                                                                                            Abstract
  AI agents are increasingly capable of reasoning, planning, using tools, and executing long-horizon tasks, yet
  many still rely on humans to identify worthwhile work and initiate it. Proactiveness adds the capacity to initiate
  purposeful action without an explicit request. We examine proactiveness as a capability that complements
  intelligence and alignment in the development of superintelligent agents. Research on proactiveness, however,
  remains fragmented across communities with different terminology, assumptions, and evaluation practices. We
  integrate its conceptual foundations and historical development across control, agent theory, ubiquitous computing,
  mixed-initiative interaction, and foundation-model research. We organize enabling mechanisms into six capacities:
  awareness, anticipation, agenda formation, arbitration, action, and adaptation. We synthesize evaluation approaches
  at the task, mechanism, and user levels. Across 13 application domains, including coding, autonomous research,
  robotics, healthcare, and education, we compare the initiative agents exercise with the authority they are granted.
  Finally, we outline future directions in capability development, safety and governance, and emerging application
  frontiers, grounding the development of calibrated proactiveness for superintelligent agents in the achievements
  and limitations of existing systems.
  V Keywords: Proactive AI, Superintelligent Agents, Self-Initiated Action, Long-Horizon Tasks
  § Project: https://empathyang.github.io/Proactive-AI-for-Superintelligent-Agents/

We use proactiveness to refer to the agent’s ability to identify worthwhile goals and initiate purposeful action with-
out a new, explicit request for that intervention. Such initiative can operate within standing objectives, predefined
responsibilities, and previously granted permissions. More precisely, proactiveness concerns the delegated discretion
an agent exercises within a task’s underspecified residual decision space, while respecting its explicitly stated goals
and constraints (Figure 2). A coding agent responds reactively when a user reports a bug and asks it to make a repair.
The agent may inspect files, implement a fix, and run tests independently, but the user has identified the work to be
done (Jimenez et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2024a). A proactive coding agent, operating under a standing responsibility
for code quality, can detect a previously unreported bug and propose a repair before the user asks (Chen et al., 2025e).
Similarly, a personal assistant might anticipate a scheduling conflict and prepare alternatives without waiting for a
request. In these proactive cases, the agent identifies the need for intervention itself.
This capability is particularly relevant to long-horizon tasks. Maintaining a software project, coordinating ongoing
care, or supporting a research program involves changing conditions, unresolved dependencies, and needs that cannot
all be specified at the outset. A plan may become outdated, a previously minor concern may become urgent, or an
opportunity may arise while attention is directed elsewhere. Supporting such objectives requires agents to preserve
context, identify emerging work, revisit priorities, and decide when to resume, revise, or abandon a commitment (Aha,
2018). Proactiveness can therefore reduce the continuing burden on humans to monitor the environment and repeatedly
translate changes into new instructions. Its value depends on whether these interventions advance the broader objective
over time. Such initiative requires agents to identify what deserves attention and determine whether, when, and how to
act within their standing objectives and granted authority.
Understanding proactiveness also requires separating capability from permission. As is shown in Figure 3, intelligence
supports reasoning and execution; alignment concerns the relationship between an agent’s behavior and human intentions
and values; proactiveness concerns its initiative in identifying and advancing useful work. None of these capabilities
alone determines what the agent is authorized to do. An assistant may proactively identify a scheduling problem while
leaving every calendar change to the user. Conversely, a system may receive broad permission to execute a task while
relying entirely on the user to select that task. We examine both the initiative an agent exercises and the authority it
is granted. Research on mixed-initiative interaction provides a foundation for studying how automated assistance can

Proactiveness has a substantial history in computer science. Classical agent research identified initiative in pursuing goals
as a defining property of intelligent agents, while goal-reasoning research examined how agents select and revise their
own objectives (Wooldridge & Jennings, 1995; Aha, 2018). Work on planning, context-aware computing, and human-
computer interaction provides approaches to anticipating needs, maintaining goals, and managing intervention (Schilit
et al., 1994; Horvitz, 1999). Ideas from philosophy, cognitive science, and control theory also help explain how
purposeful action is organized. We draw on these ideas where they inform the conceptual foundations of proactive AI.
Further, contemporary large language model-based agents provide opportunities to develop these capabilities through
architectures that combine memory, reasoning, and action (Wang et al., 2024c).
This survey focuses on computer science research on proactive AI agents. Relevant work is distributed across agent
architectures, planning and goal reasoning, context-aware computing, human-computer interaction, and more recent
systems built on foundation models. These research communities often study related capabilities using different
terminology, assumptions, and evaluation practices, making it difficult to relate their findings to the design of complete
proactive systems. We organize this literature around the mechanisms that support self-initiated action and examine how
those mechanisms are evaluated and used across application settings.
This survey makes three contributions:



                                                                                                                                                           6
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


    1. Conceptual foundations and historical synthesis. We clarify proactiveness through self-initiation, explain how
       initiative relates to granted authority, and trace its development in computer science. Concepts from related fields
       inform this account of anticipation, goal reasoning, and human control.
    2. A unified mechanism framework. We organize proactive behavior through six interacting capacities: awareness,
       anticipation, agenda (formation), arbitration, action, and adaptation. The framework connects maintaining
       context and identifying candidate goals with selecting interventions, delivering actions, and learning from their
       consequences. It provides a common basis for comparing architectures across domains.
    3. Evaluation and cross-domain analysis. We synthesize evaluation approaches at the task, mechanism, and user
       levels and examine representative systems across 13 application domains. We compare how these systems exercise
       initiative, what authority they receive, and how their interventions are assessed. This analysis identifies gaps in
       the evaluation of task discovery and examines how reliable feedback and verification constrain progress across
       domains.
Furthermore, proactive agents must judge whether an intervention is useful, when it should occur (McFarlane, 2002;
Amershi et al., 2019), and how far they are permitted to act. Acting too readily can interrupt users (Adamczyk & Bailey,
2004; Mark et al., 2008; Pu et al., 2025a), pursue mistaken goals, or exceed granted authority, while excessive hesitation
can leave important needs unaddressed. We thus use calibrated proactiveness to describe the adjustment of initiative to
uncertainty, risk, timing, user preferences, and permissions. This perspective guides our discussion of future evaluation
challenges, the connection and distinction between proactiveness, long-horizon adaptation and self-improvement, and
proactive AI’s safety and governance.
The remainder of this survey proceeds from conceptual foundations and historical development to the mechanisms of
proactive agency. We then review evaluation practices and applications across domains, followed by future directions
addressing capability development, safety, trust, and governance. The final section concludes the survey.

2     Conceptual Framework
2.1    Defining Proactiveness
A proactive AI agent is an autonomous system that initiates goal-oriented actions without a new, explicit request for
that intervention. The center of this definition is self-initiation: the agent decides to act before being explicitly told to,
and organizes that action around a goal it treats as worth pursuing.
Reactive systems set the baseline for the comparison. A reactive AI agent responds when triggered and stays idle
otherwise, a design that is efficient, controllable, and straightforward to evaluate, since the user or the environment
hands it the immediate task. However, when the user does not ask and no configured trigger calls for a response, an
emerging need remains unaddressed.
Proactive agents differ in how far they look ahead before acting. A schedule or threshold can initiate a check, after
which the agent may exercise discretion in deciding whether an intervention is warranted. More capable agents add an
anticipatory model that forecasts future states, user needs, or downstream consequences, which lets them detect needs
and risks before those become explicit. These forecasts can inform the goals an agent selects and the actions it initiates.
The goal a proactive agent pursues can come from many places. The user might state a high-level objective, for instance
keeping energy cost down, holding code quality steady, or respecting a travel constraint, and the agent later initiates
actions in service of that standing objective. In other settings the goal is fixed inside a specialized system, for instance
preserving a safety margin, preventing equipment failure, or maintaining service quality. The proactive AI agents
may even generate the goal they would serve on their own. Across these settings, proactiveness concerns the agent’s
discretion in selecting and initiating an intervention within the applicable goals, constraints, and permissions.

2.2    The Two Questions Behind Self-Initiated Action
Self-initiated action requires the agent to judge what is worth acting on and whether, when, and how to intervene.
The first is what to act on. Within an assigned task or standing objective, the agent assesses current and anticipated
needs, opportunities, and risks, and settles on something worth doing. This is inseparable from goal alignment: a



                                                                                                                            7
                                                               Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


self-generated or mistimed goal that drifts from what the user actually needs reads as unnecessary or intrusive, however
competently it is executed. Choosing the target is thus already part of the hard problem.
The second is whether, when, and how to act. Because the action is unrequested, the agent has to judge that an
intervention is warranted, timely, and acceptable before making it, then shape and deliver it in a form the user will
endorse. The agent also has to decide whether this is the right moment, whether it is confident enough, whether the
action stays within the authority it has been given, whether the user would rather be offered a suggestion than have the
agent execute on its own, and how assertively to present the result.
The task specification can settle some of these choices and leave others open. For choices delegated to the agent,
self-initiation requires judgments about the value and form of an intervention under uncertainty. For this reason,
proactiveness is a distinct capability with its own representational and evaluative demands.

Figure 4 The reactivity-proactivity spectrum. The spectrum reflects how much of a task’s residual decision space an agent can

negotiating priorities and reviewing progress. Reactivity remains necessary for incorporating new instructions and responding to
changes, so the same agent can combine reactive execution with self-initiated work.

As shown in Figure 4, reactivity and proactiveness mark the two ends of a spectrum of behavior, and most systems fall
somewhere between them. Many mix triggered response with self-initiated intervention, and the same AI agent can
move along the spectrum depending on time scale, confidence, and operational context. The useful question about a
deployed system is usually how much initiative it is allowed to take, under what conditions, and with what safeguards.
Most fielded systems are accordingly hybrid, pairing a reactive layer for time-critical response to explicit inputs and
fast-changing signals with a proactive layer for deliberation and foresight over longer horizons. For example, an
autonomous vehicle can brake or steer in response to a pedestrian stepping off the curb, a nearby car braking hard, or a
lane-level hazard. During the same journey, it may assess traffic forecasts and battery reserves, identify a need for an
additional charging stop, and propose adding that stop to the route without a new request from the passenger. A coding
assistant can respond reactively by completing the current line, answering a question about an API, or applying an edit
exactly where asked. It can exercise task-scoped initiative by identifying additional changes needed to complete the
assigned task, and initiate new work outside the current assignment by proposing a refactor, flagging an unreported bug,
or recommending a dependency update under a standing maintenance objective. Personal-productivity assistants and
industrial-monitoring systems sit at their own points on the same spectrum, each described by where its initiative falls
and how that initiative is bounded.

3    History
This section traces proactive agency as a gradual expansion in the decisions delegated to machines: from reactive systems
that respond to explicit requests or configured triggers, to proactive agents that infer what is worth acting on and decide
whether, when, and how to act without an explicit request. Earlier research communities approached these problems under
different names (Figure 5). Control theory studied self-triggered regulation around fixed objectives; symbolic planning
and world modeling studied anticipation before action; agent theory studied initiative and commitment; context-aware
computing studied persistent situation modeling; mixed-initiative HCI studied intervention under uncertainty; and goal-
reasoning and intrinsic-motivation research studied how agents generate and revise their own goals. Foundation-model
agents matter not because they invented proactiveness, but because they recombine these mechanisms in open-ended,
language-mediated environments (Wiener, 1948; Fikes & Nilsson, 1971; Wooldridge & Jennings, 1995; Schilit et al.,
1994; Horvitz, 1999; Aha, 2018). This history provides the background for Section 4 and shows which parts of proactive
agency predate current LLM systems.

Figure 5 Historical foundations of increasingly open-ended initiative. Proactive agency draws on complementary traditions that

This expansion can be understood through the economic logic of incomplete contracts. Economists have long observed
that contracts cannot specify every future contingency, which is why governance, authority, and ownership matter
(Coase, 1937; Simon, 1951; Williamson, 1975, 1985). Modern incomplete-contract theory formalized this problem
in terms of residual rights of control: the right to decide what should happen when the original agreement is silent
(Grossman & Hart, 1986; Hart & Moore, 1988, 1990; Hart, 1995). A prompt, instruction, or standing objective can be
read as a contract-like delegation from a human to a machine. It specifies some goals, constraints, and permissions, but
it cannot describe every future state the agent may encounter. When such an unspecified state arises, the key question


                                                                                                                                        9
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


is who holds the residual control right: should the machine fill the gap, or should control return to the human? Early
proactiveness was limited not because the idea of machine initiative was absent, but because delegating these residual
decisions to machines raised hard problems of state uncertainty, goal alignment, authority, and accountability. The
history below traces how different research traditions gradually made more of these decisions delegable, from planning
and state estimation to intervention timing and goal formation.

3.1   Control and Cybernetics: Self-Triggered Regulation Under Fixed Goals
The theoretical roots of proactive agents can be traced to cybernetics, the study of goal-directed systems (Rosenblueth
et al., 1943; Wiener, 1948). Its central mechanism, the feedback loop, showed how a system can compare its current
state with a desired state and adjust its behavior to reduce the gap. A thermostat is the simplest example: it senses
temperature, compares it with a reference value, and automatically turns heating on or off to maintain the target. This
perceive–compare–act cycle supplied the earliest formal model of self-triggered goal maintenance and helped shape the
later perceive–reason–act view of intelligent agents. In the terminology introduced in Section 4, cybernetic control
supplies the minimal substrate for Awareness, Action, and Adaptation: the machine can track the current state, detect a
gap from a standing objective, and adjust its behavior without waiting for a new command.

3.2   Planning and World Models: Simulating Futures Before Acting
Cybernetics explained how a system could regulate behavior around a standing objective. Early AI and cognitive science
pushed this idea further by treating intelligent behavior as symbolic problem solving and planning (Newell & Simon,
1976). The key shift was that agents were no longer limited to correcting present deviations. They could represent an
internal model of the world and use it to reason about possible action sequences before execution.
STRIPS was a milestone in this transition (Fikes & Nilsson, 1971). It formalized planning in terms of an initial state, a
goal state, and a set of actions with preconditions and effects. By representing the world as logical predicates and actions
as operators over them, STRIPS gave agents a computational form of “what-if” reasoning. This established an early
basis for anticipatory behavior, but only in a limited sense. The goal was usually supplied by a user, task designer, or
environment specification. Classical planning therefore explained how an agent could reason toward a given objective,
not how it should decide which objective to adopt.
Later world-model research generalized this anticipatory role from symbolic operators to learned dynamics. Model-based
reinforcement learning and forward models formalized how an agent can predict the next state from the current state
and a candidate action (Sutton, 1991; Jordan & Rumelhart, 1992; Wolpert et al., 1995; Moerland et al., 2023). Learned
latent world models made such prediction scalable by rolling future states forward in compact representations (Ha &
Schmidhuber, 2018; Hafner et al., 2025). These systems strengthened the Anticipation side of proactive agency: an
agent could estimate downstream consequences, compare acting with abstaining, and detect failures before they became
explicit.

3.3   BDI and Agent Theory: Initiative, Commitment, and Proactiveness
Classical planning gave agents a way to reason about future action, but usually toward a goal supplied from outside.
The next major conceptual step came from philosophy. In 1987, Michael Bratman’s theory of intention formalized how
human agents structure their behavior through interconnected mental states (Bratman, 1987):

        Beliefs       +        Desires                 Intentions                    Plans                 Actions

Intentions serve as a bridge between immediate motivation and long-term planning, ensuring both future-directedness
and coherence in action. This insight inspired AI researchers in the 1980s and 1990s to operationalize Bratman’s theory
as a computational framework: the BDI (Belief–Desire–Intention) architecture (Cohen & Levesque, 1990; Rao &
Georgeff, 1995).
The BDI model comprises three interdependent mental attitudes and their dynamic interactions: Beliefs represent the
agent’s informational state about itself, the environment, and others; Desires encode motivational states, or the situations
the agent wishes to bring about; and Intentions represent deliberative commitments to a subset of desires, which the
agent pursues through planned sequences of actions. By embedding commitment into its reasoning cycle, the BDI model
achieved a balance between proactivity and reactivity: it maintained goal stability amid dynamic environments while


                                                                                                                         10
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


remaining responsive to significant contextual changes. This commitment–reactivity trade-off remains a cornerstone of
modern proactive architectures.
The intelligent-agent literature then made proactiveness a canonical property of agents. Wooldridge and Jennings
characterized agents not only by autonomy, social ability, and reactivity, but also by proactiveness: the capacity to take
initiative in pursuit of goals rather than merely respond to environmental change (Wooldridge & Jennings, 1995). This
literature also clarifies a distinction that remains easy to blur: proactiveness concerns whether the agent can originate
initiative, while autonomy concerns how much authority it has been granted to act with less supervision. For our
mechanism account, the BDI lineage supplies the historical root of Agenda. A predicted need, opportunity, or risk
becomes proactive behavior only when the agent commits to it as something to pursue.

3.4   Ubiquitous and Context-Aware Computing: Maintaining the Situation Model
Planning and BDI explain how an agent reasons toward goals and commits to them, but a proactive agent also needs
grounding before any prompt arrives. This is the contribution of ubiquitous and context-aware computing. Weiser’s
vision of ubiquitous computing placed computation in the background of ordinary activity, while early context-aware
systems used information such as location, identity, activity, time, and device state to adapt behavior without explicit
commands (Weiser, 1991; Schilit et al., 1994). Later work sharpened context awareness as the ability to use such
situational information to provide relevant services or behavior (Abowd et al., 1999).
For proactive agency, this lineage further supplies the historical root of Awareness: the agent must maintain a
model of the user and environment rather than wait for the user to specify what matters. Such a model can include
location, calendar, current task, workflow history, preferences, sensor readings, screen state, organizational setting, and
environmental risk. It is the substrate on which later Anticipation operates, because an agent cannot forecast a latent
need without first estimating the current situation.

3.5   Mixed-Initiative Interaction: The Economics of Intervention
Context-aware systems gave machines a model of the user’s situation, but situation awareness does not by itself justify
intervention. The mixed-initiative tradition shifted the question from whether a system can take initiative to when that
initiative should enter human activity. In a mixed-initiative system, control can move between user and machine: the
system may suggest, clarify, or take over part of the work, and control may later return to the user. Horvitz framed this
movement as a decision under uncertainty, where the expected value of assistance must be weighed against the costs
of error, interruption, and reduced user control (Horvitz, 1999). Tennenhouse’s proactive-computing agenda pushed a
related vision of systems that continuously sense and act under human supervision (Tennenhouse, 2000).
The key contribution of this lineage is that initiative is not automatically valuable. A correct suggestion can still be
harmful if it arrives at the wrong moment, removes the user’s sense of control, or accumulates false positives that erode
trust. Interruption-management research made these costs measurable: interruptions impose recovery time, increase
errors, and vary sharply with timing, with task boundaries often providing more acceptable moments for intervention
than mid-task disruption (McFarlane, 2002; Adamczyk & Bailey, 2004; Iqbal & Horvitz, 2007; Bailey & Konstan,
2006). Attention-aware systems and personalized interruption models then treated the cost of a notification as a quantity
to be estimated rather than a presentation detail (Horvitz & Apacible, 2003; Horvitz et al., 2004).
For proactive agents, this literature supplies the historical root of Arbitration. Anticipation may identify a latent need,
but Arbitration decides whether that need justifies action now, at what level of autonomy, and through what form of
delivery. The agent must weigh confidence, expected benefit, timing, reversibility, and granted authority before acting.
Mixed-initiative interaction therefore provides the “whether, when, and how strongly” side of proactive agency.

3.6   Goal Reasoning and Intrinsic Motivation: Generating the Agenda
The preceding lineages explain how agents sense the present, simulate the future, commit to intentions, and gate
interventions, but they leave one burden only partly specified: where do candidate goals come from when no user has
supplied them? Goal reasoning addresses this question directly by asking where goals come from and how they should
be revised. Goal-driven autonomy studied agents that monitor expectations, detect discrepancies between expected and
observed states, explain those discrepancies, formulate new goals, and manage the resulting goal set (Molineaux et al.,
2010; Klenk et al., 2013; Vattam et al., 2013; Aha, 2018). This loop is proactive by construction: the trigger for a new
goal is not an external command, but the agent’s recognition that the world has departed from what it expected. A failed


                                                                                                                        11
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


plan, missing resource, emerging threat, or newly available opportunity can become a goal the agent adopts before the
user has named it.
A complementary lineage comes from intrinsic motivation and open-ended learning. Goal-driven autonomy generates
goals from discrepancies in the world, while intrinsically motivated agents generate objectives from internal signals such
as curiosity, novelty, uncertainty reduction, or learning progress (Barto et al., 2004; Oudeyer et al., 2007; Schmidhuber,
2010). Prediction-error curiosity drives agents toward states whose outcomes they cannot yet forecast, while learning-
progress signals steer them toward goals near the frontier of current competence (Pathak et al., 2017; Forestier et al.,
2022). These systems show that self-generated goals need not arise only from anomaly repair. An agent can form an
agenda because a region of the environment is informative, learnable, or worth exploring. Modern open-ended agents
inherit this pattern: Voyager uses an automatic curriculum to propose new skills, while autonomous research agents
generate hypotheses, experiments, or research directions as part of longer discovery loops (Wang et al., 2024a; Lu et al.,
2024). What matters here is that these agents do more than carry out long tasks. They also begin to supply the Agenda
that guides what should be pursued next.

3.7   Foundation Models: Recombination at Open-Ended Scale
The foundation-model era brings the earlier lineages together. A foundation model is a model trained on broad data at
scale and adaptable to a wide range of downstream tasks (Bommasani et al., 2021). Large language and multimodal
foundation models extend this idea by providing a common representational substrate for goals, preferences, constraints,
plans, memories, tool calls, and explanations. This substrate lets mechanisms that were historically developed in separate
communities operate inside a single agent architecture: context tracking from ubiquitous computing, future simulation
from planning and world models, commitment from BDI, agenda formation from goal reasoning, intervention gating
from mixed-initiative interaction, and adaptation from feedback.
Contemporary agents built on foundation models illustrate this recombination. Language agents interleave reasoning
and tool use, decompose natural-language objectives, maintain memory, simulate future steps, and revise plans over
extended interaction (Yao et al., 2023b; Sumers et al., 2024; Park et al., 2023). Open-ended agents generate curricula
or subgoals, proactive assistants infer latent needs from context, and autonomous research systems generate and test
hypotheses across multi-step loops (Wang et al., 2024a; Lu et al., 2025a, 2024). This generality also expands the stakes
of initiative. A narrow proactive system may adjust a thermostat or issue an alert, while an agent built on foundation
models may email a person, edit a repository, schedule a meeting, operate a browser, call an API, or change a production
system. The central question therefore becomes sharper: when should the agent move first, how far should it go, and
when must it ask, defer, or remain silent? Foundation models make proactivity more general, and for that reason make
calibrated proactivity more necessary.

3.8   Synthesis: From Historical Lineages to Mechanisms
The current LLM-driven wave of AI renews a much older agenda. Long before foundation models, proactiveness had
already appeared across cybernetics, symbolic AI, cognitive science, automation, operations research, and human-
computer interaction. These traditions studied different parts of the same problem: how a system senses a situation,
reasons about the future, commits to goals, evaluates the value of intervention, and coordinates its initiative with human
control. Many of these ideas now reappear as core ingredients in the development of more general agents. Progress on
proactive agency will therefore require more than larger models. It will require a renewed integration of the fields that
have studied initiative, decision, control, and human agency from different angles.
Seen from this perspective, proactive agency is a history of increasingly incomplete delegation. Early control systems
operated under nearly complete specifications: a fixed objective, a narrow state variable, and a small action set. Later
agents were asked to fill in more of what the instruction left open, from action sequences and future contingencies
to situation models, intervention timing, and self-generated goals. Proactiveness is the capacity to fill these gaps;
autonomy is the authority granted to act on the resulting judgments. As agents gain real authority through information,
prediction, memory, and tool use, calibrated proactivity becomes the problem of keeping that real authority aligned with
the authority humans have formally granted (Aghion & Tirole, 1997). The six-A mechanism in the next section can be
read as the machinery that makes such incomplete delegation possible.

Figure 6 Six interacting capacities for exercising proactive discretion. Awareness maintains a situation model that enables
Anticipation to identify future needs and predict the consequences of possible actions. Agenda converts these forecasts into prioritized
commitments, and Arbitration determines whether and when to intervene. Action carries out the selected intervention, while
Adaptation uses outcomes and feedback to update the other capacities.


4    Mechanism
We organize the mechanisms of proactive AI agents into six interacting capacities, abbreviated the six A’s: Awareness,
Anticipation, Agenda, Arbitration, Action, and Adaptation (Figure 6). Within this framework, Anticipation and
Arbitration address two distinctive demands of self-initiated work: identifying needs and opportunities for work that no
explicit user request or task instruction has specified, and deciding whether, when, and how to initiate an intervention
within granted permissions.
Awareness, Agenda, Action, and Adaptation have established roles in general AI agents. However, their proactive forms
can require substantial changes: maintaining context before a request arrives, generating and revising goals alongside
assigned tasks, delivering unsolicited interventions with appropriate user control, and learning from feedback on the
agent’s own initiative. Proactive behavior emerges through the interaction of all six capacities. Table 1 organizes
representative works by these six mechanisms and their subdimensions.

4.1     Awareness
Before an agent can anticipate anything, it must hold an estimate of what is currently the case (Figure 7). Awareness
is the process that builds and maintains that estimate, and we take it up in four parts: tracking state from multimodal
streams into a persistent situation model (§4.1.1), deciding what to sense or ask about next when that estimate falls short
(§4.1.2), organizing what has been learned into a hierarchical memory that later prediction can draw on (§4.1.3), and
running a cognitive loop that can fire without an incoming query (§4.1.4). For proactive agents, Awareness must support
the discovery of work before a request arrives. This changes what the agent monitors, which context it retains, and when
it gathers more information, with sensing and memory organized around continuing needs across tasks and sessions.

4.1.1    Multimodal State Tracking and Context Management
A reactive system can interpret each request as it arrives; an agent acting without a new request uses observations and
retained context to assess the current situation. A persistent, regularly updated model of user and environment state

Figure 7 Awareness grounds initiative in decision-relevant context. When instructions leave decisions unspecified, the agent
must determine what is happening, what prior experience remains relevant, and what information is missing. Persistent memory and

gaps. The central trade-off is maintaining sufficient context for sound decisions while controlling the costs of computation, energy,
privacy, and user attention.


can support this assessment, an approach that predates current foundation-model agents. Context-aware computing in
ubiquitous computing built ambient models of a user’s situation and used them to reconfigure behavior automatically
(Schilit et al., 1994; Abowd et al., 1999). Dialogue state tracking is the longest-running formalization of maintaining
a belief over a user’s goals as an interaction unfolds, running from the Dialog State Tracking Challenge through the
MultiWOZ corpus to modern neural trackers (Williams et al., 2013; Budzianowski et al., 2020; Jacqmin et al., 2022).
Proactive agents generalize this recipe along two axes at once: from a fixed schema of slot-values to open-world state, and
from discrete dialogue turns to continuous multimodal streams. Early ambient assistants already monitored a person’s
state with non-intrusive sensors and intervened when a predictive model of work pressure and exhaustion flagged trouble
(Bosse et al., 2013), and operational decision-support agents maintained a running model of the environment in order to
deliver the right information to the right person at the right time (Buchler et al., 2014). The state model is only as good
as the perception that fills it, and that perception is a general capability the proactive agent inherits from the broader
perception literature: egocentric vision (Grauman et al., 2022), wearable activity recognition (Zhang et al., 2022; Wu
et al., 2026d), and screen and interface understanding (Baechler et al., 2024), each a partial and noisy view that has to
be fused into one estimate. Feeding always-on streams into a bounded model context creates a systems tension that
streaming and context-paging architectures manage (Chen et al., 2024a; Xiao et al., 2024; Packer et al., 2023); we defer
the memory side of this tension to §4.1.3. One signal in this stream is natively anticipatory and worth singling out: gaze
precedes the action it serves, so eye movements give an early read on intention that feeds prediction directly (§4.2)
(Belardinelli, 2023; Wilson et al., 2025). Recent proactive systems already assemble these streams, fusing wearable
video and audio into the context that drives proactive predictions (Yang et al., 2025b).
Recent systems are turning this research aspiration into working prototypes, with early commercial features starting
to appear. Continuous screenshot and sensor capture is folded into queryable personal memory by systems such as
MIRIX (Wang & Chen, 2025), with commercial timeline-recall features such as Microsoft Recall, Screenpipe, and Plaud
NotePin serving as industrial exemplars of the same idea (Microsoft, 2025b; Screenpipe, 2026; PLAUD, 2026); native
interface agents track screen-state transitions as their world state (Qin et al., 2025c); and mobile agents tie on-device


                                                                                                                                         15
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


capture to user context for proactive suggestion (Yang et al., 2026e; Li et al., 2024c). The cost of capture that never
stops recurs across all of them. Tiered sensing keeps cheap sensors always on and wakes expensive ones only when
relevance is flagged (Yang et al., 2026a), and privacy-sensitive domains push the whole pipeline on-device (Ji et al.,
2025). This privacy-and-energy bill is the standing tax on awareness that the gating discussion (§4.4) and the systems
discussion (§4.1.4) return to.

4.1.2   Active Perception and Proactive Information Seeking
Choosing what to sense is itself a decision problem. Active perception couples sensing to action selection in vision and
robotics (Bajcsy, 1988; Bajcsy et al., 2017), and active learning and Bayesian experimental design choose queries to
maximize expected information gain (Settles, 2009; Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995). These classical formulations supply
the vocabulary, information gain and expected value of perfect information, that modern “should I ask?” heuristics
implicitly rediscover, and recent agent work imports the formal apparatus explicitly, casting question selection as
sequential Bayesian experimental design or as expected-information-gain maximization over a maintained belief state
(Choudhury et al., 2026; Echarghaoui et al., 2026).
When the missing information lives in the user’s head, the active-sensing act becomes a clarifying question. An
unsolicited clarification claims the user’s attention and must pass the same arbitration gate (§4.4) as any other intervention.
The design problem has two parts. Selectivity governs when an ambiguity is worth an interruption, the question that
systems for selective clarification and ambiguity detection address (Kuhn et al., 2023a; Zhang et al., 2024g; Qian et al.,
2024); utility governs which question buys the most information, which is expected value of perfect information in
conversational clothing (Aliannejadi et al., 2019; Rao & III, 2018). The literature has matured from prompted heuristics
to trained asking policies that learn when and what to ask from interaction or offline logs (Li et al., 2023a; Andukuri
et al., 2024; Wei et al., 2025a; Sun et al., 2025b). The same pattern recurs wherever underspecified instructions meet
costly downstream execution: open-domain coding agents, text-to-CAD specification, and dynamic-rule compliance
screening each report agents that clarify before they commit (Edwards & Schuster, 2026; Yuan et al., 2026a; He et al.,
2025a), and timing matters as much as content, since the value of a clarification depends sharply on when it is asked and
which kind of information is missing (Gulati et al., 2026).
When the missing information is external, the same gate becomes an in-generation retrieval decision: the agent monitors
its own uncertainty and searches only when its parametric knowledge is insufficient, the pattern established by the
adaptive-retrieval line (Asai et al., 2023; Jeong et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2023; Press et al., 2023). Agentic search and
evidence-seeking variants extend uncertainty-guided retrieval to reasoning models and to domains such as pathology
and recommendation (Li et al., 2025e; Hua et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2026a).
In embodied and interactive settings the question carries a price: it interrupts a person, spends a turn, or stalls the task,
so information seeking has to be budgeted against task progress. Ask-before-acting policies gate a query on whether the
missing information would change the next decision (Chen et al., 2024b; Wang et al., 2026k); expert-query budgets are
spent sparingly under learned uncertainty estimates (Singh et al., 2022; Igbinedion & Karaman, 2024; He et al., 2025b);
question sequences are planned to maximize expected information gain (Hu et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2026c); and the
completion-versus-interaction balance is optimized (Luo et al., 2026b), with that trade-off cast as an explicit Pareto
frontier (Yao et al., 2026). The same budgeting drives collaborative navigation and joint planning, where every dialogue
turn with a human is a cost to minimize (Taioli et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2024h; Ognibene et al., 2025; Fang et al.,
2026d; Houtti et al., 2025). Asking for clarification can resolve uncertainty before further action and gives the user an
opportunity to guide that action (§4.5).

4.1.3   Hierarchical Memory Systems
Cognitive science provides the structural basis for agent memory. The episodic and semantic distinction (Tulving et al.,
1972) and the separation of working memory from long-term declarative and procedural stores in cognitive architectures
(Anderson et al., 2004; Laird et al., 2017; Nuxoll & Laird, 2007) carry over almost directly into the memory modules
of modern agent frameworks (Sumers et al., 2024). The four memory stores are working, episodic, semantic, and
procedural.
An agent that monitors a streaming situation cannot let its context window fill passively. Staying current means
continuously deciding which elements of the live situation map are kept resident and which are paged out or expired,



                                                                                                                            16
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


the operation that operating-system-style virtual context management supplies (Packer et al., 2023) and that the agent-
memory surveys catalog in general (Zhang et al., 2024k; Hu et al., 2026f). For a proactive agent the workspace doubles
as the buffer that demand detection reads, so streaming systems pair a working store with a need detector that fires on it
(Xie et al., 2026), and long-running agents cap workspace size to keep always-on cognition affordable (Zhang, 2026a).
Anticipation (§4.2) works from recurring patterns, and those patterns have to be built before they can be used. Episodic
consolidation is what turns raw interaction history into them, through retrieval weighted by recency, importance, and
relevance together with reflection, linking, and decay (Park et al., 2023; Xu et al., 2025d; Zhong et al., 2023; Chhikara
et al., 2025; Tan et al., 2025). Recent systems make the proactive payoff concrete, distilling interaction trajectories into
reusable experiences that drive unprompted assistance (Wang & Jiang, 2026; Fiorini et al., 2025) and folding event
streams into structures that surface what the user will need next (Wang et al., 2026g; Yang et al., 2026c).
For a proactive agent a stale preference is especially expensive, because acting on it produces an unprompted wrong
intervention, and an unsolicited error costs more trust than a solicited one. Long-term stores therefore track not only
what is true of the user but when it stopped being true, through persona and preference stores (Li et al., 2025c),
temporal knowledge graphs that invalidate superseded facts (Rasmussen et al., 2025), and timestamped repositories
that detect contradictions and update on human correction (He et al., 2025a). The memory surveys frame this as the
temporal dimension of agent memory (Wu et al., 2025f), and LongMemEval quantifies the cost of getting it wrong,
reporting roughly a 30% accuracy drop over sustained interaction (Wu et al., 2025b); grounding suggestions in a group’s
accumulated history is the multi-user form of the same requirement (Wang et al., 2025e).
Deliberating from scratch makes every intervention expensive. Consolidating repeatedly successful action sequences
into reusable skills lets proactive behaviors fire habitually at low marginal cost, the procedural-memory class that
cognitive architectures and their agent descendants identify (Anderson et al., 2004; Sumers et al., 2024). Agents build
executable skill libraries (Wang et al., 2024a), induce reusable workflows from past traces (Wang et al., 2025o), compile
mastered goals into fast low-level policies (Carta et al., 2025), and store synthesized strategies for proactive dialogue
(Kim et al., 2025b). Semantic memory holds who the user is and procedural memory holds what the agent already
knows how to do; together they feed anticipation (§4.2) and execution (§4.5).

4.1.4   Runtime Architectures: Triggers, Always-On Monitoring, and Sleep-Time Compute
A chatbot’s cognition is invoked when a query arrives; a proactive agent has to decide when to wake up, and that decision
cannot itself be a response to a query. Classical lineages decoupled triggering from acting but with fixed, hand-authored
conditions: event-condition-action rules in active databases (Paton & Díaz, 1999), trigger-action programming in the
smart home (Ur et al., 2014), and interrupt-driven deliberation in belief-desire-intention architectures (Rao & Georgeff,
1995), with doctrine-driven monitors in operational decision support showing the same shape at scale (Buchler et al.,
2014). The modern question is what replaces the hand-authored trigger, and adaptive schedulers that decide when to
engage which cognitive activity are one emerging answer (Su, 2026b).
The contemporary pattern is a continuous event stream paired with a lightweight should-I-act judgment. ProactiveAgent
learns this judgment from human-labeled acceptance data and fine-tunes agents to offer assistance unprompted (Lu
et al., 2025a). The recipe instantiates across settings: sensory-context polling on wearables and smart glasses (Yang
et al., 2025b, 2026a; Liu et al., 2026n), agent-formulated trigger conditions registered against a changing environment
(Shi et al., 2026b), intent-conditioned monitoring backed by long-term memory (Xie et al., 2026), and the industrial
ambient-agent pattern of event-driven, cron-scheduled, human-in-the-loop loops (LangChain Blog, 2025). Real-time
collaboration pushes the monitor to high frequency so that adaptation can keep pace with a human partner (Liu et al.,
2026l).
Wakefulness is graded: between fully asleep and acting lies idle computation, where the agent that has already thought is
the agent that can act first. Sleep-time compute rewrites context offline to amortize test-time reasoning (Lin et al., 2025);
memory-consolidation pipelines rewrite persistent memory offline to reorganize accumulated experience (Anthropic,
2026f; Ye et al., 2026a); speculative planning pre-executes likely next steps while waiting on observations (Choi et al.,
2026a; Hua et al., 2024); and idle-time anticipation pre-fetches evidence for predicted needs (Hu et al., 2026a).
Always-on cognition runs on real silicon, and the bill comes due in scheduling, energy, and privacy. Agent operating
systems schedule and context-switch agent workloads (Mei et al., 2025); heterogeneous-SoC schedulers keep latency-
critical reactive interactions responsive while sustaining background proactive monitoring on the same device (Wei et al.,



                                                                                                                          17
                                                   Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


2026b); and the privacy cost of always-listening voice assistants is well documented, where continuous microphone
access trades exposure for convenience (Chandrasekaran et al., 2021). Edge-cloud splits with on-device sanitization keep
sensitive monitoring local (Shen et al., 2026b), and mobile agents hibernate to respect battery and platform sandboxing
while still waking for time-sensitive obligations (Kadaboina, 2026). The heartbeat scheduler reappears here as the
runtime that decides how much to spend while idle (Su, 2026b), closing the loop between an agent’s awareness of its
situation and its readiness to act on it, the readiness that the anticipation stage of §4.2 now puts to work.

Figure 8 Anticipation establishes why an intervention may be worth initiating. A useful forecast identifies not only a possible
future need but also how acting could improve on abstaining. User and world models supply the predictions, while counterfactual
comparison and scenario rehearsal connect them to expected consequences. Anticipation thus provides the predictive basis for
proposing goals and judging interventions, linking what may happen to what the agent could usefully do.

Anticipation is the first of the two distinctively proactive capacities. It takes the situation estimate that awareness
maintains and projects it forward to a latent need before that need is voiced. Two questions organize anticipation
(Figure 8): what to model, and how to operate on the model. The thing worth modeling is the interaction environment,
and which part of that environment is most salient varies by deployment. Sometimes the salient part is a person, and
anticipation reduces to inferring a user’s hidden intent and mental state (§4.2.1); sometimes the salient part is the
non-human dynamics of a system or scene, and anticipation reduces to rolling the environment forward (§4.2.2). A
user is one part of the world the agent inhabits, so these are two cases of a single modeling problem that differ only
in where the predictive weight falls. On top of whichever case supplies the forecast sit two model-agnostic inference
operations: forking the future to value a possible intervention (§4.2.3), and sampling many futures to rehearse an act
before committing to it (§4.2.4).

4.2.1        Modeling the User: Intent and Mental States
When the salient part of the environment is a person, the future the agent must predict is a hidden mental state: what
the user wants, believes, and will need next. This is Theory of Mind, the capacity to attribute unobservable mental
states to others (Premack & Woodruff, 1978), whose developmental signature is the false-belief task, in which a child
succeeds only once they can represent that another person holds a belief the child knows to be false (Wimmer, 1983;
Baron-Cohen et al., 1985). Differences between the agent’s and user’s models of the situation can reveal needs the user
has not expressed.
Inferring intent from behavior predates language models. Plan and intent recognition framed the task as inverting
observed actions back to the goal that generated them (Kautz & Allen, 1986; Sukthankar et al., 2014), and Bayesian
Theory of Mind and meta-learned agent models recast that inversion as inverse planning over a rational actor (Baker


                                                                                                                                                      18
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


et al., 2017; Rabinowitz et al., 2018). The Lumière project built a Bayesian user model to infer a software user’s goals
from their actions and shipped as the basis for the Microsoft Office Assistant (Horvitz et al., 2013a). Horvitz’s own
follow-up laid out the missing piece as principles for gated action, arguing that an inference-driven assistant should
weigh the uncertainty of its inference against the cost of a poorly timed intervention (Horvitz, 1999), previewing why
arbitration (§4.4) is inseparable from anticipation.
Whether language models possess Theory of Mind is contested, and that contest is the load-bearing caveat for a proactive
agent. Some studies report human-level false-belief performance (Kosinski, 2024); others show that trivial alterations to
the same problems collapse it (Ullman, 2023). Targeted benchmarks find the capacity brittle and shallow (Kim et al.,
2023; Chen et al., 2024d; Xu et al., 2024a), and a model can state a mental state correctly yet fail to act on it (Gu et al.,
2026). The exact regime a proactive agent operates in is the weakest one: applied Theory of Mind under information
asymmetry, where the agent must commit to an action on the inferred state and a misread propagates into a consequential
misunderstanding (Kaur et al., 2026; Qian et al., 2025a; Weisz et al., 2024).
Because emergent Theory of Mind is unreliable, deployed systems scaffold an explicit belief representation the agent
can query and audit instead of trusting the capacity to appear on its own. Perspective-taking prompts filter the context
down to what a target can actually see before the model reasons about them (Wilf et al., 2023); symbolic belief graphs
maintain a separate belief state per agent (Sclar et al., 2023); and neuro-symbolic and multimodal approaches pair a
language model with structured Bayesian inference over goals and beliefs (Jin et al., 2024a; Shi et al., 2025a; Wang
et al., 2026n). The proactive payoff is that an explicit belief state is inspectable and can be consumed directly by the
arbitration gate (§4.4): the agent can expose what it thinks the user believes before it acts on that estimate.
In deployment, user-modeling for proactivity recurs in three forms. Agents elicit intent by inference over accumulated
interaction history (Zhao et al., 2026a; Zheng et al., 2026a); they anticipate the next task the user will need help with,
whether as just-in-time information, open-future task discovery, or actionable assistance (Yang et al., 2025d; Song et al.,
2025b; Siangliulue et al., 2026); and they carry inferred intent in long-term memory to drive prosocial, well-timed
intervention, including the multi-party cooperative setting where the agent must model several people at once (Bortoletto
et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026q; Zhang et al., 2024a; Sequeira et al., 2025; Favier et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2024f). The same
anticipation logic applies when the most salient part of the environment is not a person but the surrounding system,
which is the case we turn to next.

4.2.2   Modeling the World: Environment Dynamics and Future Prediction
When the salient part of the environment is the non-human dynamics of a system or scene, anticipation needs a forward
model of how that environment evolves, and Theory of Mind plays little role. The foundation is classical and borrowed.
Forward and inverse models and model-based reinforcement learning formalize predicting the next state from the current
state and an action (Sutton, 1991; Jordan & Rumelhart, 1992; Wolpert et al., 1995; Moerland et al., 2023); learned latent
world models make imagination tractable by rolling the future forward in a compact latent space (Ha & Schmidhuber,
2018; Hafner et al., 2022, 2025; Assran et al., 2025); and generative video world models scale open-ended visual
prediction in settings such as interactive environments and autonomous driving (Bruce et al., 2024; Russell et al., 2025).
The point worth keeping at full weight for an act-first agent is the fidelity criterion: what the intervention decision needs
from a world model is predictive usefulness, so a coarse rollout that correctly flags an impending failure is worth more
than a high-fidelity video that gets the dynamics wrong (Kang et al., 2025; Amos-Binks et al., 2023).
For web, software, and dialogue settings the environment is symbolic, and this is where environment modeling becomes
natively useful to today’s agents: a language model can serve as a zero-shot simulator of state transitions (Wang et al.,
2024h; Hao et al., 2023; Zuo et al., 2026), letting a proactive agent preview the result of acting against the result of
abstaining before it commits to an irreversible step such as submitting a form, running a migration, or sending a message.
The same forward-model role a learned world model plays is obtained from a model already in the loop. The pattern
spans egocentric action anticipation, which predicts the next action and the object it will touch from first-person video
(Furnari & Farinella, 2020; Girdhar & Grauman, 2021; Grauman et al., 2022), large-scale user-behavior simulation
(Wang et al., 2024d), and multi-agent rollout that searches over plausible future task outcomes (Song et al., 2025b). This
zero-shot simulator is the substrate the next two inference operations build on.




                                                                                                                           19
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


4.2.3   Counterfactual Reasoning: Valuing the Intervention
Whichever case supplied the predictive model, the decision to act reduces to one proactively-distinctive operation: fork
the future and compare. The agent contrasts the world in which it acts with the world in which it abstains, and the
divergence between the two is the estimated value of intervention, the quantity the arbitration gate (§4.4) consumes.
Prospective comparisons of acting and abstaining concern interventions in Pearl’s hierarchy. Counterfactual reasoning
additionally asks what would have happened under an alternative action, conditional on facts observed in a particular
episode. Both can use simulation, provided the model supports the relevant causal query (Pearl, 2009, 2018; Bottou
et al., 2013; Kıcıman et al., 2024). Proactive-assistance planners already instantiate the fork explicitly, contrasting a
human’s task cost with and without help and timing a robot’s guidance by the travel time it would save (Kulkarni et al.,
2021; Lo & Thomaz, 2021).
Human counterfactual thinking is functional: upward “if only” thoughts that imagine a better outcome generate
behavioral intentions and drive future improvement (Epstude & Roese, 2008; Roese, 1997; Byrne, 2019). That is the
design rationale for an agent that self-queries how bad it would be if it did not act, turning the same upward-counterfactual
process into an intervention-valuation loop in which the imagined worse future where it stayed silent is what motivates
acting first. Deployed duty agents already compute an opportunity cost of inaction in exactly this shape (Kadaboina,
2026).
Reinforcement learning supplies off-the-shelf estimators for the act-minus-abstain delta: a counterfactual baseline
marginalizes one agent’s action to isolate its causal contribution, counterfactually-guided policy search evaluates
alternative actions on logged episodes, and hindsight relabeling treats reached states as counterfactual goals (Foerster
et al., 2024; Buesing et al., 2018; Andrychowicz et al., 2018). These estimators are off-the-shelf; the proactive content
lives in why the quantity is a fork and in what the fork is finally used for.
If a prompted model rather than an explicit estimator performs the valuation, its reliability becomes the load-bearing
question, and the evidence cautions. Models handle familiar conditionals but degrade sharply on genuine counterfactual
queries (Frohberg & Binder, 2022; Wu et al., 2024c; Jin et al., 2024c) and on presuppositional prompt perturbations (Li
et al., 2025f). A miscalibrated counterfactual yields a miscalibrated delta and therefore a wrong decision to intervene or
stay silent, and the brittleness propagates straight into the arbitration gate; agentic benchmarks confirm pronounced
failures in counterfactual reasoning under partial observability (Bharadwaj et al., 2026).
The same counterfactual that values the intervention also explains it. Explanations for automated decisions are inherently
contrastive, sought in response to counterfactual cases about what would have happened otherwise (Miller, 2018;
Wachter et al., 2017), and in the proactive setting the same "harm-that-would-have-occurred" narrative both feeds the
delta into arbitration (§4.4) and serves as a minimal explanation for the unprompted act. This is what makes anticipation
the proactively-distinctive bridge to trust: an agent that can state the averted future it imagined gives the user the handle
needed for appropriate reliance (Lee & See, 2004), a principle the deployed proactive-assistance line builds on (Lu et al.,
2025a; Kulkarni et al., 2021).

4.2.4   Generative Scenario Simulation: Mental Sandboxing
The cognitive precedent for an agent that rehearses before acting is well established: the simulation heuristic judges
likelihood by mentally running a scenario, the simulation view treats conscious thought as covert action, and episodic
future thinking pre-lives a personal future (Kahneman & Tversky, 1982; Hesslow, 2002; Schacter et al., 2007; Szpunar,
2010). The proactive payoff generalizes the counterfactual fork of the previous subsection: sampling many futures
instead of contrasting two turns pairwise deltas into distributions over outcomes that an act-first decision can be taken
against.
A language model can occupy both roles a rehearsal requires, proposing actions as the policy and predicting their
consequences as the environment, which enables tree search over self-generated futures (Yao et al., 2023a; Zhou et al.,
2024a) and anticipatory reflection that predicts a failure before the action is executed (Wang et al., 2024b). For a
proactive agent this is a generative sandbox: it can sample a distribution of what would happen if it acted, entirely
internally, before it commits.
The proactively-distinctive form of sandboxing rolls out the user: the agent simulates how the conversation or interaction
will unfold, and the strong modern move trains a proactive assistant inside large-scale persona simulations, generating
many synthetic users, letting the agent practice anticipating and clarifying against them, and shipping the policy that


                                                                                                                          20
                                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


survives. Dialogue rollouts and future-turn modeling supply the mechanism (Lewis et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2025f),
language-model user simulators scale it (Luo et al., 2024a), and proactivity is now manufactured this way across
recommendation, delegated planning, recruitment, adaptive interfaces, tutoring, and clinical consultation (Kim et al.,
2026b; Xuan et al., 2026; Jiang et al., 2024b; Sun et al., 2025b; Cao et al., 2026; Langerak et al., 2023; Deng et al.,
2024c; Feng et al., 2026d).
Scaling the sandbox from one simulated user to a population lets a proactive agent rehearse emergent social consequences
before acting in a real group, and self-play turns that population into a training ground for socially aware behavior (Wang
et al., 2024g). Populated prototypes and generative-agent societies generate group dynamics that an intervention can be
tested against (Park et al., 2022, 2023; Zhou et al., 2024c; AL et al., 2024; Piao et al., 2025), and proactive mediators
and deliberation agents are evaluated and refined inside them (Liu et al., 2026q; Nath et al., 2026; Kim et al., 2025b).
Many self-initiated interventions affect several people, so population-level simulation can help an agent examine how its
actions may alter group interactions.
LLM-simulated users can be miscalibrated proxies for human users (Seshadri et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025d). Multi-turn
experiments also find that models can persist with early mistaken assumptions (Laban et al., 2025), and sycophancy has
been observed in AI assistants (Sharma et al., 2025). When such models simulate users, an overly favorable response
may cause an agent to overestimate the value or acceptability of an unrequested intervention. Offline logs and real-world
interaction data offer a basis for checking these estimates and are used to train and evaluate proactive agents (Wei et al.,
2025a; Tang et al., 2026b). The remedy points forward: externalizing what the sandbox surfaced into explicit, revisable
goals (§4.3) lets the rehearsed need be inspected and overridden before it is silently acted on.

Figure 9 Agenda bridges foresight and sustained goal pursuit. Anticipating a need does not determine whether it should become

A forecast is not yet a plan of action. Awareness supplies a situation estimate and anticipation projects it into a latent
need, but a predicted need becomes proactive behavior only once the agent commits to it as a goal it will pursue
unprompted (Figure 9). Agenda turns identified needs and opportunities into goals the agent can maintain and pursue.
Self-initiated work expands this capacity to include generating, revising, and prioritizing goals alongside existing
assignments, and sustaining those commitments across interruptions and sessions. We trace the capacity in three steps:
how a latent need becomes an explicit goal (§4.3.1), how a committed goal is decomposed and carried across time
(§4.3.2), and how a crowded agenda is ranked when the agent’s self-generated goals compete with the user’s (§4.3.3).
