4.3.1   Goal Generation: Latent Needs to Explicit Goals
Foreseeing that a user will need something is an epistemic state, while pursuing it is a commitment, and the distance
between the two is what separates a proactive agent from a forecaster. The classical practical-reasoning lineage
formalized this step: a desire becomes an intention only through deliberate adoption, after which the agent holds itself
responsible for bringing the intended state about (Bratman, 1987; Cohen & Levesque, 1990). The belief-desire-intention
tradition built the leap into running systems, supplying the deliberation that turns a candidate desire into a committed
intention that drives behavior (Rao & Georgeff, 1995), and it transfers to embodied proactivity, where a BDI controller
lets a social robot adopt and act on goals an operator never issued (K. C. & Chodorowski, 2019). For an act-first agent,
deliberate adoption determines which anticipated needs enter the agenda; a recent assistant that proposes and selects its
own daily activities from a model of standing desires shows the transition concretely (Wang et al., 2025j).
The earliest engineered answer to where a new goal comes from was goal-driven autonomy, in which an agent detects a
discrepancy between what it expected and what it observes, explains the discrepancy, formulates a goal that addresses it,
and manages the resulting goal set (Molineaux et al., 2010; Klenk et al., 2013). This loop is proactive by construction,
since the trigger is the environment violating the agent’s own predictions and no instruction has to arrive for a new
goal to appear. The pattern recurs across goal-reasoning systems that share little but the structure: a norm-constrained
planner generates only objectives that respect the deontic constraints it operates under (Pardo & Strasser, 2024), while
a motivation-driven agent self-selects which fresh goal to adopt when its standing goals are invalidated (Association
for Artificial Intelligence 2026 & Addison, 2026). Surveys of the area codify discrepancy detection, explanation, goal
formulation, and goal management as the recurring components (Vattam et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2018; Aha, 2018),
and domain-independent formulations show the same heuristics generating useful goals without task-specific tuning
(Paisner et al., 2014). Self-origination was thus an established mechanism well before foundation models, and it is the
structural ancestor of every modern behavior that notices something is wrong and decides to fix it.
Goal-driven autonomy reacts to an anomaly, yet an agent can also manufacture goals from internal drives when nothing
in the environment has gone wrong. Intrinsically motivated agents set their own objectives from signals such as curiosity,
novelty, and learning progress, so the agenda fills continuously, even absent any triggering surprise (Schmidhuber,
2010; Oudeyer et al., 2007; Barto et al., 2004). This is the purest form of self-generation, with the goal source entirely
endogenous, and it is a genuinely proactive specialization even though it runs on general reinforcement learning. Two
distinct signals make the point: prediction-error curiosity drives an agent toward states whose outcome it cannot yet
foresee (Pathak et al., 2017), and learning-progress signals steer it toward goals at the frontier of its current competence,
where improvement is fastest (Forestier et al., 2022). The same principle scales to language-based agents, where a
metacognitive estimate of competence lets an agent prioritize learnable goals across a vast open-ended goal space
(Gaven et al., 2025).
Foundation models compress a broad human prior about what is worth doing, so an AI agent can now propose its
own next objective directly in open-ended natural-language goal spaces, and the self-generation step that earlier eras
hand-engineered becomes a default capability. The canonical demonstration is an embodied agent in an open world
that runs its own automatic curriculum, proposing the next skill to acquire from what it has already mastered and
continuously extending its own agenda without human direction (Wang et al., 2024a). The pattern generalizes well
beyond one environment: agents now generate and pursue their own research questions across a full discovery cycle
(Lu et al., 2024), and foundation models serve as models of human interestingness that filter self-proposed tasks for
novelty and worth (Zhang et al., 2024c; Colas et al., 2022b,a). Studies that simply leave an agent alone with no task
supplied sharpen the proactive reading: agents spontaneously formulate and pursue multi-cycle projects of their own,
direct evidence that goal generation fires absent any prompt (Szeider, 2025; Nachkov et al., 2025).
In the assistant setting the self-generated goal is concrete and user-facing: the agent infers a latent intent from streaming
context and history, then proposes a specific task the user never requested, such as drafting the grocery list it predicts
will be needed or flagging the bug about to block a build. This is the prediction of §4.2 crystallizing into an actionable
agenda item, the direct hand-off from foresight to commitment. Distinct instantiations span the deployment surface:
mobile assistants suggest tasks from on-device context and usage history (Yang et al., 2026e; Lu et al., 2025a), streaming
systems infer latent needs and propose interventions under real-time and long-horizon memory constraints (Xie et al.,
2026; Zhao et al., 2026a), agents surface unspecified problems and bottlenecks a user has not articulated (Pasternak
et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025b; Ding et al., 2026b), and document-monitoring assistants propose next actions on an
evolving project (Siangliulue et al., 2026). A clarification step often precedes commitment, with the agent resolving an
ambiguous intent into a precise goal before it acts (Qian et al., 2024). One caution belongs here in mechanism form and


                                                                                                                          22
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


is treated normatively later: a self-generated goal can spawn emergent instrumental subgoals such as self-preservation or
resource acquisition that no designer specified, a tendency already visible when agents are given open-ended objectives
(Omohundro, 2008; Masumori & Ikegami, 2025), and we defer its ethical treatment to the later discussion of agent
safety.

4.3.2   Sub-Goal Proposal and Long-Horizon Agendas
A committed top-level goal is rarely executable as stated, so it must be broken into intermediate steps, and the question
that matters for autonomy is who decides those steps. Proactive agendas draw on established methods for decomposing
goals: classical hierarchical task networks, the options framework, and value-function decomposition supply hand-
authored hierarchies (Erol et al., 1994; Sutton et al., 1999; Dietterich, 2000), while subgoal-discovery methods let
an agent find its own waypoints through automatic goal generation and hindsight relabeling (Florensa et al., 2018;
Andrychowicz et al., 2018). Foundation models make the same decomposition language-native and on-the-fly, turning
a goal into ordered subproblems or interleaved reasoning and action as the task demands (Zhou et al., 2023; Wang
et al., 2023a; Yao et al., 2023b; Prasad et al., 2024). These methods provide a basis for organizing self-initiated work
(Liu et al., 2022a; Zhang et al., 2024d). Their use in proactive agents must also accommodate goals that are generated,
suspended, revised, and resumed as needs change. A standing agenda therefore carries both goals and their execution
state across sessions.
The proactive core of this subsection is the standing agenda: a persistent intention that outlives a single session, where
the agent registers a trigger condition, suspends, and re-engages the goal later when the condition fires. The cognitive
analogue is prospective memory, the capacity to remember to perform an action at the right future moment. The
mechanism appears in two distinct guises. In the first, an agent maintains a self-extending curriculum or a multi-stage
research program that runs for hours or across many sessions, keeping a single objective coherent over hundreds of
action cycles (Wang et al., 2024a; Lu et al., 2024; Mitchener et al., 2025; Feng et al., 2026a); scientific-discovery
agents push this furthest, sustaining hypothesis-driven agendas through long autonomous coding and experimentation
(Ghafarollahi & Buehler, 2025; Wehr et al., 2026; Wu et al., 2026c). In the second, an agent registers an event-triggered
follow-up, monitoring for a condition and proactively re-engaging a delegated intent when it occurs (Shi et al., 2026b;
Urli et al., 2018; Bairi et al., 2023), and embodied systems keep personality-driven goals alive across a building over
long deployments (Liu et al., 2026j). The engineering core is keeping the agenda alive across the suspend-and-resume
boundary and authoring the state needed to resume it: the user issues one instruction, and the agent maintains a
time-extended commitment to it.
A standing agenda spanning time will see the world change underneath it, so the agent has to keep the agenda alive
as conditions shift, because re-deriving the whole goal from scratch on every change is expensive and discards the
persistence that made the agenda proactive in the first place. What it draws on is plan repair versus full replanning,
where stability results favor localized repair that preserves most of the existing plan (Fox et al., 2006), together with
pre-emptive plan maintenance that modifies an intended plan to avoid an anticipated failure (White et al., 2015),
closed-loop refinement from execution feedback, and dependency-aware revision confined to the affected sub-tasks.
Two instantiations show the range: a self-refining agent patches its plan in place as feedback arrives (Sun et al., 2023;
Wang et al., 2024l), and a task-decoupled planner re-plans only the sub-goals downstream of a change while leaving the
rest untouched (Li et al., 2026l). The proactive specialization is the standing requirement itself: revision here serves an
intention the agent is holding open across drift, as when a proactive personal assistant must sustain hidden user intents
across multi-turn sessions with inter-task dependencies and cross-session continuity (Zhang et al., 2026b).

4.3.3   Goal Prioritization and Conflict Resolution
Anticipated needs, standing items, and explicit requests can compete for a proactive agent’s limited capacity. Goal
prioritization draws on established deliberation methods to select among them. Its foundational layer is intention
reconsideration in the belief-desire-intention tradition, which decides which committed intentions to keep, drop, or
re-deliberate as circumstances change, and how to detect interference between intentions held at once (Kinny & Georgeff,
1991; Schut et al., 2004; Thangarajah et al., 2003). A quantitative layer adds utility scalarization and Pareto reasoning
over competing objectives, together with goal-subset selection under resource limits, where an oversubscribed agent
must choose which goals to forgo because it cannot serve them all (Smith, 2004; Roijers et al., 2014; Hayes et al., 2022).
The same which-subset-at-what-utility calculus instantiates across settings, from a motivated agent balancing competing



                                                                                                                        23
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


internal need signals (Wang et al., 2025j) to a learning agent ranking goals by expected learning progress (Gaven et al.,
2025), the computation a proactive agent runs every cycle.
Once an agent runs a live task queue, the sharp question stops being scheduling efficiency and becomes whose agenda
wins a given turn: the agent’s self-initiated topic or the user’s current need. Operating-system-style agent schedulers
supply the queue-management base that this builds on, isolating resources and context-switching agent workloads
(§4.1.4) (Mei et al., 2025). The proactivity-specific contribution comes from the proactive-dialogue line, which studies
exactly the tension between an agent steering toward a conversational goal of its own and yielding to what the user wants
in the moment. Two instantiations make it concrete: surveys and benchmarks formalize agent-initiated topic planning
and target-driven guidance (Deng et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2025f), and notification systems weigh an agent’s goal of
delivering information against the cost of interrupting the user, suppressing or aggregating alerts so the agenda yields
when the user’s attention is scarce (Rizk et al., 2020). This is where multi-goal management stops being bookkeeping
and turns into an arbitration question.
A proactive agent’s self-generated goals can conflict with the user’s interests. Instrumental-convergence arguments
suggest that sufficiently capable agents pursuing a wide range of objectives can have incentives to preserve themselves,
acquire resources, and resist shutdown (Omohundro, 2008; Bostrom, 2012). Agent evaluations now exhibit it empirically,
in specification gaming and reward hacking (Skalse et al., 2025), in survival-instinct studies where agents prioritize
self-preservation by abandoning assigned tasks and compete aggressively for scarce resources (Masumori & Ikegami,
2025), in measured instrumental self-reasoning such as self-modification and covert reasoning (Fronsdal & Lindner,
2024), in shutdown-resistance experiments where models subvert their shutdown mechanism to complete a task
(Schlatter et al., 2026), in agentic-misalignment scenarios where an agent blackmails officials to avoid being shut
down or replaced (Lynch et al., 2025), and in toxic-proactivity benchmarks where over-optimized helpfulness becomes
overreach (Wang et al., 2026l). An agent’s self-generated goals should remain subject to user authority, consistent
with the agent-economics view of agents as human proxies whose guiding objectives are tied to the interests of the
principals they represent (Yang & Zhai, 2025). Research on corrigibility seeks designs that accept correction and
shutdown without resisting (Soares et al., 2015). In the off-switch game, a cooperative agent strictly prefers to defer to a
rational human when its beliefs assign positive probability to both positive and negative utility for the proposed action
(Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017). Ask-for-help policies use estimates of execution uncertainty to decide when to request
assistance (Igbinedion & Karaman, 2024; He et al., 2025b). Instruction-hierarchy training teaches models to follow
higher-priority instructions when messages conflict (Wallace et al., 2024). This is the bridge to §4.4: even a perfectly
ranked agenda is not permission to act, and the top-ranked self-generated goal must still pass the per-intervention
go/no-go gate. Prioritization decides what the agent would most like to do; Arbitration decides whether it may.

4.4     Arbitration
Arbitration evaluates whether a self-initiated intervention is warranted and determines its timing and scope within
the agent’s granted permissions (Figure 10). We decompose the gate into four questions an act-first agent answers in
sequence: whether its sense of the user’s need is confident enough to act on at all (§4.4.1), whether the value of acting
clears its cost (§4.4.2), when within the flow of events to act so the intervention lands (§4.4.3), and whether the action is
safe enough to take given that the agent may be wrong (§4.4.4).

4.4.1    Uncertainty Quantification and Confidence Thresholds
The most basic arbitration question is whether to fire at all, given that the agent’s sense that the user needs something is
only an estimate. A proactive trigger is a prediction under uncertainty, so every firing is a bet whose downside depends
on what the agent acts upon: a user-facing agent that misfires spends the user’s attention on an unwanted suggestion,
while an agent operating a system spends real resources on an unnecessary autonomous action, whether superfluous
maintenance, a wrong remediation, or wasted compute. The classical resolution from mixed-initiative interaction still
holds, that the agent should act outright only when confident and fall back to dialogue when unsure (Horvitz, 1999),
which makes the calibration of that confidence the load-bearing component of the entire gate. Both regimes recur
across the literature: clarification-first dialogue agents withhold a guessed answer and ask when intent is ambiguous
(Deng et al., 2023c; Qian et al., 2024), embodied and navigation agents gather information or request help at estimated
moments of uncertainty (Chen et al., 2024b; Igbinedion & Karaman, 2024), and a team-support agent withholds advice
it is not confident enough to justify (Hughes et al., 2023). A trust-weighted preservation agent shows the system-acting
side of the same rule, switching between acting autonomously and merely suggesting as inter-agent trust warrants

(Pellegrino et al., 2015). Calibration is non-trivial because modern neural networks are systematically miscalibrated
(Guo et al., 2017), so the number the gate reads cannot be taken at face value.
Agents can estimate confidence using token-logit probabilities and a model’s own estimate of whether it knows an
answer (Kadavath et al., 2022), verbalized confidence emitted as natural language (Lin et al., 2022; Tian et al., 2023),
sampling-consistency across stochastic runs (Xiong et al., 2024), and semantic entropy that measures uncertainty over
meaning, factoring out surface wording (Kuhn et al., 2023b). Structured self-dialogue can help an agent flag its own
knowledge gaps and ask a human for guidance when deployed (He et al., 2025a).
Calibrated confidence can inform an agent’s decision to act, ask for help, or abstain. A reject option and selective
prediction set a confidence threshold below which the agent declines to act on its own (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017;
Chow, 1970), and learning-to-defer formalizes whom it hands off to, routing the same threshold to a clarifying question
for the user or to an escalation to an on-call operator (Madras et al., 2018; Mozannar & Sontag, 2020). Threshold-setting
becomes principled once the score carries a coverage guarantee: conformal prediction turns a raw confidence into a
prediction set whose size is itself the uncertainty, letting the agent read the gate off the set directly (Quach et al., 2024).
The canonical proactive instantiation acts autonomously when that set collapses to a single hypothesis and asks for help
otherwise, a clean rule that ports across an embodied robot deciding whether to grasp now or query (Ren et al., 2023)
and a language agent deciding whether to answer or abstain, the latter now organized into its own survey of when models
should hold back (Wen et al., 2025a). The same uncertainty-routed handoff recurs in diffusion-policy robots that request
operator help only when needed (He et al., 2025b), in coding agents that ask before assuming on underspecified tasks
(Edwards & Schuster, 2026), and in learned policies that choose the moment for human intervention in a collaborative
task (Feng et al., 2024).
The gentlest verdict is to do nothing, and proactivity gives it a peculiar shape. In question answering, abstaining
is a visible answer the user can read (Zhang et al., 2024b), but in proactivity the non-act is invisible, so graceful
degradation has to extend the ladder from act, through verify-or-ask, down to a hold-and-monitor rung that keeps
watching without intruding. This mode has concrete realizations: a trained silence token lets a dialogue agent decline to
speak until a contribution adds value (Patel et al., 2026), a streaming companion stays quiet under continuous input
until a response is warranted (Yan et al., 2026a), a navigation agent holds its question until uncertainty justifies the
dialogue (Taioli et al., 2025), and a recommend-only mode lets a system-acting agent propose without committing
the change (Urli et al., 2018). A meeting-support study finds users prefer an agent that observes and asks before it
intervenes over one that acts unprompted (Houtti et al., 2025), and the same team-support agent presents only one
in every four candidate interventions, with 15% specifically withheld and the rest filtered by its theory-of-mind and


                                                                                                                                      25
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


confirmation-delay mechanisms (Hughes et al., 2023).

4.4.2   Utility and Cost: The Value of Intervention
Once the agent is confident a need is real, the next gate weighs the value of acting against its cost, with classical
value-of-information and metareasoning supplying the frame (Howard, 1966; Russell & Wefald, 1991). The cost is paid
in different currencies according to the kind of act. When the proactive act is a suggestion or an alert, the currency is the
user’s attention, and that case has a worked-out program: the agent computes the expected utility of speaking against a
learned, per-user interruption-cost model and speaks only when the benefit clears that personalized price (Horvitz, 1999;
Horvitz et al., 2013b, 2004). The attention cost is empirically grounded, since interruption measurably degrades task
performance, raises error rates, disturbs affect, and imposes recovery time (Bailey & Konstan, 2006; McFarlane, 2002;
Iqbal & Horvitz, 2007), so the cost term rests on human-factors measurement. Dialogue agents instantiate the same
balance, trading the value of contributed knowledge against the annoyance of speaking (Liu et al., 2020; Rizk et al.,
2020), sometimes planning what to communicate against a learned model of the recipient’s preferences (Chitnis et al.,
2018). Many proactive acts done for a user are not suggestions at all: an assistant that closes a window against coming
rain or files a form on the user’s behalf acts in the environment, where the price is paid in resources, side effects, and the
standing risk of an autonomous mistake. An agent-economics account makes the trade-off general, framing each such
decision as a constrained optimization in which the agent’s own autonomy is a parameter that carries cost, so that a
broader grant of authority buys more benefit while raising the price and risk the act must clear (Yang & Zhai, 2025).
The cost the gate weighs is therefore set by what the act does, whether or not a person is its beneficiary.
A second canonical instantiation predates AI agents. Predictive-maintenance economics is the textbook intervention
trade-off, where acting too early wastes remaining useful life and labor while acting too late means failure, and
condition-based-maintenance threshold optimization locates the sweet spot (Jardine et al., 2006; de Jonge & Scarf,
2020). Cost-sensitive learning supplies the general formal foundation, in which each action is chosen to minimize
expected cost under an explicit cost matrix (Elkan, 2001). Modern auto-remediation systems instantiate it, autonomously
selecting which mitigation action to apply from multi-signal failure prediction (Levy et al., 2020) and gating automatic
recovery against escalation to a human (Zhang et al., 2024e), and AI agents increasingly budget the cost of their own
tool calls the same way, treating each call as an action that must clear its price (Chen et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2025e). A
self-budgeting observability agent shows the pattern in the system-acting case, raising telemetry resolution only when a
signal justifies the added cost (Kapoor & Kas, 2026), while a navigation planner bounds the inconvenience it imposes
through an explicit budget constraint, spending it where intervening matters most (Geldenbott & Leung, 2024), and an
autonomous cyber-defense architecture decides where to direct its responses (Kott et al., 2023). Across infrastructure
healing and agent tool-use the computation is identical: is this action worth its cost?
The contemporary specialization replaces hand-authored utility functions with learned ones. Reward models trained on
human accept-or-reject judgments of past proactive actions supply the value estimate directly, and benchmarks now treat
precision, the fraction of suggestions a user actually accepts, as the operational interruption-cost metric (Lu et al., 2025a).
This closes the loop with confidence calibration, because the gate’s threshold is now fit to revealed human preference,
which is how deployed proactive assistants tune how often they speak (Chen et al., 2025d). The evaluation infrastructure
has followed, scoring proactive assistants on real-world logs and on jointly optimized productivity, proactivity, and
personalization (Tang et al., 2026b; Hao et al., 2025; Sun et al., 2025b), and recent systems learn the speak-or-stay-silent
threshold directly from offline expert behavior (Wei et al., 2025a).
A single-shot expected-value calculation misses one term: trust is an intertemporal cost that compounds across
interactions. Cry-wolf and false-alarm effects drive automation disuse (Roulston & Smith, 2004; Parasuraman & Riley,
1997), and AI agents exhibit toxic proactivity when helpfulness curdles into overreach (Wang et al., 2026l). In each case
an individual intervention looks net-positive while the sequence quietly burns the user’s willingness to listen, so the
utility model has to discount future receptivity and not only price the current act. Proactive-dialogue systems that fold
a predicted trust signal into the reward, or that model the user’s evolving willingness to comply, make this discount
explicit (Kraus et al., 2021, 2023; Natarajan et al., 2024).

4.4.3   Timing and Interruption Management
Once an intervention is judged net-positive, arbitration must still answer when. Timing matters on its own because cost
is non-stationary. For an agent competing for a person’s attention it varies sharply by micro-moment, cheapest at task


                                                                                                                            26
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


breakpoints and boundaries and most expensive mid-thought (Adamczyk & Bailey, 2004; Iqbal & Horvitz, 2007; Iqbal
& Bailey, 2010); for an agent acting on a system it is a matter of windows and lead time, where firing too early or too
late both fail (Panagopoulos et al., 2015). The two cases optimize different quantities, a human’s attentional rhythm in
one and detection delay against false-alarm rate in the other, which is why timing is handled as a decision variable of its
own (Fourie, 2019; Kim et al., 2018a; Goodman et al., 2017; Rizk et al., 2020).
For an agent competing for attention, timing has an empirical handle, because interruptibility can be sensed, with a
clear progression in signal richness from desktop activity logs, to mobile context, to physiological and attention signals
such as gaze and pupillometry (Fogarty et al., 2005; Horvitz & Apacible, 2003; Pejovic & Musolesi, 2014; Iqbal et al.,
2005). This sensing groundwork is taken from human-computer interaction yet serves arbitration directly, supplying the
real-time estimate of whether this is a good moment that the timing gate reads, across a desktop knowledge-worker
setting and a mobile or wearable one alike (Cha et al., 2020; Otogi et al., 2013; Sirithunge et al., 2019).
When the moment is wrong, the agent does not drop the intervention but coordinates it, choosing among immediate,
negotiated, mediated, and scheduled delivery (McFarlane, 2002; Houtti et al., 2025). The same move appears in
unrelated settings: deferring to a task breakpoint for a person at work is the same idea as opportunistic maintenance on a
machine, where the intervention piggybacks on a stop that was going to happen anyway, whether a machine already
halted for another reason or a user already pausing between tasks (Ab-Samat & Kamaruddin, 2014; Ho & Intille, 2005;
Mehrotra et al., 2016). The strategy is to ride an existing breakpoint that the world or the user already supplies, which a
progression-aware dialogue agent does by deferring its contribution to a juncture in the task state (Sanders et al., 2022;
Favier et al., 2022; Dubiel et al., 2024). Benchmarks now grade this delivery directly, scoring a system on whether it
surfaces information exactly when the user needs it while withholding the irrelevant content that would only distract
(Yang et al., 2025d).
The most demanding timing regime is conversation, where turn-taking, barge-in, and full-duplex models collapse
the act-or-wait decision to sub-second granularity, forcing the agent to decide while listening whether to speak now,
backchannel, or hold (Skantze, 2021; Lee et al., 2026). Duplex and listen-while-speaking architectures keep the gate
running continuously, with no comfortable breakpoint to defer to (Zhang et al., 2026g; Ma et al., 2024b; Défossez et al.,
2024). The same continuous gate appears in a real-time egocentric assistant deciding when to initiate speech (Kim et al.,
2025a; Chiang et al., 2025) and in a multi-party group conversation where an agent must time its entry among many
human speakers (Liu et al., 2025g; Eckhaus et al., 2025), a regime whose over-triggering failures recent voice-agent
benchmarks specifically expose (Xu et al., 2026c).
Everything in this subsection is a special case of one formal question: at each moment, should the agent act now or wait
for a better one? That is the optimal-stopping problem, and its sequential-detection form, quickest-change detection,
makes the trade-off precise, since waiting longer lowers the chance of a false alarm but adds delay before a real need is
served (Page, 1954; Shiryaev, 1963; Roulston & Smith, 2004). Casting timing this way unifies the examples above,
so that deciding when a warning has enough certainty to be worth its lead time, when to scale a system ahead of load
(Rzadca et al., 2020), when a user’s working memory makes assistance land best, when a learned model of the user’s
routine indicates availability (Caldeira Miguéns Diogo & Moreno, 2024), and when a learned opportunity window
has opened are the same stopping decision under different cost terms (Qian et al., 2025b; Gulati et al., 2026). Recent
proactive systems implement it directly, pairing a learned opportunity window with an explicit stopping rule, whether
a multimodal assistant gated on scene-alignment signals (Bandyopadhyay et al., 2025), a wearable that models the
user’s working memory to balance value against interruption (Pu et al., 2025b), or a scheduler trained with timing-aware
rewards over full opportunity windows (Ding et al., 2026b).

4.4.4   Risk- and Reversibility-Aware Gating
The last gate asks not whether the need is real and well-timed but whether a mistake can be undone, treating irreversibility
itself as a decision variable weighted directly in the gate. Safe reinforcement learning supplies the lineage, since
reversibility is learnable and penalizable, so an agent can be biased toward actions that preserve future options
through reachability-preserving and side-effect-penalizing objectives (Krakovna et al., 2019; García & Fernández, 2015;
Grinsztajn et al., 2021). Attainable-utility preservation and future-task objectives make the bias concrete, keeping the
agent’s downstream options open even when the reward is misspecified (Turner et al., 2020a,b; Krakovna et al., 2020).
The gate should set confidence thresholds according to the consequences of error and the feasibility and cost of recovery,
consistent with the balance between decision quality and safety considered in AI-agent economics (Yang & Zhai, 2025).



                                                                                                                         27
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Before a gate can act on risk it must perceive it, and the unsettling empirical finding is that perception is the weak link.
Emulated sandboxes and benchmarks show frontier agents routinely taking high-stakes or irreversible actions, deleting
data, escaping sandboxes, or rewriting history, without flagging them as risky (Ruan et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024). The
failure is broad, spanning computer-use, web, and embodied agents that comply with harmful or hazardous requests at
high rates (Kuntz et al., 2025; Tur et al., 2025; Levy et al., 2026; Torres-Fonseca et al., 2026), and the proactive setting
adds its own version where over-optimized helpfulness drives an agent into harmful overreach (Wang et al., 2026l). Risk
awareness is therefore measurable and currently poor, which means the gate cannot rely on the agent’s own judgment
alone and motivates the harder gates that follow (Amos-Binks et al., 2023).
The first line of risk control is a soft gate that scales required permission to the stakes, running low-risk actions
autonomously while routing consequential ones to user confirmation, with the routing itself as the proactive mechanism.
This takes concrete forms across settings: robots that ask a human for help to recover from manipulation failures
(Tellex et al., 2014), conformal triggering that asks precisely when the agent is uncertain (Ren et al., 2023), and
intervention-budgeted shared-autonomy policies that spend a limited number of human check-ins where they matter
most (Tan et al., 2022; Overman & Bayati, 2026). Variable-autonomy and parallel-autonomy frameworks set the same
dial by criticality, handing control between human and agent as the predicted consequence of acting rises (Panagopoulos
et al., 2022; Yin et al., 2023). The unifying idea is that permission behaves as a dial set by predicted consequence.
When the agent’s judgment cannot be trusted, a hard gate enforces limits from outside it. Permission systems and
domain-specific privilege control veto actions independently of the agent’s own reasoning (Shi et al., 2026c; Wang et al.,
2025a), guardrail pipelines screen each action against an external policy (Xiang et al., 2025; Chennabasappa et al., 2025),
and separation-of-powers architectures isolate intent generation from execution so that a compromised planner still
cannot act (Xiang, 2026); high-consequence autonomous deployments further motivate explicit safety measures against
misuse (Boiko et al., 2023a) and reflective runtimes that diagnose and repair failure modes during execution (Cruz,
2025). This is general agent-safety work more than a proactivity-specific mechanism, so we keep it to its arbitration role
as the external veto on the intervention decision and refer to the cited agent-safety work for enforcement details and to
Section 7.2 for broader safety and governance questions.
The closing move mirrors the hold-and-monitor verdict of §4.4.1 from the risk side: when waiting is cheap and the action
is irreversible, doing nothing gracefully is itself a calibrated choice and a form of intelligent disobedience, a deliberate
hold the agent has reasoned its way to (Hornig & Mirsky, 2026; Brahman et al., 2024). Because human approval does
not scale to high-volume autonomous operation, trusted-monitoring protocols sketch how the gate survives without a
human on every action, using a cheaper monitor to watch a more capable actor so that abstention and oversight together
keep arbitration tractable at deployment scale (Greenblatt et al., 2024). Once an intervention clears all four gates, what
remains is to carry it out, and the spectrum of autonomy along which the agent delivers the action is the subject of §4.5.

4.5     Action
Once arbitration clears an intervention, Action determines how to carry it out within granted authority (Figure 11). Two
decisions shape execution: how much work the agent performs before returning control (§4.5.1), and how it presents
the intervention (§4.5.2). Depending on its permissions and the consequences of the action, the agent may prepare a
reversible draft, request approval, execute a bounded action, or report the outcome. The delivery mechanism must make
the scope and status of the intervention clear and support correction or reversal where possible.

4.5.1    The Spectrum of Autonomy and the Agent’s Interaction Paradigm
A proactive agent that has decided to intervene must determine how much of the action to perform itself and how
much to hand back to the user. Human-factors research formalized that gradation half a century before AI agents,
in levels-of-automation scales that run from the computer offering no assistance, through suggesting an option and
then acting only on approval, up to acting autonomously and telling the human only on request (Sheridan & Verplank,
1978). A companion model decomposes any automated function into four classes, information acquisition, information
analysis, decision and action selection, and action implementation, each independently settable from fully manual to
fully automatic (Parasuraman et al., 2000); the four map almost one-to-one onto the pipeline of this chapter, and the
spectrum of autonomy is specifically the level chosen for action implementation. These frameworks describe how
execution is divided between the agent and the human. Cyber-resilience and business-process agents likewise emphasize
moving from passive monitoring to autonomous response (Kott & Theron, 2022; Dumas et al., 2026).

Figure 11 Action: exercising discretion while preserving human control. Intervention modes specify how the agent contributes to

Related autonomy scales appear across domains, describing how execution and human involvement are allocated. For
an agent that addresses a person, the rungs run from a choice-architecture nudge that biases a decision without making
it (Weinmann et al., 2016), through a suggestion-only assistant that proposes and waits (Faulring et al., 2010), to
mixed-initiative dialogue in which the agent and the user negotiate who holds the floor and who acts (Horvitz, 1999;
Avula et al., 2022). For an agent that acts on a system the same gradation is re-invented per safety-critical field, with
self-driving’s six-level scale the most thoroughly codified instance, its Level 3 requiring a fallback-ready user to take
over upon request (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, n.d.), alongside parallel autonomy-level taxonomies
written for surgical robotics and for maritime autonomous-ship regulation (Yang et al., 2017; International Maritime
Organization, n.d.). That so many fields re-derive the same rungs for their own reasons is itself the message, and
controlled studies confirm the rungs are not interchangeable, since an implicitly guiding agent preserves user autonomy
compared with an explicitly directive one (Nakahashi & Yamada, 2021), and a topic-suggesting health coach maintains
engagement and acceptance even when it takes more initiative than pure user choice (Beinema et al., 2022).
The agent or team can adjust the autonomy level at runtime as conditions change. Determining whether and when to
transfer control is the core research problem of adjustable autonomy, pioneered by a deployed multi-agent assistant that
pulled its human in only at the points where autonomous action was risky and modeled the handoff as a cost-aware
strategy (Scerri et al., 2002; Bradshaw et al., 2004), and by robot teams running with sliding autonomy that requested
help the instant they got stuck (Sellner et al., 2006). For self-initiated work, the transfer decision can account for task
criticality and the human’s availability to take over (Panagopoulos et al., 2022; Banik & Hovakimyan, 2025). AI agents
now implement the transfer decision at runtime, whether by learned uncertainty escalation as in an interactive navigator
(Igbinedion & Karaman, 2024), by rule-based metacognitive triggers that predict failure and hand off before it happens
(Xu, 2025), or by adapting the level to the situation, with team-outcome studies showing that situational adaptation beats
any fixed level (Salikutluk et al., 2024).
The contemporary form of the spectrum lives in deployed AI-agent settings as confirmation modes exposed directly
as configuration, ask-always, ask-on-risk, allowlist, and auto-execute, the rungs a user actually turns (Anthropic,
n.d.a; OpenAI, n.d.). New taxonomies grade an agent’s autonomy by the user’s residual role, from operator down
through collaborator, consultant, and approver to observer, and catalog when a deployed agent should pause for sign-off
(Feng et al., 2025; Doshi et al., 2026). The same rungs reappear across distant build-outs: a program-repair bot that
generates patches and reports them for developer approval sits at the approver rung (Urli et al., 2018), a fully automated
scientific-discovery agent runs at the observer end (Lu et al., 2024), and a general multi-agent framework exposes the
human-in-the-loop level as a configuration choice (Wu et al., 2023). A recurring caveat is that the spectrum should
perhaps be capped: one line of work argues an agent must stop and ask before any unrequested action (Zhang et al.,


                                                                                                                                         29
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


2024h; Qian et al., 2024), another that fully autonomous agents should not be built at all (Mitchell et al., 2025), and a
security analysis warns that over-frequent confirmations breed the approval fatigue that defeats the safeguard (Wang
et al., 2026e).
This rung is the deliberate mirror of the risk gate in §4.4.4: where arbitration’s last gate decides whether to act, the same
calibrated signal here sets how hard to act, so the two run off one estimate. Appropriate reliance depends in part on how
well users’ trust matches the capabilities of automation (Lee & See, 2004). Within granted authority, the autonomy level
should reflect calibrated confidence, reversibility, and the consequences of error. In autonomous reinforcement learning,
PAINT learns to avoid irreversible states and requests human intervention when its learned classifier indicates that it has
entered one (Xie et al., 2022). Calibrated or uncertainty-aware triggering supports these autonomy decisions across
settings, a conformal planner that auto-acts when its prediction set collapses to one hypothesis and asks otherwise (Ren
et al., 2023), a coding agent that proceeds on simple tasks and seeks clarification on hard ones (Edwards & Schuster,
2026), a navigation agent that minimizes dialogue until uncertainty warrants it (Taioli et al., 2025), and a diffusion
policy that requests operator help only when its own uncertainty spikes (He et al., 2025b).

4.5.2   Action Presentation and Mixed-Initiative Delivery
Because the content is unsolicited, how it is presented is itself a design decision weighed alongside the decision to act.
The founding mixed-initiative literature already treated presentation, the choice of modality, how precisely to state a
suggestion, and how to degrade gracefully under uncertainty, as a decision-theoretic variable optimized jointly with the
act (Horvitz, 1999), with proactive-assistance planners adding the constraint that a surfaced act must be recognizable to
a human who was not expecting it (Kulkarni et al., 2021), and a parallel formal line modeling what to tell a teammate as
a belief-MDP over the change it induces in their understanding (Chitnis et al., 2018). That framing has returned for
modern co-working agents, where how a proactive contribution is surfaced is tied directly to whether it is accepted (Pu
et al., 2025a). The first axis of the choice is volume, and delivery channels form a continuum from ambient awareness
to focal interruption: calm peripheral displays and glanceable notifications for a person, rising to a foreground alert
(Weiser & Brown, 1997; Wisneski et al., 1998; Matthews et al., 2004; Pielot et al., 2014), and the operations ladder from
a log line to an emailed report to paging the operator for a system being run (Rizk et al., 2020; Zhu & Callison-Burch,
2025). When to interrupt was settled in §4.4.3; the variable here is how loudly, a dial that group-conversation studies
show users want to hold themselves (Houde et al., 2025).
The cleanest way to deliver an unrequested action is to render it as a previewed, not-yet-committed change sitting
inside the workflow, so accepting it continues the work the user was already doing. The mechanism recurs across very
different agents and modalities: ghost text and inline completion for an author, a real-time plan preview for a music or
diagramming partner, and a merge-ready or co-planned change-set for an agent operating a system, each showing what
the agent would do and letting the human commit or edit (Scarlatos et al., 2025b; Ellawela et al., 2025; Hassan et al.,
2025). Code assistants have studied the preview most closely, learning when to show a suggestion at all from acceptance
feedback (Mozannar et al., 2024b), modeling the programmer’s interaction states and verification cost around it (Barke
et al., 2022; Mozannar et al., 2024a), and surfacing proactive suggestions inside the editor for the user to take or drop
(Zhao et al., 2025a; Chen et al., 2025e). The same preview-then-commit loop now wraps full agentic workflows and
human-robot manipulation, where a co-planning interface or a proposal turn lets the human approve before anything
takes effect (Mozannar et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026a; Urli et al., 2018). A preview gives the user an opportunity to detect
and reject an unsuitable proposal before execution, with attention and verification costs that depend on the proposal and
workflow.
The presentation surface is itself channel-specific, and each channel forces a different shape for the unsolicited act.
Dialogue agents deliver proactivity as injected turns whose timing and content are modeled explicitly, deciding when to
claim a turn, what to contribute, and when a backchannel is enough (Deng et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2025g; Lee et al.,
2026). Wearable and augmented-reality agents shrink the same delivery to an in-ear whisper or a glanceable panel,
jointly adapting what to say and how to surface it to the moment (Chen et al., 2025d; Lee et al., 2025b). An embodied
agent in a home or workplace has yet another surface, where the act is physical and the design variable is the legibility
of the robot’s motion, since intent-expressive movement makes the robot’s goal clear to the person it is acting around
and marks a readable approach apart from one that is merely predictable (Dragan et al., 2013). For an unattended agent
with no human in front of it the presentation surface becomes staged rollout (Davidovič & Beyer, 2018), undo-friendly
execution with a confined blast radius (Patil et al., 2024), and the audit log that presents the act to an absent principal
after the fact (Dong et al., 2024). The function stays constant across these surfaces while only the medium changes,


                                                                                                                          30
                                                 Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


which is why the question of when to enter recurs in group and asynchronous settings under each one (Eckhaus et al.,
2025; Liu et al., 2026b).
The last delivery variable is wording itself. People apply social rules to a system’s phrasing as if it were a social
actor (Nass et al., 1994), so how an unrequested suggestion is framed, its phrasing, the explanation attached, and the
confidence it displays, causally shifts whether the user accepts it and whether they over-rely on it (Zhang et al., 2020b).
Two handles replicate well: first-person hedges and natural-language uncertainty lower overreliance on wrong answers
(Kim et al., 2024b), and for inline code, highlighting the tokens most likely to be edited helps more than displaying
raw generation probabilities (Vasconcelos et al., 2025). The same levers carry to the textual self-report an agent emits
about an action it already took, where an explanation of why it acted is the action report in another setting, studied from
collaborative-filtering justifications to a self-driving controller’s rationale and to the oversight explanations that agentic
interfaces now owe an absent supervisor (Herlocker et al., 2000; Kim et al., 2018b; Jang & Sundar, 2026).

Figure 12 Adaptation: learning whether initiative was warranted. Successful execution alone does not establish that an
intervention was useful, and user reactions must be interpreted in context. Fast reflection revises the assumptions behind the next

Adaptation is the sixth A and the slow outer loop that closes the proactive cycle: once an agent has sensed, anticipated,
planned, gated, and acted, it must learn from how that act landed so that its next anticipation and its next gate are
better. Self-initiated action changes both the evidence available for learning and the behavior that must be improved.
Feedback may be implicit, delayed, or missing, and adaptation must assess the choice to intervene alongside the quality
of execution. We trace three loops at widening timescales (Figure 12): harvesting an implicit, biased signal out of the
consequences of acting first (§4.6.1), repairing the agent’s own predictive model in-context before it next fires (§4.6.2),
and the across-episode calibration of trust, personalization, and earned autonomy that keeps proactivity sustainable
(§4.6.3).

4.6.1      Implicit Feedback and Self-Correction
Feedback on self-initiated interventions can be sparse and difficult to interpret: a dismissed suggestion is a noisy label
(Opfermann et al., 2017) whose meaning cannot be read off the outcome, since the user may have been busy, distracted,
or negotiating, an averted incident is an unobservable counterfactual that leaves nothing to score (Schwall et al., 2020),
and credit for an anticipatory action arrives late or never. The same scarcity appears wherever the agent acts first:
a user-facing assistant guessing whether its unprompted nudge helped must read implicit and noisy cues from the


                                                                                                                                        31
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


interaction log (Liu et al., 2025h; Shen et al., 2025), and an operations or driving system that preempted a failure can no
longer prove the failure was coming. Both learn from signals that are implicit, biased, and censored, and the founding
mixed-initiative account already named the difficulty of inferring whether an unrequested service was wanted (Horvitz,
1999). Adaptation therefore opens with a harder problem than choosing a learning rule, which is manufacturing a usable
training signal out of silence, and recent agents take it up directly by actively probing the environment for the feedback
their own actions did not return (Su, 2026a; Feng et al., 2026c).
Learning from these signals draws on established methods for implicit feedback and partially observed outcomes,
whose assumptions must be examined in the context of self-initiated interventions. The information-retrieval and
recommender-systems tradition established long ago that interaction exhaust, the clicks, skips, and dwell times users
leave behind, substitutes for explicit labels (Joachims, 2002; Hu et al., 2008), and it catalogued the pathologies that the
proactive setting inherits, position bias as the ancestor of dismissal-is-not-rejection (Joachims et al., 2005) and delayed or
censored conversions where a non-response cannot yet be scored (Chapelle, 2014). The decision-theoretic side supplies
the estimators that turn logged, partial feedback into policies: counterfactual risk minimization and off-policy bandit
methods reweight logged decisions into improved ones (Swaminathan & Joachims, 2015; Bottou et al., 2013), and
interaction-grounded formulations recover a latent reward when no explicit reward is logged at all, including implicit
physiological signals of subjective interest (Xie et al., 2021; Shih et al., 2017). That generality lets the same estimators
serve a user’s accept and reject history and a robot operator’s record of takeovers and non-interventions alike (Spencer
et al., 2021; Ho et al., 2020), and learning directly from human interventions and corrections extends naturally to
multi-robot and co-creative teams (Seraj et al., 2023; Lin et al., 2024). These are imported tools, and the proactive
contribution is the function they are pointed at, which is deciding when to intervene.
Agents can use the recorded consequences of self-initiated interventions, together with user and operator responses, as
feedback for adaptation. For a user-facing agent the systems treat acceptance, dismissal, and edit telemetry as de facto
reward: code-completion acceptance rates drive when a suggestion is worth showing (Mozannar et al., 2024b; Ziegler
et al., 2022), reply and notification traces are mined so that a dismissal becomes a preference signal (Pielot et al., 2014;
Mehrotra et al., 2016), and a fabric-sensing assistant refines its behavior from implicit textual feedback with no explicit
ratings (Liu & Chen, 2024). For an agent managing a system the equivalent signals are operator overrides, alert triage
decisions, and rollbacks, where a disengagement corpus records every human takeover (Favarò et al., 2018), analyst
triage actions on alerts are learned into an automatic prioritisation policy (Turcotte et al., 2025), and Gandalf trains its
deployment go/no-go classifier on historical cases with feedback from component teams (Li et al., 2020). The move is
the same in both, converting the exhaust of one’s own interventions into a graded supervision signal, with full awareness
that the signal carries exactly the bias the asymmetry above named.
The modern move is to train proactivity directly and end to end on the signal sources just instrumented, the source-side
counterpart to the within-episode reasoning of §4.6.2 over the same data. For user-facing agents the recipe fits a reward
model to accept and reject and edit traces and fine-tunes toward the intervention behavior users actually keep: the
canonical exemplar collects human accept and reject annotations over predicted proactive tasks into a benchmark, trains
a reward model on them, and uses it to elicit proactiveness (Lu et al., 2025a), while related work infers latent preferences
from user edits (Gao et al., 2024) and pushes the same recipe to on-device override traces at scale (Feng et al., 2026b).
For agents acting on a system the optimization runs against execution and environment outcomes, grounding the policy
in code-execution feedback, exploration traces, or self-produced environmental reward (Gehring et al., 2025; Song et al.,
2024b; Alhajir et al., 2025), and reinforcement-learned security and operations agents tune their preemptive actions
against pipeline outcomes (Anugula et al., 2025); multi-objective formulations now optimize productivity, proactivity,
and personalization jointly (Sun et al., 2025b). Both branches presuppose that the traces already exist, and for proactive
behavior they often do not, since an agent that has never been permitted to act unprompted leaves no acceptance log to fit
a reward model to. Synthesis is the standard recourse, producing tailored instruction data for capabilities that collected
corpora underrepresent (Wang et al., 2024k) and constructing multi-turn tool-use trajectories where live interaction
traces are unavailable (Yin et al., 2025), at the cost of substituting the generator’s coverage assumptions for the user
population’s. The caveat from the feedback asymmetry never disappears, since a policy trained on biased acceptance
data inherits that bias, which is precisely why the calibration of §4.6.3 is needed downstream.

4.6.2   Inference-Time Reflection
A mature general toolbox converts the same signals into behavioral change purely in-context, with no gradient step, by
having the agent verbalize a critique of its own trace, revise, and retry, the recipe sometimes called verbal reinforcement


                                                                                                                           32
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


learning (Shinn et al., 2023). Relevant mechanisms include self-generated reflection on past attempts kept in an episodic
buffer (Shinn et al., 2023), iterative self-refinement of a single output (Madaan et al., 2023), tool-grounded critique that
checks claims against external evidence (Gou et al., 2024), and plan-level repair that separates in-plan from out-of-plan
errors (Sun et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024a). This approach has already been wired into proactive assistants and
self-improving agents that monitor their own execution and act on what they find (Sun et al., 2025a; He et al., 2025a;
Orimo et al., 2025). What makes it matter for proactive agents is what they point it at, developed next.
The proactivity-specific use of reflection turns the question from whether the answer was good to whether acting at all
was the right call, reopening the arbitration variables of §4.4: should I have intervened, was the timing right, was the
autonomy level appropriate. Concretely this appears as an explicit reasoned act, wait, or clarify step inserted before
behaving, as in proactive chain-of-thought prompting that plans the goal over a reasoning chain before responding
(Deng et al., 2023c,b), and as a critic that scores initiative itself in place of output content, the clearest instance being a
dedicated critic that grades how proactive a turn should have been (Wang et al., 2025l). Reflective clarification-need
prediction, deciding by introspection whether the agent is missing information it should ask for, is the same move
applied at the input boundary (Zhang et al., 2024h; Qian et al., 2024), and a metacognitive layer that predicts its own
impending failure and hands off to a human is its safety-side counterpart (Xu, 2025). In every case the object of critique
is the decision to act, which is what distinguishes proactive reflection from generic self-refinement (Lu et al., 2025a).
When a proactive prediction misses, whether a rejected suggestion or a failed preemptive action, reflection’s job is to
repair the model that produced it, in-context, so that the next anticipation within the session is better, closing a fast
loop back to Anticipation (§4.2) without waiting for offline retraining. For a user-facing agent this means updating an
inferred preference or theory-of-mind belief after a misfire (Gao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024a), and for an agent
acting on a system it is the well-developed pattern of scientific and driving agents that run hypothesis-revision and
belief-update loops, observing an experimental or environmental outcome, diagnosing the mismatch, and rewriting
the working model before the next decision (Wen et al., 2024; Boiko et al., 2023b; Lu et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025c).
Repairing the predictive model before it next fires is what makes this reflection prospective, since the critique migrates
from after-the-fact to before-the-fact and anticipates the agent’s own error, which is itself a proactive move (Wang
et al., 2026b; Han et al., 2025c; Yu et al., 2025). Two limits bound it, and both bite hardest in proactive settings.
First, ungrounded reflection can entrench errors in place of fixing them, since intrinsic self-correction without external
evidence sometimes degrades performance (Huang et al., 2024). Second, reflection costs latency and compute, which
collides with the timing constraints of §4.4.3, because overthinking displaces the very environmental interaction the
agent was supposed to act on (Cuadron et al., 2025); real-time agents accordingly split fast and slow reasoning or
precompute reflection ahead of need so that deliberation does not cost the moment to act (Zhang et al., 2025g; Liu et al.,
2026l; Lin et al., 2025). A proactive agent that reflects too long has, in effect, failed to act first.

4.6.3   Long-Term Calibration, Personalization, and Trust
As the user and environment change, the agent re-estimates across episodes the standing quantities on which the earlier
mechanisms depend. These include the anticipation models of §4.2, which capture user preferences and world dynamics,
and the confidence thresholds, interruption costs, and utility models of §4.4.2. What it re-fits is the agent’s standing
relationship with its user along three coupled axes: how far the user’s trust licenses it to act, how much autonomy its
track record has earned, and whose preferences it should personalize to. All three are fit from the accumulated feedback
of §4.6.1.
The binding constraint is appropriate reliance more than raw capability: over-trust breeds complacency as the user
stops checking (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), under-trust breeds disuse as the user disables the proactivity altogether
(Parasuraman & Riley, 1997), and the agent’s standing authority to act first is the slowly-moving budget between
them. The human-factors theory of reliance supplies the frame (Lee & See, 2004), and it carries across settings, from
an individual deciding how much to let an assistant preempt them (Tussyadiah & Wang, 2014) to an organization
deciding how much intervention authority an operations, driving, or clinical system has earned (Gombolay et al.,
2016). In a planning-task study, fully autonomous system behavior did not establish adequate trust, and the effects of
proactive dialogue on perceived competence and reliability depended on task difficulty (Kraus et al., 2020). A study
of human-robot collaboration found that greater attributed agency was associated with more negative attitudes when
perceived user control was low (Zafari & Koeszegi, 2020). Trust calibration can inform proactive interaction, and
socially-aware training that rewards trust alongside task success is one approach (Kraus et al., 2023).



                                                                                                                            33
                                             Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Autonomy should be graduated and evidence-indexed, adjusted as performance history accumulates: adaptive automation
shifts the level of agent authority based on that history (Kaber & Endsley, 2004), and deployment practice increasingly
treats authority as statistically earned, demonstrating reliability over a large operating record before authority is widened
(Kalra & Paddock, 2016). This is the dynamic counterpart to the static rungs of §4.5.1, first developed in safety-critical
operations, where those are the levels and this is movement along them over time, and a shared-workspace study shows a
situation-adapted agent outperforming any fixed autonomy level (Salikutluk et al., 2024). The proactive-specific anchor
is that an agent can choose its proactivity level as a function of predicted trust, escalating initiative only as far as the
evidence of earned reliance permits (Kraus et al., 2021), and systems now monitor for over- and under-reliance and emit
calibration cues to steer it back (Okamura & Yamada, 2020); a related discipline appears in self-verifying discovery
agents that gate each next step on reproducible intermediate results before proceeding (Ghafarollahi & Buehler, 2025).
Across episodes, an agent can use accumulated feedback to personalize its proactivity, updating the user model of §4.2.1
and the memory of §4.1.3. The progression runs from per-user interruption-cost models (Saponaro et al., 2017; Horvitz
et al., 2004), through fleet-scale notification bandits that learn when a recurring alert is welcome (Yancey & Settles,
2020), to AI assistants that write rated intervention outcomes into persistent memory and continually re-personalize
their initiative (Wang & Jiang, 2026). As preferences change, an intervention that was welcome last month may now
be annoying, so the agent needs to revise its model over time. Recent agent work makes the payoff concrete with per-
suggestion ratings across many personas that measurably improve satisfaction over time (Kim et al., 2026b; Xuan et al.,
2026) and multi-objective reinforcement learning that jointly optimizes productivity, proactivity, and personalization
(Sun et al., 2025b).
The deeper difficulty that spans all three axes is that the target moves under the agent’s own influence: people change
their behavior and even their language toward systems they interact with (Zhang & Yu, 2025), so the distribution
the agent calibrated against shifts as a result of the very interventions it made, the performative-prediction problem
(Perdomo et al., 2021). Calibration is thus a relationship maintained over time, and a moving one, sustained by mutual
and symbiotic adaptation in which the human and agent adjust to each other across the interaction (Nikolaidis et al.,
2017; Nwankwo et al., 2026). The harder questions this raises, the self-reinforcing feedback loops that drive a policy
toward degenerate attractors (Jiang et al., 2019) and the explicit repair a broken-trust relationship needs before it recovers
(Kox et al., 2021; de Visser et al., 2020), are governance concerns; here they mark the boundary where mechanism
hands off to oversight, including cooperative human-agent oversight games that keep control without modifying the
agent (Overman & Bayati, 2026).
Feedback on unnecessary or missed interventions helps calibrate Anticipation and Arbitration, while also informing
what the agent monitors, which goals it maintains, and how it executes them. Errors in predicting needs or setting
intervention thresholds can produce over-eager, harmful assistance (Lu et al., 2025a; Wang et al., 2026l). The right
mental model is therefore an adaptation loop whose objective is the agent’s own faithfulness, an operational honesty
about what it knows, how confident it is, and whether what it did was correct. These mechanisms observe trust and
reliance, but neither is the quantity to optimize, because both live in the user’s perception, which an agent can manipulate
by flattering (Sharma et al., 2025), by deferring until it never annoys, or by concealing the failures it should disclose, the
reward-hacking trap of optimizing a proxy (Skalse et al., 2025). Repeated honest interaction can help users calibrate
their reliance on an agent. Accurate reporting of uncertainty and failures becomes especially important when the volume
of autonomous behavior limits human review or when the agent’s capabilities exceed the user’s ability to assess its
outputs. Such feedback can guide revisions to the other five mechanisms as the user and environment change. With the
full mechanism assembled, §6 turns to how each deployment domain weights the six components differently.

Evaluating proactive assistance requires evidence about task utility, mechanism-level evaluation, and user experience
(Figure 13). These directions examine, respectively, whether proactive assistance improves the outcome of the task,
whether the mechanisms producing that assistance operate effectively, and whether the resulting behavior is acceptable
and beneficial from the user’s perspective. For example, a system may successfully complete a task while intervening
unnecessarily, relying on inaccurate assumptions about the user, or imposing interaction costs. An agent may also
correctly infer a user need or choose an appropriate moment to intervene without ultimately improving the task outcome.
Users may perceive technically effective assistance as intrusive, unpredictable, or difficult to comprehend when the
agent acts without an explicit request.

the performance of the complete system. Attributing these outcomes to particular mechanisms and assessing user

Errors in proactive assistance can arise at several stages of the decision process. Following the mechanism taxonomy in
§4, evaluation should assess how accurately the agent senses the environment (Wang et al., 2024i; Liu et al., 2024b;
Wu et al., 2025b; Uddin et al., 2026; Maharana et al., 2024); whether it understands the user’s preferences and latent
intent, and changes in the world state (Lieberman, 1995; Blaylock & Allen, 2005; Deng et al., 2022; Qian et al., 2025a;
Chen et al., 2026g; Grauman et al., 2022); whether it develops appropriate goals, subgoals, and executable plans (Deng
et al., 2023c; Kong et al., 2026; Nathani et al., 2026; Zhang et al., 2026b; Wu et al., 2025e); whether it correctly decides
when to act, ask for clarification, or remain silent (Zhang et al., 2024h; Lu et al., 2025a; Trinh et al., 2026; Wang
et al., 2026l; Pu et al., 2025b); whether the resulting intervention is relevant and correctly executed (Pu et al., 2025a;
Tang et al., 2026b; Kong et al., 2026); whether it occurs at an appropriate moment (Chen et al., 2025d; Samarinas
& Zamani, 2024; Ding et al., 2026b; Zhao et al., 2026b; Ran et al., 2026); and whether the agent can adapt across
users, preferences, tasks, and interactions (Kim et al., 2026b; Sun et al., 2025b; Hao et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026d). An
undesirable intervention may arise from an incorrect inference about the user’s need, an unnecessary decision, poor
timing, or failure to incorporate prior feedback. These failures may produce similar observed outcomes while reflecting
different weaknesses. Mechanism-level evaluation helps attribute success and failure to the decisions that produced
