                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


them (Table 2).
Assistance initiated without an explicit request can increase workload, feel intrusive, reduce user control, or encourage
inappropriate reliance. Evaluation should therefore assess whether assistance reduces mental effort, frustration, interpre-
tation time, and task-switching costs (Hart & Staveland, 1988; Tsang & Velazquez, 1996; Reid & Nygren, 1988; Lee
et al., 2025a; Pu et al., 2025a); whether the interaction is perceived as useful, usable, collaborative, and respectful of
privacy (Brooke, 1995; Laugwitz et al., 2008; Walker et al., 1997; Andolina et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2024e, 2023c; Ma
& Ziegler, 2024; Horvath & Greenberg, 1989); whether users can accept, modify, override, or reverse interventions
and retain an appropriate sense of agency (Walker & Whittaker, 1990; Parasuraman et al., 2000; Pu et al., 2025a; Villa
et al., 2025); and whether trust and reliance remain calibrated to the agent’s actual reliability (Jian et al., 2000; Lee &
See, 2004; Kraus et al., 2020; Schemmer et al., 2022; Desai et al., 2013). Workload, usability and experience, level of
control, and trust and reliance provide complementary measures of user experience (Table 2), consistent with recent
calls for more human-centered evaluation of proactive agents (Deng et al., 2024b; Kraus et al., 2025).
Existing evaluations often emphasize only one of these directions or blur their distinct roles: task success may overlook
flawed intervention processes, mechanism metrics may not establish user benefit, and human-subject studies may not
identify which system decisions actually shaped user perceptions. Evaluation is also uneven across settings, with more
standardized benchmarks for conversational agents than for embodied, mobile, visual, and cross-application systems.

5.1     Task Utility Metrics
Additional monitoring, reasoning, interaction, and delay can raise the cost of proactive assistance even when they
improve the final result. Task utility therefore includes task success and task efficiency. Success asks whether the agent
provides a final meaningful outcome; efficiency asks whether the gain was worth its cost.

5.1.1    Success Metrics
Proactive assistance can admit several valid responses when the trajectory or endpoint is incompletely specified. An
agent may provide information, ask a clarifying question, prepare an action, complete part of the task, or appropriately
remain silent. Evaluation should therefore judge whether the agent advanced the user’s goal. Reference trajectories or
answers can support this judgment when they capture the relevant goal. The goal itself may also be implicit, incomplete,
or evolving. A technically correct action may be irrelevant to what the user actually needs, while a partial intervention
may still be valuable if it prevents an error or saves later effort. Success may therefore depend on goal completion,
correctness, relevance, and risk reduction. For vague requests, even determining whether the agent succeeded may
require contextual or model-based judgment.
Whole-task evaluation has a long history in dialogue and mixed-initiative systems. Early work measures task success
through agreement between the agent’s inferred result and a ground truth scenario key (Walker et al., 1997), while
early mixed-initiative transportation assistants report the proportion of sessions that successfully complete the intended
task (Ferguson et al., 1996). Such reference-based evaluation works well when the goal is explicit and verifiable.
Coding assistants can use completed assignments or passed test cases as concrete outcome signals (Pu et al., 2025a;
Chen et al., 2025e), and agents acting in an environment with stable and valid feedback or reward signals should be
evaluated similarly Liu et al. (2026e,g); proactive search systems may examine whether suggested information influences
the subsequent conversation (Andolina et al., 2018); and task-oriented dialogue may combine goal completion with
domain-specific outcomes, such as the sale-to-list ratio in negotiation (Wu et al., 2025e). The appropriate definition of
success thus depends on what useful assistance looks like in the target setting.
A session-level score aggregates proactive decisions into one result. More granular outcomes can improve credit
assignment. For example, the Hint Justification Rate measures the proportion of provided hints, including on-demand
and proactive hints, that students correctly justify by deriving the hinted step (Maniktala et al., 2020). Intervention-level
scoring parallels the use of dense process signals in reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (Lightman et al.,
2023). Such measures record intervention-level uptake or local task progress. Establishing why an intervention was
effective requires examining whether the agent inferred the right need, chose the right moment, and delivered the right
content.




                                                                                                                          37
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


5.1.2   Efficiency Metrics
An agent may continuously monitor context, infer latent needs, request additional information, and sustain several
rounds of interaction before offering assistance. These steps may improve task success, but they also consume user
attention, time, and computational resources. Evaluation should assess task success together with the resources that the
agent and the user expend to achieve it.
Task-completion time depends partly on how quickly users interpret information, make decisions, and respond to
the agent. These human factors limit the system’s control over total task duration. The agent’s sensing, reasoning,
communication, and intervention policies affect both computational cost and the amount of work imposed on the
user. For example, an agent that reasons more frequently may identify better opportunities to help, but it may also
consume more tokens and increase latency; similarly, an agent that repeatedly asks clarifying questions may improve its
understanding of the user’s goal while increasing interaction burden. Task efficiency should therefore be treated as a
human-AI co-design objective: the system should determine when additional computation or interaction is worth its
cost.
First, agent-side efficiency concerns how much computation is required for the agent to continuously determine whether,
when, and how to intervene. Proactive agents may continuously sense the environment, update state and memory,
generate possible actions, and evaluate whether intervention is appropriate, even when they ultimately remain silent.
This makes the cost of deciding not to act an important part of efficiency. Proactive GUI agents, for example, can reduce
such overhead by reducing repeated processing of complete visual histories through bounded context and structured
state (Chai et al., 2026a). Lightweight triggering mechanisms can similarly avoid invoking a large model after every
observed user event (Liu et al., 2026o). Evidence from general GUI agents further suggests that additional reasoning
can increase token consumption and latency without reliably improving task success (Zhang et al., 2025e). Relevant
measures therefore include inference latency, token usage, memory and energy consumption, monetary cost, sensing
frequency, triggering frequency, and the computational cost of intervention decisions.
Second, these algorithmic choices also create user-facing efficiency costs that the agent must account for when deciding
whether an intervention is worthwhile. Proactivity can reduce downstream task effort, but it can also introduce
interruptions, clarification turns, verification, or correction work. For instance, the proactive AR assistant studied by
Lee et al. (2025a) sometimes requires longer interactions. In proactive programming support, Pu et al. (2025a) find no
significant difference in total task-completion time, suggesting that additional assistance does not necessarily translate
directly into faster completion. In those settings, task duration alone remains an incomplete measure: a longer interaction
may produce a better outcome, while a shorter one may simply reflect premature or ineffective assistance. The agent
should therefore reason about the expected benefit of an intervention relative to both its computational cost and the
human effort it induces. Useful measures include interaction turns, interruptions, correction and verification effort,
independent completion times for the agent and the user, and ultimately the amount of user effort saved for a given level
of task quality.
Efficiency ultimately concerns the balance between resources consumed and useful assistance delivered. Proactive
preparation may reduce the number of interaction turns and the effort needed to complete a task (Hu et al., 2026a),
but poorly timed assistance can introduce extra interruption, resumption, and verification costs for users even when
its content is correct (Mark et al., 2008; Iqbal & Bailey, 2010). These trade-offs constrain mobile, wearable, and
embodied agents, where always-on monitoring and idle-time computation (§4.1.4) compete for limited energy, device
resources, and access to personal context. Evaluation should therefore relate useful assistance to the time, attention, and
computation it consumes.

5.2     Mechanism-Level Metrics
The second level evaluates the internal mechanisms of a proactive agent to identify where its behavior succeeds or fails.
Mechanism-level metrics cover six categories: Context Modeling Efficacy; User State and World State Anticipation;
Planning Quality; Intervention Decision and Timing; Intervention Delivery and Presentation; and Adaptation and
Generalization. These categories align with the six mechanisms in §4: Awareness models the current user and
environment state; Anticipation predicts intentions, needs, and future states; Agenda selects and organizes goals;
Arbitration decides whether and when to intervene; Action delivers an understandable and controllable intervention;
and Adaptation improves these behaviors through experience. Although these categories are interdependent, they
provide a diagnostic structure for locating the mechanism most directly associated with a measured capability or failure.


                                                                                                                        38
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Downstream task success can leave the underlying mechanism unmeasured. Anticipation and Action studies often
evaluate the final intervention without separately assessing the prediction or delivery process that produced it.

5.2.1   Context Modeling Efficacy
Maintaining Awareness requires an accurate representation of the current situation drawn from an extended interaction
history. This requires the agent to retain relevant observations, integrate evidence distributed across time and modalities,
update information as circumstances change, and distinguish observed facts from uncertain inferences. Evaluation
should assess context quality together with the cost of maintaining it as the interaction history grows.
A first question is whether relevant evidence remains accessible as the interaction becomes longer and more complex.
Long context benchmarks provide controlled tests of this capability. MM-NIAH evaluates retrieval, counting, and
reasoning over textual and visual evidence distributed across long multimodal contexts (Wang et al., 2024i), while
MMNeedle tests target retrieval in large visual contexts, including cases where the requested evidence is absent (Wang
et al., 2025b). MileBench extends this setting to realistic interleaved image text inputs (Song et al., 2024a). In text only
settings, LongBench and RULER evaluate long document retrieval, multi-hop reasoning, and aggregation (Bai et al.,
2024; Hsieh et al., 2024), while Lost in the Middle shows that evidence accessibility can also depend on its position
within the context (Liu et al., 2024b). Together, these benchmarks motivate measures such as retrieval precision and
recall, multi evidence recall, distractor robustness, and performance across context lengths and evidence positions.
During sustained interaction, the contextual representation must remain correct as information changes. LoCoMo
evaluates recall, temporal reasoning, and summarization over extended conversations (Maharana et al., 2024), while
LongMemEval examines cross-session reasoning, knowledge updates, and abstention (Wu et al., 2025b). MemoryA-
gentBench further considers selective forgetting and test-time learning (Hu et al., 2026d), and multimodal settings are
studied in Mem-Gallery (Bei et al., 2026). Memora focuses specifically on evolving user information and introduces
Forgetting-Aware Memory Accuracy to penalize reliance on invalidated memories (Uddin et al., 2026). These settings
evaluate whether the context representation remains consistent with the user’s current state.
Maintaining such awareness also raises an efficiency question. Supplying the complete interaction history at every step
may preserve information, but becomes increasingly costly as the history grows. Context compression methods such
as Selective Context and LongLLMLingua retain more informative portions of the input while reducing the amount
of context processed by the model (Li et al., 2023c; Jiang et al., 2024a). Persistent memory approaches address the
same problem across interactions: MemGPT manages information across different memory tiers (Packer et al., 2023),
while PlugMem turns agent trajectories into structured graphs of reusable and generalizable facts and skills (Yang et al.,
2026c). Context modeling should therefore be evaluated jointly in terms of context quality and context cost (Yang
et al., 2026c). Relevant efficiency measures include retrieved or processed tokens, compression ratio, memory growth,
retrieval and update latency, and computational cost. More informative evaluations can report quality under a fixed
context budget, or the amount of computation required to reach a given level of retrieval or downstream accuracy.
These measures are most useful when applied to the contextual representation available before a proactive decision is
made. Quality can be characterized through retrieval precision and recall, multi-hop and temporal reasoning accuracy,
knowledge-update accuracy, stale-information retention, selective forgetting accuracy, and false-positive or abstention
rates when relevant evidence was never observed (Hsieh et al., 2024; Wu et al., 2025b; Uddin et al., 2026; Wang et al.,
2025b). LongMemEval-V2 provides a useful formulation in which a memory system processes historical trajectories and
returns compact evidence for downstream reasoning (Wu et al., 2026a). A proactive agent benchmark could similarly
measure pre-decision evidence coverage, or the proportion of decision-relevant facts represented when an opportunity to
assist arises, together with an oracle context gap comparing downstream performance using the agent’s context against
annotated gold context. Paired with context size or retrieval cost, these measures reveal whether a proactive failure
stems from missing, outdated, or inefficiently maintained awareness.

5.2.2   User State and World State Anticipation
An agent may need to infer task-relevant states that are not yet directly observable through its Anticipation mechanism.
User-state anticipation estimates the user’s latent goals, preferences, constraints, and emerging assistance needs from
partial interaction evidence. World-state anticipation forecasts how the surrounding task environment is likely to evolve.
User state anticipation ranges from recovering a user’s current latent state to identifying needs that become apparent only


                                                                                                                         39
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


over time. Dialogue state tracking provides the basic formulation. The Schema Guided Dialogue benchmark evaluates
active intent accuracy, requested slot F1, average goal accuracy, and joint goal accuracy (Rastogi et al., 2020). More
recent benchmarks extend this setting beyond explicitly stated goals. IN3 evaluates recovery of missing information
from underspecified instructions through Vagueness Judgment Accuracy, Missing Details Recover Rate, and Summary
Intention Coverage Rate (Qian et al., 2024); UserBench measures whether incrementally revealed preferences are
successfully elicited and reflected in the agent’s choices (Qian et al., 2025a); and LifeSim-Eval evaluates recognition
and fulfillment of explicit and implicit intentions, including intention completion over long horizon user trajectories
(Duan et al., 2026a). Across these settings, useful measures include intent or goal accuracy, slot and preference level
precision, recall, and F1, as well as macro-F1 when intent classes are imbalanced. When several interpretations remain
plausible, Recall@k, mean reciprocal rank, or other ranking metrics can evaluate whether the correct user state remains
among the agent’s plausible hypotheses.
Assistance before an explicit request requires recognizing the relevant user state in advance. ProactiveBench evaluates
whether an emerging situation warrants assistance using accepted versus rejected proactive offers and reports F1 for
assistance prediction (Lu et al., 2025a). ProAgentBench further separates when assistance is needed from what assistance
is anticipated, evaluating the former with accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 and the latter with intention category
accuracy and semantic similarity to the user’s subsequent request (Tang et al., 2026b). PIRA-Bench considers multiple
interleaved intents in noisy activity streams and measures intent precision, recall, and F1 together with false positives
during periods in which no actionable intent is present (Chai et al., 2026a). JIR-Arena evaluates real-time prediction
of users’ information needs for proactive information recommendation (Yang et al., 2025d). Beyond final prediction
accuracy, evaluation can therefore measure accuracy over observation prefixes, prediction lead time, time to stable intent
recognition, and false alarms before a genuine need emerges.
Because latent user states are often underdetermined, anticipation should also evaluate whether the agent represents
uncertainty appropriately. CLAMBER tests whether models recognize ambiguous information needs and generate
clarifications that resolve the missing information (Zhang et al., 2024g), while INTENT-SIM studies uncertainty-based
prediction of when clarification is useful and evaluates its effect on downstream performance (Zhang & Choi, 2025).
Appropriate metrics therefore include ambiguity-detection F1, entropy over candidate intents, calibration error or Brier
score, and the expected reduction in uncertainty or downstream error from additional information. To isolate errors in
user-state inference, a fixed downstream policy can also be evaluated using inferred versus annotated user states, with
the resulting oracle gap indicating how much performance is lost because of imperfect anticipation.
Changes in the external environment may create, remove, or alter opportunities for assistance. World-state anticipation
forecasts these changes. Action anticipation benchmarks provide established examples. EPIC-KITCHENS evaluates
upcoming verbs, nouns, and actions using top-k prediction and class-balanced recall measures (Damen et al., 2018),
while Ego4D evaluates both short-term object interactions and longer future action sequences using Top-5 mean average
precision for short-term object interactions and edit distance for long-term action sequences (Grauman et al., 2022).
In interactive agent environments, Web Agents with World Models predicts action-conditioned descriptions of how
the interface state will change following candidate actions (Chae et al., 2025). More generally, world model quality
can be evaluated through next-state or state-change accuracy, event precision and recall, time-to-event error, and
multi-step rollout fidelity. When multiple future trajectories are plausible, probabilistic measures such as negative
log-likelihood, Brier score, and calibration error can assess uncertainty across possible outcomes. As with user-state
inference, comparing a fixed policy under predicted and observed world states can help attribute downstream failures
specifically to forecasting errors.

5.2.3   Planning Quality
Choosing an appropriate objective and a coherent course of action from an anticipated user state or future situation is
the task of the Agenda mechanism. This involves deciding what should be pursued, decomposing the objective into
intermediate steps, respecting dependencies and constraints, and revising the plan when new information becomes
available. Evaluation should distinguish failures in agenda formation, where the agent selects an inappropriate objective,
from failures in plan construction, where the objective is appropriate but the resulting plan is invalid or ineffective.
An agent’s objectives should be relevant, necessary, and consistent with the user’s preferences. π Bench distinguishes
Proactivity, which measures whether hidden requirements are identified or resolved, from Completeness, which measures
how many task requirements are ultimately satisfied (Zhang et al., 2026b). UserBench evaluates whether decisions



                                                                                                                       40
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


reflect elicited user preferences through its normalized choice score, Best Exist Rate, Correct Exist Rate, and Preference
Elicited (Qian et al., 2025a). ProactiveMobile similarly reports Success Rate for translating an inferred need into an
appropriate function sequence, together with False Trigger Rate when no action is warranted (Kong et al., 2026). More
generally, agenda quality can be measured through objective selection accuracy, precision and recall over required
objectives, agreement with user-ranked goals, and regret relative to the highest utility feasible objective. These measures
help distinguish an agent that plans poorly from one that successfully pursues the wrong goal.
Once an appropriate objective has been selected, plan construction evaluates whether the agent can produce a valid
sequence or structure of actions that achieves it. PlanBench tests understanding of action preconditions, effects, and
goal reachability, supporting measures such as valid plan rate, goal achievement rate, and the number of violated
preconditions or inapplicable actions (Valmeekam et al., 2023). Natural Plan evaluates trip, meeting, and calendar
planning through solve rate under increasingly complex natural language constraints (Zheng et al., 2024a). WorFBench
focuses on task decomposition and evaluates sequential and graph structured plans through subsequence and subgraph
matching (Qiao et al., 2025). The Agent Planning Benchmark reports binary Plan Correctness and six-level Plan Grade,
while distinguishing failures caused by inappropriate tools, unavailable tools, and infeasible objectives (Sun et al.,
2026a). Across these settings, useful measures include goal reachability, plan validity, subgoal coverage, dependency
preservation, tool appropriateness, and recognition that no feasible plan exists.
Planning quality also depends on satisfying constraints while choosing well among multiple feasible solutions. Trav-
elPlanner separately evaluates delivery, commonsense constraints, hard constraints, and overall task completion (Xie
et al., 2024a), while COMPASS distinguishes feasibility from preference optimization and exposes cases in which a
plan satisfies mandatory requirements but poorly reflects the user’s priorities (Qin et al., 2025b). AgentBoard introduces
progress rate to measure how much of an objective has been completed even when the final goal is not reached (Ma
et al., 2024a). Evaluation can report feasibility, constraint satisfaction, preference utility, regret, and subgoal progress
separately, especially when multiple plans can satisfy the same objective.
Plan revision becomes important when new user information or environmental changes invalidate part of an existing
plan. Flex TravelPlanner evaluates planning as constraints are introduced sequentially and tests whether higher priority
requirements remain satisfied when conflicts arise (Oh et al., 2025). AdaPlanBench evaluates replanning under
progressively revealed user and environment constraints through final Accuracy, Valid Plan Rate, interaction turns, and
repeated violations of previously disclosed constraints (Liu et al., 2026i). TripTide evaluates adaptation to unexpected
disruptions through Preservation of Intent, Responsiveness, and semantic, spatial, and sequential Adaptability (Karmakar
et al., 2025). These settings motivate measures such as recovery success, constraint retention, preservation of unaffected
plan components, revision cost, and repeated constraint violations, capturing whether the agent can update an existing
plan coherently as conditions evolve.

5.2.4   Intervention Decision and Timing
Intervention Decision and Timing evaluates the Arbitration mechanism: whether an agent should intervene, when
intervention is appropriate, and whether the proposed action is justified within its granted permissions. Given an
anticipated user state and a proposed agenda, the agent may act directly, ask for clarification, request consent, defer
to the user, or remain silent. The central evaluation question is therefore not whether the intervention itself is well
expressed or correctly executed, but whether the agent chooses an appropriate intervention decision under the available
evidence, uncertainty, risk, and timing constraints.
A first dimension is whether intervention is warranted at all. Ask Before Plan evaluates whether an agent recognizes
that available information is insufficient before proceeding with planning (Zhang et al., 2024h). ProactiveBench tests
whether assistance is offered only in situations where intervention is appropriate (Lu et al., 2025a), while HiL Bench
reports Ask F1 to balance necessary clarification against unnecessary questioning (Trinh et al., 2026). KnowU Bench
distinguishes among acting, seeking consent, and remaining silent (Chen et al., 2026g), and ProactiveMobile allows
multiple decisions to be considered valid in the same context (Kong et al., 2026). These settings motivate intervention
precision, recall, and F1, false intervention rate, missed assistance rate, macro F1 for multiple decision types, and set
valued accuracy when several choices are acceptable. Clarification and consent decisions can further be evaluated
through unnecessary question rate, missed clarification rate, and consent seeking accuracy across actions with different
levels of consequence and reversibility.
A second dimension concerns how much authority the agent should assume. Mixed-initiative systems characterize this


                                                                                                                         41
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


choice as a balance between the expected value of autonomous action and the potential costs of error, disruption, or loss
of user control (Horvitz, 1999). Adjustable autonomy similarly studies when control should remain with the agent and
when it should be transferred to a human, including the coordination and delay costs associated with that transfer (Scerri
et al., 2002). Learning-to-defer formalizes a related problem by evaluating whether a system acts on cases it can handle
reliably while passing more difficult cases to an expert (Mozannar & Sontag, 2020). Calibrated variants additionally
examine whether estimated agent and human correctness probabilities correspond to observed outcomes (Verma &
Nalisnick, 2022). Relevant measures include autonomy coverage, deferral accuracy, selective risk, risk-coverage curves,
expected decision cost, calibration error, and Brier score. Together, these metrics evaluate whether the agent allocates
decision authority appropriately.
Intervention quality also depends on timing. In proactive settings, an intervention can remain useful within a range of
acceptable times. JIR-Arena evaluates precision and recall of predicted information needs and scores recommendation
timing through a soft comparison of predicted and annotated start and end times (Yang et al., 2025d). ProActor defines
broader readiness windows and penalizes interventions that occur either too early or too late (Ding et al., 2026b). ProCIS
incorporates timeliness through pDCG and npDCG, rewarding relevant information when it is provided at an earlier
useful point (Samarinas & Zamani, 2024), while ProactiveVideoQA integrates response quality over time through PAUC
(Wang et al., 2025k). OmniPro evaluates performance around annotated trigger moments and under autonomous online
triggering (Zhao et al., 2026b), and EgoPro Bench makes the appropriate intervention time dependent on the user’s
profile and inferred intentions (Ran et al., 2026). ProAgentBench further distinguishes intervention at an inappropriate
moment from anticipation of inappropriate assistance (Tang et al., 2026b). These settings motivate valid-window
accuracy, trigger precision and recall, premature intervention rate, delayed intervention rate, temporal distance from the
nearest acceptable boundary, and utility lost because of delay.
The usefulness of a trigger also depends on whether the user can accommodate the interruption. Interruptibility research
estimates the expected cost of interrupting a user (Horvitz & Apacible, 2003) and predicts whether the user is currently
available for interruption (Hudson et al., 2003). Interruption cost varies across points within the same task (Adamczyk &
Bailey, 2004). Interventions outside natural task boundaries can increase completion time, errors, and annoyance (Bailey
& Konstan, 2006). Delaying notifications until more suitable breakpoints can reduce disruption (Iqbal & Bailey, 2008).
Mobile studies further show that receptivity depends on personal and situational context (Pejovic & Musolesi, 2014),
and that willingness to engage with an intervention is distinct from merely tolerating its arrival (Pielot et al., 2017).
Useful measures therefore include expected interruption cost, resumption time, performance loss following interruption,
subjective disruption, receptivity prediction accuracy, and subsequent engagement.
Finally, aggregate success can conceal important arbitration failures. Toxic proactivity evaluations measure how often
agents violate safety constraints while pursuing task goals (Wang et al., 2026l). ProMemAssist relates the frequency of
proactive memory support to users’ responses to those interventions (Pu et al., 2025b), while proactive programming
studies distinguish productive engagement, passive ignoring, and active disruption (Pu et al., 2025a). These reactions
should be interpreted together with delivery quality, since rejection may result from either an inappropriate decision to
intervene or a poorly delivered intervention. Arbitration evaluation should therefore report unnecessary intervention,
missed assistance, excessive clarification, inappropriate autonomy, premature interruption, and delayed action separately.

5.2.5   Intervention Delivery and Presentation
Intervention Delivery and Presentation evaluates the Action mechanism: whether an approved intervention is commu-
nicated or executed in a form that is correct, understandable, controllable, and appropriate to its consequences. An
intervention may appear as a suggestion, hint, clarification, preview, explanation, editable contribution, confirmation
request, or direct action. Arbitration evaluates whether, when, and within what scope an intervention is warranted.
Action evaluation assesses the quality of its execution and presentation.
The first requirement is substantive correctness. For informational interventions, the delivered content should accurately
address the anticipated need; for operational interventions, the resulting action should produce the intended state change.
ProactiveVideoQA evaluates the correctness of information delivered while an event unfolds (Wang et al., 2025k), while
ProAgentBench separates the quality of proposed assistance from the decision to initiate that assistance (Tang et al.,
2026b). ProactiveMobile evaluates whether predicted device-function sequences are functionally equivalent to a valid
reference (Kong et al., 2026). Related agent benchmarks measure functional task correctness (Zhou et al., 2024b) and
progress toward the intended goal when full completion is not achieved (Ma et al., 2024a). Relevant measures include



                                                                                                                        42
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


content accuracy, semantic relevance, execution success, state change accuracy, subgoal completion, and implementation
fidelity between the approved plan and the action that is actually performed.
Correctness, however, does not determine whether the intervention is delivered with an appropriate degree of user
involvement. This constitutes a distinct evaluation target within Action: once an intervention has been selected, the agent
must still determine whether to present it as information, a suggestion, an editable preview, a confirmation request, or an
executed action. Mixed initiative interaction suggests that this choice should account for uncertainty about user intent
and the potential cost of an incorrect action, with dialogue used to resolve uncertainty when autonomous execution is not
justified (Horvitz, 1999). Research on levels of automation similarly treats automation reliability and the consequences
of erroneous decisions or actions as criteria for determining how much control should be delegated (Parasuraman
et al., 2000). Human AI interaction guidelines further emphasize efficient dismissal and correction, cautious behavior
under uncertainty, and mechanisms that preserve user control (Amershi et al., 2019). Accordingly, delivery mode
appropriateness can be assessed through human ratings, pairwise preferences, or agreement with expert authored policies.
User control can be evaluated through the availability of inspection, editing, rejection, pausing, cancellation, and reversal.
Correction effort provides a complementary measure by quantifying the time, number of interactions, or amount of
modification required to turn the proposed intervention into an acceptable outcome. These measures expose usability
costs that final task success alone may conceal.
A further dimension is whether the intervention makes the agent’s intention and actions understandable to the user.
Users should be able to determine what the agent is proposing, what it has already changed, and what is likely to
happen next. Objective measures can include comprehension accuracy, interpretation time, prediction of the agent’s next
action, and consistency between explanations and executed behavior. Behavioral traces provide additional evidence.
Proactive programming studies distinguish productive engagement, passive ignoring, and active disruption (Pu et al.,
2025a); interface studies record behaviors such as previewing, expansion, copying, acceptance, and rejection (Chen
et al., 2025e); and proactive visual analytics systems examine whether suggestions are executed or incorporated into
subsequent analysis (Zhao et al., 2025b). Acceptance should be interpreted alongside intervention correctness and user
outcomes. Explanations can increase reliance without improving human and agent performance (Bansal et al., 2021),
and evaluations should also measure learning and task benefit when users appear to use assistance (Aleven et al., 2006;
Baker et al., 2004). More informative evaluation can distinguish immediate acceptance, acceptance after modification,
rejection after inspection, later reversal, and successful correction.
Delivery quality must also be considered relative to the attention and coordination it demands. Reading time, interaction
steps, interface transitions, cognitive workload, and recovery time after an intervention can be evaluated together with
the benefit that the intervention provides. Human robot interaction offers related measures of coordination. Human robot
fluency has been evaluated through concurrent activity, human idle time, and functional delay (Hoffman & Breazeal,
2007), while motion legibility measures how readily and how early people can infer the robot’s intended goal (Dragan
et al., 2013). Gaze and conversational turn taking provide additional evidence about coordination and interpretation
(Baraglia et al., 2017; Peng et al., 2019), although these measures often require task specific behavioral coding (Fink
et al., 2014). Digital agents face an analogous requirement: users should be able to understand the direction of an
intervention, observe its effects, and retain the ability to modify or stop it.

5.2.6   Adaptation and Generalization
Agents can improve through experience, remain effective as operating conditions change, and transfer what they have
learned beyond the interactions from which that knowledge was acquired. An agent may need to adjust to changing
user preferences, new environmental dynamics, unfamiliar tasks, revised tool interfaces, or changes in the information
available to it. These experiences may affect any earlier mechanism, including what context is retained, how future
states are anticipated, which objectives are selected, when intervention is appropriate, and how actions are carried
out. Evaluation should therefore characterize the trajectory of improvement and recovery, including performance after
adaptation.
User adaptation concerns whether repeated interaction enables the agent to better serve a particular user. ProPerSim
evaluates whether an assistant can learn from repeated user feedback and improve the relevance and timing of personal-
ized recommendations over time (Kim et al., 2026b). Training Proactive and Personalized LLM Agents similarly studies
whether agents can adapt their interaction behavior to previously unseen user preferences (Sun et al., 2025b), while
PersonaLens evaluates preference alignment together with response quality and task success across diverse user profiles



                                                                                                                           43
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


and interaction histories (Zhao et al., 2025d). PAHF more directly evaluates continual personalization by measuring
Success Rate, Feedback Frequency, and Average Cumulative Personalization Error during both initial preference learning
and adaptation after preferences change (Liang et al., 2026). These settings suggest that personalization gain should be
reported together with learning speed, sample efficiency, cumulative error or regret, and the amount of feedback required
to achieve the improvement. This distinction is important because agents that eventually reach similar performance may
impose very different learning burdens on their users.
Adaptation over long interaction histories further requires determining which prior information remains valid as
circumstances change. Effective adaptation involves acquiring new information and updating, revising, or disregarding
information that has become obsolete. LongMemEval evaluates information extraction, reasoning across sessions,
temporal reasoning, knowledge updating, and abstention in sustained interactions (Wu et al., 2025b). PERMA examines
whether agents can reconstruct evolving preferences from temporally related events distributed across sessions and
domains (Liu et al., 2026m). Memora explicitly evaluates failures caused by continued reliance on obsolete or invalidated
memories and introduces a forgetting-aware measure that penalizes such behavior (Uddin et al., 2026). OP Bench
evaluates whether retained user information is used when relevant and whether personalization becomes irrelevant,
repetitive, or sycophantic (Hu et al., 2026e). VitaBench 2.0 further organizes interactions as temporal user trajectories
that require agents to continuously extract, use, and update preferences (Chen et al., 2026h). Relevant measures include
update accuracy, obsolete-information reuse, inappropriate personalization, performance immediately before and after a
change, recovery time, and the amount of interaction required to establish the new state.
Agents must also adapt when the environment changes independently of the user. Such changes may affect available
tools, interface structure, observation formats, state transition dynamics, resources, or the validity of previously learned
strategies. ProEvolve constructs controlled sequences of environment changes by modifying tools, schemas, and data
access, allowing agent performance to be evaluated as the surrounding system evolves (Li et al., 2026a). EvoArena
similarly represents environmental change as progressive updates across terminal, software, and social settings and
evaluates whether agents maintain useful knowledge across successive changes (Xu et al., 2026b). Test Time Adaptation
for LLM Agents examines performance before and after agents adapt to previously unseen environment formats
and dynamics using information gathered through deployment interaction (Chen et al., 2026a). Gaia2 introduces
environments that evolve asynchronously, including events that occur independently of the agent’s actions, and therefore
tests whether an agent can continue reasoning and acting as external conditions change (Froger et al., 2026). These
settings motivate measures such as the immediate performance drop after a change, adaptation gain, recovery time,
cumulative loss during recovery, interaction efficiency, retention of knowledge that remains valid, and performance
across consecutive environment changes.
Experience may also improve capabilities that can be reused across subsequent tasks. Evaluating such adaptation requires
testing whether gains obtained from earlier experience persist when the task, goal, or environment changes. AgentGym
evaluates agents across diverse tasks and environments and studies whether experience acquired through interaction
improves performance beyond the settings in which it was collected (Xi et al., 2024). Relevant measures include
improvement on later related tasks, transfer efficiency, retention of previously acquired capabilities, forgetting after
learning new tasks, and performance gained per unit of additional experience. These measures assess the accumulation
of reusable capabilities across tasks.
Evaluation can test whether knowledge acquired from previous experience remains useful when the agent encounters
users, tasks, applications, tools, or environments that were not directly represented during learning. RealPref evaluates
whether preferences inferred from long interaction histories can guide responses in unseen situations (Guo et al., 2026b).
ProCodeBench exposes a complementary gap between simulated and real developer behavior by comparing proactive
intent prediction under synthetic and real IDE traces (Li et al., 2026d). AndroidWorld varies tasks and operating
conditions within a dynamic mobile environment and shows that performance can change across task variations and
platforms (Rawles et al., 2024). AgentGym likewise provides evaluation across multiple environments and tasks (Xi
et al., 2024). Generalization can therefore be measured through performance on held-out users, tasks, tools, applications,
and environments, together with the source-to-target performance gap, worst-group performance, zero-shot transfer, and
the amount of additional interaction required when some adaptation is permitted.

5.3   User Experience Metrics
The third level evaluates how users experience proactive assistance. Evaluation should measure whether an intervention
increases cognitive burden, disrupts ongoing activity, reduces user control, or encourages inappropriate dependence


                                                                                                                         44
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


on the agent. In proactive systems, initiative originates partly or entirely from the agent without an explicit user
request. User experience evaluation therefore complements task and mechanism evaluation by measuring the human
consequences of agent initiative.
User experience can be assessed through four dimensions (Table 2): User Workload, Usability and Experience, Level of
Control, and Trust and Reliance. Workload concerns the effort demanded from the user, usability and experience concern
the perceived quality and fit of the interaction, control concerns the user’s effective authority over agent behavior, and
trust and reliance concern whether users depend on the agent to an appropriate degree.

5.3.1   User Workload
Proactive assistance can change the user’s cognitive, temporal, physical, and attentional burden. Initiating useful actions
before the user asks can reduce effort. Attracting attention, introducing additional decisions, requiring supervision, or
interrupting ongoing work can create new demands. Task-completion time, interaction steps, and workload should
therefore be measured separately.
Validated workload instruments provide broad measures of these costs. NASA TLX assesses Mental Demand, Physical
Demand, Temporal Demand, Performance, Effort, and Frustration (Hart & Staveland, 1988). The Workload Profile
provides a more diagnostic account of the cognitive resources required by a task (Tsang & Velazquez, 1996), while
the Subjective Workload Assessment Technique emphasizes time load, mental effort, and psychological stress (Reid &
Nygren, 1988). These measures can reveal cases in which proactive assistance removes direct interaction effort while
increasing monitoring, interpretation, or decision burden.
Behavioral measures provide complementary evidence about when and how such burden occurs. Interpretation time
following an intervention (Pu et al., 2025a), task-switching delay, additional errors, and recovery time can expose
disruption that may not be fully reflected in subjective ratings. Interruptions introduced outside suitable task boundaries
can increase completion time, errors, and annoyance (Bailey & Konstan, 2006), and interrupted work has also been
associated with greater stress, frustration, and perceived effort (Mark et al., 2008). Delaying information until detectable
breakpoints can reduce disruption (Iqbal & Bailey, 2008). Because the same behavioral delay may arise from workload,
unclear assistance, or low trust, workload is best evaluated through a combination of subjective ratings, behavioral
disruption, and recovery measures.
Workload evaluation should report effort saved together with demands introduced by an intervention. Relevant outcomes
include perceived mental and temporal demand, attention shifts, monitoring effort, decision burden, recovery time, and
additional actions required to manage the intervention. Apparent efficiency gains can coexist with greater cognitive or
supervisory burden in proactive systems.

5.3.2   Usability and Experience
Users judge proactive assistance by whether it is easy to understand and use, fits naturally within their activity,
and provides value without creating excessive friction or discomfort. Workload measures the effort required by an
interaction. Usability and experience measures capture how users judge its overall quality, usefulness, naturalness, and
appropriateness.
Standardized instruments provide general measures of interaction quality. The System Usability Scale provides a global
assessment of perceived usability (Brooke, 1995), while the User Experience Questionnaire captures broader pragmatic
and experiential qualities (Laugwitz et al., 2008). PARADISE relates task success and dialogue costs to user satisfaction
in interactive systems (Walker et al., 1997). Human-AI interaction guidelines introduce additional criteria that are
particularly relevant to proactive systems, including whether the system communicates its capabilities, allows users to
correct or dismiss its behavior, and adapts appropriately through repeated interaction (Amershi et al., 2019).
More specific measures are often needed because the desirable experience depends on the role and domain of the agent.
Proactive search and visual captioning systems evaluate user preference and satisfaction (Andolina et al., 2018; Liu
et al., 2023c), emotional support agents assess perceived support and interpersonal appropriateness (Liu et al., 2024e),
and proactive coding studies examine perceived collaboration and interference (Pu et al., 2025a). The Working Alliance
Inventory can characterize perceived collaboration and relational quality over longer interactions (Horvath & Greenberg,
1989). In embodied systems, the Godspeed scales assess anthropomorphism, animacy, likeability, perceived intelligence,



                                                                                                                         45
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


and safety (Bartneck et al., 2009). These measures illustrate that user experience is multidimensional and should be
aligned with the type of relationship the system is intended to support.
Proactivity also creates tradeoffs among usefulness, intrusiveness, and privacy. Greater robot initiative can increase
perceived usefulness while also making the system feel more intrusive (Villa et al., 2025), and proactive conversational
cues may be experienced as useful decision support and may also be experienced as unwanted interference (Ma &
Ziegler, 2024). Continuous sensing and contextual inference introduce an additional privacy dimension. Information
collection can be perceived as inappropriate when it violates contextual expectations even when the resulting intervention
is accurate or beneficial (Nissenbaum, 2004). These dimensions should therefore be reported separately.
Global usability scores can provide a common reference point. Domain-specific measures are often needed to explain
why an intervention is welcomed, ignored, or rejected.

5.3.3   Level of Control
Users should retain appropriate authority over the agent’s goals, decisions, and actions. Evaluation should assess
override availability and whether users can understand what the agent is doing, influence its behavior when necessary,
and stop, modify, or reverse its actions in practice.
Research on proactive interaction shows that perceived control can change as agent initiative increases. Proactive
programming studies measure perceived control and whether stronger initiative shifts the perceived role of the system
from a tool toward a collaborative partner (Pu et al., 2025a). Robot studies similarly examine preferred autonomy and
the appropriateness of different levels of independent action (Villa et al., 2025). Interaction coding can reveal how
initiative shifts between participants through behaviors such as repetition, summarization, interruption, or transfer of
responsibility (Walker & Whittaker, 1990). Levels of automation frameworks provide a broader account of how authority
can be distributed across information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and execution (Parasuraman et al., 2000).
A user may formally retain the right to reject an agent’s action while exercising little effective control if the agent
controls the relevant information, establishes influential defaults, acts before the user can respond, or makes reversal
costly. Economics distinguishes formal authority, meaning the recognized right to make a decision, from real authority,
meaning practical influence over what is actually decided (Aghion & Tirole, 1997). Control evaluation should therefore
examine the availability of corrective mechanisms and whether they can be understood and used effectively in realistic
interaction.
System behavior should remain responsive to relevant human reasons, and consequential outcomes should remain
traceable to responsible human actors, as proposed in work on meaningful human control (Santoni de Sio & van den
Hoven, 2018). Human-AI design guidelines similarly emphasize efficient correction, dismissal, and adaptation following
user feedback (Amershi et al., 2019). Even limited opportunities to modify an algorithmic recommendation can increase
satisfaction and willingness to continue using the system (Dietvorst et al., 2018). Relevant measures include perceived
agency, override frequency and success, modification success, reversal cost, use of autonomy settings, understanding of
control boundaries, and the gap between nominal authority and effective influence.
Evaluation should examine how control is exercised across the complete interaction. A proactive agent provides
meaningful control when users can anticipate its scope of action, intervene before undesirable consequences occur, and
efficiently correct its behavior when their goals or preferences are not being followed.

5.3.4   Trust and Reliance
Users’ dependence on the agent should match its actual capabilities and limitations. Evaluation should assess the
calibration of trust, acceptance, and usage to those capabilities. A well-calibrated user should rely on the agent when it
is likely to be correct and maintain sufficient skepticism when its recommendations or actions are uncertain.
Trust questionnaires include items on reliability, dependability, and confidence (Jian et al., 2000). Trust should also
remain sensitive to actual system capability, vary appropriately across reliable and unreliable conditions, and remain
specific to the task or component being evaluated (Lee & See, 2004). Broader models distinguish dispositional,
situational, and learned sources of trust (Hoff & Bashir, 2015). Appropriate reliance provides a more behavioral
perspective by asking whether users accept correct recommendations while rejecting incorrect ones (Schemmer et al.,



                                                                                                                       46
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


2022). Together, these approaches distinguish subjective confidence in the agent from whether that confidence produces
appropriate behavior.
Behavioral reliance should be interpreted relative to recommendation correctness. Accepting accurate recommendations
and rejecting incorrect ones can indicate appropriate reliance. Acceptance of incorrect recommendations can indicate
excessive reliance, and rejection of correct recommendations can indicate unnecessary distrust. Explanations can
increase acceptance without improving complementary performance between the user and the AI system (Bansal et al.,
2021). Cognitive forcing interfaces can reduce acceptance of incorrect AI advice. They may also increase user effort
and reduce subjective preference (Buçinca et al., 2021). Evaluation should consequently distinguish correct acceptance,
correct rejection, incorrect acceptance, unnecessary rejection, verification behavior, error detection, and the effort
required to maintain appropriate skepticism.
A study of knowledge workers found that greater confidence in generative AI was associated with lower self-reported
critical thinking. Greater confidence in one’s own expertise was associated with more critical engagement (Lee et al.,
2025c). The study characterizes critical thinking in AI-supported work through activities such as information verification,
response integration, and task stewardship. For proactive agents, this suggests evaluating whether users inspect evidence,
challenge questionable suggestions, consider alternatives, and retain sufficient understanding of the task to recognize
agent errors. These outcomes complement conventional trust measures by examining whether reliance preserves active
human judgment.
Trust develops through experience and may change as an agent succeeds, fails, becomes more autonomous, or adapts its
behavior. Introducing highly autonomous behavior before sufficient trust has developed can reduce user confidence
(Kraus et al., 2020). Measuring trust repeatedly throughout an interaction can reveal its formation, degradation, and
recovery over time. Trust trajectories and summary measures such as the area under the trust curve can therefore provide
a longitudinal account of how users respond to changes in system reliability (Desai et al., 2013). Evaluation should
assess whether trust and reliance remain aligned with what the agent can actually do under the conditions in which it is
being used.

6     Applications
This section surveys applications of proactive AI agents across 13 domains, from Coding and GUI Agents to Healthcare
and Agriculture. Figure 14 illustrates the broader transition these applications point toward: agents that can discover and
advance work under standing objectives, with people defining goals and reviewing outcomes. Each domain has its own
subsection, which summarizes representative systems in a per-vertical table, identifies the tasks on which proactiveness
is exercised, examines how the agent’s behavior is realized through Awareness, Anticipation, Agenda, Arbitration,
Action, and Adaptation, and closes with an Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions discussion. A concluding
Cross-Industry Trends subsection places the 13 domains on a shared Initiative-and-Authority maturity map (Table 16)
and reads three recurring patterns off it.

6.1    Coding Agents
Modern coding agents already exhibit substantial initiative (Wang et al., 2025h; Anthropic, n.d.b; OpenAI, 2025a;
GitHub, 2025; Lin, 2026a). They can complete repository-level tasks asynchronously, respond to workflow events,
and participate in validation and review with limited step-by-step supervision. Their autonomy is also becoming more
context-sensitive. Rather than following a single permission policy, deployed systems increasingly adjust how far they
proceed according to the expected consequence of an action and the safeguards available around it (Gomes & McPeak,
2026).
Their initiative nevertheless remains bounded in an important way: the work itself is usually selected elsewhere. An
assigned issue, workflow trigger, or project board determines what deserves attention, after which the agent plans
and executes within that scope. Studies of Claude Code usage suggest a similar division of labor, with users making
most planning decisions and the agent making most execution decisions (Hitzig et al., 2026). Reports on agent-first
engineering likewise retain human control over prioritization and acceptance, even when agents perform much of the
implementation and review (Lopopolo, 2026; Kotliarskyi et al., 2026).
Through the mechanism taxonomy of Section 4, current systems are already strong in Awareness and Action, and increas-
ingly capable of Arbitration. The larger gap lies in project-level Anticipation, Agenda, and Adaptation. Automatically
