repairing a triggered CI failure, for example, demonstrates autonomous execution. Recognizing that recurring failures
reveal a broader reliability problem, deciding that the problem deserves attention, and sustaining the resulting work
across later changes call for a stronger form of proactivity.
At the project level, a proactive coding agent operates under standing project objectives and bounded authority, identifies
work that has not yet been explicitly assigned, decides which work deserves attention, selects an appropriate form of
intervention, and maintains unfinished commitments as the project evolves. These standing objectives may be less
specific than an assigned issue. Specifically, a project may ask the agent to preserve reliability, reduce security risk, or
keep maintenance costs under control without specifying which component to inspect or what change to make. However,
such objectives express project priorities rather than a single execution path. The agent therefore needs to translate
them into concrete engineering work while accounting for the conventions and trade-offs of the project. The following
sections organize this progression around proactive work discovery, engineering agenda formation and prioritization,


                                                                                                                                                                                                       48
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


risk-aware intervention and coordination, and long-running project stewardship. Table 3 compares selected coding
systems across the six mechanisms, including the scope of their agendas and the controls on code changes.

6.1.1   Proactive Discovery of Unassigned Engineering Work
Task-scoped initiative can extend into project-level discovery when the agent identifies work beyond the current
assignment. Current agents already exhibit substantial task-scoped anticipation: given a high-level issue, they can
recover repository context, infer the affected scope, and determine how the requested outcome should be validated (Zhang
et al., 2023; Wu et al., 2024a; Yang et al., 2024a; Zhang et al., 2024j; Wang et al., 2025h). An interface change may
require updates to downstream call sites and regression tests even when neither is stated explicitly. Such work can span
much of a repository while remaining subordinate to an objective selected by someone else.
Moving beyond this boundary calls for project-level understanding: relating local evidence to the architecture, history,
and standing objectives of the repository, in the way experienced engineers recognize when repeated local fixes reveal
a deeper reliability problem or when a temporary workaround is becoming structural debt. Observational evidence
from Claude Code suggests that such high-level judgment remains strongly associated with human expertise, with users
making most planning decisions and domain experts providing more effective direction per interaction (Hitzig et al.,
2026). Industrial harnesses and academic work are beginning to externalize this expertise through repository-local
documentation, reusable skills, and distilled procedural knowledge (Lopopolo, 2026; Zhang et al., 2025b; Li et al.,
2026j; Ning et al., 2026d), though SWE-Skills-Bench shows that generic or mismatched skills often provide little benefit
and can interfere with the current project context (Han et al., 2026a). The research challenge is therefore to select and
ground the engineering experience relevant to a newly observed concern.
A discovery goes beyond the assigned task when the concern can be accepted, deferred, or rejected as an independent
project decision, separate from completing the current task. In comparison, work necessary to complete the current
objective remains within the assigned task, even when it was omitted from the original request. An architectural weakness
discovered during a bug fix meets this bar, since the project can choose separately whether to address it. TEBench
operationalizes this setting for testing, requiring agents to identify stale or missing tests even when no immediate failure
exposes the need (Shang et al., 2026). Code security offers a second setting where such discovery is already measurable:
Big Sleep, Revelio, and RFCAudit search a well-scoped coding domain for previously unstated concerns and ground
them through executable evidence or external specifications (Big Sleep team, 2024; Hou et al., 2026; Zheng et al.,
2025c). Both settings suggest that credible proactive discovery today rests on a well-defined domain scope and a strong
verification loop.
Recent products are beginning to extend discovery beyond repository-local signals. OpenAI describes Dots (Table 4) as
monitoring recurring customer feedback, scoping improvements and bug fixes, and preparing tested pull requests for
review (OpenAI, 2026c). This workflow illustrates a move from executing assigned issues toward identifying candidate
engineering work from ongoing product context. However, the product description alone does not establish how reliably
such candidates are selected or whether they deserve priority over competing project needs.
Proactive discovery can also be decoupled from execution. An agent whose task is to surface candidate work does not
need authority to act on it: its output can be a scoped, evidence-backed engineering claim that the project accepts, defers,
or rejects at a later stage. GitHub’s agentic autofix follows this pattern by validating a proposed repair in a sandbox
and returning it as a draft pull request for review (GitHub, 2026a). Structuring proactive discovery this way keeps each
candidate reviewable in isolation; whether it becomes a project commitment is the next question, handled by agenda
formation.

6.1.2   Engineering Agenda Formation and Prioritization
The proactive move at this stage is commitment formation. Execution-oriented systems such as the Codex app and
Symphony primarily organize work around externally supplied tasks (OpenAI, 2026a; Kotliarskyi et al., 2026). The
Codex app, for example, isolates concurrent agents through worktrees, while Symphony dispatches project-board items
into persistent agent workspaces. Both systems increase throughput, but neither removes the prior need to decide which
concerns deserve a place on the agenda.
A proactive agenda therefore involves three additional decisions beyond execution: which candidate to commit to, how it
depends on other work, and how to sequence it under standing project priorities. Some tasks can proceed independently,


                                                                                                                         49
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


whereas others rely on an interface change or a validation result that has not yet arrived. Prioritization must also account
for delayed feedback and limited execution, testing, and review capacity. A security hardening task, a maintainability
refactor, and a documentation improvement may all be useful, but the agenda must determine which best serves the
project’s current needs and which should wait.
Recent multi-agent coding systems make dependency-aware planning the central mechanism that lets a proactive
agenda run in parallel. CAID plans independent subtasks for asynchronous execution and integrates them through
branch-and-merge with executable verification (Geng & Neubig, 2026). Anthropic’s parallel compiler project similarly
coordinated sixteen agents across nearly two thousand sessions through explicit decomposition and tests (Carlini, 2026).
These systems do not yet decide which concerns should enter the agenda, but they show that useful parallelism depends
on isolating dependencies and validating integration rather than merely assigning more workers.
Proactive scheduling must handle bottlenecks beyond model inference: compilation, integration tests, merge resolution,
and human review can dominate the critical path. Cursor’s self-driving codebase experiment reports that static
dependency graphs became too rigid under these constraints, the system stalled on its slowest worker, and large-
scale compilation created shared-resource contention (Lin, 2026b). The agenda must therefore use waiting time
productively while avoiding downstream work whose assumptions are not yet stable. This makes scheduling a continual
resource-allocation problem rather than a one-time ordering of tasks.
A proactive planning policy can itself become a learned artifact when execution traces from prior project commitments
are treated as training signal, though distilled planning experience must remain revisable as project assumptions change.
Cursor reached its eventual orchestration design by analyzing execution logs, identifying recurring coordination failures,
and repeatedly revising the harness rather than trusting its initial organizational analogy (Lin, 2026b). Trajectory-based
methods such as CODESKILL offer a path for distilling successful decomposition and validation procedures into
reusable planning knowledge (Li et al., 2026j). Yet the limited and sometimes negative gains observed in SWE-Skills-
Bench caution against treating every historical strategy as a permanent rule (Han et al., 2026a). Planning experience is
therefore most useful when retained together with the assumptions under which it succeeded.
A proactive agenda is therefore a dependency-aware and resource-bounded plan whose structure changes as execution
produces new evidence. It records which candidate concerns have become project commitments, how those commitments
depend on one another, and how they compete for project resources. In doing so, it indicates what may proceed now,
what can run in parallel, what remains provisional, and which plausible improvements are better deferred. The result is a
revisable execution structure, not a growing backlog.

6.1.3   Risk-Aware Intervention and Coordination
Deployed coding products have moved from a single global autonomy setting toward action-specific authority, exposing
the authority decision as a first-class control surface for proactive intervention (Hughes, 2026; OpenAI, 2026b). This
separation is particularly important for unassigned work: choosing a task does not authorize every action needed to
implement it. Claude Code ranges from plan mode and manual permission prompts to sandboxed or unrestricted
execution, while its auto mode uses a classifier to distinguish routine project-local actions from actions that exceed the
user’s authorization. Codex similarly separates the sandbox, which defines the technical boundary of execution, from
the approval policy, which determines when an action stops for review.
For proactive interventions executed in the background, automated review can enforce the authority decision after
execution, but the runtime cost of this safeguard grows with the depth of testing and review it invokes (Gomes & McPeak,
2026). Sandboxed execution allows an agent to act provisionally while withholding acceptance until a proposed change
has been checked against authorization, safety, and quality criteria. The system may still execute the change, run tests,
and invoke several reviewers before determining that the intervention was unsuitable. A learned value model could
move part of this judgment earlier by estimating, from the proposed plan and repository context, whether an intervention
is likely to remain within project policy and user intent. Such a model would complement sandboxes, explicit rules, and
final review; its role would be to prevent some unsuitable plans from reaching the more expensive execution stage.
A second axis of the proactive intervention decision is request ambiguity: current agents systematically guess when
instructions are underspecified, so a proactive agent should weigh interruption cost against downstream error cost
before acting (Ji et al., 2026; Fang et al., 2026e). UnderSpecBench finds that underspecified DevOps instructions cause
coding agents to guess rather than consistently clarify or defer, with more than half of evaluated runs violating at least



                                                                                                                         50
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


one action boundary. ClarifyCodeBench likewise shows that strong code-generation ability does not imply strong
requirement-clarification ability. Reversible exploration may proceed under uncertainty, whereas a high-blast-radius
action with an unclear target may require a plan, clarification, or explicit approval.
When a proactive agent intervenes while other developers and agents are also acting on the codebase, session provenance
becomes the shared artifact that carries the intent behind each intervention alongside its final diff (GitHub, 2026b,d).
Current interfaces increasingly expose agent sessions in this way. GitHub’s Agents tab places session histories beside
issues and pull requests, while agent-authored commits can link permanently to the session log that produced them.
This provenance allows reviewers to recover the evidence and assumptions behind a change and gives another agent or
developer a basis for continuing work initiated elsewhere.
Because a proactive agent may intervene in parallel with other agents and developers, the coordination problem shifts
from message-passing to whether its actions remain attributable and recoverable; recent systems address this through
prompt-level rollback and workspace isolation (GitHub, n.d.b; Khatua et al., 2026; Geng & Neubig, 2026). GitHub
Copilot CLI records prompt-level workspace snapshots and can rewind both the conversation and modified files when an
intervention goes wrong. CooperBench finds that two coding agents perform substantially worse when coordination is
required, whereas CAID obtains better results by isolating workspaces and centralizing integration. The deeper problem
is whether concurrent actions remain compatible with shared state when their assumptions diverge.
Intervention and coordination can therefore be governed by the expected cost of correction: subject to authorization as a
hard boundary, a proactive agent may proceed as far as its understanding and rollback guarantees make economical, and
clarify or escalate beyond that point. This policy seeks calibrated and correctable intervention rather than the maximum
amount of autonomous action. Within its permissions, the agent may choose among exploration, proposal, execution,
clarification, escalation, and abstention according to its uncertainty, the action’s blast radius and reversibility, and the
likely cost of being wrong.

6.1.4   Long-Running Project Stewardship
Proactive coding extends into stewardship when the agent holds commitments that span sessions, releases, or handoffs
and must preserve the meaning of unfinished work across those gaps. A background agent may spend hours completing a
fixed issue while its goal and success condition remain externally supplied. Stewardship instead concerns commitments
such as a migration that pauses for an upstream dependency and resumes after the repository has changed. The challenge
is not merely to keep a process alive, but to preserve why the work remains worth pursuing.
For a proactive agent to carry a commitment across fresh sessions, project state must persist independently of any single
model context; current long-running harnesses achieve this by externalizing plans, decisions, and open commitments
into versioned repository artifacts (Lopopolo, 2026; Young, 2025; Rajasekaran, 2026; Ning et al., 2026c). OpenAI’s
harness-engineering workflow makes the repository itself the system of record, while Anthropic’s long-running harness
asks each fresh session to leave structured progress artifacts for its successor. A later planner–generator–evaluator design
applies the same principle to multi-hour application development. These systems provide useful building blocks for
continuity without assuming that one context can contain the project indefinitely.
Because a proactive commitment must also survive within-session context compression, the compression policy has
to retain the evidence and open questions needed for future decisions, whether through explicit guidance or a learned
policy (Rajasekaran et al., 2025; Gao et al., 2026f). Anthropic’s context-engineering guidance emphasizes retaining
high-signal architectural decisions and unresolved problems while discarding redundant interaction history. SWE-MeM
goes further by training coding agents to decide when, what, and how to compress their trajectories rather than relying
on a fixed summarization rule. The objective is not token reduction alone: a useful representation must preserve the
current commitment, the evidence behind it, rejected hypotheses, unresolved questions, and the conditions under which
future work may resume.
Handoff between agents is the concrete test of whether stewardship state supports the next proactive decision, and
Handoff Debt shows that successors resume work substantially more efficiently when they receive prospective contextual
notes than when they inherit repository state alone (KC & Budathoki, 2026). Code records what changed, but may
not reveal why a path was chosen, which hypotheses were rejected, or why the remaining work is blocked. State
management should therefore prepare the next agent to decide and act, rather than merely summarize what the previous
agent did.



                                                                                                                         51
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


A proactive commitment can be invalidated as the repository continues to evolve during its execution horizon. Long-
horizon benchmarks show that this failure mode already appears when the coding tasks themselves are externally
assigned (Thai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026c). SWE-EVO and SWE-CI expose errors that compound across release-
scale changes and long sequences of repository evolution, yet both still specify the work to be performed. Proactive
stewardship extends the problem by requiring the agent to resume, revise, reprioritize, or abandon commitments that it
selected for itself. It is, therefore, best understood as continuity of engineering intent under changing state, extending
beyond persistence of the original plan.

6.1.5   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Existing coding benchmarks measure the execution of assigned work at increasing scale and duration, but rarely require
the agent to decide what deserves attention on its own (Jimenez et al., 2024; Thai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026c; Shang
et al., 2026). SWE-bench measures issue resolution, while SWE-EVO and SWE-CI extend assigned-task execution
toward coordinated release changes and continued repository evolution. TEBench moves closer to proactive discovery
by including stale and missing tests that are not exposed through an immediate failure. These benchmarks broaden the
work agents perform, but they still usually specify what deserves attention.
Evaluating proactive discovery requires examining pre-implementation decisions, since outcome-only benchmarks
reward completion regardless of whether the action was warranted (Gloaguen et al., 2026). FixedBench shows that agents
often modify code even when the reported issue has already been resolved, exposing an action bias that task-completion
benchmarks do not penalize. Evaluation should therefore ask whether a concern is grounded, worth attention, and better
acted on than deferred or ignored. Passing tests can show that a patch works, but not that the patch was worth making.
Standing objectives such as improving maintainability or reducing security risk may admit several valid interventions
with different costs and priorities, making developer preferences over which concerns to pursue and which plans to
accept an important source of supervision.
A proactive intervention benchmark should measure whether the coding agent’s authority is calibrated to its uncertainty,
since ambiguous requests currently draw action from agents that should clarify or defer (Ji et al., 2026; Fang et al.,
2026e). UnderSpecBench and ClarifyCodeBench provide useful components by testing whether agents act, clarify, or
defer under ambiguity. Runtime review can catch unsafe or unauthorized actions after background execution, but may
require substantial testing and rubric-based checking. A learned value model could complement these safeguards by
identifying some unsuitable plans before execution, reducing unnecessary trials without replacing sandboxes, explicit
permissions, or final review.
Proactive coordination and stewardship require project-trajectory evaluation, since coding competence does not nec-
essarily translate into successful collaboration or efficient handoff (Khatua et al., 2026; KC & Budathoki, 2026).
CooperBench shows that coding competence does not automatically produce successful collaboration, while Handoff
Debt demonstrates that repository state alone may be insufficient for efficient takeover. Training this behavior also
introduces a data bottleneck. Issue histories, patches, CI logs, reviews, and agent traces record how assigned work was
completed, but rarely indicate which unassigned concerns were worth pursuing or how commitments should change as
the repository evolves. Synthetic trajectories may provide supervision at scale, but they would need to preserve realistic
repository changes, competing concerns, delayed feedback, and developer judgments rather than merely generating
longer coding traces.
An increasingly proactive coding agent is expected to work under standing project objectives in an evolving repository,
requiring it to discover, schedule, execute, and preserve work as the project changes, which requires the corresponding
evaluation protocols to provide useful system development signals. Rather than presenting one preselected issue, the
environment would require the agent to decide what merits investigation, which concerns should become commitments,
how those commitments should be scheduled, how far the agent should intervene, and whether unfinished work should
continue as conditions change. Executable tests could assess whether an intervention works, while developer preferences
could assess whether it was worth making. The central question would then shift from how many assigned tasks the
agent completes to whether it discovers, schedules, executes, and preserves useful work as the project evolves.

GUI agents translate user goals into sequences of reasoning, planning, and execution steps within digital environments
by operating graphical interfaces (Nguyen et al., 2024), increasingly in combination with complementary programmatic
interfaces such as command-line tools and code execution (Li et al., 2026i; Zhou et al., 2026b). Their ability to
continuously observe and act within users’ digital environments creates opportunities for proactiveness beyond simply
following fully specified instructions. We distinguish two forms of such behavior. First, an agent may take initiative
within an explicitly stated but underspecified goal: for example, identifying intermediate objectives, acquiring missing
information, exploring an unfamiliar interface, coordinating multiple applications or tools, or revising its plan after
execution failures. Second, an agent may take initiative beyond the explicit instruction by inferring latent user needs
from ongoing activities and context. For example, it may recognize from an incoming dinner invitation that the user
may also need a calendar event, transportation arrangements, or a reminder. Existing work on proactive GUI agents has
predominantly studied the former setting, particularly in long-horizon tasks where users provide a high-level objective
but leave substantial execution details unspecified (Agashe et al., 2025; Tang et al., 2026b; Chai et al., 2026a). The latter


                                                                                                                                                                 53
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


form, in which agents anticipate useful actions before they are explicitly requested, remains less extensively explored
in current GUI benchmarks, but is central to the longer-term vision of personal agents that continuously reason over
users’ activities, environments, and evolving needs. These two forms of initiative shift part of the burden of intermediate
decision-making from the user to the agent, reducing the need for continuous specification and supervision.
How such proactiveness can be acquired and exercised, however, depends strongly on the computational platform in
which the agent operates. Desktop environments provide comparatively mature and tool-rich software ecosystems,
making autonomous execution across applications and interaction modalities increasingly feasible (Xie et al., 2024b;
Agashe et al., 2025; Li et al., 2026i). Agents can combine graphical actions such as mouse clicks and keyboard
input with command-line interfaces, code execution, and other structured tools, enabling flexible coordination over
long-horizon workflows (Li et al., 2026i; Zhou et al., 2026b). Web environments are more open and dynamic: although
agents can exploit structured representations such as HTML, accessibility trees, and the DOM, they must operate
across heterogeneous websites, adapt to changing page states, and often discover relevant information, interaction
paths, or site-specific procedures before determining how to proceed (Zhou et al., 2024b; Koh et al., 2024). Mobile
environments, in contrast, expose especially rich personal and contextual signals that can support anticipation of latent
needs (Kong et al., 2026; Chai et al., 2026a), while imposing tighter constraints on screen space, computation, latency,
and execution robustness (Rawles et al., 2024; Chai et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026c). Recent work therefore explores
lightweight or on-device agents, reusable application knowledge, and efficient interaction strategies to make proactive
behavior practical under these constraints (Chai et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2025i). Accordingly,
we organize proactive GUI agents by deployment platform, focusing on the platform-specific challenges involved in
acquiring proactiveness and the mechanisms proposed to address them. Table 4 compares selected research systems and
commercial products across these platforms and the six mechanisms.

6.2.1   Desktop GUI Agents
Desktop environments provide a representative setting for GUI-based proactive agents, where agents perform long-
horizon computer tasks such as processing emails, editing documents and spreadsheets, managing files, and using
development tools as part of routine workflows (Xie et al., 2024b; Bonatti et al., 2024). Although users may specify only
the overall goal, these environments are relatively stable and the intended outcome is often clear. Proactiveness therefore
centers on interpreting underspecified instructions, inferring intermediate objectives, and coordinating the required
applications and tools to complete the task. In this setting, initiative primarily lies in filling in the missing steps between
a user’s high-level goal and successful execution. Existing benchmarks capture different aspects of this challenge.
OdysseyBench evaluates cross-application dependencies spanning Word, Excel, PDF, Email, and Calendar (Wang
et al., 2025g), while OfficeBench studies coordinated operations across productivity applications (Wang et al., 2024m).
OS-Marathon further emphasizes extremely long and repetitive workflows, such as processing receipts or entering
grades (Wu et al., 2026b), and OSWorld 2.0 extends desktop evaluation to realistic workflows involving hundreds of
interactions, dynamically arriving information, and persistent constraints (Yuan et al., 2026b). Professional domains can
extend these horizons even further: CADWorld, for example, requires agents to preserve geometric and engineering
constraints while manipulating persistent CAD artifacts over long execution trajectories (Dong et al., 2026b). Together,
these desktop-specific challenges suggest that proactive desktop agents are primarily about maintaining ownership of an
extended workflow: determining intermediate objectives, carrying information across applications, and completing the
work without repeatedly returning task decomposition to the user. OpenAI’s dots illustrate this direction in industrial
systems by maintaining ongoing projects, responding to new information, and preparing work such as tested fixes and
pull requests for review (OpenAI, 2026c). Their background “proactive research” uses read-only tools, distinguishing
the discovery of useful work from its subsequent execution under the applicable permissions.
The first capability required for maintaining such workflow ownership is proactive planning: agents must identify
what may be missing from underspecified user instructions and construct or revise a plan from limited input. Agent-S
combines hierarchical planning with external knowledge and past experience (Agashe et al., 2024), while Agent S2
continuously revises plans across multiple temporal scales (Agashe et al., 2025). DeskCraft further allows agents
to clarify requirements and adapt ongoing professional work in response to interruptions or user feedback (Wang
et al., 2026j). LEGOMem stores procedural experience at both the orchestrator and execution levels to improve task
decomposition and delegation across office workflows (Han et al., 2025a). UI-Copilot instead reduces the burden of
long-horizon reasoning by separating persistent memory from transient execution context and invoking retrieval or
computation tools only when needed (Lu et al., 2026b). OSWorld-Human highlights why such efficiency matters: much



                                                                                                                            54
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


of the latency in current computer-use agents arises from repeated planning and reflection, while leading agents still
require substantially more steps than human trajectories (Abhyankar et al., 2025). Thus, while stronger planning is
central to proactive desktop agents, sustained workflow ownership also requires recognizing and avoiding repeated
low-level reasoning that makes long-horizon execution inefficient and difficult to scale.
Beyond proactively deciding what steps are needed, desktop agents must also decide how those steps should be
executed. Many operations that require long and fragile graphical interaction can instead be completed through
terminals, code, APIs, or structured tools, shifting desktop interaction from pure GUI control toward hybrid GUI–CLI
execution. Proactiveness in this setting therefore includes recognizing when direct manipulation is unnecessarily costly
and switching to a more suitable execution mechanism. UFO2 and ComputerRL combine visual interaction with
native APIs or programmatic functions (Zhang et al., 2025c; Lai et al., 2025), while MCPWorld and OSWorld-MCP
study hybrid GUI–tool execution and show both its potential and the difficulty of consistently invoking the right
tools (Yan et al., 2025b; Jia et al., 2025). WeaveBench and CUA-Universe extend this paradigm to long-horizon
trajectories that interleave GUI actions, command-line operations, and code execution (Li et al., 2026i; Shi et al., 2026a),
while CLI-Anything exposes applications through machine-oriented command interfaces that can bypass repetitive
graphical actions altogether (Yang et al., 2026g). Controlled GUI–CLI comparisons further suggest complementary
bottlenecks: GUI agents struggle with grounded long-horizon interaction, whereas CLI agents are constrained more by
skill coverage (Zhou et al., 2026b). Recent work on hybrid GUI–MCP agents and EE-MCP therefore treats execution
modality itself as a learned decision, requiring agents to determine when tools should be invoked and how their outputs
should be integrated with the current visual state (Fan et al., 2026a; He et al., 2026b). Taken together, these works
suggest that desktop proactivity should extend from planning the workflow to selecting the most effective way to carry
out each step: generating code to replace repetitive mouse actions, invoking an API when an operation is well specified,
or returning to GUI interaction when spatial or transient interface state makes visual control necessary.
Such proactive execution, however, still assumes that the agent already possesses an appropriate procedure or skill.
In open-ended desktop environments, this cannot be guaranteed, making proactive adaptation a further requirement:
agents must recognize when their current repertoire is insufficient and respond by retrieving, adapting, or acquiring new
procedural knowledge rather than immediately returning the capability gap to the user. CUA-Skill and VISUALSKILL
represent reusable procedures as structured execution graphs or multimodal skills that can be retrieved and verified during
new tasks (Chen et al., 2026f; Jiang et al., 2026), while OS-Copilot and HyMEM accumulate experience from previous
trajectories and reuse it for later decomposition and adaptation (Wu et al., 2024d; Zhu et al., 2026c). When stored
knowledge is insufficient, GUI-Bee explores unfamiliar interfaces to acquire grounding knowledge (Fan et al., 2025),
OSExpert investigates software functionality and converts verified discoveries into reusable skills (Liu et al., 2026h),
and SEAgent improves through iterative interaction and automatically generated curricula in unseen software (Sun et al.,
2026b). EvoCUA-1.5 pushes this further through online interaction with executable desktop sandboxes (Huang et al.,
2026b), while EE-MCP accumulates application-specific experience to improve future GUI–tool decisions (He et al.,
2026b). These approaches point toward a broader hierarchy of desktop proactiveness: agents should first plan how to
advance the workflow, then select the most effective execution modality, and finally adapt or learn new procedures when
their existing capabilities are insufficient. Proactiveness at this level therefore means progressively reducing the number
of decisions that must be returned to the user, from task decomposition to execution strategy to capability acquisition.

6.2.2   Web GUI Agents
Web proactiveness centers on continually assessing whether changing interface states still support the user’s objective
and taking the initiative to adjust the workflow when its assumptions become unreliable. Websites differ in layout,
navigation structure, terminology, and functionality, while execution states can change as content is updated, actions fail,
or unexpected conditions arise. These conditions require agents to interpret emerging mismatches and determine an
appropriate response before further actions compound the problem. Mind2Web evaluates cross-task, cross-website, and
cross-domain generalization (Deng et al., 2023a), while WebArena spans heterogeneous interactive websites including
shopping, forums, content management, maps, and collaborative development (Zhou et al., 2024b). VisualWebArena
further shows that some tasks depend on visual information unavailable from textual structure alone (Koh et al., 2024).
HTML, DOM trees, accessibility information, and page text provide useful structure, but real-world HTML can itself be
large and noisy (Deng et al., 2023a), and AgentOccam demonstrates the importance of carefully designed observation
and action representations (Yang et al., 2025c). These challenges make situational judgment central to Web proactivity:
an agent must determine when to continue, recover, replan, explore, or seek clarification, without requiring the user to



                                                                                                                         55
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


diagnose every unexpected state.
The first capability required for such situational judgment is proactive monitoring: agents must detect emerging
deviations from expected execution and determine whether recovery is needed before those deviations undermine
the task. Existing interaction-based learning methods provide part of the foundation for such behavior. Early work
used workflow-guided exploration to cope with sparse Web rewards (Liu et al., 2018), while WebRL learns through
online reinforcement learning and a self-evolving curriculum partly generated from failed attempts (Qi et al., 2025).
WebAgent-R1 similarly optimizes complete multi-turn browser trajectories from task-level outcomes (Wei et al., 2025b),
with WebServ and WebGym providing infrastructure and realistic environments for scaling browser interaction and
training (Lu et al., 2025b; Bai et al., 2026). These approaches help agents learn from failed trajectories and improve
subsequent decisions, but outcome rewards typically reveal that something has already gone wrong rather than explicitly
teaching the agent to anticipate when a plan is becoming unreliable. The stronger proactive capability is to detect early
signals of mismatch, such as an unexpected page state or altered workflow, interpret their implications for the current
objective, and intervene before the deviation propagates.
Beyond detecting deviations, proactive Web agents must recognize when missing environmental knowledge prevents
reliable progress and initiate targeted exploration to resolve that uncertainty. An unfamiliar page or unexpected transition
may require the agent to investigate available functions, relationships between interface states, or alternative navigation
paths before continuing. WebPilot searches alternative routes when the correct path is uncertain (Zhang et al., 2024i),
while Go-Browse more systematically explores Web environments to construct useful trajectories (Gandhi & Neubig,
2025). SAGE makes this process increasingly autonomous by first acquiring structural knowledge of a website and
then generating progressively more difficult tasks for continued practice (Yang et al., 2025e). The important proactive
decision is to determine when exploration is warranted. An effective Web agent should continue with the current
workflow when observations remain consistent with the plan, perform local recovery or replanning when a specific
step fails, explore more broadly when missing environmental knowledge prevents reliable progress, and seek user
clarification when the remaining uncertainty cannot be resolved safely or depends on preferences or decisions that
should not be inferred autonomously. Proactivity therefore lies in diagnosing the source of uncertainty and selecting the
appropriate response.
Sustained Web proactiveness also requires retaining useful discoveries and recognizing when prior procedures can be
reused or adapted to guide the response to a new situation. Agent Workflow Memory extracts recurring procedures from
prior trajectories and retrieves them for later Web tasks (Wang et al., 2025o), while SkillWeaver explores new websites,
discovers useful operations, and distills successful behavior into reusable APIs (Zheng et al., 2025a). SAGE similarly
connects autonomous exploration with skill acquisition (Yang et al., 2025e), and WebRL generates new tasks around the
evolving boundaries of the agent’s capabilities (Qi et al., 2025). An industrial counterpart appears in Edge’s Copilot
Mode: Journeys groups related browsing activity to help users resume earlier tasks (Microsoft, 2025a). This illustrates
contextual continuity across sessions, complementing research on retaining and reusing procedural knowledge.
These capabilities support proactive response selection: the agent must determine whether the current situation warrants
continuing with a known procedure, adapting it, investigating further, or involving the user. Acquired skills and memory
provide a basis for this judgment by helping the agent recognize both familiar situations and the limits of its existing
repertoire. When unexpected states involve ambiguous preferences, consequential choices, authorization boundaries, or
risks that the agent cannot reliably evaluate, the proactive response should be to seek clarification before proceeding.
Web proactiveness can therefore be understood as an adaptive decision hierarchy: maintain the current workflow while
its assumptions remain valid; detect and interpret deviations when they arise; recover or replan when the problem
is understood; explore when missing environmental knowledge prevents reliable action; reuse or acquire procedural
knowledge when appropriate; and involve the user when the uncertainty cannot or should not be resolved autonomously.

6.2.3   Mobile GUI Agents
Mobile proactiveness centers on anticipating latent information and assistance needs from the rich personal context
available on devices closely embedded in users’ everyday lives. With appropriate access, agents can connect calendar
events, emails, alarms, travel bookings, notifications, and application activity to anticipate what information or assistance
would help the user next (Kong et al., 2026; Chai et al., 2026a). Initiative therefore begins with identifying a useful
assistance objective: interpreting how an emerging event relates to the user’s plans, recognizing a possible need, and
deciding whether it warrants attention. Meta’s Muse illustrates this broader direction by using persistent context about



                                                                                                                          56
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


users’ goals and connected services to offer proactive suggestions; it is accessed through its app or WhatsApp and
executes tasks through a dedicated cloud virtual machine (Meta, 2026). Such systems highlight how personal context
can support assistance beyond the immediate interaction. Mobile proactiveness consequently spans three connected
decisions: what the user may need, whether and when assistance is warranted, and how to deliver it effectively.
Proactive need inference is the first ability required for such anticipation: agents must connect fragmented and evolving
contextual signals to identify a useful assistance objective before the user fully articulates it. ProactiveMobile evaluates
latent-intent inference from on-device context and its translation into executable API sequences (Kong et al., 2026), while
Act2Intention connects intention understanding, personalized prediction, and execution through continuous intention–
action trajectories (Yan et al., 2026b). These approaches suggest that anticipating useful assistance requires connecting
current observations with prior activity and user preferences. For example, a flight cancellation may imply a need to find
alternative transportation, check an affected booking, or reconsider an upcoming appointment. AppAgent-Pro addresses
a related form of initiative by extending broad user requests into additional cross-application information seeking when
further work is judged useful (Zhao et al., 2025c). Commercial features illustrate complementary forms of contextual
assistance: Google Magic Cue retrieves relevant information across personal applications, such as surfacing flight details
during an airline call, while Samsung Now Nudge uses screen content and stored context to suggest actions such as
adding an event or sharing relevant photos (Kugler, 2025; Samsung, 2026). HONOR’s YOYO combines automatic
schedule extraction with tasks that execute when user-specified contextual conditions occur (HONOR, 2026). These
examples distinguish anticipating an immediate information need from carrying out a previously expressed conditional
intention. In general, they show how mobile initiative can emerge from an unexpressed need, an incomplete request, or a
remembered instruction whose triggering context has arrived.
Beyond inferring a possible need, proactive mobile agents must assess its relevance and timing to decide whether,
when, and how to intervene. Mobile activity includes incidental browsing, repeated notifications, task switching, and
intentions that may already have been fulfilled, making continuous observation insufficient grounds for intervention.
PIRA-Bench evaluates proactive intent recommendation from noisy visual trajectories with interleaved intentions
and user-profile context, while its PIRF baseline uses memory and state tracking to interpret ongoing activity (Chai
et al., 2026a). PRPF explicitly separates intervention gating from assistance generation, using a lightweight perception
stage to activate more expensive reasoning only when warranted (Ding et al., 2026c). Qwen-UI-Agent extends this
direction through a lightweight harness supporting proactive service initiation and stateful workflows across mobile
and computer environments (Zhou et al., 2026a), connecting the decision to offer assistance with the agent’s execution
capabilities. The proactive decision is therefore whether to remain silent, retain a possible need for later reassessment,
offer timely information, or propose an executable action. When the appropriate response depends on uncertain
preferences or consequential commitments, focused clarification can establish the user’s intended outcome. Effective
mobile proactiveness requires both sensitivity to emerging needs and restraint when the evidence or timing is insufficient.
Turning anticipated needs into useful assistance requires proactive capability development: agents must acquire and
adapt the interaction policies needed to fulfill emerging objectives across changing applications. Mobile tasks often cross
applications and depend on transient interface states, motivating executable environments such as AndroidWorld (Rawles
et al., 2024). Online reinforcement learning strengthens this execution foundation: MobileGUI-RL combines self-
exploration with trajectory-aware optimization of completion and efficiency, while MobileRL uses difficulty-adaptive
replay, curriculum filtering, and trajectory-length-aware rewards (Shi et al., 2025c; Xu et al., 2025e). AgentCPM-GUI
combines supervised trajectory learning with reinforcement fine-tuning, Mobile-Agent-v3.5 extends training across
environments and model scales, and WM-R1 uses learned world models to reduce reliance on costly real-device
rollouts (Zhang et al., 2025i; Xu et al., 2026a; Han & Qian, 2026). These methods develop the ability to execute
assistance after a useful objective has been identified. Exploration and self-evolution further help agents maintain
that ability as applications change: UI-Voyager improves supervision from successful and failed trajectories, while
MobileGUI-RL generates learnable tasks through autonomous exploration (Lin et al., 2026b; Shi et al., 2025c). From a
proactive perspective, their value lies in building the execution capabilities needed to fulfill anticipated needs.
Sustained mobile proactiveness further requires recognizing recurring assistance needs and reusing accumulated
knowledge and procedures to address them efficiently under device constraints. UI-KOBE explores applications in
advance and represents their states and transitions as reusable knowledge graphs, while SkillDroid compiles successful
trajectories into parameterized skills that can be replayed without repeated language-model calls (Chai et al., 2026b;
Chen et al., 2026d). Such reuse supports timely assistance under mobile constraints on model size, memory, latency,
energy, connectivity, and privacy (Chai et al., 2026b; Huang et al., 2026c; Zhang et al., 2025i). AgentCPM-GUI reduces


                                                                                                                         57
                                                            Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


generation overhead through a compact action representation; MobileExplorer overlaps lightweight exploration with
model inference and stores traces as structured memory; and Mobile-Agent-v3.5 explores multiple model sizes and
cloud–edge collaboration (Zhang et al., 2025i; Huang et al., 2026c; Xu et al., 2026a). Combined with PRPF’s selective
activation of deeper reasoning (Ding et al., 2026c), these approaches suggest an architecture in which relevant context
is maintained efficiently, stronger reasoning is invoked when a meaningful need emerges, and familiar procedures are
reused during execution. Mobile proactiveness thus connects contextual anticipation with selective intervention and
adaptive execution, reducing the user’s effort in recognizing, formulating, and initiating useful assistance.

6.2.4      Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Evaluation of proactive GUI agents should assess whether agents exercise appropriate initiative throughout the assistance
process, while reflecting the distinctive demands of each platform. For desktop agents, this means evaluating whether
they infer missing intermediate objectives, coordinate long-horizon workflows, select suitable execution mechanisms,
and address capability gaps without unnecessary user supervision. For Web agents, evaluation should examine whether
they detect deviations, distinguish execution failures from missing knowledge, and appropriately choose among recovery,
replanning, exploration, procedural reuse, and clarification. For mobile agents, it should assess whether contextual signals
support the inferred information or assistance need, whether intervention is timely and useful, and whether the resulting
assistance fulfills that need. Existing benchmarks capture complementary parts of this process: ProAgentBench and
PIRA-Bench assess the appropriateness and timing of assistance (Tang et al., 2026b; Chai et al., 2026a), Act2Intention
links intention prediction to subsequent GUI execution (Yan et al., 2026b), OpenComputer emphasizes verification of the
resulting application state (Wei et al., 2026a), and OSWorld-Human highlights interaction length and latency (Abhyankar
et al., 2025). A complete evaluation should therefore connect the quality of the proactive decision to its execution
outcome, accounting for unnecessary actions, computation, supervision, and interruption alongside task success.
These distinctions motivate platform-specific open directions within a shared challenge of deciding when and how to
take initiative. Desktop agents should strengthen sustained workflow ownership by adapting plans, selecting among GUI,
terminal, APIs, and stored skills, and acquiring procedures when their current capabilities are insufficient (Li et al., 2026i;
Shi et al., 2026a). Web agents should improve situational judgment by recognizing when workflow assumptions no
longer hold and determining whether uncertainty calls for local recovery, broader exploration, knowledge acquisition, or
user clarification (Yang et al., 2025e; Zheng et al., 2025a). Mobile agents should better connect evolving personal context
with latent needs, calibrate intervention to relevance and timing, and deliver assistance through reusable procedures and
selective reasoning (Kong et al., 2026; Chai et al., 2026a; Ding et al., 2026c; Chai et al., 2026b; Chen et al., 2026d;
Huang et al., 2026c). Across platforms, stronger initiative must remain aligned with user intent and authorization,
especially when objectives are inferred or external content introduces competing instructions (Levy et al., 2026; Evtimov
et al., 2025). The central research direction is therefore to develop agents that take responsibility for advancing desktop
workflows, adapt appropriately to changing Web situations, and anticipate useful mobile assistance, while recognizing
when further action requires user involvement.

Information access is one of the oldest settings for proactive behavior: recommender systems offer items no one asks
for (Resnick et al., 1994), filtering systems decide what to deliver instead of waiting to be queried (Belkin & Croft, 1992),
and early retrieval tools surface documents from a user’s working context before any search box is used (Rhodes et al.,
1996). These systems already perform the two operations that define proactive behavior: predicting a latent information
need (Anticipation, §4.2) and deciding whether and when to present unrequested information at an acceptable cost in
attention, relevance, and trust (Arbitration, §4.4). What they share with ordinary information retrieval (IR) is general
machinery: ranking, relevance modeling, query understanding, and session modeling. What makes them proactive is
that the action comes before any request, which forces the system to decide for itself what to act on and whether acting
is worth the interruption. Today this proactiveness works over short horizons: what ships at scale is contextual pre-fetch
and zero-query retrieval keyed to immediate context, such as recent app usage or the current document, alongside
recommenders that predict the next item from recent behavior (Peng et al., 2025), each serving the need the user has right
now rather than a goal it holds and revises over time; the most prominent product that inferred such goals from memory
and researched them overnight, ChatGPT Pulse, was retired within a year in favor of tasks the user schedules (OpenAI,
2025b; Digit, 2026). The current wave of adaptive and agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) (Asai et al., 2023;
Li et al., 2025e) and deep-research agents (Zheng et al., 2025d) points toward multi-source anticipation that holds a
user’s evolving goals over longer horizons, gathers evidence across many sources on its own initiative, and revises what
it surfaces as those goals change. Information access is therefore anticipation-rich but agenda-shallow relative to the
other verticals here: its ability to predict an immediate need is mature and widespread, yet it rarely maintains a longer
intent on the user’s behalf. Table 5 compares selected systems for contextual information delivery, recommendation, and
retrieval across the six mechanisms. We take the two faces of information access in turn, recommendation and search,
then ask how proactiveness is evaluated and what risks it raises.

6.3.1   Recommendation as Proactive Filtering
Recommendation is proactive by design, because it presents items when the user has issued no query at all. This is
the classic push model of information access rather than the pull model of search. Belkin & Croft (1992) describe
recommendation as the mirror image of retrieval and named it information filtering, a system that serves a standing
interest profile by choosing what to deliver rather than answering a one-off query. Early collaborative filtering
systems such as Tapestry and GroupLens do exactly this, predicting which items in an incoming stream a user would
value (Goldberg et al., 1992; Resnick et al., 1994), and later work organizes the area around the push-versus-pull
distinction (Hanani et al., 2001). In our terms, the recommender’s Anticipation is a model of the latent need encoded in
past behavior, and its Arbitration is the choice of which few items to surface within limited screen space. Whether to
surface them at all is a permission set by the platform, which is the capability-versus-autonomy distinction of §4.5.1.
Sequential and session-based recommenders sharpen the Anticipation step by predicting the next interaction from an
unfolding session (Hidasi et al., 2016; Kang & McAuley, 2018; Sun et al., 2019), which is the core of anticipatory
recommendation: predicting a need before the user acts on it. Feed and notification systems make the Arbitration
step explicit, since sending too much is directly costly and a heavy notification load lowers user mood (Pielot et al.,
2014), so bandit and reinforcement-learning controllers decide when to send a notification at all, balancing engagement
against fatigue (Yancey & Settles, 2020; Rizk et al., 2020); STEPS, a push agent deployed on Douyin, also schedules its
own next wake-up and counts permission disablement as the cost of interruption (Zhang et al., 2026m). LLM-based
and agentic recommenders carry the same structure forward (Peng et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2026e): a tool-augmented
recommendation agent checks whether it has enough evidence about the user and the items, then gathers more before
recommending, which mirrors the idea of retrieving only when uncertain (Zhang et al., 2026a), while interactive
recommenders optimize engagement over many turns (Feng et al., 2026c; Zhong et al., 2026). Recommendation also
turns proactive in dialogue: proactive cues can prompt a user to try decision aids they would otherwise miss, and users
tend to accept these prompts (Ma & Ziegler, 2024), while target-driven conversation planning orders the system’s
dialogue moves to lead the user toward a chosen item, a self-generated Agenda (§4.3) aimed at a system-side goal (Wang
et al., 2022).

6.3.2   Proactive Search: From Zero-Query to Agentic Retrieval
Search is the active, query-driven side of information access, and it turns proactive in three ways: by anticipating the
need before any query, by asking before it answers, and by self-initiating retrieval inside its own reasoning. The first
move is to stop waiting for a query. Just-in-time retrieval agents monitor the user’s current activity, such as the document
being written or the page being read, and offer related material with no query and without interrupting (Rhodes &


                                                                                                                          59
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Maes, 2000). The Remembrance Agent is the canonical early example: it runs continuously and shows short summaries
relevant to the user’s current text, on the premise that ordinary search cannot help when the user does not yet know
enough to ask (Rhodes et al., 1996). Watson reads the user’s activity in everyday applications, infers the task from the
text on screen, and retrieves related documents without a query (Budzik & Hammond, 2000), while Letizia browses
ahead of the user to find the links they are likely to want next (Lieberman, 1995). In all of these the need is read from
context rather than typed, so Awareness of the user’s task state (§4.1.1) is the enabling layer and Anticipation is the
distinctive act; wearable versions such as Jimminy carry the same idea to physical context like location and time of
day (Rhodes & Maes, 2000). The line continues into contextual mobile assistants, with Google Now’s predictive cards
as the best-known commercial case of surfacing the right card before it is requested (Rubin, 2012), and Pixel’s Magic
Cue carries it on device, surfacing a fact or action from mail, calendar, or messages when the current exchange needs
it (Kugler, 2025) (Table 4).
The second move is to ask before answering. When a query is unclear or underspecified, a well-calibrated system
can hold back its answer and ask a clarifying question instead, trading one extra turn against the risk of confidently
answering the wrong question. Learning to ask good clarifying questions in search and question answering is a research
area of its own, from the Qulac and ClariQ datasets to rankers that score a candidate question by how much it is expected
to reduce uncertainty (Aliannejadi et al., 2019; Rao & III, 2018; Aliannejadi et al., 2021). The proactive part is again an
Arbitration decision, namely when to ask rather than answer (§4.4.1). CLAM asks for clarification only when a request
is ambiguous (Kuhn et al., 2023a), CLAMBER tests whether models can even tell that clarification is needed and finds
that they often cannot (Zhang et al., 2024g), and related work trains agents to judge how vague a task is and to recover
the user’s implicit intent before acting (Qian et al., 2024). Asking too often is as poorly calibrated as never asking,
the same two-sided failure that runs through proactive behavior. The posture extends to multi-turn settings, where a
conversational system can volunteer suggestions, anticipate follow-up needs, and guide the discussion (Deng et al.,
2023b): Andolina et al. (2018) studied this directly, surfacing relevant information into an ongoing conversation without
being asked, and PACIFIC casts proactive question answering in which the system opens a clarification over mixed table
and text data (Deng et al., 2022). Recent information-gathering agents push the gate further, learning policies for which
question reduces uncertainty the most (Choudhury et al., 2026; Echarghaoui et al., 2026), and icebreaker agents study
how to open an interaction with a user the system knows nothing about (Zheng et al., 2026a), while IntentRL trains a
deep-research agent to clarify latent intent before committing to an expensive run (Luo et al., 2026b).
The third move folds retrieval into the agent’s own reasoning: instead of always retrieving, the agent decides from
its own uncertainty when and what to fetch. Self-RAG learns special tokens that decide when to retrieve and whether
a passage helps (Asai et al., 2023), FLARE retrieves whenever it is about to generate a low-confidence span (Jiang
et al., 2023), and Adaptive-RAG routes a query to no retrieval, a single retrieval step, or several steps according to its
predicted difficulty (Jeong et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025n). At longer horizons the same decision becomes a multi-step
plan: Self-Ask has the model raise and answer its own follow-up questions, sending them to a search engine when
useful (Press et al., 2023); Search-o1 lets a reasoning model trigger retrieval mid-chain whenever it reaches a point
it is unsure about (Li et al., 2025e); and deep-research agents run many rounds of self-directed search and synthesis
over the open web, trained end to end to do so (Zheng et al., 2025d; Zhong et al., 2026), and Omakase runs such
research in the background, issuing queries as a user’s project documents evolve and distilling the reports into a few
actionable suggestions (Siangliulue et al., 2026). Each of these applies the Arbitration gate of §4.4.1 to the act of
retrieving, so the agent reaches for outside information only when answering without it is the riskier choice. The
capability-versus-autonomy line matters here (§4.5.1): an agent that issues many unrequested queries is exercising
self-initiated capability, but the freedom to spend that compute, and to act on what it finds, is autonomy that its operator
grants. What is new compared with early just-in-time retrieval is that the agent can read, reason over, and re-query its
own retrieved evidence.

6.3.3   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Evaluating proactive information access takes more than standard IR metrics, which reward the right answer to a stated
query. A proactive system must also be scored on predicting a need early and surfacing it without over-triggering, so
evaluation has to account for timing and for need prediction (§5). ProCIS provides timing annotations and normalized
proactive discounted cumulative gain (npDCG) for evaluating whether useful documents are retrieved at appropriate
moments in a conversation (Samarinas & Zamani, 2024). PREVAL instead jointly rewards early proactivity and the
quality of subsequent suggestions (Sen et al., 2018), while JIR-Arena defines the just-in-time recommendation task



                                                                                                                         60
                                                              Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


across modalities (Yang et al., 2025d). The common point is that acceptance and interruption cost, not relevance alone,
become the targets, and that a proactive system can fail in two opposite ways: missing a need it should have served, or
surfacing too aggressively. The same power to choose what the user sees also carries risks. Some are shared by any
system that surfaces content, and we treat them with the governance directions (§7.2). What is specific to information
access is that surfacing corrupts its own evidence: personalized surfacing narrows exposure into filter bubbles (Pariser,
2011), and a recommender that learns from the behavior it shapes falls into degenerate feedback loops that corrupt the
very signal Anticipation depends on (Jiang et al., 2019). These risks make Arbitration (§4.4) not only a utility one but a
normative gate. Several open directions are specific to this domain. Agents could hold a persistent, revisable model
of a user’s evolving goals across sessions, instead of reading each need from the immediate moment. Surfacing could
be made diversity- and privacy-aware by design, resisting filter bubbles and feedback loops and keeping always-on
awareness on the device. Evaluation still needs benchmarks that score need prediction, timing, and interruption cost
together, and that reward the correct decision to stay silent. In information access, mature proactiveness is not surfacing
or retrieving more, but understanding a user’s evolving goals well enough that its silence is as deliberate as its initiative.
