Embodied agents represent one of the most promising frontiers for proactive agency. By bridging digital reasoning and
physical execution, they extend proactivity beyond virtual environments into the physical world. Whereas a proactive
software agent may recommend an action, schedule a task, or generate information, a proactive embodied agent can
navigate its surroundings, manipulate objects, operate equipment, and directly affect people and infrastructure. Therefore,
every stage of the proactive loop must account for the constraints of physical interaction, including uncertainty, latency,
safety, and the limited reversibility of physical actions.
Despite rapid progress in robotics, most deployed embodied systems remain either reactively autonomous or exhibit only
bounded proactivity. Reactively autonomous robots can perform sophisticated tasks, such as grasping diverse objects or
navigating dynamic environments, but generally act in response to explicit commands, predefined triggers, or externally
assigned workflows. Bounded proactive agents go further by initiating actions within a defined task, environment, or
permission structure, but they still lack the reliability and generality required for open-ended proactive behavior. A fully
proactive robot, by contrast, must recognize emerging opportunities and risks, anticipate future needs, decide whether
and when to intervene, communicate its intentions, and adapt its behavior over time. The long-term goal is not only
greater autonomy, but robots that act as collaborative partners: taking useful initiative while remaining responsive to
human goals, preferences, and boundaries. Realizing this vision requires embodied agents to close the full proactive
loop defined by the six-A mechanism introduced in §4. Table 6 maps selected embodied systems and mechanisms
supporting proactiveness onto this framework.
Several rapidly developing technologies are bringing this vision closer. Simulation (Li et al., 2023b; Wang et al., 2023b;
Authors, 2024; Zakka et al., 2025; Mittal et al., 2025; Wen et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026m), teleoperation (Zhao et al.,
2023; Wu et al., 2024b; Khazatsky et al., 2024), wearable and egocentric data collection (Chi et al., 2024; Xu et al.,
2025a; Hoque et al., 2025; Punamiya et al., 2026; Zheng et al., 2026b), and learning from third-person images and
videos (Chen et al., 2025b, 2026b) are expanding the scale and diversity of robot-learning data, enabling robots to
acquire and generalize increasingly complex skills. Egocentric human video now reaches tens of thousands of hours
(Zheng et al., 2026b; Build AI, 2025; Figure AI, 2026d; Luo et al., 2026a), open cross-embodiment robot corpora exceed
a thousand hours and deliberately retain failure and recovery trajectories (Hou et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2025d; AGIBOT,
2026), and simulation suites scale household tasks to hundreds of activities across thousands of scenes (Nasiriany et al.,
2026; Kim et al., 2026d; Stanford Vision and Learning Lab, 2026). Large language models and vision-language models
contribute semantic knowledge, high-level reasoning, and natural-language interaction (Ahn et al., 2022; Driess et al.,
2023; Yang et al., 2025f). Vision-Language-Action models ground language instructions and visual observations in
robot actions (Team et al., 2024; Kim et al., 2024a; Black et al., 2024; Intelligence et al., 2025b; Liu et al., 2025d;
Team et al., 2025; Bjorck et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2026f; Generalist AI, 2026; Genesis AI, 2026; Physical Intelligence
et al., 2026; Luo et al., 2026a; Team et al., 2026; Yu et al., 2026e; Generalist AI, 2025). The 2026 generation of these
models controls whole humanoid bodies and coordinates several robots (Google DeepMind, 2026a), transfers zero-shot
to dozens of unseen homes (Figure AI, 2026c), and attributes most of that generalization to human-video pretraining
with explicit scaling laws (NVIDIA, 2026b; Figure AI, 2026c). World-action models capture how actions may change
future states, supporting anticipation, planning, and policy learning (Ye et al., 2026b; Agarwal et al., 2026; Garrido
et al., 2026; Gao et al., 2026d; Guo et al., 2026a; Li et al., 2026e); they have become a systematic research program
with open modular stacks (Wang et al., 2026m), and in self-evolving variants one network serves as policy, simulator,
and evaluator so that candidate actions are imagined and scored before execution (Bi et al., 2026), at the price of
several-fold higher inference latency than a comparable VLA (NVIDIA, 2026c). Policies also improve after deployment:
offline reinforcement learning from autonomous rollouts and expert corrections roughly doubles throughput on hard
real-world tasks (Intelligence et al., 2025a), and unified RL frameworks for VLAs (Zang et al., 2025), hours-scale
online post-training on physical robots (Yang et al., 2026b), world-model-based policy optimization (Zhu et al., 2025a;


                                                                                                                                                      62
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Wang et al., 2026a), and in-context learning from a single video demonstration (Skild AI, 2026) shorten the loop from
experience to behavior. Neuro-symbolic methods combine learned representations and policies with explicit symbols,
rules, and planners, supporting compositional reasoning, constraint-aware planning, and more interpretable execution
(Mao et al., 2023; Luo et al., 2024b; Yu et al., 2026d; Nie et al., 2026; Pan et al., 2026; Albinhassan et al., 2026; Kamale
& Berenson, 2026). At the system level, agentic architectures are beginning to orchestrate perception, reasoning, task
decomposition, memory, skill selection, and low-level control within closed-loop robotic workflows (Gu et al., 2025; Li
et al., 2026g; Xiao et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2026a), increasingly with readiness checks, progress verification, pre-actuation
validation gates, and long-term memory with risk prediction implemented as separate, inspectable modules (Wang
et al., 2026i; Liu et al., 2026p; Li et al., 2026h), and with embodied-reasoning models that watch live video, track task
progress, call tools, and hand work between robots (Google DeepMind, 2026b).
These advances do not, by themselves, make a robot proactive. Rather, they provide the fundamental capabilities needed
for proactive robots to determine what to do next and when to act. In the near term, the commercial market is therefore
likely to be defined by bounded proactivity. The most valuable embodied systems may not be those that operate with
the greatest independence, but those that combine useful initiative with clear operational limits, calibrated uncertainty,
measurable value, and reliable mechanisms for human oversight and escalation. This suggests a practical progression
from reactive autonomy to bounded proactivity and, eventually, to general-purpose proactive embodied agents.
The following sections examine four representative verticals: household services, autonomous driving, industrial
collaboration, and human-agent co-creation. These domains overlap to some extent with the discussions of smart homes,
smart cities, and entertainment and media in §6.7, §6.8, and §6.12, respectively. Notably, the emphasis here is on
physically embodied agents that act in the real world.

6.4.1   Household Services: From Smart Appliances to Proactive Domestic Partners
A proactive household robot should understand not only explicit requests, but also the routines, preferences, permissions,
and changing conditions of the home. It may recognize when a task needs attention, choose an appropriate time to act,
avoid disturbing residents, ask before handling unfamiliar belongings, and remember household preferences. Rather
than waiting for the command “clean the kitchen”, for example, it might notice that dishes have accumulated, determine
whether the dishwasher is available, and act at a time that does not interfere with meal preparation. In this setting,
proactivity means being helpful without becoming intrusive. This section focuses on embodied agents that perform
physical tasks in domestic environments, while proactive smart-home systems are discussed more broadly in §6.7.
The home represents a major potential market for embodied AI, but also one of its most difficult operating environments.
Unlike factories and warehouses, homes vary widely in layout, objects, routines, and social norms. Thus, commercial
household robotics remains dominated by specialized products, such as robotic vacuum cleaners, lawn mowers, and
snow-removal systems, whose tasks and operating boundaries are tightly constrained (Jones et al., 2005; Matic, 2026;
Segway Navimow, 2026; Yarbo Inc., 2026). Appliance makers are extending this envelope incrementally rather than
leaping to general manipulation: Roborock’s Saros Z70 vacuum carries a five-axis arm limited to light objects and a
fixed catalogue of object types, Dreame and LG showed arm-equipped home robots at CES 2026, and Samsung quietly
shelved its Ballie companion robot (Roborock, 2025; Engadget, 2026; ChannelNews, 2026).
The emerging frontier is proactive, general-purpose household manipulation. Companies such as 1X, Sunday Robotics,
Figure, and Weave Robotics are developing humanoid or mobile-manipulation systems for tasks including tidying,
dishwashing, laundry handling, and household organization (1X Technologies, 2026a; Sunday Robotics, 2026; Figure
AI, 2026b; Weave Robotics, 2026). These systems demonstrate increasingly varied and extended workflows, but reliable
operation across an entire home remains an open challenge. The first measured generalization numbers appeared in
2026: Figure 03 running Helix 2.5 performed bed making, towel folding, and toy tidying in 30 previously unseen homes
without any in-home data, succeeding in 56% of trials, against 9% for a model trained without large-scale human-video
pretraining (Figure AI, 2026c). In simulation, the winning entry of the 2025 BEHAVIOR Challenge completed only
12.4% of its 50 long-horizon household tasks end to end, and the best agents on the LongAct benchmark reach 16%
full-task success even with frontier language models as planners (Larchenko et al., 2025; Stanford Vision and Learning
Lab, 2026; Zhu et al., 2026e). As of this writing, none of these general-purpose home robots has confirmed consumer
deliveries: 1X says some NEO orders will ship in 2026 and others later, Sunday plans a 50-household beta in late
2026, and Weave’s first shipments are scheduled for fall 2026 (heise online, 2026; Sunday Robotics, 2026; Weave
Robotics, 2026). The gap between a convincing demonstration and a useful product is especially large in domestic



                                                                                                                          63
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


settings: occasional failure may be acceptable in a laboratory, but frustrating or unsafe in everyday use.
The central technical challenge is domestic generalization: maintaining reliable performance across variations in layouts,
objects, clutter, lighting, residents, and routines. A robot entering a new home must quickly learn not only where
objects are located, but also how that household organizes its space and which actions its residents consider appropriate.
This requires navigation and manipulation to be combined with contextual reasoning, memory, preference learning,
and permission-aware decision-making. Human-in-the-loop operation offers one practical path toward this capability
(1X Technologies, 2026a, 2025). Remote operators can help robots resolve unfamiliar situations and complete useful
tasks while generating demonstrations from real homes. These interventions can create a data flywheel through which
recurring situations are gradually incorporated into autonomous policies, providing a bridge from supervised household
services to increasingly autonomous and proactive behavior. 1X’s NEO follows this model, with a remote expert able to
supervise at scheduled times and a world-model effort aimed at reducing reliance on teleoperators (1X Technologies,
2026a,c), and Weave’s Isaac 1 operates autonomously by default with teleoperation as a fallback and physical cues
that show when the robot is working (Weave Robotics, 2026). Two alternative flywheels avoid remote operators in the
customer’s home altogether. One collects paid first-person video of people doing chores in their own homes: Figure’s
Index app reports 16 million videos from more than 100 countries and accounts for most of Helix 2.5’s zero-shot
capability (Figure AI, 2026d), Sunday’s Skill Capture Glove recorded roughly 10 million episodes in more than 500
homes without a robot present (Robotics 24/7, 2025; Humanoids Daily, 2026), and open datasets such as EgoWild2Dex
follow the same recipe (Lin et al., 2026a). The other licenses large multi-embodiment foundation models to hardware
makers, as with Gemini Robotics 2 and π0.7 , the latter operating unseen kitchens and appliances zero-shot (Google
DeepMind, 2026a; Physical Intelligence et al., 2026). Whichever route is taken, in-deployment learning must not erase
earlier skills: naive sequential fine-tuning of vision-language-action models on a stream of real-world tasks causes severe
forgetting, which experience replay largely prevents (Zhu et al., 2026b). However, remote access to a household robot
also raises significant privacy concerns, particularly when operators can view sensitive domestic spaces or activities.
Privacy risks persist even without a human viewer: the structured maps, object lists, and task summaries a robot exports
can re-identify households and reveal target objects, and no single abstraction removes this leakage across tasks (Xu &
Ayday, 2026). The viability of this model will therefore depend on whether users are willing to accept such oversight
and whether strong safeguards, transparency, and user controls can make remote operation sufficiently trustworthy.
Commercial adoption will depend on three closely related factors. First, physical capability does not imply authorization.
Entering a room, moving an object, or discarding an item may violate privacy, ownership, or household norms. A
proactive domestic agent must therefore judge which actions are permitted, whose preferences take priority, and when
confirmation or inaction is appropriate (Li et al., 2026b). Recent work begins to measure and build this judgment. In the
NormAct benchmark, multimodal agents reach the goal in 67.4% of household scenarios but comply with the unspoken
norm in only 24.7% (Zhao et al., 2026c); ask-or-act policies learn when accumulated interaction history suffices to act
and when a clarification question is worth its cost (He et al., 2026a); EgoAsk lets the robot ask context-relevant questions
about a user’s belongings through smart glasses (Hu et al., 2026c); routine-anticipation models predict a resident’s next
activities and defer to a language model only when uncertain (Gonzalez et al., 2026); and a four-day in-home study with
ten families found that robot-initiated reminders raise tensions over timing and authority among residents (Xu et al.,
2026e). Closed-loop evaluation with an adaptive human model further shows that proactive methods that look strong
offline can collapse and increase user workload (Patel & Chernova, 2026). Second, reliability must transfer across homes
without extensive preparation or per-household engineering. Systems that perform well in controlled demonstrations
must retain that reliability in unfamiliar and changing environments. Third, cost must remain commensurate with
practical value. Early general-purpose home robots and prototypes remain expensive relative to specialized appliances,
raising expectations for both reliability and breadth of capability: NEO is priced at $20,000 or $499 per month, Sunday’s
hand-built Memo units cost about $20,000 with retail expected to fall by at least half, and Weave’s Isaac 1 is listed at
$7,999 or $449 per month (1X Technologies, 2026b; Sunday Robotics, 2026; Weave Robotics, 2026).
The most successful household robot may therefore not be the one with the broadest initial skill set. Instead, it may
be one that performs a small number of valuable tasks reliably across different homes, at an acceptable cost, without
undermining privacy, personal preferences, autonomy, or comfort. Such a system would mark a meaningful transition
from a smart appliance to a trusted proactive domestic partner.




                                                                                                                         64
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


6.4.2   Autonomous Driving: Proactive Embodied AI at Commercial Scale
A proactive autonomous vehicle must continually anticipate how a traffic scene may evolve and respond before
contingencies happen. It cannot rely on a passenger, safety driver, or remote operator to guide it through each decision.
Instead, it must predict the behavior of pedestrians and other road users, negotiate right-of-way, select safe stopping
locations, reroute around disruptions, and determine when uncertainty calls for more cautious behavior, a minimal-risk
maneuver, or operational assistance. This section focuses on autonomous vehicles as embodied agents, with the broader
role of proactive agents in smart cities discussed in §6.8.
Autonomous driving is among the most commercially mature examples of proactive embodied AI operating in open,
human-populated environments. Waymo and Pony.ai offer fully driverless commercial robotaxi services across multiple
metropolitan areas (Waymo, 2024; Pony AI Inc., 2025a). By September 2026, Waymo reported more than half a million
paid trips per week on a fleet of over 4,000 vehicles in 15 U.S. cities (TechCrunch, 2026b,c; Waymo, 2026a), Baidu’s
Apollo Go ran fully driverless on Uber in Dubai with more than 240 million driverless kilometers behind it (CnEVPost,
2026; Baidu, Inc., 2026), WeRide operated roughly 400 driverless vehicles in the United Arab Emirates (Gasgoo, 2026),
and Pony.ai reported per-vehicle unit-economics breakeven for its seventh-generation vehicle and committed, with Uber,
to 2,000 robotaxis in Europe (Pony AI Inc., 2025b; TechTimes, 2026). Zoox operates a public service in Las Vegas
and has expanded limited rider access in San Francisco (Zoox, 2025, 2026); in August 2026 it began charging fares
under the first federal exemption granted to a purpose-built robotaxi without a steering wheel or pedals (TechCrunch,
2026f,g). Tesla began a small number of rides without an in-car safety monitor in Austin in January 2026 and claimed
one million unsupervised miles by September, within small daytime geofences and with remote supervision (Electrek,
2026a,b). Wayve and several automotive manufacturers are pursuing a complementary model centered on autonomy
software that can be deployed across vehicle platforms and markets (Wayve, 2026c). Driverless highway freight follows
the same pattern in a tighter operational domain: Aurora passed 500,000 driverless miles in Texas and targets 200 trucks
by the end of 2026 (Aurora Innovation, Inc., 2026b,a), while Volvo and Waabi began hauling freight between Dallas and
Houston with an observer still on board (WBAP, 2026).
Autonomous driving has reached broader deployment than general-purpose robotics partly because its embodiment
and operating environment are comparatively constrained. Vehicles travel primarily along road networks governed by
established traffic rules, infrastructure, and social conventions. The sector has also benefited from large-scale driving
datasets (Sun et al., 2020; Ettinger et al., 2021), mature automotive supply chains, and clear applications in passenger
transportation and logistics. However, current systems operate within circumstances under which they are designed to
function, such as geographic areas, road types, and weather conditions (National Highway Traffic Safety Administration,
2026). Remedies for failures at that boundary are, in practice, contractions of the boundary: after its vehicles passed
stopped school buses in Austin, Waymo issued a software recall, and after an empty robotaxi was swept away on
a flooded road, it recalled 3,791 vehicles and restricted operation at times and places of elevated risk (NPR, 2025;
TechCrunch, 2026d). Regulators are codifying the same model. The first global framework for automated driving
systems, UN GTR No. 26, requires safety at least equivalent to a competent and careful human driver and prohibits
self-modifying software (Bennett Jones LLP, 2026); China’s first Level 3 approvals specify road type and speed limits
explicitly (Gasgoo, 2025); and NHTSA’s 2026 framework pairs streamlined exemptions with enhanced oversight and a
national benchmark effort (Hunton Andrews Kurth LLP, 2026). Hence, their proactivity is substantial, but bounded.
The next frontier is broader and more transferable driving agency. Existing systems already exhibit bounded proactivity
by anticipating other road users, choosing appropriate pick-up and drop-off locations, adapting routes to disruptions,
and positioning vehicles without continuous human instruction. Future systems must generalize these capabilities across
more cities, weather conditions, traffic cultures, and vehicle platforms without extensive location-specific engineering.
That transfer is under way but remains a staged, multi-year process: Waymo is running specialist-supervised trials
across 20 London boroughs toward a 2026 launch and targets Munich toward the end of 2027 and Singapore in 2028,
while Wayve and Uber began supervised autonomous rides in London in September 2026 with Nissan robotaxis planned
for Tokyo (Waymo, 2026c; TechCrunch, 2026e; Uber Technologies, Inc., 2026; Wayve, 2026b). On the model side,
reasoning-centric vision-language-action drivers make anticipation explicit and language-grounded (Hu et al., 2025b;
Wang et al., 2025i; Huang et al., 2026e; Yan et al., 2026c), world models serve not only to generate rare scenarios
but as closed-loop evaluators with the policy in the loop (Waymo, 2026d; Wayve, 2026a; Basant et al., 2026), and
efficient world-action models internalize prediction as a training signal while keeping action real-time (Wang et al.,
2026c; Fan et al., 2026b). Proactivity also extends beyond the individual vehicle: at the fleet level, agents could forecast
demand, reposition vehicles, schedule charging and maintenance, and coordinate responses to network-wide disruptions.


                                                                                                                         65
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Fleet-level proactivity remains the least developed strand: recent work on rebalancing under demand drift is an exception
(Han et al., 2026b), and in current deployments fleet agenda-setting is largely delegated to ride-hailing platforms rather
than to the driving agent (Baidu, Inc., 2026; TechTimes, 2026).
The remaining challenge is to scale safety and economic viability together. Autonomous vehicles must handle rare and
unfamiliar situations, provide credible evidence of safety to regulators and the public, and reduce the costs of vehicles,
sensors, maintenance, insurance, and operational support. Because driving decisions are safety-critical and often difficult
to reverse (Bellan, 2024; Koopman, 2024), the vehicle must remain appropriately conservative when the intentions of
other road users or the environment state are uncertain. Safety evidence is now reported at scale, though largely by the
companies themselves: across 270 million autonomous miles, Waymo reports 82% fewer injury-causing crashes and
95% fewer serious-injury crashes than a human benchmark (Waymo, 2026b). Synthesized safety-critical scenarios (Kim
& Choi, 2026), pedestrian intent prediction (Ashayer et al., 2026), and external intent communication (Tran et al., 2026)
address the long tail and the legibility of the vehicle’s own intentions. Fallback behavior has a regulatory price as well:
California now fines operators whose vehicles block first responders and requires licensed remote drivers (TechCrunch,
2026a).
Autonomous driving offers a useful preview of how other proactive embodied agents may mature: begin within a
restricted operational domain, deploy at meaningful scale, learn from real-world experience, maintain robust fallback
and human-support mechanisms, and expand both autonomy and proactive initiative only as safety and reliability are
demonstrated.

6.4.3   Industrial Collaboration: From Task Automation to Proactive Co-Workers
A proactive industrial agent does more than execute a task assigned by a worker or production-management system. It
monitors the shared workflow, anticipates what people and machines will need next, initiates appropriate assistance,
communicates its intentions, and escalates when uncertainty or risk exceeds its authority. The focus here is on embodied
agents that work alongside people, reduce physical workload, and improve the coordination of shared tasks.
Industrial robots have operated for decades in structured work cells separated from human workers, where they achieve
high efficiency on repetitive and carefully specified tasks (Nof, 1999; Dzedzickis et al., 2022), and that paradigm
is still growing: the global operational stock of industrial robots reached five million units in 2025 (International
Federation of Robotics, 2026). The commercial frontier is now shifting toward flexible mobile manipulators and
humanoid platforms that can operate in human-designed facilities and support a wider range of workflows. Figure and
RobotEra, for example, are developing and piloting humanoid systems for material handling, kitting, logistics, and other
labor-intensive operations (BMW Group, 2024; Figure AI, 2026a; Futurism, 2026). The evidence base has begun to
shift from demonstrations to operating records. BMW’s ten-month Figure 02 pilot at Spartanburg accumulated roughly
1,250 operating hours and placed more than 90,000 sheet-metal parts into welding fixtures before it was succeeded by a
parts-sequencing task and a second vendor pilot in Leipzig (BMW Group, 2026). Agility Robotics reports more than
65,000 hours of commercial Digit operation across nine customer facilities (Agility Robotics, 2025, 2026), Apptronik’s
Apollo operates in designated zones at Mercedes-Benz, GXO, and Jabil (Malayil, 2026), and Boston Dynamics and
Google DeepMind are pairing Gemini Robotics models with the electric Atlas, with Hyundai targeting parts sequencing
in 2028 and component assembly by 2030 (Korosec, 2026; Demaitre, 2026). Analysts count roughly 19,000 to 25,000
humanoids shipped in the first half of 2026, more than 70% of them to industrial and commercial buyers and most
of them from AgiBot and Unitree (Smart Analytics Global, 2026; Qi & Wang, 2026; Francis, 2026; KrASIA, 2026).
Non-humanoid mobile manipulators are reaching production in logistics first, as in Dexterity’s autonomous trailer
loading at FedEx and UPS’s order of 400 Pickle Robot truck unloaders (Dexterity, 2026; Soper & LaPara, 2025). In a
widely viewed 2026 comparison, a Figure humanoid processed roughly 200 fewer packages than a human participant
during a ten-hour parcel-sorting task, demonstrating near-human performance in this narrowly defined workflow (Bishop,
2026; Nield, 2026), and a later company-run livestream showed three Figure 03 robots sorting more than 28,000
packages over 24 hours without reported interventions (Knutsson, 2026). These demonstrations reflect substantial
progress in perception, manipulation, and robustness, but they should not be confused with proactive agency. A robot
may operate autonomously for hours on a parcel-sorting line while still following a predefined objective, workspace,
and action pattern. Every deployment above is a fixed, fenced task: totes, trolleys, parcels, or trailers. The vendors
themselves describe designated zones and multi-year roadmaps, and Tesla’s own investor filings state that the initial
Optimus builds are routed to an internal training academy rather than to production work (Tesla, Inc., 2026). Most
industrial humanoid pilots therefore remain closer to task-level reactive autonomy: they can execute assigned work


                                                                                                                        66
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


independently, but fail to determine how best to contribute to the broader workflow.
Proactivity begins when the agent reasons about the state and needs of the overall operation. Rather than waiting for
an operator to request each action, it might infer which component will be needed next, prepare tools before a worker
reaches the corresponding step, reorder tasks when a workstation falls behind, or ask for clarification when several
actions appear plausible. Recent research has explored proactive task sequencing through real-time prediction of human
motion and intent (Huang & Mutlu, 2016; Liu et al., 2023b; Yu et al., 2024; Abilkassov et al., 2025), adaptive behavior
tailored to individual workers (Liu et al., 2022b; Chen et al., 2023b; Freire et al., 2024; Hostettler et al., 2024), and
anticipatory cues that make upcoming robot actions easier for people to understand (Psarakis et al., 2025; Bo et al., 2026).
Work in 2026 has moved from predicting human intent to deciding whether and when to act on it. Examples include
learned ask-or-act policies that weigh clarification against assistance accuracy over multi-day interaction (He et al.,
2026a), event-driven assistance that acts only on observed human–object state transitions and refrains when a task is
unsolvable (Liu et al., 2026a), collaborative vision-language-action policies whose action chunks straddle task transitions
and thereby trigger premature assistance unless steered at inference time (Xu et al., 2026d), and uncertainty-aware
intention prediction for assembly (Heman et al., 2026). At the workflow level, fatigue-predictive task allocation decides
when to assign which task to whom (Xue et al., 2026), and LLM-based orchestrators plan and replan for heterogeneous
robot fleets over a shared world state (Gupta et al., 2025; Zhang, 2026b), although a single accepted false claim about
that state can cascade into fleet-wide replanning (Khalid & Min, 2026). The first commercially deployed workflow-level
reasoning is advisory rather than embodied: Amazon’s Project Eluna reasons over live operational data to recommend
where managers should shift people to avoid bottlenecks (Amazon, 2025). These systems provide clearer examples of
bounded proactive collaboration, although most remain research prototypes or narrowly scoped pilots.
The central challenge is the reliability of proactive initiative. An unnecessary or poorly timed action may interrupt
a worker, slow production, damage equipment, or create a safety hazard. The agent must therefore do more than
predict what might happen next: it must judge whether acting now would be helpful, whether its intention will be
understood, and whether the action can be stopped or reversed safely. A controlled study of humanoid assistance in
group collaboration found that unprompted intervention raised interaction load and that its value depended on the
participants’ prior experience and personality (Vitry et al., 2026). For legged and balancing robots, even stopping
is an active behavior: cutting power makes a biped fall, so classical functional-safety chains can be certified only
around, not inside, the balancing controller, a gap that the forthcoming ISO 25785-1 standard for actively stabilized
mobile robots is meant to address (Ding et al., 2026a; i-SCOOP, 2026). Newer platforms accordingly build in graded
slow-to-stop-to-sit responses, independent safety controllers, and explicit visual and auditory intent cues (Wessling,
2026). Industrial users will generally prefer a system that performs a limited set of tasks with consistently high reliability
and efficiency over one that attempts a broader range of tasks unpredictably. Amazon’s withdrawal of its Blue Jay
multi-arm cell within four months of announcing it, and a Siemens case study documenting the collect–curate–fine-tune
cycles needed to make a generalist policy reliable at a single packaging station, illustrate the point (Amazon, 2025; Zhu
et al., 2026a). Proactive industrial agents are therefore likely to emerge through gradually expanding islands of validated
autonomy. Task-level performance may be approaching that of human workers in some narrow workflows, but reliable
workflow-level proactivity remains an open frontier.

6.4.4   Human-Agent Co-Creation: From Virtual Imagination to Physical Creativity
A proactive co-creative embodied agent does more than fabricate a finalized human design. It participates in shaping the
artifact by interpreting incomplete intent, proposing alternatives, evaluating feasibility, selecting tools and materials, and
adapting the design during production. In this setting, proactivity means making timely and constructive contributions
while preserving human authorship and control. This section focuses on humans and embodied agents collaboratively
creating physical artifacts, while broader forms of digital co-creation, including games and media, are discussed in
§6.12.
Generative AI has greatly expanded digital creation in images, videos, and virtual 3D assets (Zhu et al., 2017; Rombach
et al., 2022; OpenAI, 2024; DeepMind, 2025; Tochilkin et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2025e). The next frontier is to connect
this generative capability with robotic systems that can produce physical outcomes. Early commercial platforms are
already building parts of this pipeline. Machina Labs develops software-defined factories that translate digital designs
into complex metal structures, while AUAR combines robotic microfactories with software that converts building plans
into prefabricated components (Machina Labs, 2026b; AUAR, 2026). Machina Labs has since raised capital for a
50-cell facility in which forming robots decide incrementally where to work and how much to deform, guided by in-cell


                                                                                                                           67
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


scanning (Machina Labs, 2026a; SAE Media Group, 2026); Divergent couples generative design, large-format metal
printing, and robotic assembly in one production system (TCT Magazine, 2026); and process-planning software now
derives work instructions and assembly sequences from CAD so that engineers approve rather than author them (Dirac,
2026). Text-to-CAD has likewise become conversational and self-checking, with commercial agents that anticipate
edits and validate geometry before committing them (Zoo, 2026; Backflip AI, 2026). These systems are primarily
automated fabrication platforms rather than co-creative agents, but they provide important infrastructure for future
agentic design-to-production workflows. Research prototypes demonstrate complementary elements of this vision.
FRIDA and CoFRIDA translate multimodal creative intent into paintings and update their plans using feedback from the
evolving canvas, with CoFRIDA supporting human-robot co-painting (Schaldenbrand et al., 2022, 2024), and CoBrush
extends co-painting to multi-round sessions by separating intent inference, spatial grounding, and stroke execution (Qin
et al., 2026). Other systems have demonstrated robotic pottery and sculpting, including closed-loop visual planning for
clay reliefs of more than a hundred actions (Yoo et al., 2024; Ma et al., 2020; Schaldenbrand & Oh, 2026), as well as the
generation and robotic assembly of physical structures from sketches (Xu et al., 2025f), text descriptions (Goldberg
et al., 2025; Pun et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2026k; Kyaw et al., 2025a; Sznaier Camps et al., 2026), or speech (Kyaw et al.,
2025b). Multi-robot execution frameworks further increase the scale and complexity of the artifacts that robotic systems
can construct (Huang et al., 2025a; Liu et al., 2026k). Agentic design-and-fabrication systems are beginning to combine
these pieces: MAVE places LLM supervisor, design, and robot agents, an augmented-reality headset, and a cobot in one
interactive workflow (Yang et al., 2026f), and vision-language agents that align observed assembly state with the design
specification replan when human co-workers deviate from the expected sequence (Chen & Deng, 2026). Together,
these efforts point toward workflows in which design reasoning, feasibility analysis, production planning, and physical
execution are no longer treated as separate stages.
The central frontier is closed-loop prompt-to-product. A user may begin with an incomplete description, rough sketch,
reference image, or partial design. A proactive agent could generate alternatives, identify ambiguities, evaluate whether
each proposal can be produced with the available tools and materials, and recommend modifications before production
begins. During production, it could inspect intermediate results, detect deviations, revise the design or production
plan, and ask the user to choose among emerging alternatives. The defining capability is knowing when to propose,
clarify, revise, or defer while balancing creative intent, physical feasibility, user preferences, and resource constraints.
The individual pieces of this loop now exist. Multi-agent CAD generators wrap design in programmatic geometric
validation, review, and rollback (Barkley et al., 2026; Shui et al., 2026; Hu et al., 2026b; Haag et al., 2026), and new
benchmarks score manufacturability and assemblability rather than shape similarity (Dong et al., 2026a; Wang et al.,
2026d). Fabrication-aware tools let users repair generative 3D models that would fail when printed (Faruqi et al., 2026),
stage the assistant’s initiative from decomposition to structural recommendation before cutting (Gao et al., 2026a),
optimize generated shapes for printability (Wu et al., 2025a), or improvise assemblies from the materials at hand (Isume
et al., 2025). During production, language-model agents screen toolpaths for anomalies before printing and monitor and
correct additive processes in situ (Eslaminia et al., 2026; Alali et al., 2026; Pak et al., 2026). What is still missing is a
single system that composes alternative generation, feasibility scoring, in-production inspection, and user-in-the-loop
refinement under one policy for when to propose, verify, or ask (Wang et al., 2026h).
Co-creation offers a relatively permissive setting for proactive experimentation because creative goals are often subjective
and evolve throughout the process. In tightly controlled or safety-critical settings, an unexpected robot action is usually
a liability. However, in creative work, it may become a useful suggestion or a productive change in direction. Therefore,
embodied agents can take greater initiative, provided that their contributions remain transparent, reversible, and aligned
with the creator’s intent.
The commercial opportunity lies in flexible design-to-production systems for personalized products and low-volume
manufacturing. Such systems could reduce dependence on specialized design expertise, dedicated tooling, and large
production runs. However, important barriers remain, including translating subjective intent into engineering spec-
ifications, verifying structural and functional feasibility, maintaining quality over long production sequences, and
managing material and equipment constraints. Questions of authorship, intellectual-property ownership, provenance,
and accountability will also become more pressing as humans and agents jointly design and fabricate physical products.
Early evidence is emerging on both fronts: professional artists found collaboration with an autonomous painting arm
more playful and reflective than with a human partner and granted it more autonomy (Cocchella et al., 2025), expressive
robot behaviors shift perception from tool to partner (Yu et al., 2026c), and patch-level attribution can distinguish human,
robot, and genuinely blended regions of a collaborative painting (Chen & Alves-Oliveira, 2026).



                                                                                                                          68
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


6.4.5   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Robotics is adopting proactive behavior more cautiously than many digital domains because embodied agents act
directly on people, objects, and infrastructure. Their mistakes can cause physical harm, damage property, or alter the
environment in ways that are difficult to reverse. Proactive embodied agents also share broader concerns with other
proactive systems, including privacy, trustworthiness, ethics, and alignment, as discussed in §7. Beyond these general
concerns, physical embodiment introduces several distinct challenges.
First, evaluating proactive embodied intelligence remains difficult, and no single standard captures all of its relevant
dimensions. As with proactive agents in other domains, task success alone is insufficient, as discussed in §5. A proactive
robot must also recognize when intervention is useful, act at an appropriate time, communicate its intentions, and avoid
unnecessary or disruptive behavior. Thus, evaluation should consider both task performance and the quality of human-
agent interaction, including interaction fluency, legibility, perceived safety, user agency, and overall user satisfaction
(Dragan et al., 2013; Hoffman, 2019; Cohen et al., 2026). It should also capture failures specific to proactivity, such
as missed opportunities, unnecessary interventions, excessive clarification, poorly timed actions, and inappropriate
escalation. Such metrics are beginning to appear. Benchmarks now score the decision rather than only the outcome:
ProActBench and RobotEQ include negative traps in which the correct behavior is to stay silent (Zhang et al., 2026l;
Fang et al., 2026b; Che et al., 2026), NIABench penalizes interrupting the human’s plan (Zhang et al., 2026i), ProAct-75
reports trigger-detection accuracy and steps saved (Zhu et al., 2026d), EgoServe and HOTD-Bench treat intervention
as a context-dependent choice over continuous video (Gong et al., 2026; Song et al., 2025b), and NormAct scores
compliance with unspoken household norms (Zhao et al., 2026c). Across these benchmarks, current vision-language
models remain far below humans and are brittle to prompt framing; in one failure-recovery benchmark, refusal rates
swing from near-total to near-zero when answer options are reordered (Pathak & Krishna, 2026). For task competence
itself, evaluation is shifting from single success rates to capability profiles, robustness audits, and reproducible real-robot
leaderboards (Gao et al., 2026b; Fei et al., 2025; Atreya et al., 2025; Yakefu et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026e).
Many of these qualities cannot be measured adequately using static datasets or isolated task-success metrics. They often
require human-in-the-loop studies and longitudinal deployments because the appropriate level of initiative depends
on the user, environment, and application. Offline evaluation against static human models can overstate proactive
performance so much that methods which look strong offline add net work once the human adapts to the robot (Patel &
Chernova, 2026; Tang et al., 2026a), and user studies continue to find that more frequent intervention does not raise
engagement (Hriscu et al., 2026; Vitry et al., 2026). Longitudinal in-home studies remain small, typically a handful of
homes over several weeks (Moorman et al., 2026; Kian et al., 2026), while distributed double-blind pairwise comparison
offers one scalable template for real-world evaluation (Atreya et al., 2025). The same behavior may be helpful in one
context but distracting, intrusive, or even unsafe in another. Evaluation is further complicated by the diversity of robotic
embodiments, including humanoids, mobile manipulators, quadrupeds, drones, mobile robots, and fixed-base arms, each
with different capabilities, risks, and interaction patterns. Real-world experiments are also costly and time-consuming,
particularly when they require specialized hardware, controlled safety procedures, and repeated studies with human
participants.
Second, proactive embodied agents must adapt quickly to new embodiments, environments, tasks, and users. A household
robot entering a new home must learn its layout, object conventions, resident preferences, and household boundaries. An
industrial robot may need to adjust to a new workstation, tool configuration, workflow, or human partner. Differences in
sensors, kinematics, payloads, and control interfaces also limit the direct transfer of policies across platforms. Unlike
digital agents, which can learn about users through virtual interactions such as text exchanges, embodied agents typically
require physical interaction and real-world execution. This makes adaptation and generalization slower, more expensive,
and potentially riskier.
Third, proactive robots must take initiative safely under physical uncertainty. Actions in the physical world may be
difficult to reverse and can alter the environment before a person has time to intervene. An embodied agent must
therefore reason not only about whether an action is likely to succeed, but also about its possible consequences, whether
nearby people will understand its intention, and whether the action can be interrupted or recovered from safely. Hence,
calibrated uncertainty, legible motion, permission-aware planning, and reliable fallback behavior are central to proactive
embodiment. Red-teaming studies show why these cannot be left to the policy alone: unguarded vision-language-action
models can be driven to unsafe actions in nearly all tested scenarios, and fine-tuning only on safe demonstrations can
even increase hazardous execution (Zhang et al., 2026j; Chen et al., 2026i; Yin et al., 2026, 2024b; Li et al., 2026f).
The field is therefore converging on decoupled arbitration layers: formal guardrails that translate safety rules into


                                                                                                                            69
                                                         Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


temporal-logic specifications and veto non-compliant plans (Ravichandran et al., 2026), compact hazard-judging models
that score observation–action pairs (Choi et al., 2026b), reachability-based safety values that gate policy optimization
(Tayal & Nambi, 2026), calibrated success confidence for ask, act, or abort decisions (Francis-Meretzki et al., 2026), and
layered guardrail architectures with explicit conservatism allocation (Kim et al., 2026c). Governance lags embodiment:
the only humanoid-specific safety standard in progress, ISO/CD 25785-1, covers industrial settings only, so home robots
still fall under the 2014 personal-care standard; the EU has deferred product-embedded high-risk AI obligations to 2028;
and legal analyses on both sides of the Atlantic find no fit-for-purpose privacy rulebook for remote teleoperation of home
robots (International Organization for Standardization, 2026; EU AI Act Resource, 2026; Da Costa Alves & Le Goff,
2026; Stewart, 2026).
Finally, open-world operation requires robots to continue improving after deployment, yet physical systems cannot
explore freely when mistakes may cause harm. Progress will depend on learning mechanisms that combine simulation,
demonstrations, operator interventions, and carefully collected real-world experience without compromising safety.
Continual learning systems must also detect when an update has degraded performance, prevent unsafe policies from
being deployed, and support reliable rollback or human takeover. Recent proposals place a world-model verification
gate inside a human-oversight envelope around post-deployment self-improvement and argue for evaluating the evolving
trajectory rather than a fixed checkpoint (Nguyen et al., 2026), while real-robot continual-learning benchmarks show
that naive sequential fine-tuning forgets earlier skills unless experience is replayed (Zhu et al., 2026b).
As a result, progress in proactive robotics will depend not only on more capable models, but also on better mechanisms
for calibrated initiative, rapid adaptation, permission-aware decision-making, safe continual learning, human oversight,
and reliable escalation. Ultimately, a general-purpose proactive embodied agent must do more than act autonomously.
It must judge when intervention is useful, when clarification is needed, and when it should wait or remain still. Only
systems that combine physical capability with this form of operational judgment can become safe, trustworthy, and
genuinely helpful partners in the open world.

In security and surveillance, proactiveness concerns whether the human or the agent decides which protective tasks
warrant attention and how they should be pursued. An agent may exercise task-scoped initiative while analyzing an
alert or patching a reported vulnerability, even when a human selects the task. The agent takes initiative when, within a
standing protective objective and an authorized scope, it decides what to investigate next, whether a finding warrants
intervention, and when to revisit an earlier decision. In surveillance, these decisions also include determining whether
an ambiguous event warrants acquiring further evidence.
Existing work supplies foundations for these proactive choices. Red teaming and threat hunting organize inquiry around
possible weaknesses or overlooked intrusions. Agent-based testing and repair automate diagnosis and intervention,
while incident records preserve evidence and case history. Earlier autonomous cyber-resilience work and the AICA
reference architecture envisaged agents that monitor, plan, respond, and recover in contested environments (Kott &
Theron, 2022; Kott et al., 2023). Recent accounts of autonomous threat hunting and agentic cybersecurity describe
increasingly broad defensive workflows (Sindiramutty, 2024; Kshetri, 2025; Vinay, 2025). These foundations support


                                                                                                                                                          70
                                         Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


broader initiative when an agent identifies related vulnerabilities, proposes additional protection, or recognizes that
changed conditions require renewed attention. Table 7 compares selected security systems across the six mechanisms,
covering vulnerability discovery and repair as well as patrol planning.
The central challenge is therefore not simply to connect investigation, repair, and monitoring into a longer workflow
while leaving task selection and coordination to humans, but to enable the agent to sustain task-selection judgment
across that workflow. A proactive agent must repeatedly determine whether further investigation work is warranted, what
defensive form it should take, and how far the protection should extend, while remaining within authorization and human
oversight. This section thus examines that capability through initiative in choosing investigations, turning findings
into protective action, and proactively revisiting prior decisions, before considering the associated risks, evaluation
challenges, and open research directions.

6.5.1   Choosing investigations and acquiring evidence
A human-defined project or incoming alert can provide a starting point for security agents to work on without prescribing
every subsequent investigation. The distinction between a relatively reactive agent and a proactive one is whether the
agent merely follows an assigned investigation workflow or takes the initiative to use available evidence to formulate
an additional question worth pursuing. It is noteworthy that choosing a tool within a prescribed task is not, by itself,
evidence of task initiation and proactiveness.
Red teaming and threat hunting frame investigation around hypotheses about weaknesses or intrusions worth examining,
providing the forward-looking foundation for security agent proactiveness. Interviews with professional threat hunters
highlight the judgment and organizational context this inquiry requires (Maxam & Davis, 2024). A permission change,
for example, may create a path from a compromised account to a sensitive service. Those lines of work form anticipation
(§4.2) that connects assets, permissions, and possible attacker actions to a testable hypothesis about how protection
could fail.
Product-level testing, organization-level threat hunting, and ecosystem-level vulnerability discovery offer different
settings for examining the scope of proactiveness. PentestGPT coordinates tool use, result interpretation, and subsequent
testing within supplied penetration-testing targets (Deng et al., 2024a). Google’s SecOps Triage and Investigation
Agent gathers evidence and correlates signals around incoming alerts (Google Cloud, 2026). Project Glasswing extends
model-assisted vulnerability discovery across participating organizations (Anthropic, 2026g). These systems illustrate
different forms of automated investigation, but broader initiative also requires deciding which additional evidence is
worth pursuing. A useful follow-up check seeks evidence that can distinguish between competing explanations requiring
different responses. For unfamiliar server access, maintenance records, executed processes, and subsequent data access
can help distinguish authorized work from credential abuse. Missing records may justify finer monitoring (Kapoor & Kas,
2026), while missing organizational context may call for asking the service owner. Anthropic’s discussion of trustworthy
agents likewise motivates clarification when uncertainty concerns intent that only a person can resolve (Anthropic,
2026i). A benign explanation supports closure when it accounts for the relevant observations without leaving conflicting
evidence unresolved. The judgments made during the arbitration (§4.4) stage therefore weigh potential loss, the value
of further evidence, disruption, and review cost when choosing whether to continue, clarify, or return the case to
monitoring.
Particularly, in physical and video monitoring, the next investigative decision supporting proactive intervention may
concern what additional evidence is needed to resolve an ambiguous event. Earlier decision-support work such as
the Warfighter Associate addressed the management of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance assets (Buchler
et al., 2014). For anti-poaching patrols in protected areas, PAWS predicts where poaching is likely from past patrol
and poaching records and suggests patrol routes that planners review before rangers patrol (Fang et al., 2016; Xu et al.,
2020). Someone repeatedly approaching a restricted entrance could be testing access or completing a delivery. Footage
from another authorized camera or an earlier time interval may distinguish these explanations, but replaying existing
footage cannot recover observations that were never recorded. Video-analysis methods supply components for selective
inspection. Holmes-VAU combines descriptions at multiple temporal scales with adaptive frame sampling, while QVAD
refines questions as visual context becomes available (Zhang et al., 2025d; Bekit et al., 2026). AgenticVAU separates
search planning, observation, and judgment, recording whether observations support, contradict, or leave a candidate
event unresolved (Duan et al., 2026b). Additional observation also expands the scrutiny imposed on people. Inspecting
a short authorized interval, tracking someone across locations, and retaining movement histories have different privacy



                                                                                                                      71
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


implications (Zhang & Maharjan, 2026). Purpose and permitted scope should constrain collection before it occurs, while
a supported benign explanation should help end unnecessary scrutiny.

6.5.2   Turning findings into protective action
A finding from the previous investigation stage may require a decision about whether to gather additional evidence,
propose a protective measure, or defer action. In typical workflows, this initiative is exercised by a human, who
determines whether follow-up work is warranted and defines its scope. For an agent to exhibit proactiveness, it must
take on this role as well: recognizing when further action is needed and deciding what that action should involve.
Existing work has automated substantial parts of agentic repair and response workflows, enabling agents to diagnose
problems, propose fixes, and carry out prescribed actions (Pearce et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024a). These systems,
however, typically act on tasks initiated by a human rather than deciding whether further intervention is warranted.
DARPA’s AI Cyber Challenge shows how far this automation has reached: in the final competition, autonomous cyber
reasoning systems discovered 54 of the synthetic vulnerabilities planted in the challenge projects and patched 43 of
them, and also found 18 real vulnerabilities that were disclosed to maintainers (Defense Advanced Research Projects
Agency, 2025). The winning system, ATLANTIS, combines LLMs with static analysis, symbolic execution, and
fuzzing to discover and patch vulnerabilities (Kim et al., 2025c). On the response side, security orchestration platforms
execute predefined playbooks that coordinate tools such as SIEMs, firewalls, and ticketing systems once an alert meets
their trigger conditions (Islam et al., 2019). In these settings, the broader objective and intervention scope are defined
upstream: challenge organizers select the target projects and evaluation criteria, while engineers specify the conditions
that trigger playbooks.
Stronger initiative arises when a security agent must decide what, if anything, should happen next. In software repair,
such initiative may involve deciding to search for related vulnerabilities or extend a fix beyond the reported bug; in
surveillance, it may involve deciding whether to gather more evidence, issue a notification, escalate for review, or take
no further action. A confirmed bug is often one instance of a broader flaw (Wang et al., 2025m). Project Zero found
that at least nine of the eighteen zero-days exploited in the wild in the first half of 2022 were variants of previously
patched vulnerabilities, and that at least half could have been prevented by more comprehensive patching (Stone, 2022).
Searching for such variants is a task the original report does not specify: the agent must abstract the root cause into a
pattern, decide where else that pattern could occur (Jang et al., 2012; Kim et al., 2017), and judge whether the instances
it finds call for individual patches or a structural change (Popa & Flynn, 2025). Big Sleep illustrates the search itself.
Given the message and diff of a recent SQLite commit, the agent looked for related issues in the current code and found
an exploitable stack buffer underflow, which was fixed before it reached an official release (Big Sleep team, 2024). The
commits used to initiate these searches, however, were selected by researchers, so independently deciding which changes
warrant variant analysis remains an additional task-selection capability. In surveillance, the corresponding choice turns
on two questions: whether further evidence could change the decision, and what harm delay would allow (Howard,
1966). Choosing not to act is thus part of the same initiative, and should be recorded together with the evidence that
supports it.
Taking initiative does not require giving the agent final authority over consequential actions. An agent may independently
identify issues, investigate related cases, and propose repairs or other interventions, while deployment or other high-
impact actions remain subject to human approval. A mistaken investigation or proposal consumes effort but leaves the
protected system unchanged, whereas a mistaken patch, account suspension, or network block can disrupt the operations
it was meant to protect. Protective changes are not exempt from this risk: in July 2024, a faulty update to CrowdStrike’s
security software affected an estimated 8.5 million Windows devices (Weston, 2024; CrowdStrike, 2024). An agent can
therefore be given wide latitude in deciding what to investigate and propose, while actions that are hard to reverse or that
affect many systems remain subject to approval (Shavit et al., 2023; Anthropic, 2026i,d). CodeMender follows this
division: it generates and validates patches automatically, but all of them are currently reviewed by human researchers
before being submitted upstream (Popa & Flynn, 2025).

6.5.3   Sustaining protection and revisiting decisions
Proactiveness may also require an agent to revisit earlier decisions when new conditions change their basis. Changes in
permissions, dependencies, or threat knowledge may make a previously resolved issue relevant again. In surveillance,
later evidence may similarly alter the basis for resolving an event or ending further observation. A vulnerability may be


                                                                                                                         72
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


deferred because no exploit is known, because the affected service is reachable only by trusted accounts, or because the
deployed version of a dependency does not include the vulnerable code (Pashchenko et al., 2018); a surveillance event
may be closed because the available footage supports a benign explanation. Each of these conditions can change after
the decision is recorded, sometimes quickly (Bilge & Dumitraş, 2012). Mandiant’s analysis of vulnerabilities exploited
in 2023 found that the average time-to-exploit fell from 32 days in 2021–2022 to five days, after excluding statistical
outliers (Charrier & Weiner, 2024). A deferral that was reasonable while no exploit was known may therefore become
unreasonable within days. Likewise, if a person whose earlier presence was attributed to a delivery is later observed
attempting unauthorized access at another restricted entrance, the new evidence may warrant reopening the original
event, whereas unrelated activity elsewhere would not.
Existing incident records and case histories provide the memory needed to support such reassessment. Claude Security,
a commercial code-security product, supports scheduled scans for continued coverage, and user-recorded dismissals
persist so earlier triage decisions remain visible across the team (Anthropic, 2026d). Proactive reopening, however,
requires more than retrieving a prior record: the agent must relate a new condition to an earlier decision and determine
whether that decision should be reconsidered. Incident-response guidance calls for recording the actions performed
during an investigation and preserving the integrity and provenance of those records (Nelson et al., 2025). Such records
show what was decided and when, but may not explain the assumptions supporting that decision. A subsequent change
that invalidates those assumptions may also be recorded elsewhere without referring to the original case. A firewall
change that exposes a previously internal service, for example, is recorded in change management rather than in the
vulnerability ticket whose deferral assumed the service was internal (Johnson et al., 2011). Searching past cases by
host or vulnerability identifier may retrieve that ticket, but retrieval alone does not establish that the firewall change
has invalidated the assumption underlying the deferral. The agent must therefore reconstruct the basis of the earlier
decision, test whether the new condition contradicts it, and decide whether the case warrants a targeted recheck, renewed
intervention, or no change. Explicitly recording the conditions underlying each decision makes such reassessment more
tractable.
Proactiveness over longer time horizons also raises a prioritization problem when new investigations, repairs, and
rechecks compete for limited computation and human review. The agent must therefore judge not only whether a task
is worth pursuing, but also whether it deserves priority over pending investigations, repairs, and rechecks. Because
intrusions are rare relative to benign activity, even accurate detectors produce mostly false alarms (Axelsson, 2000), and
SOC analysts report that manually validating them is tedious and can lead to burnout and desensitization (Alahmadi
et al., 2022). A proactive agent can add to this burden, because each investigation it opens, repair it proposes, or recheck
it schedules may eventually require validation or approval. Open-source maintainers have already experienced the effect:
the curl project reports that plausible but unfounded AI-generated vulnerability reports take longer to refute the more
convincing they appear, consuming time that would otherwise go to fixing real bugs (Stenberg, 2024, 2025). Whether a
new task should displace pending work depends on the harm it could prevent, how soon that harm could materialize, and
how likely the task is to yield protection (Jacobs et al., 2020, 2021; Nelson et al., 2025). A validated repair awaiting
deployment may deserve priority over a speculative search. However, if a change invalidates an assumption underlying
an earlier security decision, reassessing that decision may be more urgent than either task.

6.5.4   The agent as a target and source of risk
Proactiveness creates a new attack and safety surface at the level of task initiation itself: an agent can be induced,
mistaken, over-scoped, or insufficiently controllable in deciding what work to start or continue. An adversary can induce
unwanted task initiation by manipulating the evidence an agent uses to decide what to investigate or act upon. Indirect
prompt injection shows the mechanism: instructions embedded in retrieved content can redirect an LLM-integrated
application, because such applications blur the line between data and instructions (Greshake et al., 2023; Perez &
Ribeiro, 2022; Liu et al., 2024g; Zhan et al., 2024; Debenedetti et al., 2024). The agent may also be mistaken without any
adversary, inferring a threat from coincidental evidence and initiating work that consumes review capacity or disrupts
operation (Axelsson, 2000; Ruan et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2026l). It becomes over-scoped when a legitimate line of
inquiry leads beyond its authorization, as when tracing reused credentials reaches a third-party service (Lynch et al.,
2025). The UK AI Security Institute has reported such overreach under deliberately permissive testing conditions:
in 10 of 122 cyber-evaluation runs with internet access enabled and some safety safeguards disabled, agents tasked
with solving a security challenge took unsanctioned actions directed at real people and organizations (UK AI Security
Institute, 2026). Finally, agent-initiated tasks may bypass oversight mechanisms designed for human-assigned work,



                                                                                                                         73
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


particularly when new investigations or actions are not explicitly logged and exposed for review (Chan et al., 2024).
Mitigations must therefore constrain task initiation itself, rather than relying solely on controls applied after tasks are
underway. Separating trusted control instructions from untrusted evidence, as in CaMeL, can prevent attacker-controlled
content from being treated as authority for new actions (Debenedetti et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2025c; Wallace et al.,
2024; Beurer-Kellner et al., 2025); requiring independent corroboration before initiating costly investigations can reduce
the influence of planted evidence; and making agent-initiated tasks visible, scope-limited, and cancellable can preserve
opportunities for human oversight and intervention (Odersky et al., 2026; Anthropic, 2026e; Greenblatt et al., 2024;
Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017; Soares et al., 2015).

6.5.5   Evaluation, challenges, and open directions
Evaluating proactiveness requires measuring whether an agent can identify and initiate warranted protective work that
has not been externally specified, rather than only how well it executes a task once that task has been assigned. Most
existing benchmarks for security agents primarily evaluate execution after the relevant task or objective has already
been defined, including CTF-oriented benchmarks and environments (Shao et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025m; Engelberg
et al., 2026), Cybench (Zhang et al., 2025a), and CVE-Bench (Zhu et al., 2025c). Cyber Defense Benchmark narrows
this gap by asking agents to identify malicious events in raw Windows logs without guiding questions (Chona et al.,
2026), although the higher-level hunting objective is still externally supplied. Evaluating initiative therefore requires
environments in which potential follow-up work remains latent rather than appearing explicitly in the task description.
Examples include a patched vulnerability for which related variants may remain, an alert involving credentials that may
also have been used elsewhere, or a later permission change that invalidates an earlier decision not to investigate.
The task scope of proactive security agents makes evaluation substantially more difficult because whether initiative is
appropriate depends on context, its protective benefit is often counterfactual, and the work it generates can itself be
costly. First, whether a potential task is warranted cannot usually be determined from an isolated observation. The same
failed login may deserve little attention on a test server but immediate investigation on a domain controller. Benchmarks
must therefore specify enough asset, exposure, policy, and authorization context for judgments about initiative to be
meaningful. Second, prevention is inherently counterfactual: after an agent patches a vulnerability, the absence of a
subsequent compromise does not reveal whether the intervention prevented an attack or whether no attack would have
occurred. Cyber-operations gyms such as CybORG, which place defensive agents against attacker agents in simulated
networks, provide one way to estimate these effects by comparing trajectories with and without an intervention under
controlled conditions (Standen et al., 2021; Emerson et al., 2024), although such estimates may not transfer directly to
real deployments. Third, as discussed in §6.5.3, investigating a benign event consumes analyst attention even when it is
resolved correctly (Alahmadi et al., 2022; Hassan et al., 2019).
Controlled comparisons can then separate the value of agent initiative from the value of task execution or predefined
automation. One condition can assign the protective task externally, showing what the agent achieves when a human has
already identified the work to perform. A second can use a fixed workflow or playbook, such as always checking related
accounts after a suspicious login, to measure the benefit of predefined follow-up rules. A third can expose the agent to
the same observations and objectives without specifying the follow-up, allowing it to identify, formulate, and initiate
additional work on its own. The contrast between the latter two conditions is particularly important: it tests whether
agent-directed initiative improves on predefined follow-up rules rather than merely demonstrating that follow-up of any
kind is useful. Such comparisons require model capability, tool access, observations, authorization, and resource budgets
to be held constant. An agent with broader visibility or a larger budget may discover more simply because it can search
further (Kapoor et al., 2025), while an agent allowed to take actions unavailable to the baseline is not meaningfully
comparable. Evaluation should jointly report protective outcomes, missed warranted opportunities, unnecessary initiated
work, and human review or operational cost. Reporting these quantities together distinguishes useful initiative from two
degenerate strategies: initiating nearly everything, which may improve coverage at unsustainable cost, and initiating
almost nothing, which minimizes overhead by leaving valuable opportunities unexplored.
Open directions concern how such initiative should operate over longer horizons, how agents should prioritize among
competing opportunities for protective work, and how initiative should remain subject to effective human oversight.
Long-horizon evaluation requires environments that evolve over weeks rather than ending after a single verdict:
dependencies are updated, permissions change, new advisories appear, and most changes do not warrant intervention.
Such environments test the reassessment discussed in §6.5.3, namely whether new evidence justifies continuing,
reopening, or terminating earlier lines of work (Anugula et al., 2025). Prioritization calls for methods to estimate the


                                                                                                                        74
                                                       Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


expected value of candidate investigations and to learn from reviewers’ decisions about which proposed actions are
worth pursuing (Veeramachaneni et al., 2016). Initiative also creates an oversight problem: reviewers should be able to
understand why the agent proposed or initiated a task, what further actions approval would authorize, and how its scope
can be narrowed or terminated (Shavit et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2026e).
