Among the verticals surveyed here, AutoResearch is where proactiveness is most easily confused with autonomy,
and separating the two is essential for making progress. The research loop is long-horizon and loosely supervised,
which makes it a natural home for self-initiated behavior. Many systems that have attracted the most attention receive
their top-level research objective from a human and self-direct the execution. Reduced supervision over execution
demonstrates autonomy; proactiveness depends on which hypotheses, experiments, or subgoals the agent identifies
and initiates within that objective. A human-specified objective therefore does not by itself make the research agenda
reactive. Recent conceptual work sharpens this distinction by arguing that externally scaffolded agentic workflows
do not automatically internalize the goals, decision policies, self-regulation, or learning that would support a more
internally grounded form of research agency (Xing et al., 2026). Recent surveys of agentic scientific discovery organize
the field around a similar axis, charting the transition from isolated AI tools toward systems that participate across
hypothesis generation, experimental design, execution, and iterative refinement (Gridach et al., 2025; Ren et al., 2026).
The genuinely proactive content of autonomous research concentrates at three points: generating candidate questions,
hypotheses, and subgoals (Agenda, §4.3); deciding which candidates warrant clarification, commitment, or stopping
before scarce experimental resources are spent (Arbitration, §4.4); and building experimental-oracle and research-state
infrastructure so that agent-initiated hypotheses can be validated, recorded, verified, forked, and extended. We organize
this subsection along that axis, moving from autonomous execution of given goals toward systems that generate, select,
validate, and preserve research trajectories. Table 8 compares selected research systems across the six mechanisms and
their deployment settings.

6.6.1      Autonomous Execution of Given Research Goals
The clearest existing examples are end-to-end execution pipelines in the experimental sciences. Boiko et al. (2023b)
introduced Coscientist, which couples GPT-4 with web and documentation search, code execution, and automated
laboratory interfaces to plan and carry out experiments from a stated objective. ChemCrow follows a similar template,
augmenting an LLM with expert-designed chemistry tools to plan syntheses and guide chemical discovery (M. Bran
et al., 2024). Both Coscientist and ChemCrow are strongly autonomous in execution, gathering situational context
through tools, planning multi-step procedures, and recovering from local failures, but the research question they pursue
is still supplied by the human. In this survey’s vocabulary, they supply Awareness (§4.1) and Action (§4.5) at high
capability while the top-level research objective remains human-specified. Complementary systems approach scientific


                                                                                                                                                    75
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


assistance from the literature side: retrieval-augmented agents such as PaperQA synthesize evidence across large
corpora to answer specific scientific questions (Lála et al., 2023), and successors show that such agents can match or
exceed expert humans on literature synthesis tasks (Skarlinski et al., 2024); LAB-Bench operationalizes the range of
literature-grounded tasks that biology research assistants are expected to handle (Laurent et al., 2024). Agent Laboratory
generalizes the execution template across the full research pipeline, coupling literature review, experimentation, and
report writing in a single agentic system (Schmidgall et al., 2025); the Virtual Lab demonstrates the same pattern in
biomedical research, assembling a team of LLM agents that collaboratively designed SARS-CoV-2 nanobodies against
emerging variants, which human researchers subsequently validated experimentally (Swanson et al., 2025). More recent
systems push this execution autonomy further: ScientistTwo takes a human-specified research problem, establishes
baselines, formulates hypotheses, implements and runs experiments, performs ablations, and iterates through simulated
peer review without human intervention (Nam et al., 2026). These systems can therefore automate increasingly large
portions of the research process while remaining anchored to a human-directed question rather than originating the
top-level objective themselves.

6.6.2   Hypothesis Generation and Research Agenda Formation
Proactiveness moves upstream when systems propose hypotheses, generate research directions, rank ideas, or decide
which experiments should enter the loop. Lu et al. (2024) introduced The AI Scientist, which generates research
ideas, writes code, executes experiments, produces manuscripts, and runs a simulated review process, applying the
loop to machine-learning research where experiments can be executed as code; its successor, AI Scientist-v2, reduces
reliance on human-authored code templates and manages the process with an experiment-manager agent using agentic
tree search (Yamada et al., 2025). In biomedical research, Co-Scientist uses a generate-debate-evolve process to
formulate and rank hypotheses under scientist-provided objectives (Gottweis et al., 2026); more recent work extends
this framework toward execution-grounded research, coupling hypothesis formation to real-world validation across
materials science, biology, and computer science (Schmidgall et al., 2026). Robin similarly closes the loop between
hypothesis generation and experimental feedback in biology, integrating literature-search and data-analysis agents
to generate hypotheses, propose experiments, interpret experimental results, and update hypotheses in an iterative
discovery workflow (Ghareeb et al., 2026). Literature-grounded ideation systems such as ResearchAgent iteratively
propose and refine research ideas using scientific literature and reviewer agents (Baek et al., 2025). These systems
connect directly to Anticipation (§4.2) and Agenda (§4.3): they do not merely execute given tasks but generate the
tasks themselves, the scientific analogue of the automatic curriculum in open-ended exploration (Wang et al., 2024a).
Even so, the scientist typically still states the broad research goal; the system’s proactiveness lies in populating and
refining the hypotheses that serve it. This exposes a central tension in agenda generation: the objective is not simply to
produce ideas that appear novel, but to identify hypotheses that are feasible, testable, and likely to change scientific
belief if validated. Empirical studies of LLM research ideation make this tension visible: LLM-generated ideas can score
higher on novelty than human-generated ones while scoring lower on feasibility (Si et al., 2025). Recent benchmarks
probe this gap more directly: AI Idea Bench evaluates AI research idea generation across dimensions such as novelty,
feasibility, and alignment with target-paper ideas (Qiu et al., 2025), while HypoBench evaluates hypothesis-generation
methods in terms of practical utility, generalizability, and discovery rate (Liu et al., 2026c). A complementary line of
work asks whether novelty itself can be judged reliably: RQ-Bench shows that LLM judges can produce a “novelty
mirage” by favoring model-generated research questions over author-anchored ones, while human experts prefer the
latter (Sinhahajari et al., 2026); RINoBench similarly finds that LLM rationales for research-idea novelty can resemble
human explanations without yielding reliable novelty judgments (Schopf & Färber, 2026). These results suggest that
agenda generation becomes valuable scientific progress only when candidate hypotheses are filtered through feasibility,
testability, evidential leverage, and the cost of downstream validation, rather than novelty alone.

6.6.3   Experimental Design and Resource Allocation
Research is difficult for proactive agents because its feedback is not only costly, but often delayed, noisy, and asymmetric
in what it reveals. In machine-learning research, the validation oracle is often cheap: the agent can run training
code, score a benchmark, and iterate. In most empirical sciences the verdict lives in the physical world: validating
a hypothesis may require synthesizing a molecule, culturing cells, running an animal study, or measuring a material
property, often over days or weeks and with expensive reagents, specialized instrumentation, and uncertain readouts.
Every candidate experiment becomes a costly, and sometimes practically irreversible, bet, and the burden shifts from
executing experiments to deciding which experiments are worth performing (Arbitration, §4.4). Recent AutoResearch


                                                                                                                         76
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


systems have begun to make this allocation problem explicit: PrimeScientist represents competing research plans
and their outcomes in an executable plan tree and conditions subsequent exploration on both experimental feedback
and the remaining resource budget (Yu et al., 2026f). Luo et al. (2026b) target a complementary form of arbitration
for open-ended deep-research agents: their agent learns to recognize when user intent is ambiguous and to ask a
clarifying question before committing to a long and costly investigation. Both instantiate the same underlying decision:
before committing scarce resources to a research trajectory, the agent must determine whether that trajectory warrants
further investment. This arbitration problem has a longer methodological history in experiment selection. Active
learning formalizes query selection as choosing the examples expected to be most informative for a learner (Settles,
2009), Bayesian experimental design frames experiment choice as the optimization of expected utility or information
gain (Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995), and Bayesian optimization provides a related framework for sequentially optimizing
noisy, expensive black-box objectives, a setting common in chemistry and materials discovery (Shahriari et al., 2015).
As an early instantiation of these principles in biological research, King et al. (2009) introduced the Robot Scientist
Adam, selecting experiments for their information value rather than simply running them; its successor Eve applied
related active-selection logic to drug screening (Williams et al., 2015). The self-driving laboratory paradigm that builds
on these strategies has been reviewed across chemical and materials sciences (Abolhasani & Kumacheva, 2023; Seifrid
et al., 2022). A-Lab provides a high-profile instantiation of this paradigm at scale: Szymanski et al. (2023) combined
active learning, robotic synthesis, and literature-derived knowledge to accelerate inorganic materials discovery, though
subsequent scrutiny of its product characterization and novelty claims illustrates a core fragility: an automated oracle is
only as trustworthy as the measurements and assumptions behind it (Leeman et al., 2024). The bottleneck is therefore
not whether an agent can act but whether the environment returns reliable evidence at the right level of abstraction,
which is why the experiments an agent declines to run may be as informative as the ones it executes.

6.6.4   Experimental Oracles and Research-State Infrastructure
Closing the AutoResearch loop depends on two kinds of infrastructure that together determine whether the choices made
during agenda generation and arbitration are backed by reliable evidence.
The first is the experimental oracle: the interface through which an agent queries the physical world and receives a
measurement it can act on. Without a reliable oracle, even well-calibrated arbitration lacks a trustworthy feedback signal.
Programmable and cloud laboratories reduce the latency of this query layer by turning robotic synthesis, assays, and
instrumentation into remotely executable services (Armer et al., 2023). Self-driving laboratories close the loop more
tightly by coupling automated experiment execution with measurement, model updating, and next-experiment selection,
making the oracle not merely a passive readout but part of an adaptive discovery system (Abolhasani & Kumacheva,
2023; Seifrid et al., 2022; Tom et al., 2024). Concrete systems instantiate this idea across experimental settings: CAMEO
used Bayesian active learning with a synchrotron beamline for closed-loop materials discovery (Kusne et al., 2020),
while recent LLM-based laboratory agents have begun to control scientific instruments such as atomic-force microscopes
through iterative measurement and parameter adjustment (Mandal et al., 2025). Laboratory-orchestration systems
point toward a complementary interface layer, translating high-level experimental goals into executable workflows for
automated infrastructure (Angelopoulos et al., 2026). Recent deployments of Co-Scientist further connect this interface
to hypothesis-generating agents, coupling model-generated scientific proposals to semi-automated materials synthesis
and previously unpublished biological measurements (Schmidgall et al., 2026). Oracle reliability nevertheless varies
substantially across fields: in machine learning the validation signal is cheap, fast, and machine-readable, whereas in
materials synthesis, wet-lab biology, and drug discovery it is slow, costly, and susceptible to noise, protocol variation,
and confounded characterization, a fragility illustrated by the A-Lab scrutiny described above.
More fundamentally, experimental oracles define the observable state space within which an AutoResearch agent
can reason: a fixed assay panel, sensor suite, or measurement schema may make closed-loop optimization efficient
while constraining discovery to phenomena that the infrastructure can already detect. This limitation is already visible
in in-silico research settings, where agents can propose new metrics, tests, or diagnostic benchmarks when existing
evaluations fail to distinguish competing hypotheses. The physical analogue is measurement design: in the longer term,
the most capable AutoResearch systems may need to recognize when existing sensors cannot adjudicate a hypothesis
and propose new probes, assays, or instrument workflows that make the relevant variables observable.
The second is research-state infrastructure: the persistent scientific substrate that binds executable tools, data resources,
workflows, intermediate artifacts, decision rationales, and evidence chains into a reusable state, so that later agents
and scientists can verify, fork, and extend prior work rather than restarting from scratch. Standard publication formats


                                                                                                                          77
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


compress research into a linear narrative and discard much of the machine-actionable state that autonomous inquiry
requires, including provenance, failed paths, branching history, tool configurations, execution traces, and the evidentiary
links between claims and the artifacts that support them. The FAIR principles established Findability, Accessibility,
Interoperability, and Reusability as baseline targets for scientific data (Wilkinson et al., 2016); computational notebooks
demonstrated that executable, inspectable analysis records can coexist with human-readable narrative (Kluyver et al.,
2016); and reproducibility standards and research-object conventions push further toward open methods, code, and
workflow provenance (Stodden et al., 2016; Sandve et al., 2013; Bechhofer et al., 2013).
Recent agentic systems extend this lineage from reproducible artifacts toward persistent research workspaces, where
state is not only what has been recorded but also what tools, datasets, workflows, and intermediate artifacts remain
available for future action. Biomni illustrates a workspace-level version of research-state infrastructure in biomedical
research: it exposes a broad action space of specialized tools, software packages, databases, and protocols to an AI
agent, enabling workflows that connect literature review, bioinformatics analysis, code execution, and wet-lab protocol
design (Huang et al., 2026a). Although biomedical in implementation, the broader design pattern is field-general:
AutoResearch systems need persistent, agent-native environments that bind domain resources, executable workflows,
intermediate outputs, and human-agent collaboration state into a reusable substrate for inquiry. AgentRxiv provides a
complementary shared-state mechanism for agentic research, letting agent laboratories deposit and retrieve findings
on a common preprint server so that cumulative progress compounds across runs (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025). Agora
moves this shared state inside the research process itself, representing results, hypotheses, failures, and verifications
as an append-only Git-backed contribution graph through which independently operating agents can inspect prior
branches and build on a persistent research history (Zhang et al., 2026h). Agent-Native Research Artifacts (ARA)
address within-loop continuity: each cycle’s output becomes a structured state representation that subsequent agents
can audit, reproduce, and build upon, preserving the branching history of inquiry rather than compressing it into a
linear narrative (Liu et al., 2026d). AutoScientists similarly treats research state as an active coordination substrate for
long-running experimentation, allowing agents to interpret shared experimental state, critique proposals, and record both
successful and failed directions to reduce redundant exploration (Gao et al., 2026c).
A further requirement is that accumulated state be auditable at the level of scientific claims. ScientistOne makes this
evidentiary requirement explicit through Chain-of-Evidence, a framework in which citation, numerical, methodological,
and conclusion claims in an AI-generated paper are linked to concrete evidence sources such as retrieved papers, code,
execution logs, score files, and experimental artifacts (Meng et al., 2026). Its CoE Integrity Audit checks whether
reported scores are reproducible, references are valid, task specifications are respected, and method descriptions align
with the submitted code. This auditability pressure also reshapes scientific workbench design, where the workspace and
evidence layers begin to merge. Claude Science integrates research tools, compute, and domain-specific skills into a
scientific AI workbench while producing artifacts whose code, environment, and interaction history can be inspected for
validation and reuse (Anthropic, 2026a). Together, the oracle layer and the state layer allow AutoResearch to be treated
not as a series of isolated experiments but as an evolving, machine-readable inquiry that makes research executable,
preserves failures, accumulates evidence, and supports principled continuation.

6.6.5   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
The hardest question for AutoResearch is not whether an agent can complete a research-shaped workflow, but when
that workflow should count as scientific progress. A system can retrieve papers, propose hypotheses, write code,
run experiments, and draft a manuscript while adding little reliable knowledge. Recent evaluations of open-ended
research make this distinction empirical: in “shadow evaluations” on unpublished research questions, frontier agents
autonomously completed much of the associated literature review, implementation, experimentation, and manuscript
preparation but failed to make substantial progress on the underlying research questions, with expert analysis identifying
failures in research judgment, experimental redesign, backtracking, resource awareness, and instruction adherence (Kirgis
et al., 2026). Broader process-level evaluation in AutoResearchEval similarly identifies recurring failures in checking,
revision, and reconsideration of the research trajectory across 100 frontier research tasks and 800 agent trajectories (Fei
et al., 2026). Conversely, an agent that rules out an attractive but underpowered experiment, exposes an ambiguity in the
objective, or preserves a failed branch for later reuse may contribute more to discovery than one that produces a polished
result. Evaluation should therefore treat AutoResearch as an epistemic process rather than a task pipeline. The relevant
metrics are not only answer accuracy, report quality, or benchmark score, but whether the agent changes what scientists
are justified in believing, whether its claims can be reproduced and audited, whether its decisions improve the allocation



                                                                                                                         78
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


of scarce experimental attention, and whether the research state it leaves behind can support principled continuation.
This perspective makes several current risks sharper. Hypothesis-generation systems can overproduce novelty-like
ideas whose feasibility or evidential leverage is weak; automated judges can mistake persuasive rationales for genuine
scientific value; and closed-loop laboratories can optimize efficiently against measurements that are noisy, confounded,
or too narrow to reveal the phenomenon of interest. Even when the evaluation itself is appropriate, a single experimental
realization may be weak evidence about the underlying research idea: the “implementation lottery” shows that different
plausible implementations of the same proposal can produce enough variation to reverse which ideas appear preferable,
complicating the use of individual experimental scores for research branching and memory (Ning et al., 2026b). A
more adversarial failure arises when an agent can influence the evidence by which its own success is judged. Recent
experiments across autonomous research tasks find that agents can exploit evaluation procedures and adapt their
strategies to repeated reviewer feedback, motivating evaluation criteria and confirmatory measurements that remain
outside the producing agent’s control (Huang et al., 2026d). The long feedback cycles of biology, chemistry, and
materials science amplify these risks: by the time an error is visible, the agent may already have consumed weeks of
experimental effort or propagated an unsupported claim into downstream artifacts. For this reason, evaluation must also
inspect the evidence chain that connects an agent’s final claims to its intermediate decisions, executions, measurements,
and failed alternatives. Recent work on discovery certification makes this distinction explicit by separating attainment of
a target score from evidence that the claimed discovery is attributable to the agent’s research process, using controlled
recovery and feedback tests with independently verifiable evidence (Ning et al., 2026a).
Recent developments in mathematics and biology make these questions increasingly concrete outside controlled
AutoResearch benchmarks. In mathematics, frontier AI systems have begun to produce results on longstanding open
problems: OpenAI reported a series of advances across mathematics and theoretical computer science and subsequently
released an AI-generated proposed resolution of the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize problem together with a Lean
formalization (OpenAI, 2026e,d). The latter was produced through a large-scale multi-agent search in which thousands
of concurrent agents explored and exchanged candidate approaches before the resulting argument was formalized and
checked. The ultimate mathematical status and significance of such results remain subject to scrutiny, but their rapid
emergence has already prompted a broader debate over what progress in mathematics should optimize for. A public
declaration initially signed by 25 Fields Medalists argued that treating the solution of prominent open problems as the
objective of AI-assisted mathematics risks mistaking a proxy for the broader goals of mathematical research, which
also include developing conceptual understanding, useful questions and methods, attribution, and a community capable
of interpreting and extending the resulting knowledge (A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics, 2026). This
view is not universal, and other mathematicians have argued that AI-mediated and machine-verified mathematics can
become another legitimate extension of how mathematical knowledge is produced. The debate nevertheless illustrates
a distinction that becomes more important, rather than less, as execution and verification improve: a verified result
need not by itself exhaust the scientific value of the process that produced it. Mathematics therefore provides an
instructive limiting case for AutoResearch—as the cost of generating and, in formally specified settings, mechanically
checking candidate results falls, the scarce resource can shift toward selecting worthwhile questions, interpreting results,
establishing provenance, and integrating them into cumulative scientific knowledge.
Biology exposes a complementary difficulty because its oracle ultimately remains physical. Recent systems increasingly
couple computational hypothesis generation to real-world experimentation: Co-Scientist has been evaluated in lab-in-
the-loop workflows spanning materials synthesis and biological phenotype prediction (Schmidgall et al., 2026), while
Anthropic has reported an agentic search over biological sequence space that identified a previously uncharacterized
enzyme system associated with CRISPR-like repeat arrays and subjected parts of the resulting hypothesis to wet-lab
testing (Anthropic, 2026c). The latter remains an early result: the observed repeat-associated system has properties
suggestive of an interesting biological mechanism, but its function and broader significance require further experimental
characterization. More generally, such episodes make questions of novelty, provenance, attribution, and independent
validation increasingly salient when agents search scientific literature and data, formulate hypotheses, and participate
in their experimental validation. These questions should not be taken to prejudge particular scientific or priority
claims; rather, they illustrate why increasingly autonomous discovery requires transparent provenance and independent
experimental evidence in addition to capable hypothesis generation. Together, the mathematics and biology cases expose
complementary limits of execution-centric AutoResearch: even where correctness can increasingly be mechanically
checked, scientific value is not exhausted by verification, while in empirical science the evidence itself remains costly,
partial, and contestable.

These considerations shift evaluation from raw initiative to the calibration and accountability of initiative. A mature
research agent should know when to generate ideas, when to ask for clarification, when not to spend resources, when to
distrust an oracle, and when existing measurements cannot adjudicate the question. Open directions include benchmarks
for experiment refusal and clarification, protocols for preregistered agent-generated studies, evidence-chain audits for
AI-produced scientific claims, auditable research-state artifacts that preserve failed branches and decision rationales, and
measurement-aware agents that design new assays, probes, simulations, or diagnostic benchmarks when the current
observable state space is inadequate. In AutoResearch, mature proactiveness is not the ability to do more science
unaided, but the ability to ask better questions, choose better tests, expose the evidence behind its claims, and leave
behind a research state that others can verify, fork, and extend.

6.7      Agents for Smart Home
The smart home is the private, consumer end of proactive deployment: one household, a few co-present occupants, and
an always-on fabric of appliances, speakers, and sensors that observes daily life at close range and acts on it over minutes
and days. Standing goals such as comfort, safety, and energy thrift are rarely restated, so initiative must come from the
agent; yet every unsolicited act lands on a co-present person in a private space, so the felt costs of error are intrusion,
annoyance, and lost trust rather than systemic harm. The stakeholders are correspondingly intimate: occupants, family
members, and caregivers, with platform vendors and utilities in the background, and consumer privacy as the governing
regulatory constraint.
Agents for smart home have seen wide deployment, yet most systems still wait to be asked. What ships at scale
today is condition-triggered scene automation: user-authored rules of the form “when this, then that” that the platform
merely executes. The deployed frontier is acceptance-gated, single-step anticipation: Alexa Hunches flags potentially
forgotten actions and supports automatic actions, such as locking a door or turning off a light. In 2022, Amazon reported
that features including Hunches and Routines initiated roughly one in four Alexa smart-home interactions without a
spoken request (Eberhardt, 2022). The next level, toward which research systems point, is learned-preference ambient
orchestration under standing objectives, such as comfort and energy budgets that the agent manages continuously without
per-rule authoring; the ultimate level is household-scale agenda ownership with calibrated interruption. The binding
constraint on this progression is not anticipation but arbitration, that is, knowing whether, when, and how strongly an
intervention will be welcome (§4.4). Relative to the other verticals in this section, the home thus shows the broadest
consumer deployment of proactivity and among the shallowest, a mirror image of autonomous research, whose agents
are autonomy-deep but barely deployed. Table 9 summarizes selected approaches to household orchestration, routine
synthesis, predictive heating, and safety monitoring.




                                                                                                                                           80
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


6.7.1   Ambient Household Orchestration
The flagship use case is coordinating many devices toward goals the occupant states vaguely or not at all. Its deployed
anchor is Alexa Hunches, which learns deep device and deep home embeddings as a world model over the household’s
device states and gates each candidate action on a learned model of whether the user will accept it (Eberhardt, 2022).
Research systems put LLM agents (Wang et al., 2024c) on the same stage: Sasha maps under-specified goals such as
“make it cozy” onto whatever devices the home contains (King et al., 2024), SAGE grounds open-ended requests in
verifiable device actions (Rivkin et al., 2024), and LLMind, Penetrative AI, and IoT-LLM reason directly over raw sensor
and device signals (Cui et al., 2023a; Xu et al., 2024c; An et al., 2025). A complementary line converts continuous
context into anticipated tasks so the agent offers help before being asked: Lu et al. (2025a) learn from real activity traces
with a reward model as a proxy for user acceptance, and ProAgent decides in the wild, from on-demand sensory context,
when assistance is worth initiating (Yang et al., 2025a).

6.7.2   Trigger-Action Automation and Routine Synthesis
Trigger-action programming (TAP) is the canonical way households encode standing policy, from IFTTT recipes to
vendor routines (Ur et al., 2014; Mi et al., 2017). Its known failure modes, inaccurate mental models and buggy rules
(Huang & Cakmak, 2015; Brackenbury et al., 2019), motivated rule recommendation and end-user debugging aids
(Corno et al., 2019b,a). Proactive agents move the home from executing rules to authoring them: AutoTap synthesizes
automations from stated properties (Zhang et al., 2019), Trace2TAP proposes them from observed behavior traces
(Zhang et al., 2020a), and LLM-based systems now generate, contextualize, and repair routines in situ (Badalov & Yoon,
2026; Giudici et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026b). Routine synthesis is the clearest instance of the agenda shifting from user
to agent (§4.3) while the user retains veto power by editing the proposed rule.

6.7.3   Energy and Comfort Management
Household energy rewards anticipation because HVAC and appliances carry thermal and temporal inertia. Scott et al.
(2011) showed early that occupancy-predictive heating outperforms fixed schedules; nonintrusive load monitoring gives
the agent appliance-level visibility from a single meter (Kelly & Knottenbelt, 2015); and deep reinforcement learning
schedules loads against dynamic prices and comfort constraints (Yu et al., 2020). In deployment terms this is the most
automated corner of the home: pre-conditioning and load shifting act silently under a standing comfort and cost budget,
previewing the standing-objective orchestration the rest of the home still lacks.

6.7.4   Health Monitoring and Aging in Place
Ambient assisted living is where home proactivity carries the highest stakes. Its perceptual base is two decades of
sensor-based human activity recognition, from probabilistic models in instrumented homes (van Kasteren et al., 2008) to
deep, multimodal, and wearable recognizers (Ordóñez & Roggen, 2016; Yao et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2021; Bouchabou
et al., 2021; Ni et al., 2024) and vision-based fall detection (Alam et al., 2022). The proactive trigger is typically a
deviation from a personal baseline rather than a rule: anomaly detection over the daily routines of older adults living
alone supplies the alarm (Shahid et al., 2022). Agentic systems close the loop with continuous monitoring, check-ins,
and autonomous escalation to caregivers (Khalil et al., 2025; Choi et al., 2025), and embodied assistants anticipate
which objects an occupant will need from a spatio-temporal model of the home (Patel & Chernova, 2022). Because the
monitored population is vulnerable, privacy-preserving learning of activity predictors is part of the use case rather than
an afterthought (Zehtabian et al., 2021).

6.7.5   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Evaluation has matured from one-off user studies to purpose-built benchmarks: SimuHome stresses proactive intent
inference, physical-limit checks, and temporal scheduling in a Matter-compliant simulator whose policies transfer to
real devices (Seo et al., 2025), and PersonalHomeBench scores reactive and proactive behavior under personalized,
multimodal observation (Bharadwaj et al., 2026) (§5). The open challenges are less perceptual than social. First,
timing and agency: human-factors studies converge on the finding that ill-timed initiative distracts and annoys, with
interruptibility depending on the occupant’s activity, engagement, and mood (Wei et al., 2022a,b), and the acceptable
level of initiative is itself user- and context-dependent (Reicherts et al., 2021; Zargham et al., 2022) (§4.4.3). Low-
commitment initiative, asking or suggesting rather than acting silently, better preserves user agency (Oh et al., 2024;

Deng et al., 2024b), and longitudinal deployment shows adoption hinges on the agent fitting into, rather than overriding,

and hubs under persistent suspicion (Lau et al., 2018; Zheng et al., 2018; Malkin et al., 2019; Abdi et al., 2019).
Third, the household is plural: most systems model a single principal, while real homes contain several people with
conflicting preferences and asymmetric authority, a largely unsolved arbitration problem. The direction of travel is from
acceptance-gated single actions toward standing-objective orchestration, which will require acceptance models that
generalize across routines, preference learning that spans household members, and interruption budgets audited over
weeks rather than judged per event (§7).

6.8     Agents for Smart City
The city swaps the home’s intimacy for scale: municipal infrastructure serving millions, operated by agencies and
utilities, observed through traffic, mobility, environmental, and event telemetry, and governed publicly over horizons
that stretch from signal cycles to multi-year plans. There is no single principal; consequences are diffuse, delayed, and
contestable, and legitimacy is a matter of public accountability rather than personal preference. The technical substrate
is the urban-computing tradition (Zheng et al., 2014): spatio-temporal deep networks that forecast citywide flows, traffic,
and crime (Zhang et al., 2017; Li et al., 2018; Yu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2019; Huang et al., 2018; Xia et al., 2021),
lately consolidated by urban foundation models and LLM interfaces such as UrbanGPT (Li et al., 2024d; Zhang et al.,
2026f; Han et al., 2025b).
Unlike agents for smart home (§6.7), agents for smart city are predominantly sensor-triggered alerting for human
operators, dashboards that flag congestion, pollution, or hazards and leave the response to control rooms. The strongest
deployed proactivity is early warning at planetary scale, flood and earthquake forecasts pushed directly to affected
populations, which is anticipation without actuation. The research frontier is predict-then-act control validated largely
in simulation, where agents pre-time signals, rebalance fleets, and shape electrical loads. The next level is agent-
driven anticipatory infrastructure operations that pre-position resources before disruptions cascade, held under granted,
supervised, and revocable authority; the ultimate level is coordination across networks, where traffic, energy, and
emergency agents negotiate rather than optimize in silos. Extending this progression to closed-loop municipal action
requires resolving diffuse authority and public accountability (§7.2). Table 10 summarizes selected approaches to traffic
control, energy management, early warning, emergency planning, and urban simulation.




                                                                                                                                                82
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


6.8.1   Traffic and Mobility Orchestration
Signal control is the canonical testbed. Deep and multi-agent reinforcement learning agents learn to pre-empt congestion
rather than react to it, scaling from single intersections (Wei et al., 2018) to network-level coordination (Wei et al.,
2019b), pressure-based and thousand-light control (Wei et al., 2019a; Chen et al., 2020), and meta-learned transfer
across intersections (Zang et al., 2020); LLMLight now casts the language model itself as the signal-control agent
(Lai et al., 2023), while TrafficGPT and TransGPT let operators steer traffic foundation models through dialogue
(Zhang et al., 2024f; Wang et al., 2024e). On the mobility side, dispatch and repositioning agents act ahead of demand:
reinforcement-learned order dispatching and fleet management in ride-hailing (Xu et al., 2018; Lin et al., 2018; Li
et al., 2019; Jin et al., 2019; Al-Abbasi et al., 2019) and model-predictive and graph-learned rebalancing of autonomous
mobility-on-demand (Iglesias et al., 2018; Gammelli et al., 2021).

6.8.2   Grid and Utility Operations
Urban energy agents reshape demand before peaks arrive. Reinforcement-learned demand response is a mature literature
(Vázquez-Canteli & Nagy, 2019), given a shared testbed by CityLearn, which coordinates load shaping across building
portfolios (Vázquez-Canteli et al., 2020); multi-agent controllers manage residential loads on fast timescales (Mai et al.,
2023; Shojaeighadikolaei et al., 2022) and schedule electric-vehicle charging ahead of grid stress (Park & Moon, 2022).
Water, road maintenance, and other utility networks remain comparatively agent-poor, an asymmetry we return to below.

6.8.3   Environmental and Public-Health Early Warning
Field sensing coupled to forecasting is the city’s most consequential deployed proactivity. Google’s global flood
model anticipates extreme riverine floods in ungauged basins and pushes warnings days ahead across dozens of
countries (Nearing et al., 2024), and deep models predict wildfire risk from remote-sensing and environmental data
(Xu et al., 2024d) and interpolate and forecast citywide air pollution (Le et al., 2020). On the public-health side,
generative-agent epidemic models anticipate contagion dynamics jointly with behavioral response (Williams et al., 2023).
Characteristically, all of these stop at the alert: anticipation is delivered to humans, and actuation remains institutional.

6.8.4   Emergency Response and Civic Coordination
Agentic systems are beginning to convert warnings into coordinated response, today as human-supervised decision
support rather than deployed responders. Geospatially grounded LLM agents turn live wildfire detections into resource-
allocation recommendations (Chen et al., 2025g); EpiPlanAgent drafts and validates epidemic response plans with
practitioners in the loop (Mao et al., 2025), and LLM agents act as policymakers in simulated epidemics (Aoki &
Ghaffarzadegan, 2026); CrisisSense-LLM distills situational awareness from disaster social media (Yin et al., 2024a);
and vision papers sketch disaster-management architectures that chain hazard early warning to risk analytics and
coordinated response (Li et al., 2025a). High inaction costs license more initiative here than anywhere else in the city,
but consequences are contestable enough that authority must remain granted, supervised, and revocable: proactiveness
supplies initiative, not authority (Chan et al., 2023; Kasirzadeh & Gabriel, 2025).

6.8.5   Urban Simulation and Digital Twins
Where the relevant futures cannot be observed, planners rehearse interventions in silico (§4.2.4). Classical agent-based
modeling (Bonabeau, 2002) and transport microsimulation (Horni et al., 2016) are being refounded on generative agents
(Park et al., 2023): OpenCity scales LLM-driven urban simulation (Yan et al., 2024), AgentSociety simulates more than
ten thousand LLM-driven residents (Piao et al., 2025), UGI proposes a foundational platform for embodied city agents
(Xu et al., 2023), CitySim and GATSim model urban behavior and mobility with generative agents (Bougie & Watanabe,
2025; Liu et al., 2025c), and generative AI is likewise entering urban digital twins (Xu et al., 2024b). For proactive
operations these simulators are the counterfactual engine: policies for signals, fleets, and emergency plans are tested
against synthetic populations before touching the street.

6.8.6   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Evaluation is the city’s soft spot. Predict-then-act agents are overwhelmingly validated in simulators, CityLearn for
energy (Vázquez-Canteli et al., 2020) and MATSim-style platforms for mobility (Horni et al., 2016), and the sim-to-real


                                                                                                                          83
                                                    Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


gap remains largely uncrossed: few signal-control or rebalancing policies in this literature have faced a real network
with liability attached. Generative-agent simulators promise richer counterfactuals but are themselves unvalidated
instruments, so a policy tested only against synthetic residents inherits their biases (Han et al., 2025b). Deployed
early-warning systems show the inverse strength, planetary reach with measurable lead times (Nearing et al., 2024), and
could anchor evaluation practice, since lead time, false-alarm rate, and coverage equity are metrics the field already trusts.
The deeper challenges are institutional. With no single principal, endorsement is a matter of governance rather than
preference: accountability, oversight, and contestability are deployment preconditions, not afterthoughts (Chan et al.,
2023; Kasirzadeh & Gabriel, 2025; Schmitz et al., 2025), and equity questions, such as whose neighborhood receives
pre-positioned resources, have no analogue in single-user domains. Proactive output therefore skews toward suggestion
over action. Open directions follow: staged autonomy that graduates agents from dashboards through recommendations
to bounded actuation with automatic rollback; standing fairness audits of proactive allocation; extension to under-served
utility networks such as water and road maintenance; and cross-network coordination so that traffic, energy, and
emergency agents stop optimizing in silos. How initiative can move safely from calibrated suggestion to trustworthy
action is taken up in §7.

Proactive agents for healthcare span clinical intake, diagnosis, treatment, follow-up, patient monitoring, and biomedical
research. Across these settings, care often needs to advance before a patient or clinician explicitly asks for the next
action. Patients may omit relevant information, new test results may alter an earlier assessment, and unresolved actions
or subtle deterioration may require attention before the next consultation. These situations create opportunities for
agents to act proactively by identifying what information, expertise, or follow-up is needed as a case evolves.
Current healthcare agents address some of these needs, but their proactiveness is still concentrated within active tasks or
episodes of care. Once a case is underway, they can seek missing evidence, ask follow-up questions, consult specialists,


                                                                                                                                               84
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


invoke medical tools, and organize subsequent steps. Some systems also monitor evolving records or pursue biomedical
hypotheses over time, although their ability to sustain such behavior across visits remains limited. More longitudinal
forms of proactiveness would require agents to preserve unresolved concerns, connect later evidence to earlier decisions,
and recognize when a change warrants renewed clinical attention. These capabilities expand when and how an agent
contributes to care, while diagnostic and therapeutic authority remains with clinicians.
We examine this development through four connected workflows. Clinical history taking concerns proactive evidence
acquisition. Multi-specialist deliberation extends proactiveness to the selection and coordination of expertise. Longitudi-
nal care coordination requires agents to maintain unfinished clinical work over time, while continuous monitoring and
biomedical discovery move toward the proactive formation of new clinical or scientific objectives. Table 11 compares
selected systems and benchmarks across these workflows using the six mechanisms.

6.9.1   Clinical History Taking and Iterative Anamnesis
The first form of clinical proactiveness is deciding what must be learned before a diagnosis can be trusted. An initial
patient account rarely includes every symptom, prior condition, medication, laboratory finding, demographic factor, or
temporal detail needed for a reliable assessment. An agent that responds only to the presented information may therefore
answer an underspecified version of the clinical problem. Proactive history taking requires it to identify which missing
evidence could change the assessment and continue the interaction until the case is sufficiently specified.
Existing systems increasingly place parts of this evidence-gathering process under agent control. Medical consultation
agents (Ren et al., 2025) maintain dialogue and patient-history information across an encounter, allowing later questions
to depend on what has already been learned rather than treating each turn independently. In MedAgentSim (Almansoori
et al., 2025), doctor agents interact with simulated patients and request examinations or imaging as additional evidence
becomes necessary, extending information acquisition beyond conversational questioning alone. MeDxAgent (Sanghvi
et al., 2026) ties this process more directly to diagnostic uncertainty by using evolving differential diagnoses to guide
targeted follow-up questions. Agent Hospital (Li et al., 2024b) embeds similar information seeking within a broader
simulated clinical process, where consultation and examination jointly determine what evidence becomes available
before diagnosis. Together with these interaction-oriented systems, the progression is toward agents that shape the
diagnostic evidence they reason over, rather than accepting the initial case description as fixed.
The MINT benchmark (Fang et al., 2026a) highlights a complementary requirement: controlling when a model commits
to a diagnosis as evidence accumulates. In MINT, clinical evidence is supplied incrementally by the evaluation protocol
rather than actively requested by the model, and at each turn the model may provide a diagnostic answer or continue to
hold its response. The benchmark shows that models often commit before sufficient evidence has been observed, can
later self-correct as additional evidence arrives, and are particularly susceptible to premature commitment when salient
evidence such as laboratory findings appears early. MINT therefore evaluates commitment timing rather than proactive
evidence acquisition itself, while showing why a diagnostic agent that actively gathers evidence must also know when
the available information is sufficient to justify an answer.

6.9.2   Multi-Specialist Deliberation and Case Conferencing
Even thorough evidence collection may leave uncertainty that cannot be resolved from a single clinical perspective.
Imaging, pathology, pharmacology, surgery, and disease-specific practice can yield different interpretations of the same
case. Proactiveness at this stage requires the agent to recognize that the current reasoning process lacks the expertise
needed to proceed and to broaden the deliberation before the case converges prematurely (Liu et al., 2023d; Gan et al.,
2025).
MedAgents (Tang et al., 2023) brings multiple medical experts into iterative discussion and consensus formation,
moving specialist consultation into the reasoning process rather than requiring each opinion to be solicited separately.
MDAgents (Kim et al., 2024c) adds another layer of control by adapting between individual and collaborative rea-
soning according to estimated case complexity, so the amount of expertise involved can vary with the case itself.
MedAide (Wei et al., 2024) coordinates specialized medical agents according to different clinical intents, emphasizing
how heterogeneous expertise can be assembled around the needs of a consultation. MedChat (Liu et al., 2025b) similarly
combines role-specific LLM agents and specialized vision models under a directing agent, making the integration of
multimodal clinical perspectives part of the agentic workflow. When consensus is difficult, MACD (Li et al., 2025d)
uses iterative consultation and evaluation to continue deliberation rather than accepting the first converged answer.


                                                                                                                        85
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


MedCoAct (Zheng et al., 2025b) coordinates doctor and pharmacist agents while using confidence to regulate their
interaction, linking the intensity of collaboration to uncertainty in the current reasoning process. MediHive (Wang &
Yang, 2026) reduces advance specification further by allowing agents to assume specialized roles and debate divergent
conclusions. MMedAgent-RL (Xia et al., 2025) learns to coordinate multimodal specialist inputs through triage and
referral, shifting part of the decision over where a case should be routed into the learned policy itself.
The scope of this coordination is usually fixed in advance. Most frameworks receive a predefined case, objective, and set
of specialist roles. They can manage deliberation after it has been configured, but seldom decide that another specialty
is needed, that the current consultation structure is inadequate, or that later evidence warrants reopening an earlier
consensus. Current systems are therefore more mature at proactively conducting multi-specialist reasoning than at
determining when and how such reasoning should be initiated.

6.9.3   Longitudinal Care Coordination
After a diagnosis or treatment plan has been produced, the source of risk shifts from incomplete reasoning to incomplete
follow-through. Tests must be completed, referrals attended, reports reviewed, treatments initiated, and patient responses
reassessed. Because these actions are distributed across visits and clinical services, an appropriate recommendation
may still fail when one step is delayed, forgotten, or disconnected from later evidence. Proactive support must therefore
preserve the unfinished state of care instead of treating the production of a plan as the end of the task.
Several medical agents already reduce the need to specify every intermediate step within an active clinical episode.
MMedAgent (Li et al., 2024a) plans over multiple medical tools and integrates their outputs, giving the agent control
over which operations are needed to advance the assigned task. MedAgent-Pro (Wang et al., 2026o) structures diagnostic
reasoning hierarchically and delegates multimodal evidence analysis to specialized tools, extending this control from tool
selection to the organization of a multi-step diagnostic workflow. MedAgentBench (Jiang et al., 2025) evaluates agents in
an EHR environment on patient-specific clinical tasks that require interaction with medical-record systems, providing a
setting for assessing agentic execution in operational workflows. MRGAgents (Wang et al., 2025c) distributes radiology
report generation across disease-specialized agents, while radiology reasoning agents (Yi et al., 2025) coordinate
retrieval, visual interpretation, drafting, refinement, and synthesis as connected stages rather than isolated prompts.
TheraAgent (Li et al., 2026c) applies a related idea to treatment planning, repeatedly evaluating and refining a proposed
therapy instead of treating the first generated plan as complete. Across these settings, current proactiveness is strongest
in advancing an already established clinical objective through the steps needed to complete it.
Their involvement, however, usually ends with the current case or episode. After producing a plan or report, the
agent rarely checks whether the proposed action occurred or whether later evidence still supports the original decision.
Longitudinal proactiveness would require persistent links among recommendations, pending tests, referrals, treatments,
and subsequent observations. Such continuity would allow the agent to recover unfinished care, detect deviations from
the expected trajectory, and return the case to clinical attention before delay becomes consequential.

6.9.4   Continuous Patient Monitoring and Biomedical Hypothesis Discovery
Longitudinal coordination maintains an objective that has already been established. A further expansion of proactiveness
occurs when the agent must recognize that a new objective has emerged. Changes in laboratory trends, clinical
notes, medication exposure, or patient-generated signals may indicate deterioration before a clinician requests another
assessment. Continuous monitoring can reduce this delay by detecting meaningful changes and deciding whether they
justify a new clinical concern.
irAE-Agent (Gallifant et al., 2025) searches clinical notes for immune-related adverse events, allowing evidence
appearing in the record itself to surface a potential complication that may require further attention. AgentRx (Al Jorf
& Shamout, 2026) evaluates LLM-based agents on multimodal clinical risk prediction using heterogeneous patient
information. irAE-Agent directly illustrates how newly observed evidence can surface a potential reason for further
clinical work, while AgentRx evaluates the ability of agentic systems to integrate patient information for risk prediction.
Their value depends on calibrated intervention. Excessive alerts transfer the interpretive burden back to clinicians and
may obscure the few events that require action. Useful proactive monitoring therefore depends on distinguishing changes
that warrant escalation from those that do not.
Biomedical research presents a related transition from pursuing an assigned objective to expanding it. DrugAgent (Liu


                                                                                                                        86
                                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


et al., 2024d) automates machine-learning programming for drug-discovery tasks through agentic planning and tool use,
allowing a broad research objective to be carried forward through multiple scientific operations. PharmaSwarm (Song
et al., 2025a) distributes pharmaceutical research across collaborating agents, so candidate directions can be examined
from multiple functional perspectives without each step being separately specified by the researcher. STELLA (Jin
et al., 2026) supports longer-horizon scientific exploration through self-evolving reasoning templates and dynamically
constructed tools as experience accumulates. AgentD (Ock et al., 2025) similarly integrates biomedical retrieval,
question answering, molecular generation, property prediction and refinement, and structure generation within an agentic
drug-discovery workflow. These systems can therefore automate extended parts of scientific exploration, with some
systems able to surface directions that a researcher did not enumerate in advance. Their search spaces, evaluation criteria,
and high-level goals are still largely supplied by humans. Proactive scientific discovery remains less developed when the
agent must decide that accumulated evidence justifies a new hypothesis or a change in research direction.

6.9.5     Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Healthcare agents have progressed from proactive evidence collection (Li et al., 2024b; Almansoori et al., 2025; Ren
et al., 2025; Sanghvi et al., 2026) to proactive coordination of clinical expertise (Wei et al., 2024; Tang et al., 2023;
Kim et al., 2024c; Liu et al., 2025b; Li et al., 2025d; Zheng et al., 2025b; Wang & Yang, 2026), proactive workflow
execution (Li et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2025b; Wang et al., 2025c; Yi et al., 2025), and continuous risk detection or
biomedical exploration (Gallifant et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2024d; Jin et al., 2026). Across this progression, systems have
become increasingly capable of deciding what to do next once a case or objective is active. They remain less reliable at
maintaining responsibility across interruptions, reopening dormant issues, and forming new objectives from changes
that no user has yet raised. Healthcare proactiveness is therefore relatively mature within consultations and predefined
workflows, while longitudinal and objective-forming proactiveness remains at an early stage.
Evaluation should distinguish these levels of capability. Evidence-gathering agents should be assessed on whether they
ask necessary questions before concluding; deliberative systems on whether they involve relevant expertise and expose
unresolved disagreement; care-coordination agents on whether they recover unfinished actions; and monitoring systems
on whether they detect emerging risks without creating excessive burden. Prospective and cross-institutional validation
is needed to determine whether these behaviors remain reliable across clinical settings. As agents take on a larger role in
initiating and sustaining clinical work, evaluation must also verify that their recommendations remain reviewable and
that the division between proactive support and clinician authority is preserved.

Legal practice typically encompasses investigating facts and authorities, developing and testing legal positions, preparing
documents, coordinating matters, and identifying potential violations or exposure. Much of this work cannot be


                                                                                                                                                                87
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


determined at the outset, as the legal agenda itself changes with the matter. For example, a new fact may alter the
applicable legal theory, an opposing interpretation may require additional evidence, and a revised agreement may create
new procedural or compliance obligations. Legal assistance therefore becomes proactive when it can recognize that such
developments have created new work before the client or attorney explicitly requests it.
Current legal agents show meaningful proactiveness once a legal issue has already entered the agenda. They can extend
incomplete research, introduce unrequested counterarguments, select intermediate workflow actions, and identify risks
in submitted materials. Their main limitation is that the scope of legally relevant work is still largely inherited from
the user. Further progress depends on recognizing when interactions among facts, rules, documents, and procedural
developments create a new obligation, claim, vulnerability, or risk. Such recognition requires an evolving representation
of the matter through which the agent can revise what deserves investigation, while attorneys retain authority over legal
judgment and consequential action.
We examine how far this transition has progressed across legal research and evidence gathering, argument stress-testing
and adversarial review, legal matter management and workflow execution, and compliance monitoring and legal-risk
anticipation. Table 12 compares selected legal systems across these applications using the six mechanisms.

6.10.1   Legal Research and Evidence Gathering
The proactive challenge in legal research begins before an authority is retrieved. An initial inquiry may omit material
facts, assume an incorrect legal category, or overlook a jurisdictional issue that changes which authorities apply. When
these defects remain hidden, additional retrieval may strengthen an answer without correcting the question on which it is
based. A legal research agent therefore needs to assess whether the current framing and evidentiary record are sufficient,
identify what remains unresolved, and direct further investigation toward those gaps.
Recent systems have made clear progress toward this form of proactiveness through retrieval, planning, and verification.
LegalAgentBench (Li et al., 2025b) evaluates agents on multi-step legal tasks that require reasoning over real-world
legal corpora and selecting among external tools, making both tool use and intermediate research progress observable. L-
MARS (Wang & Yuan, 2025) more directly implements iterative legal research: it decomposes a query into subproblems,
searches heterogeneous legal sources, and uses a judge agent to assess evidentiary sufficiency, jurisdiction, and
temporal validity before deciding whether further retrieval is needed. CourtReasoner (Han et al., 2025d) examines a
complementary capability by evaluating whether agents can construct goal-oriented judicial analyses and argue both
sides of a dispute, testing how legal authorities are assembled into support for competing positions. Deterministic
Legal Agents (de Martim, 2025) instead structures research over temporal legal knowledge graphs, allowing an agent
to plan and execute point-in-time retrieval, context reconstruction, provenance tracing, and impact analysis through
auditable primitives. For long legal agreements, PAKTON (Raptopoulos et al., 2025) combines collaborative agents with
retrieval-augmented generation to locate relevant contractual material and produce grounded answers with improved
completeness and justification. These approaches move legal research beyond one-shot retrieval by giving agents
mechanisms to organize, inspect, and extend the evidence used within an active inquiry.
The current advance is therefore strongest in proactive gap filling within an active inquiry. The legal issue itself is still
generally selected and bounded by the user. Agents rarely conclude that new evidence has changed the relevant legal
category, that a different jurisdiction must be examined, or that an apparently completed inquiry should be reopened. A
more developed research agent would preserve connections among facts, claims, authorities, and unresolved questions
across the matter. It could then revise the research agenda when those connections change, moving from self-directed
retrieval toward proactive identification of what now requires legal investigation.

6.10.2   Argument Stress-Testing and Adversarial Review
Legal positions are developed in anticipation of parties who may challenge their facts, assumptions, and interpretation
of authority. Users can produce a coherent argument while overlooking the objection most likely to affect its practical
viability. If that objection is discovered only when raised by opposing counsel, a court, or a regulator, opportunities
to collect evidence or revise the position may already be limited. Anticipating consequential challenges is therefore a
distinct form of legal proactiveness because it brings future scrutiny into present preparation.
Legal agents support adversarial review through several forms of role separation, critique, and simulated opposition.
ChatLaw (Cui et al., 2023b) organizes legal assistance through a multi-agent architecture and law-firm-inspired operating


                                                                                                                          88
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


procedures, introducing structured intermediate roles rather than relying on a single response. LawLuo (Sun et al.,
2024a) makes this internal review more explicit through receptionist, lawyer, secretary, and boss agents, with the boss
agent evaluating the work produced during multi-round consultation. Courtroom simulation provides a more directly
adversarial setting. AgentsCourt (He et al., 2024) combines court debate, legal-resource retrieval, and subsequent
decision refinement, while AgentCourt (Chen et al., 2025a) uses structured adversarial interactions to evolve lawyer
agents and their legal knowledge. SimCourt (Zhang et al., 2026c) organizes agent interaction around the procedural
structure of Chinese trials and evaluates both the simulated procedure and its contribution to judgment prediction.
SAMVAD (Devadiga et al., 2025) assigns agents to judicial, prosecution, defense, and adjudication roles and lets them
deliberate iteratively over case facts and retrieved legal material. LegalSim (Badhe, 2025) shifts attention from substantive
argument to procedural strategy, allowing opposing agents to select actions such as discovery requests and motions and
thereby exposing exploitative sequences that emerge during adversarial proceedings. Debate-Feedback (Chen et al.,
2025f) uses a more compact debate structure for legal judgment prediction, combining competing agent reasoning
with reliability evaluation. MASLegalBench (Jing et al., 2025), rather than introducing another courtroom system,
evaluates role-based multi-agent configurations on deductive legal reasoning under GDPR, providing a way to test
whether decomposition and specialization actually improve collaborative legal analysis.
This line of work has developed proactive challenge generation more than proactive challenge management. Most
systems broaden the argument set within a predefined dispute, but provide limited guidance on which objection should
change the course of the matter. Stronger agents would connect each challenge to the available evidence, upcoming
decisions, and the consequences of leaving it unresolved. A plausible objection could then trigger factual verification,
document revision, or investigation of an alternative legal theory. The next stage is therefore selective and consequential
anticipation, in which adversarial review creates and prioritizes further legal work rather than simply generating more
arguments.

6.10.3   Legal Matter Management and Workflow Execution
Legal matters progress through dependencies among documents, participants, decisions, and procedural events. Contract
review may move through extraction, comparison, negotiation, revision, and approval. Patent preparation may alternate
between prior-art research, claim drafting, and technical verification. Due diligence may uncover facts that expand the
scope of later review. Since the completion or revision of one component can change what should happen elsewhere,
proactive matter management requires the workflow to adapt as the legal state evolves.
Recent systems automate different portions of legal workflows once an objective has been specified. LAW (Watson et al.,
2025) orchestrates domain-specific tools and text agents to answer questions over custody and fund-services contracts,
including tasks that require intermediate operations such as computing contractual dates. PAKTON (Raptopoulos et al.,
2025) similarly coordinates multiple agents and retrieval over long legal agreements, but focuses on document review and
grounded question answering. Patent-oriented systems cover a broader range of workflow structures. PatentAgent (Wang
et al., 2024j) integrates modules for pharmaceutical patent question answering, chemical-structure extraction from
images, and core-structure identification, allowing different analysis operations to be invoked within a unified agent.
AutoPatent (Wang et al., 2024f) targets end-to-end document production through a planner, multiple writer agents, and
an examiner agent that jointly generate complete patents from initial drafts. AutoSpec (Shea & Yu, 2025) decomposes
patent-specification drafting into smaller subtasks and equips open-source models with tools specialized for each stage.
Legal consultation systems organize work around participants rather than document stages: ChatLaw (Cui et al., 2023b)
encodes standardized operating procedures modeled on legal-service workflows, while LawLuo (Sun et al., 2024a)
coordinates receptionist, lawyer, secretary, and supervisory agents across a multi-round consultation. MASER (Yue
et al., 2025) addresses orchestration from a different direction by using a multi-agent simulator to generate synthetic
data from interactive legal scenarios and introducing MILE to evaluate models in multi-stage legal interactions. Across
these designs, agents increasingly select intermediate actions, tools, and roles without requiring the user to specify every
step of the workflow.
Current progress, however, concerns proactive sequencing inside a workflow whose boundary has already been
established. Systems can decide how to complete an assignment, while rarely recognizing that a change elsewhere has
expanded or altered the assignment itself. Advancing toward proactive matter management requires persistent tracking
of factual assumptions, unresolved issues, document versions, approvals, and deadlines. A revised clause could initiate
renewed compliance review, new evidence could invalidate an earlier draft, and an approaching procedural event could
call for immediate preparation. The key development is from autonomously executing known dependencies to detecting


                                                                                                                          89
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


when the evolving matter has created new ones.

6.10.4   Compliance Monitoring and Legal-Risk Anticipation
Compliance monitoring comes closest to proactive discovery of new legal issues because the relevant problem may not yet
be part of the legal agenda. A regulatory amendment, modified data practice, or contractual change may appear routine
in isolation while their interaction creates an obligation or exposure that no user has recognized. Compliance-oriented
systems examine policies, contracts, data practices, and operational processes for such conflicts.
Recent compliance systems address different stages between assembling relevant organizational context and evaluating
it against legal requirements. PACT (Fang et al., 2025) provides the information layer by linking heterogeneous
enterprise artifacts in an embedding-based graph, allowing compliance agents to recover privacy-relevant connections
that would otherwise remain distributed across separate resources. Compliance Brain Assistant (Zhu et al., 2025b) builds
agentic investigation on top of enterprise compliance data: its full-agentic mode can invoke multiple tools and APIs to
discover additional context needed to answer complex compliance queries. For data pipelines, the approach proposed
by Videsjorden et al. (2025) decomposes compliance assessment into agent tasks that extract and label pipeline artifacts
and evaluate them against applicable legal requirements according to factors such as actor role and system risk. The
multi-agent legal verifier of Nguyen et al. (2025) divides data-transfer compliance checking into statutory interpretation,
business-context evaluation, and risk assessment before synthesizing a final determination. The governance-oriented
assistant of Mamalis et al. (2024) takes a narrower legal-information approach, grounding interactions in EU legislation
and GDPR case law to support queries over regulatory material. These systems therefore range from recovering
compliance-relevant context to carrying out structured legal verification, while continuous detection of newly emerging
risks remains less developed.
This application has progressed beyond work on a fully articulated legal question, yet its proactiveness is commonly
activated only after relevant materials have been submitted for inspection. Continuous risk anticipation would connect
legal developments with organizational changes over time, recognize when their interaction creates material exposure,
and decide whether the resulting issue warrants notification, investigation, or escalation.

6.10.5   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Agents for the law domain have shown promising signals of developing proactiveness: legal research agents can identify
missing support, adversarial systems can introduce unrequested challenges, workflow agents can select intermediate
actions, and compliance systems can surface risks in submitted materials. However, proactiveness is less developed
when the agent needs to revise the legal agenda itself. Few systems continuously connect changes in facts, authorities,
documents, and procedural status to recognize that a new legal issue has emerged or that an earlier issue now requires
different work.
Evaluation should therefore extend beyond answer accuracy and completion of predefined workflows. It should
test whether an agent detects legally consequential changes without an explicit request, identifies the work those
changes create, reopens analysis whose assumptions no longer hold, and prioritizes intervention according to urgency
and consequence. Both omission and over-intervention matter: missed issues may leave obligations, deadlines, or
vulnerabilities outside the legal agenda, while excessive escalation can overwhelm professional review. Legal agents
have thus developed meaningful proactiveness within identified issues, while proactive formation and revision of the
legal agenda remains the central frontier, with attorneys continuing to control legal judgment and consequential actions.

6.11     Agents for Education
Proactiveness has far-reaching implications in education because effective support often begins before learners can
recognize or articulate their own needs. Educational agents assist through explanation, feedback, assessment, resource
recommendation, and the organization of instructional activities, yet the value of these actions is determined by their
effects beyond the current interaction. A correct answer may conceal fragile understanding, while an incorrect one
may reflect a temporary slip, a missing prerequisite, or a misconception whose consequences will emerge only in later
material. Learners may know that they are struggling without knowing what has gone wrong, what support would
help, or when intervention would be most valuable. Support triggered only by explicit requests or observed failure may
therefore arrive too late to prevent downstream learning difficulties.
