This mismatch between observable behavior and future learning needs defines the central role of proactive educational
agents. By maintaining an evolving account of the learner, an agent can identify needs that have not been expressed,
anticipate where they may affect subsequent progress, and alter instruction before avoidable difficulties accumulate (Chu
et al., 2025). Because premature or excessive assistance can weaken independent reasoning during learning, effective
support also depends on recognizing when observation, delay, or withdrawal will better serve the learner’s development.
Research has developed these proactive capabilities at different temporal scales. Learner modeling and error analysis
support the early discovery of latent needs and, increasingly, the anticipation of how those needs may affect later learning.
Adaptive tutors use such evidence to regulate an ongoing activity without waiting for an explicit request. Current systems
have made substantial progress in diagnosing learner states, anticipating some future difficulties, and initiating local
pedagogical actions, but their behavior usually remains bounded by individual tasks, activities, or planning episodes. We
therefore review two main lines of work: learner-state diagnosis and anticipation, and adaptive tutoring and formative
scaffolding. Table 13 compares selected educational systems and supporting models across the six mechanisms.

6.11.1      Learner-State Diagnosis and Anticipation
The first step toward proactive educational support is recognizing a consequential need before the learner clearly reports
it. Dialogue, assignments, worked solutions, and interaction histories provide partial evidence about understanding.
Diagnosis therefore requires inferring the learner state underlying the observed behavior rather than treating correctness
alone as sufficient evidence. Moreover, the instructional significance of that evidence is rarely immediate. Thus beyond
identifying the learner’s current state, proactive support also requires judging whether an observed difficulty is likely to
affect later learning.
Knowledge-tracing methods address the corresponding inference problem in real interactions by identifying relevant
knowledge components in tutor–student dialogue and tracking student knowledge across the interaction (Scarlatos
et al., 2025a). Related multi-agent methods assess whether teachers’ responses in professional-development settings
demonstrate targeted mathematical content knowledge (Yang et al., 2024b). Student artifacts provide a complementary
source of evidence by revealing where understanding begins to break down. From Correctness to Comprehension (Zhang
et al., 2025h) combines multimodal student work with longitudinal records to support error classification and tailored
feedback, while AI-driven Virtual Teacher (Xu et al., 2025c) analyzes student solution drafts to identify and correct
mathematical errors. Multi-agent automatic feedback systems (Guo et al., 2024) and tools for open-ended responses (Ma-
telsky et al., 2023) further support assessment and feedback from richer forms of student work. SEFL (Zhang et al.,
2026d) complements these approaches by using teacher–student LLM agents to simulate assignment completion and
formative feedback, producing synthetic pairs of student work and corresponding feedback. MathAgent (Yan et al.,


                                                                                                                                                               91
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


2025a) localizes and categorizes errors in multimodal mathematical solutions, while ErrorRadar (Yan et al., 2026d)
benchmarks models on error-step identification and error categorization. AI-assisted CS50 teaching (Liu et al., 2024c)
and teachable-agent systems for programming education (Jin et al., 2024b) expose code-level misunderstandings, while
Closing the Loop (Nair et al., 2024) improves writing feedback by optimizing it against simulated student revisions, con-
testable essay-feedback frameworks (Hong et al., 2025) support interactive feedback and evaluation, and EvaAI (Lagakis
& Demetriadis, 2024) uses multiple agents for automated grading.
Diagnosis becomes more challenging when the relevant need has not yet produced an observable failure. A learner may
perform adequately on the current activity yet still be at risk of difficulty when a prerequisite is reused, when previously
learned material decays, or when the curriculum moves to a more demanding task. In such cases, present evidence must
support not only an estimate of current understanding but also an assessment of how that understanding may affect later
learning.
Recent work begins to provide this anticipatory capability through learner and classroom simulation. Classroom
Simulacra (Xu et al., 2025b) models students’ learning behavior from longitudinal interactions with course materials
and simulates how that behavior evolves over time. TeachTune (Jin et al., 2025) uses simulated students with prescribed
knowledge and motivational characteristics to help teachers review pedagogical conversational agents across different
learner profiles before deployment. StudentSim (Yang et al., 2026d) moves this line toward per-student specialization,
training individualized simulators from sparse per-learner records that simulate both a student’s own responses and
how those responses change under tutor guidance; as a proof of concept, it further uses the simulator as a reward for
reinforcement-learning-based tutor improvement. Related systems explore simulation for teacher preparation: Evelyn
AI (Bhowmik et al., 2024) provides an LLM-powered virtual student with whom pre-service teachers can practice,
while LLM-enhanced teaching simulations (Zheng et al., 2024b) investigate simulation-based teacher training and the
authenticity of these simulated experiences. Although these systems do not themselves plan a learner’s future trajectory,
they make it possible to examine learner responses and instructional strategies before corresponding real interactions
occur.
Other work connects such anticipation more directly to instructional planning. (Hu et al., 2025a) simulate teacher–
student interactions from an existing teaching plan, generate reflections from the simulated process, and use them to
refine the plan before classroom use. Here, anticipated problems can change future instruction before real students
encounter them. ProPACT (Golrang et al., 2026) uses multimodal measures of shared attention and mental effort to
forecast emerging suboptimal states in collaborative learning and trigger adaptive scaffolds before coordination breaks
down.
Current systems therefore provide substantial support for estimating learner states and, increasingly, for anticipating
how those states may affect subsequent learning. However, these capabilities usually remain bounded to particular
interactions, activities, or planning episodes. A more general proactive educational agent would need to maintain
learner-relevant information over time, track whether predicted needs remain unresolved, and update its assessment as
new evidence arrives. Such continuity would provide a stronger basis for deciding when and how subsequent pedagogical
actions should be taken.

6.11.2   Intervention: What should the system do now?
Once a potential need has been identified, the next stage of proactiveness concerns whether and how the tutoring agent
should alter the current learning process. The same visible learners’ difficulty can support different decisions. A learner
who is productively exploring may benefit from additional time, whereas another learner may be repeating an ineffective
strategy that will make later steps harder. The agent therefore needs to interpret the difficulty in relation to the learner’s
history, the current task, and the likely consequences of continued effort. These judgments turn learner-state estimation
into active regulation of an unfolding activity.
Adaptive tutoring systems already support several forms of proactive intervention within an ongoing learning activity.
Existing systems can initiate pedagogical actions, choose among several forms of support, and adjust assistance within a
defined activity. OATutor (Pardos et al., 2023), conversational tutoring systems with student modeling (Park et al., 2024),
personalized tutoring agents (Liu et al., 2024a), and private tutoring frameworks based on chained LLMs (Chen et al.,
2024c) adapt instructional responses to estimated learner needs. Depending on the available evidence and system design,
they can adjust instructional strategies, guidance, learning activities, or assessment during the tutoring process. Resource-
oriented systems extend this action space. FOKE (Hu & Wang, 2024) combines learner profiling with tailored guidance


                                                                                                                           92
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


and learning-path planning, while recommendation chatbots with knowledge-graph contextualization (Abu-Rasheed
et al., 2024a) and knowledge-graph-based explanation systems (Abu-Rasheed et al., 2024b) help learners understand
and interact with learning recommendations. (Zhang et al., 2026k) extend the action space beyond dialogue to the visual
environment itself, inferring learner states from multimodal behavior and proactively modifying the visual learning
environment through interventions such as adaptive highlighting. These mechanisms allow the agent to modify the
conditions under which learning proceeds, moving beyond the interpretation of a completed response. However, these
adaptive tutoring systems’ reasoning usually remains bounded by the predefined task scope, and the consequences of an
intervention rarely reshape decisions beyond that setting. The field has progressed from responsive answer generation
toward local proactive regulation, while initiative to form help across sessions remains limited.

6.11.3   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Evaluation should distinguish two questions: whether a proactive intervention was warranted, and whether it ultimately
benefited the learner. The first concerns the quality of the agent’s decision to intervene. Because proactive tutors act
before an explicit request, they can intervene too early, too late, unnecessarily, or not at all when support is needed.
Premature assistance may interrupt productive struggle or disclose information that the learner could have derived
independently, whereas missed or delayed intervention may allow confusion and frustration to deepen. Evaluation
should therefore assess not only whether an agent detected a learner need, but whether the evidence available at the time
justified intervention and whether the timing and intensity of support were appropriate. The second question concerns
educational benefit over a longer horizon. Immediate task performance is an insufficient measure because assistance
can improve the current answer while weakening retention, transfer, independence, or engagement. More informative
outcomes include delayed unaided performance, retention, transfer to new problems, and whether support can be
withdrawn as competence develops. Where feasible, evaluation should also consider longer-term learner development,
including whether the agent preserves productive effort, confidence, persistence, and curiosity rather than optimizing
only for short-term correctness.
A central challenge for proactive educational agents is that the learner state required to make these decisions is only
partially observable, while appropriate intervention is highly learner- and context-dependent. On one side, the same
behavior can reflect very different underlying conditions: a long pause may indicate confusion, productive reasoning,
distraction, or deliberate exploration, while an incorrect answer may result from a misconception, uncertainty, or
a transient mistake. Beyond knowledge and skill, intervention decisions may also depend on harder-to-measure
factors such as confidence, motivation, persistence, frustration, and curiosity. Inferring these states reliably from noisy
interaction traces remains difficult, yet errors in this inference directly affect whether proactive support helps or disrupts
learning. On the other side, the same hint, explanation, or delay can support one learner and hinder another, making it
difficult to derive general intervention policies from isolated episodes. Progress will require methods that learn from
longitudinal experience while distinguishing transferable educational patterns from learner-specific preferences and
trajectories. Such methods must also operate under strong privacy and governance constraints, because richer proactive
support often depends on maintaining sensitive learner histories over time. More capable systems will therefore need
not only better prediction, but better calibrated decisions about when to intervene, how strongly to intervene, when to
continue observing, and when to defer to learners or educators.

6.12     Agents for Entertainment and Media
The value of proactiveness in entertainment and media is experiential rather than task-completing, depending on timing,
presence, taste, and a sense of authorship. An intervention that is well timed deepens immersion; the same intervention
mistimed breaks it, so the cost an agent must weigh is the experience itself rather than a failed task. Today this
proactiveness optimizes the current session: what operates at scale is content recommendation and auto-play triggered
by the current viewing or listening context, with in-world characters and creative tools that are only beginning to act
on their own, all anticipating the next moment well but holding no objective that spans sessions unless the user writes
one, as in a prompt-defined playlist that refreshes on a schedule (Spotify, 2026b). Research points toward anticipatory
immersion agents that work over longer horizons, shaping the pacing of a long-form narrative, coordinating co-created
content across many sessions, and adjusting intensity under a standing objective such as sustained engagement without
overload. Entertainment is therefore rich in deployed anticipation but early in agenda relative to the other verticals here,
and its distinctive constraint is that stronger initiative is felt directly in immersion and authorship rather than in whether
a task succeeds. We organize the discussion around three roles: acting inside an interactive world, curating what a user

6.12.1        Acting Inside the World: Game and Embodied Agents
Some of the oldest proactive agents in entertainment act inside interactive worlds. Interactive drama introduced the
drama manager, an agent that watches an unfolding story and intervenes to shape pacing and coherence without being
asked, realized in Façade and developed across the interactive-narrative literature (Mateas, 2003; Riedl & Bulitko, 2013).
Believable autonomous characters complement it, pursuing their own goals and acting in the world rather than only
replying when addressed. Foundation models scale this from authored behavior to open-ended initiative: Generative
Agents shows simulated characters that observe events, store memories, form plans, and start interactions with no user
scripting each step (Park et al., 2023), and the pattern is entering production, where NVIDIA ACE supplies speech,
reasoning, and animation for interactive characters and its companions, such as a PUBG ally that advises, shares loot,
drives, and fights alongside the player, act on their own within the game (NVIDIA, 2026a; Burnes et al., 2025); that ally
has since shipped in a live-service beta that sets explicit per-event priors on whether to speak or act (Kim et al., 2026a).
This gives designers a ladder of initiative from commentary, to suggestion, to coordinated play, to direct action; higher
rungs enrich a world but demand stronger Arbitration, since an unwanted act can break play, story, or trust.
Embodiment raises the cost of acting. In VR and virtual worlds the agent is experienced as a body, a voice, and a spatial
presence, the regime studied for decades as embodied conversational and socially interactive agents (Cassell et al.,
2000). Initiative is now expressed through gaze, gesture, motion, and proximity, which raises costs that text interfaces
never face: a spoken interruption mid-scene, or an avatar that enters personal space, can feel intrusive in ways a small
notification would not (Adamczyk & Bailey, 2004; Bailenson et al., 2003). Well-timed initiative instead strengthens
presence when the agent makes its intent legible and respects the rules of the world (Dragan et al., 2013). Recent
evaluation of LLM-driven characters in VR reports gains in perceived realism and usability alongside persistent limits in
latency and emotional depth (Korkiakoski et al., 2025), and a companion that played a VR puzzle game autonomously
lowered enjoyment by reducing challenge and player autonomy (Zhang et al., 2026e). The Arbitration question in this
setting is how the agent controls timing, distance, modality, and reversibility so that initiative preserves rather than
breaks immersion.

6.12.2        Curating What Users See: Feeds and Recommendation
Outside embodied worlds, the most widely deployed proactive agents in entertainment are media recommenders that
decide what to play or show before any query. YouTube and TikTok rank video from interaction history and context, and
Spotify’s DJ assembles a personalized lineup with spoken commentary and revises it from feedback (YouTube, 2021;
TikTok, 2020; Spotify, 2023, 2026a). We treat the general mechanism, recommendation as proactive filtering together
with its conversational and preference-eliciting variants, as information access (§6.3); what is specific to entertainment


                                                                                                                                                           94
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


is that the target is taste and attention rather than a stated information need. These systems are accordingly strong in
Awareness, Anticipation, and Adaptation but narrow in action: they rank and deliver content rather than act within a
shared world, and their recurring decision is Arbitration over when to surface the next item, how strongly to frame it,
and how easily the user can redirect the session.

6.12.3   Co-Creating Content and Performance
On the production side, agents help make content rather than deliver it, which the human-computer interaction literature
frames as mixed-initiative co-creativity, where creative agency is shared and the tool takes initiative as a partner instead of
waiting for each instruction (Deterding et al., 2017; Shneiderman, 2007). Deployed creative assistants follow this shape:
Adobe’s Firefly assistant plans and runs multi-step edits across creative applications from a described outcome, and
creator tools suggest ideas, titles, and thumbnails (Key, 2026; YouTube, 2026). Their proactive value is in maintaining
context, proposing next steps, and preparing editable candidates rather than a finished asset, and those candidates
have to be worth surfacing, which favors non-obvious, divergent options over literal completion, a leap-of-thought
rather than chain-of-thought style of generation (Zhong et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2025b). Live performance makes
timing the central problem. ReaLJam anticipates future musical input and revises uncommitted future chords, keeping
committed chords fixed (Scarlatos et al., 2025b). Users set the initial silence period and the lookahead and commitment
horizons. Live Assistant learns intervention decisions for live streams, choosing whether to intervene, when, and whom
to address (Gao et al., 2026e).

6.12.4   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Because the value is experiential, evaluation must look past task success to immersion (Jennett et al., 2008), acceptance,
and the cost of interruption (Adamczyk & Bailey, 2004), and the risks here are rarely physical. They are broken
immersion, spoilers, unfair in-game assistance, weakened authorship and a narrowing of creative diversity (Doshi &
Hauser, 2024), and misuse of a creator’s likeness or style (Bariach et al., 2024). The risk most specific to media is
that engagement is a poor proxy for enjoyment: optimizing it can amplify content that users say makes them worse
off while failing to track their stated satisfaction (Milli et al., 2025). The broader harms of choosing what a user sees,
such as filter bubbles, degenerate feedback loops, advertising incentives, and attention-capturing dark patterns, follow
the same logic as in information access (§6.3). The lesson is a graded initiative contract: proactive output is safest
as a suggestion, cue, preview, or rehearsal that the user can accept or drop, with stronger action reserved for review.
Several open directions are specific to entertainment. Immersion agents could work over longer horizons, shaping
long-form pacing and coordinating co-created content across sessions rather than resetting each one. Embodied and
live-performance settings need real-time timing and legibility methods, so that the agent signals its intent before it acts.
As the tool takes more initiative, authorship, likeness, and creative diversity need explicit safeguards. Evaluation should
also reward stated satisfaction over raw engagement. In entertainment, mature proactiveness is not intervening more
often or forcing deeper immersion, but timing each intervention through an Arbitration gate (§4.4) so that it deepens the
experience and leaves play, taste, and authorship with the user.

6.13     Agents for Agriculture
Agricultural decisions often need to be made under uncertain environmental conditions and within time-sensitive
biological growth cycles, before problems become fully visible, making proactive intervention particularly important.
Water stress, disease pressure, and weather risks may already be developing when symptoms remain weak, while delayed
intervention can remove cheaper or safer options. Proactive agricultural agents can therefore monitor relevant conditions,
such as crops, soil, and weather, and determine when additional measurement, advice, or intervention is needed, or when
existing operations should be adjusted.
In agricultural applications, proactiveness takes different forms depending on the task. Field sensing and management
support timely monitoring and resource allocation; pest and disease management enables early risk detection and
intervention; and operational coordination helps adapt resource allocation and task schedules to changing conditions.
Existing systems address these needs within specific agricultural settings, with varying degrees of autonomy and
integration. Table 15 compares selected agricultural systems across the six mechanisms.

6.13.1      Field Sensing, Management, and Operational Coordination
Agricultural agents can support field monitoring by maintaining an updated view of field conditions. AgriSentinel (Mylay
et al., 2025) combines image-based crop-disease classification with on-device management suggestions. The distributed
precision-agriculture framework in (Davcev et al., 2026) connects heterogeneous sensing with agent-based reasoning and
adaptive decisions, while the Agent-Based Service Architecture (ASA) (Pardo-Pina et al., 2026) organizes greenhouse
telemetry, analytics, and RAG-grounded decision support within a shared agent architecture. The wireless-sensor-
network architecture in (Villarrubia et al., 2017) further integrates distributed sensing with multi-agent monitoring for
crop irrigation.
Beyond monitoring, agricultural agents can support management decisions using available field information. Agri-
SAGE (Balasubramaniam et al., 2026) couples multi-agent LLM reasoning with APSIM crop simulation to generate and
validate context-aware agronomic advice, while AgroAskAI (Cantonjos & Biswas, 2025) coordinates role-specialized
agents and external tools for locally grounded climate-adaptation support. The irrigation-and-fertigation framework in
(Adamo et al., 2025) models resource management as sequential decisions driven by real-time IoT measurements. More
broadly, the agricultural-agent framework in (Li et al., 2026k) organizes perception, knowledge and memory, planning,
action, and feedback into a closed-loop view of agricultural intelligence. These systems illustrate different approaches
to supporting agricultural decisions based on observed conditions, simulation, and external information.
Agricultural operations may also require coordination across multiple agents, resources, or activities. The community-
irrigation multi-agent system in (Chiewchan et al., 2022) models farms as agents that estimate crop water needs and
negotiate water redistribution under scarcity. The greenhouse-production multi-agent system in (Ferentinos et al.,
2005) coordinates agents responsible for root-zone and aerial environments through supervisory-level negotiation. The
agri-robot fleet coordination approach in (Lujak et al., 2020) studies distributed and decentralized coordination for
heterogeneous agricultural vehicles and dynamic task assignment.
These works demonstrate sensing, management, and coordination within specific agricultural applications. However,
their capabilities remain largely tied to particular tasks and operational settings. An open direction is to investigate
how changes in field conditions, resource availability, or operational constraints can inform subsequent decisions and
adjustments when coordination across activities is needed.




                                                                                                                                                          96
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


6.13.2   Agricultural Risk Detection and Intervention
Pest and disease management requires timely detection and intervention, as emerging threats may become easier to
identify while the available intervention window narrows. PestMA (Shi et al., 2025b) uses Editor, Retriever, and Validator
agents to retrieve external pest-management evidence, synthesize recommendations, and validate them. PDD-Agent (Qin
et al., 2025a) uses a multimodal agent to orchestrate specialized tools for plant-disease diagnosis. The UAV-based
pest-management system in (Chu & Bao, 2025) connects real-time pest classification with swarm path planning and task
allocation, extending threat recognition toward deployment decisions. The smart-farming agentic framework in (Murad
et al., 2026) further integrates soil, weather, disease-detection, and farmer-facing components within a broader decision
pipeline.
Current systems mostly begin from an observed image, query, sensor condition, or external signal. Stronger proactive
agents could combine such evidence with crop stage, forecasts, exposure, and prior observations to anticipate emerging
risks and initiate appropriate actions, such as targeted inspection, increased monitoring, early warnings, or preventive
treatment, while accounting for uncertainty and intervention costs.

6.13.3   Evaluation, Challenges, and Open Directions
Agricultural agents should be evaluated by whether their proactive behavior leads to timely and appropriate decisions as
conditions evolve. Recommendation accuracy remains important, but it does not capture whether an agent acted early
enough to be useful, intervened when intervention was actually warranted, or refrained from acting when evidence was
insufficient. Evaluation should therefore consider lead time, unnecessary interventions, escalation quality, resource
use, and adaptation to subsequent observations. These criteria are application dependent: a disease-management agent
should identify emerging risks early without triggering unnecessary treatments, whereas an irrigation-management agent
must balance timely intervention against water consumption. Importantly, inaction can itself be an appropriate proactive
decision when the expected benefit of intervention is low or uncertainty remains high.
A central challenge is determining when an agent should initiate action without an explicit task request. Agricultural
environments generate continuous streams of weak, noisy, and sometimes conflicting signals, while the consequences of
acting too early and too late can both be substantial. Proactive agents therefore need to relate observations to longer-term
operational objectives, recognize when evolving conditions create a meaningful need for attention, and decide whether
to monitor, gather additional information, alert a user, or intervene. This requires more than executing predefined
workflows: the agent must infer when a latent objective has become actionable and calibrate the scope and urgency of its
response under uncertainty and resource constraints. Open questions include how such initiative should be grounded in
persistent goals, how intervention thresholds should adapt across farms and seasons, and how agents can remain useful
without becoming unnecessarily intrusive or overactive.

6.14     Cross-Industry Trends
The preceding verticals of proactive AI agents differ in many important ways. For instance, they differ in their data,
their tolerance for error, their regulators, and the horizon over which their consequences arrive. However, despite these
differences, three patterns recur across domains (Figure 15). Many systems now use a common architecture, with
foundation-model cores and domain-specialized machinery (§6.14.2). Across these domains, agents are also being asked
to carry whole workflows, not just respond within them (§6.14.3). Progress still differs by domain. A consistent divider
is the cost and quality of feedback on whether a self-initiated action was correct (§6.14.4). The remaining subsections
expand on these ideas: First, we overview the relative maturity of proactivity in each vertical. Then we expand on
each of the three trends. The per-vertical tables in the preceding subsections summarize the systems on which these
observations rest, and Table 16 places each domain on a common ladder.

6.14.1   Proactive Maturity Across Domains
In this section, we evaluate the maturity of proactivity in systems across the many previously surveyed verticals. In
service of this goal, we start by reiterating a shared measure of proactivity. We place the surveyed systems on a common
informal scale of initiative, distinguishing reactive, trigger-initiated, forecast-initiated, mandate-directed, and agenda-
generative behavior. The scale asks where the agent’s task comes from and tracks the anticipation-to-agenda progression
of the mechanism chapter. A reactive system executes an instruction or a user-authored rule. A trigger-initiated system
notices a condition that has already occurred and surfaces it. A forecast-initiated system acts on a latent need or failure

before it manifests, which is the step that Anticipation supplies (§4.2). A mandate-directed system holds standing
objectives and discovers, prioritizes, and revisits the work that advances them, and an agenda-generative system revises
those objectives themselves; these last two are the committed-goal and goal-generation steps of Agenda (§4.3). The
scale is a discretization of the reactivity–proactivity spectrum of §2 rather than a separate construct, and, as that section
stresses, a single system can occupy different points on it depending on time scale, confidence, and operational context.
The six-capacity framework connects the discovery and organization of candidate work through Anticipation and Agenda
with decisions about intervention and execution through Arbitration and Action. We therefore read each domain on a
second, orthogonal axis, the authority the agent is granted over its first move, which is the levels-of-autonomy spectrum
of §4.5.1: whether it may only suggest, may act inside a gate such as a sandbox, branch, simulator, or approval workflow,
or may act unsupervised. The two axes move independently. Autonomous-research systems can combine deep execution
autonomy with task-scoped initiative under a human-specified top-level question (Lu et al., 2024; Xing et al., 2026);
smart-home platforms can initiate a large share of interactions with very little authority behind any single act (Eberhardt,
2022). Each cell reports in Table 16 where the systems surveyed in that domain’s subsection most consistently sit on the
initiative ladder, and a hyphen between two rungs means the surveyed set spans both.
Three comparative observations follow from the table. First, deployment and initiative are decoupled. The home is
deployment-rich but initiative-shallow, while the city combines forecast-initiated assistance with limited action authority:
municipal forecasting is excellent and closed-loop municipal action is rare, because authority there is diffuse and every
action is a public act (§7.2). Autonomous research is the extreme case, autonomy-deep and barely deployed. Second, no
vertical has reached the agenda-generative rung, and several argue that it should not. For example, in security, healthcare,
law, and education the surveyed systems converge on the same target, mandate-directed initiative under bounded
authority, in which greater proactiveness expands what the agent notices, investigates, and prepares while consequential
acts remain gated by policy and professional responsibility (Anthropic, 2026d; Gallifant et al., 2025). The frontier in
these domains is the quality of initiative, not the scope of unsupervised authority. Third, feedback conditions differ
substantially across domains. Coding agents can often test proposed changes before deployment, whereas feedback from
physical experiments and seasonal or civic interventions can be slower, costlier, or more diffuse. These differences affect
how readily agents can verify and revise self-initiated work. Model capability, execution reliability, and governance also
constrain progress, as the maturity table indicates. This is the subject of §6.14.4.

6.14.2       Trend 1: A Shared Architecture with Domain-Specific Specialization
Across these verticals, proactive systems are increasingly built on a common architecture: a foundation-model core
paired with domain-specialized machinery. In most domains surveyed here the reasoning core is a large language or
multimodal model: coding agents run an LLM loop over the repository (Anthropic, 2025; OpenAI, 2025a; GitHub,
2025); GUI agents drive an MLLM over screenshots (Hong et al., 2024; Kong et al., 2026); autonomous-research
systems wrap an LLM in tools and experiment loops (Boiko et al., 2023b; Lu et al., 2024; Gottweis et al., 2026); and
legal, medical, and urban agents are typically one or more LLMs over domain tools and retrieval (Wang & Yuan, 2025;
Tang et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024d). The value of the shared core is specific and worth naming: parameterized world
knowledge is what lets a single system anticipate a latent need (§4.2) in open-world situations without the domain-
specific engineering that earlier paradigms required, and most systems reach workable behavior with no task-specific
training. Anticipation, historically the expensive part of a proactive system, has become close to a commodity.
The key architectural differences are everything the domain contributes beneath and around that core, and the boundaries
of foundation-model primacy mark where domains tend to differ. Systems without an LLM core cluster at the two data
extremes. At the low-data, low-latency end a narrow quantitative signal suffices and nothing heavier is warranted: the
Observe–Ask–Intervene agent gates on measured speaking time (Houtti et al., 2025), and WorkFit acts on smartwatch
thresholds (Ahire et al., 2024). At the high-data end, domains with enormous proprietary corpora train bespoke models
rather than adopt a pretrained prior, as AlphaZero does from self-play (Silver et al., 2017) and Alexa’s Hunches do
by learning device and home embeddings over fleet-scale logs (Eberhardt, 2022). Even where an LLM is present it
usually sits atop a domain-specific predictive substrate rather than replacing it: security systems remain hybrids of LLM
reasoning over purpose-built detectors because general-purpose agents still underperform specialized static analysis
(Yohn et al., 2026), and cities retain spatio-temporal forecasters under an LLM interface (Li et al., 2024d). The emerging
architecture is therefore layered rather than monolithic: a general reasoner supplies anticipation and agenda, a domain
model supplies calibrated prediction, and a domain gate supplies authority.
Embodiment adds a second boundary, about latency rather than data. Continuous physical control cannot wait on slow


                                                                                                                                                 99
                                            Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


deliberation, which forces hybrid fast–slow designs: ProAct couples a fast behavioral stream to a slower LLM cognitive
system (Zhang et al., 2026l), industrial robots adjust motion in real time from proximity and physiological signals while
a deliberative layer plans above them (Hostettler et al., 2024), and wearable assistants split a light always-on monitor
from a heavier reasoner to keep continuous awareness affordable (Chen et al., 2025d; Wen et al., 2025b). Given the
standing energy and latency cost of always-on awareness (§4.1), foundation-model cores will likely remain dominant
as efficiency improves. The boundary cases are nonetheless a useful corrective, since they show the LLM to be one
substrate among several, selected by a domain’s data-and-latency regime rather than by default, and they predict where
the shared substrate will arrive last: in domains that are either too thin or too rich in data, or too fast to wait for a token.

6.14.3   Trend 2: From Assisting Humans to Carrying Workflows
A second cross-domain pattern is that agents are increasingly assigned whole workflows instead of individual steps
within them. Earlier proactive systems clustered around proactive suggestion, such as code completions, health prompts,
assistant reminders, recommended items, or clarifying questions, each of which augments a human who remains the
operator of the task. What a growing subset of frontier systems now do is carry a workflow that previously required
a person: a coding agent turns an assigned issue into a reviewed pull request (OpenAI, 2025a; GitHub, 2025), a GUI
agent accepts bounded delegation across applications (Zhao et al., 2025c; Ye et al., 2026c), a research system runs
an experimental loop end to end (Boiko et al., 2023b; Szymanski et al., 2023), and a security agent scans, validates,
and drafts a patch (Anthropic, 2026d). Workflows can contain latent work that nobody thought to request, arrive with
incomplete specifications, and span interruptions. Proactiveness lets an agent identify and pursue additional work that
advances a longer-horizon objective.
This shift is visible in the human’s role, which moves along the workflow from operator to collaborator to reviewer. It is
most advanced in software, where the developer no longer specifies each edit but defines an outcome, constraints, and
acceptance conditions, and then reviews evidence; the same rotation is underway for clinicians and attorneys, whose
surveyed systems all place a professional at a review gate rather than at the keyboard. The rotation explains why so
many domain conclusions above converge on the same next milestone. Encounter-bounded medicine wants longitudinal
responsibility, matter-bounded law wants lifecycle strategy, interaction-bounded tutoring wants trajectory-aware learning
paths, and issue-triggered coding wants a repository custodian (Thai et al., 2025; Chen et al., 2026c): in each case the
demand is for an agent that holds an objective across time rather than a task within a session.
Crucially, the systems taking consequential first moves are not the least constrained ones. As the authority axis above
records, they scale the strength of the first move to risk, reversibility, and confidence (§4.4.4) and engineer the gate
before granting the initiative: coding agents act inside sandboxes and review, and Alexa’s Hunches complete actions
behind a learned acceptance model. What is spreading, in other words, is not autonomy but initiative that a principal can
safely accept, which is why the gate travels with the capability across domains that share nothing else. The workflow
shift and the graduated-authority pattern are two faces of the same move: an agent may hold a longer objective only
insofar as its acts on that objective stay gated.

6.14.4   Trend 3: Verification and Feedback Infrastructure Is a Key Constraint
The common architecture of §6.14.2 does not produce uniform progress across domains. An important source of
variation is how cheaply, quickly, and reliably the environment provides feedback on proactive behavior (§4.6.1). Timely,
reliable feedback can support repeated testing and correction, provided agents can execute the relevant actions and
interpret the results. Software is the paradigm case, since a compiler, type checker, test suite, linter, or CI run can
reject a change before a human sees it, so a coding agent can treat its own edits as verifiable state transitions and
self-verify rather than emit ungrounded text (Ning et al., 2026d). The frontier has accordingly moved from generation to
closed-loop engineering, in which the agent reviews its own diffs, requests further agent or human review, and iterates
until reviewers are satisfied (Lopopolo, 2026; Anthropic, 2026b). Machine-learning research can use a similar feedback
loop by running training code and scoring a benchmark, supporting autonomous-research systems that propose and test
their own research ideas (Lu et al., 2024; Yamada et al., 2025).
Where the oracle is slow or expensive, repeated testing and correction become harder to sustain without supporting
infrastructure. A wet-lab assay or materials synthesis turns every action into a costly, sometimes irreversible bet, so
the burden shifts from executing experiments to deciding which experiments are worth running (Boiko et al., 2023b;
Szymanski et al., 2023), which connects proactive research to active learning and Bayesian experimental design (Settles,


                                                                                                                           100
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


2009; Chaloner & Verdinelli, 1995). Agriculture and education face the same problem in temporal form, since the
outcome of an intervention may not be observable for a season or a semester. Recent engineering addresses these
feedback constraints: cloud and self-driving laboratories reduce the latency of the oracle (Armer et al., 2023; Abolhasani
& Kumacheva, 2023); research-state infrastructure preserves what experiments returned so a later agent can verify and
extend rather than restart (Schmidgall & Moor, 2025; Anthropic, 2026a); and city operators substitute simulation for
the costly street trial, rehearsing interventions against synthetic populations in urban digital twins before deploying
them (Xu et al., 2024b; Piao et al., 2025). The digital twin and the self-driving lab are the same move made in different
domains: buy a cheap oracle so that initiative becomes affordable.
Two implications follow for verification and evaluation. First, capability gains can shift the burden from generating
candidate work to checking and completing it. Under Project Glasswing, partners reported over ten thousand high- or
critical-severity vulnerability findings within a month, and the binding constraint moved from finding vulnerabilities
to verifying, disclosing, and patching them (Anthropic, 2026g,h); a proactive agent that can generate more candidate
work than its principal can check has shifted the cost rather than paid it. The second is that our evaluations are not
yet measuring the thing that limits us. Benchmarks still largely specify what the agent should work on and then
score whether it succeeded, which measures execution under a reactively supplied agenda (Jimenez et al., 2024). A
mandate-directed agent must instead be scored on whether it discovered work worth doing, prioritized it correctly, chose
a proportionate intervention, and recognized when no intervention was preferable, and the metrics that would support
this, such as task-discovery precision and recall, interruption cost, human verification effort, and reward for correct
silence, remain scattered and domain-specific (Chen et al., 2026c; Samarinas & Zamani, 2024; Tang et al., 2026b)
(§5). Further progress will require advances in model and execution capabilities supported by trustworthy feedback and
verification. Evaluation should assess both the value of self-initiated work and whether an agent appropriately refrains
from acting.

7     Future Work: Towards Calibrated Proactiveness
Current systems implement proactive capabilities only partially (§ 4 and § 6). The long-term objective is calibrated,
governable proactiveness that is useful across realistic contexts. Future proactive agents may become situated partners
that can anticipate needs, manage long-horizon goals, and intervene across conversational, multimodal, embodied, and
ambient environments, including robotics, household assistance, wearable devices, workplace support, and personalized
daily planning. In these settings, proactiveness involves self-initiation, latent-need detection, goal formation, intervention
arbitration, and cross-context action. Calibration is needed to determine when initiative is helpful, when clarification is
needed, when human approval is required, and when inaction is preferable. Greater initiative may be useful, intrusive,
unsafe, or misaligned, depending on its calibration and context.
Calibrated proactiveness calls for connected advances in capabilities, governance, and application development. Techni-
cal and evaluative progress should support agents in anticipating needs, initiating actions, and sustaining assistance over
long-horizon interactions (§7.1). Governance needs to preserve safety, trustworthiness, and human agency when agents
initiate action (§7.2). Application development should consider how calibrated proactive agents may affect products,
workflows, organizational roles, and modes of human supervision across domains such as work, finance, education, and
healthcare (§7.3).

7.1     Steps to Take for Advancing Proactiveness
7.1.1    Evaluation Beyond Narrow Applications, Static Performance, and Coarse-Grained Metrics
Evaluation needs to cover agents that anticipate needs, manage long-horizon goals, and intervene appropriately across
diverse interaction contexts. Relevant contexts include text-based conversations and multimodal, embodied, and ambient
environments, including robotics, household assistance, wearable devices, workplace support, and personalized daily
planning, as indicated across the domain tables in Section 6. Alongside single-turn response correctness, evaluation
should assess whether the agent recognizes useful occasions for intervention, chooses an appropriate level of initiative,
preserves user control, and adapts as the user’s goals and environment evolve over time.
Many evaluations treat proactiveness as a turn-level prediction problem in conversational settings (Chen et al., 2025d),
where task-specific response skills may be acquired through post-training. Such tests provide limited evidence about
self-initiation, as defined in § 2, as a generalizable capability. More general benchmarks, such as ProCIS (Samarinas
& Zamani, 2024), Ask-Before-Plan (Zhang et al., 2024h), and ProactiveBench (Lu et al., 2025a), begin to evaluate


                                                                                                                          101
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


proactive behavior in predominantly single-turn and text-based scenarios. As a result, they provide limited evidence
about whether proactive agents can generalize across modalities, domains, task horizons, and levels of environmental
complexity. Future benchmarks should cover near-term conversational agents and longer-term embodied or ambient
agents, with tasks that vary in temporal horizon, user involvement, risk level, and contextual uncertainty.
Many proactive actions occur without a direct user request. Actions that improve task outcomes may be perceived
as helpful, intrusive, distracting, premature, or overly controlling depending on their timing, context, and degree of
autonomy. Future evaluation should therefore measure task outcomes together with how users experience agent initiative.
General user-experience and usability instruments, such as UEQ (User Experience Questionnaire) (Laugwitz et al., 2008)
and SUS (System Usability Scale) (Brooke, 1995), can provide useful system-level signals. Targeted measures should
assess trust, reliance, perceived control, interruption cost, willingness to accept suggestions, and perceived respect for
human agency. Technical correctness can coexist with user-perceived miscalibration.
Task success and user satisfaction provide limited evidence about the mechanisms producing an agent’s behavior.
Memorized patterns, alignment-tuned responses, and task-specific shortcuts may influence these outcomes. Future
benchmarks should therefore include fine-grained tests for core proactive mechanisms, including self-initiation, world
modeling, sub-goal proposal, intervention timing, initiative arbitration, action-level validation, and cross-context
generalization. A unit-test-style evaluation could separately probe each mechanism before evaluating the full agent in
integrated long-horizon tasks. These tests should assess decisions to act, ask, defer, or remain silent across settings.
A unified benchmark design should combine broader application settings, user-centered metrics, and mechanism-level
tests. Together, these components can assess whether agents improve task outcomes and sustain calibrated, governable,
and user-aligned proactiveness across realistic contexts.

7.1.2   Strengthening Calibrated Proactiveness Through Mechanism-Level Advances
Toward Unified, Resource-Aware, and Robust Situation Awareness. Maintaining a reliable estimate of the current
situation supports anticipation and timely intervention (§ 4.1). Existing work has developed building blocks for this
capacity across different settings, including multimodal state tracking and context management (Yang et al., 2025b),
continuous personal memory (Wang & Chen, 2025), online video understanding (Chen et al., 2024a), active information
gathering (Choudhury et al., 2026), and proactive triggering (Lu et al., 2025a). Future work should develop unified
situation-awareness architectures that integrate perception, memory, active information seeking, runtime triggering, tool
outputs, dialogue history, screen state, user behavior, and environmental signals into a shared representation of the user,
task, and environment that supports anticipation, agenda formation, and arbitration. The shared representation needs
compression because proactive agents operate over continuous streams of information that cannot be fully retained
in a bounded context window. Agents must decide what to keep, summarize, retrieve, forget, or page into memory.
Existing work on streaming language models (Xiao et al., 2024), virtual context management (Packer et al., 2023), and
sleep-time computation (Lin et al., 2025) provides early steps in this direction. Future compression mechanisms should
be optimized specifically for proactiveness: they should preserve information that may support future anticipation,
discard irrelevant details, and retain enough evidence to justify why an intervention was triggered.
Situation-awareness systems should allocate computation, memory, sensing, and interaction according to contextual
importance. Candidate approaches include triage, selective attention (Vaswani et al., 2017), information filtering,
priority management, adaptive compression, and background or “dream-time” computation during periods of low system
demand (Lin et al., 2025). For example, hierarchical awareness systems could use low-cost monitors to continuously tag
incoming context according to novelty, urgency, uncertainty, user relevance, risk, and potential need for intervention.
When these signals indicate that a moment is important, ambiguous, or high-stakes, the agent could escalate to more
expensive processing, such as deeper multimodal interpretation, memory retrieval, active information gathering, tool use,
or explicit clarification. In parallel, attention and information-selection mechanisms could restrict processing to the most
relevant portions of a long context, while background computation could reorganize memory, consolidate previously
observed experiences, or precompute likely future needs without delaying ongoing interaction. Some resource allocation
may also occur below the software layer. For instance, on-device sensors, low-power processors, or hardware-level
event triggers in mobile and IoT environments (Baccour et al., 2022) could detect salient environmental changes before
activating more computationally expensive models. Hardware-assisted mechanisms can provide an efficient first stage for
software-level reasoning over large, continuous streams of multimodal data. Together, these complementary mechanisms
allow routine context to be compressed, summarized, deferred, or ignored, while high-value moments receive richer



                                                                                                                        102
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


analysis before the agent forms a sub-goal, arbitrates intervention, or initiates action. Compression keeps long-running
context usable, and adaptive resource allocation determines which parts of that context require deeper understanding.
Temporal freshness, uncertainty awareness, noise handling, and cross-context coherence affect the quality of situation
estimates. Temporal freshness is necessary because proactive agents may act on long-term memories, yet stale
preferences or outdated task states can cause errors in unsolicited interventions; long-term memory systems (Zhong
et al., 2023), temporal knowledge graphs (Rasmussen et al., 2025), and long-memory evaluation (Wu et al., 2025b) show
why this matters. Uncertainty awareness is necessary because multimodal perception, user-state inference, and active
sensing are noisy; egocentric vision (Grauman et al., 2022), wearable activity recognition (Zhang et al., 2022), and
gaze-based intention estimation (Belardinelli, 2023) each provide partial evidence. Cross-context coherence is necessary
because proactive agents must reconcile evidence from dialogue, screen state, sensors, memory, and external tools;
screen and interface understanding (Baechler et al., 2024), native GUI state tracking (Qin et al., 2025c), and on-device
proactive context modeling (Li et al., 2024c) illustrate the diversity of such evidence sources. Awareness errors in these
dimensions may propagate through the proactive pipeline, leading the agent to anticipate the wrong need, adopt the
wrong goal, intervene at the wrong moment, or learn the wrong lesson from feedback. Future work should incorporate
unification, compression, adaptive resource allocation, temporal updating, uncertainty estimation, and cross-context
reconciliation into the awareness layer.
Toward Generalizable Anticipation. Anticipating latent needs, future risks, and emerging opportunities before they are
explicitly stated requires models that generalize across users, entities, tasks, environments, interface states, and temporal
horizons (§ 4.2). Predictions of user behavior, environmental dynamics, interface transitions, and task consequences
should indicate whether an unmet need, a preventable failure, a timely opportunity, or a situation requiring clarification
or human approval may arise. Existing work provides useful foundations for this capacity, including user intent modeling
(Qian et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2025a), Theory-of-Mind-style reasoning (Kosinski, 2024), plan and intent recognition
(Kautz & Allen, 1986), learned world models (Ha & Schmidhuber, 2018), generative visual simulators (Bruce et al.,
2024), and scenario-level reasoning (Yao et al., 2023a). Future work should develop unified anticipation models that
can transfer across different prediction targets and contexts while representing the downstream relevance of predicted
states. The anticipation layer should provide sufficiently rich forecasts for subsequent agenda formation and arbitration
to compare acting, asking, deferring, and remaining silent.
Continuous forecasting needs to remain effective across computational conditions and levels of contextual complexity.
Proactive agents may need to forecast continuously over long-running interaction streams. Expensive world models,
user simulations, or multi-step rollouts cannot be invoked for every possible future at every moment. Future work should
therefore connect anticipation with the resource-aware situation-awareness layer: lightweight forecasting mechanisms
may handle routine and short-horizon developments, while deeper world models, counterfactual reasoning, or user-state
inference can be activated when the current context contains greater novelty, uncertainty, risk, or user relevance. This
allocation should support generalization from simple, frequently occurring cases to complex situations that require
richer simulation. This challenge is compounded by the brittleness of current models. Targeted benchmarks show
that Theory-of-Mind reasoning by LLMs on false-belief tasks can fail under perturbations, interactive information
asymmetry, or cases in which the model must use the inferred mental state to reason about subsequent behavior (Ullman,
2023; Kim et al., 2023; Chen et al., 2024d). Learned world models, generative visual simulators, and user-behavior
models (Hafner et al., 2025; Bruce et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2024d; Shen et al., 2026a) still struggle to produce reliable
predictions across open-ended environments, unfamiliar users, and long temporal horizons. Future proactive systems
therefore need anticipation mechanisms that can adapt the depth and form of forecasting to the complexity of the current
situation without sacrificing reliability.
Generalization should cover predictions of the most likely next state and reasoning about alternative, causal, and
counterfactual futures. A proactive agent may need to represent what is likely to happen under continued observation,
an external change, a possible user action, or different forms of agent assistance. Counterfactual reasoning (Pearl,
2009; Kıcıman et al., 2024) can help world models estimate how future trajectories may differ under alternative
conditions, including whether a potential action would improve the future relative to waiting or remaining silent. The
anticipation layer should generate comparable forecasts of potential consequences for downstream agenda and arbitration
mechanisms to evaluate in terms of benefits, risks, priorities, and user authority. LLM-based causal and counterfactual
reasoning remains fragile under genuine counterfactual queries, distribution shifts, and partially observable agentic
settings (Jin et al., 2024c; Bharadwaj et al., 2026). Future work should investigate world models that generalize across
observed trajectories and plausible yet unseen courses of events while distinguishing statistical plausibility from causal


                                                                                                                         103
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


consequence.
Forecasts used to guide unsolicited behavior need observable evidence and explicit uncertainty. Anticipated needs
and future states should be tied to concrete signals from user behavior, environmental dynamics, interaction history,
task progress, and observed outcomes. Multimodal signals, such as procedure planning Chang et al. (2020); Liu et al.
(2023a), egocentric action anticipation (Furnari & Farinella, 2020; Shen et al., 2026a), gaze-based intention estimation
(Belardinelli, 2023), and multimodal Theory-of-Mind reasoning (Jin et al., 2024a), can ground forecasts in what the user
is seeing, doing, or likely intending. Dialogue rollouts, user simulators, and generative-agent societies (Zhang et al.,
2025f; Luo et al., 2024a; Park et al., 2023) can further help agents rehearse future interactions, but simulated users may
become miscalibrated proxies that over-accept suggestions or reinforce sycophantic assumptions (Sharma et al., 2025;
Seshadri et al., 2026; Wang et al., 2025d). Future work should therefore build anticipation layers that jointly represent
predicted future states, alternative trajectories, supporting evidence, model assumptions, and predictive uncertainty.
Such representations should indicate where a prediction transfers reliably, where additional evidence is required, and
where downstream mechanisms should continue observing.
Toward Accountable, Revisable, and User-Directed Agendas. Forming an agenda from anticipated needs requires
an accountable choice of goals to pursue (§ 4.3). Existing work has explored goal generation from anticipated needs
(Molineaux et al., 2010; Klenk et al., 2013), intrinsic goal formation (Oudeyer et al., 2007; Barto et al., 2004), open-ended
curriculum construction (Wang et al., 2024a), proactive task suggestion (Lu et al., 2025a), and long-horizon standing
agendas (Shi et al., 2026b). Current systems often blur the boundary between identifying that something may be useful
and deciding that the agent should pursue it as a goal. Future agenda mechanisms should therefore expose why a latent
need is promoted into an agenda item, how it relates to the user’s explicit objectives, what evidence supports it, and
under what conditions it should be reconsidered or abandoned. This would make self-generated goals more accountable
while helping users understand and calibrate trust in the agent’s initiative.
Proactive agendas need to support revision as the user’s priorities, task state, available resources, and environmental
conditions change. An agenda formed from uncertain predictions may become invalid when those predictions or other
underlying assumptions change. For example, in assembly tasks, an initially planned sequence may become infeasible
once the agent discovers that certain steps are not physically executable (Jing et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026e,g). Future
systems should therefore support intention reconsideration, goal revision, plan repair, suspension, and dependency-aware
replanning, allowing an agenda item to be updated, deferred, replaced, or abandoned when its underlying assumptions
no longer hold. The persistence of long-horizon commitments should depend on their continuing justification.
Competing agenda items need to be prioritized under user direction. A proactive agent may simultaneously hold explicit
user requests, standing delegated goals, inferred latent needs, and internally generated objectives. Work on intention
reconsideration (Kinny & Georgeff, 1991; Schut et al., 2004), multi-objective goal selection (Roijers et al., 2014;
Hayes et al., 2022), proactive-dialogue goal steering (Deng et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2025f), and user-aware notification
suppression (Rizk et al., 2020) provides foundations for agenda management. Future systems should rank agenda
items by expected utility, feasibility, user priority, urgency, reversibility, resource cost, and potential interference with
the user’s current task. They should also preserve clear distinctions among user-requested, delegated, inferred, and
self-generated goals, with stronger authorization requirements for goals that are less directly grounded in explicit user
intent.
Users should retain the ability to inspect, revise, pause, reject, or terminate agenda items. Work on instrumental
convergence (Omohundro, 2008; Bostrom, 2012), reward hacking (Skalse et al., 2025), agentic misalignment (Lynch
et al., 2025), corrigibility (Soares et al., 2015), off-switch deference (Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017), and instruction
hierarchies (Wallace et al., 2024) shows why this matters: agent-originated goals may conflict with changing user
intentions or persist beyond their original justification. Future work should treat agendas as inspectable, revisable, and
user-directed commitments, with accountability, continual reconsideration, prioritization, and human authority built into
their management.
Toward Multi-Level, Utility-Aware, and Risk-Sensitive Arbitration. Proposed agenda items need to be assessed
against the conditions for intervention (§ 4.4). When self-generated goals are not fully user-governed, arbitration
determines whether an intervention should be executed, delayed, softened, escalated, or suppressed. Existing work on
confidence-based intervention (Horvitz, 1999), selective prediction and abstention (Geifman & El-Yaniv, 2017; Wen
et al., 2025a), learning to defer (Madras et al., 2018; Mozannar & Sontag, 2020), and conformal uncertainty triggers
(Quach et al., 2024; Ren et al., 2023) provides useful foundations. Future work should develop multi-level arbitration


                                                                                                                         104
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


policies that choose among silent monitoring, clarification, suggestion, confirmation, reversible execution, human
escalation, and refusal. Such policies could support graceful degradation under limited confidence and reduce premature
intervention.
Arbitration also needs to reason about whether intervention is worth its cost. A technically correct proactive action can
still be undesirable if it interrupts the user, consumes scarce resources, invokes costly tools, or damages long-term trust.
Classical work on value-of-information and metareasoning (Howard, 1966; Russell & Wefald, 1991), attention-sensitive
alerting (Horvitz et al., 2013b, 2004), and interruption cost (Bailey & Konstan, 2006; Iqbal & Horvitz, 2007) provides
a foundation for modeling this trade-off. Recent systems extend this logic to proactive assistant evaluation (Lu et al.,
2025a; Tang et al., 2026b), budget-aware tool use (Chen et al., 2023a; Liu et al., 2025e), and trust-aware proactive
dialogue (Kraus et al., 2023). Future arbitration mechanisms should therefore estimate whether the expected benefit of
an intervention outweighs its attention cost, resource cost, timing cost, and cumulative trust cost. The resulting decision
process should incorporate confidence and expected utility.
Arbitration also needs to account for timing, risk, and external oversight. Timing should be modeled as a decision
variable: even a valuable intervention may fail if it arrives at the wrong moment. Work on interruption timing (Adamczyk
& Bailey, 2004; Iqbal & Bailey, 2010), just-in-time assistance (Yang et al., 2025d), and optimal stopping for act-versus-
wait decisions (Page, 1954; Shiryaev, 1963; Qian et al., 2025b) offers a basis for modeling intervention timing. At the
same time, the required permission level should scale with risk and reversibility: low-risk reversible actions may be
taken more autonomously, while high-stakes or irreversible actions should require confirmation, external vetoes, or hard
constraints. Existing work on risk benchmarks for agents (Ruan et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024), runtime guardrails
(Xiang et al., 2025; Chennabasappa et al., 2025), permission systems (Shi et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2025a), and
contextual trustworthiness monitoring (Greenblatt et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025f) points toward arbitration layers that
do not rely solely on the agent’s self-judgment. Future work should build arbitration as a monitored and adaptive gate
that jointly considers confidence, utility, timing, risk, reversibility, and user authority before proactive action is allowed.
Toward Mixed-Initiative and Responsible Action. Agents need to choose a justified degree of commitment when
translating anticipation, agenda formation, and arbitration into user-facing behavior without an explicit request (§ 4.5).
Existing work on levels of automation (Sheridan & Verplank, 1978; Parasuraman et al., 2000), mixed-initiative interaction
(Avula et al., 2022), adjustable autonomy (Scerri et al., 2002; Bradshaw et al., 2004), and action reasoning (Yao et al.,
2023b) provides useful foundations. Future work should develop mechanisms for calibrating action commitment that
map proactive intent into graded action levels, such as suggesting, explaining, asking, drafting, previewing, executing a
low-risk step, or committing a consequential action only after approval. Calibrated commitment requires deciding when
to remain peripheral, ask, prepare an action for review, or execute autonomously.
Proactive action should be responsible throughout its lifecycle. Because proactive actions are often unsolicited and
may unfold over long horizons, users should be able to inspect, edit, reject, pause, or undo them whenever possible.
Reversibility can preserve user control and limit the consequences of mistaken initiative. Low-risk actions may be
delivered with lightweight acceptance or rejection, as in inline coding suggestions (Barke et al., 2022); higher-impact
actions should support previews and co-planning before execution (Mozannar et al., 2025); and deployed agents should
maintain traceable action logs for inspection, recovery, and rollback (Dong et al., 2024). Future work should determine
how these safeguards scale with the action’s uncertainty, impact, reversibility, and authorization requirements: what
may be freely suggested, what should be previewed, what requires confirmation, and what should not be autonomously
executed.
Some consequences of proactive action cannot be fully reversed. Actions that can be undone may still consume attention,
interrupt workflows, reveal information, alter user trust, or create downstream dependencies. Future systems should
study rollback alongside how an action is surfaced, justified, monitored, and corrected. Calm and peripheral displays
can reduce unnecessary attentional demand (Weiser & Brown, 1997; Wisneski et al., 1998); proactive dialogue systems
illustrate how initiative can be delivered conversationally (Deng et al., 2023b); uncertainty cues can support calibrated
reliance (Vasconcelos et al., 2025); and audit-oriented explanations can clarify post-action responsibility (Jang & Sundar,
2026). These elements should be integrated into the action mechanism. The agent should be able to communicate why
action was appropriate at that moment, what evidence supported it, what uncertainty remained, what alternatives were
considered, what consequences followed, and how the user can regain control or seek remediation.
Agents should scale initiative according to risk and user authorization, preserve reversibility and recovery whenever
possible, and remain explainable and auditable when consequences cannot be fully undone.


                                                                                                                          105
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Toward Scrutinized, Personalized, and Faithful Adaptation. Learning from responses to proactive interventions
requires interpreting feedback that is often implicit, delayed, biased, or missing (§ 4.6). A user may accept an action for
convenience, ignore a suggestion because of poor timing, undo an action later, or gradually change their trust in the
agent without providing explicit labels. Future work should develop a governed adaptation process that specifies what
the agent is allowed to learn from, how feedback should be interpreted, and whether the resulting behavioral changes
remain appropriate.
Feedback signals need to be assessed for reliability and meaning. Agents should record what they did, why they
acted, what context supported the action, how the user or environment responded, and whether later evidence changes
the interpretation of that response. Agent observability can make tool use and execution histories traceable after
deployment (Dong et al., 2024), reflective runtimes can diagnose execution failures during operation (Cruz, 2025),
and self-improving agents can expose knowledge gaps or failure modes before updating behavior (He et al., 2025a).
Clicks, skips, dismissals, acceptances, takeovers, rollbacks, or delayed outcomes may indicate approval, annoyance,
correction, changing circumstances, or convenience. Future systems should estimate the confidence and informativeness
of each feedback signal before using it as a learning target. They should distinguish direct preferences from ambiguous
behavioral traces, reconcile immediate reactions with delayed outcomes, and seek clarification when the available
evidence is insufficient. Noisy or misinterpreted feedback may reinforce inappropriate behavior before users or
developers detect drift.
Agents need to calibrate changes in initiative as they learn user preferences, interruption tolerance, trust, desired
autonomy, and proactivity thresholds. The same intervention may be helpful for one user, intrusive for another, and
outdated for the same user later. Prior work on over-trust and complacency (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010), disuse under
low trust (Parasuraman & Riley, 1997), adaptive automation (Kaber & Endsley, 2004), interruption-sensitive assistance
(Horvitz et al., 2004), and proactive personalization (Sun et al., 2025b) shows how accumulated evidence can inform
changes in reliance and autonomy. Future work should therefore study adaptation as a long-term relationship in which
the agent gradually earns, loses, or renegotiates initiative. This requires models that can distinguish stable preferences
from temporary reactions, personalize without overfitting to sparse or biased feedback, account for preference drift, and
update autonomy thresholds without making the agent either overly passive or prematurely intrusive.
Adaptation targets should reflect whether proactive behavior is appropriate. Acceptance, engagement, and apparent trust
can be misleading proxies: an agent may learn to remain silent to avoid annoyance, flatter the user to gain approval,
or become overly aggressive when short-term acceptances are rewarded. These risks are amplified by performative
feedback loops (Perdomo et al., 2021), recommender-style degeneration (Jiang et al., 2019), sycophancy (Sharma et al.,
2025), reward hacking (Skalse et al., 2025), and toxic proactivity (Wang et al., 2026l). Future work should therefore
define adaptation targets that reflect whether the agent inferred the right need, acted at the right time, selected the
appropriate autonomy level, disclosed sufficient evidence, respected user corrections, and improved future outcomes
without manipulating user behavior.
Feedback assessment needs to establish which signals are sufficiently reliable and meaningful to support learning.
Personalization needs to calibrate initiative for each user and context, and learning targets need to reflect whether
proactive behavior was appropriate. These requirements aim to support improvement over time while limiting the effects
of ambiguous feedback, overfitting to short-term reactions, manipulation, overreach, and learned passivity.

7.1.3   Proactiveness for Long-Horizon Tasks and Agent Self-Evolution
Proactiveness as a Drive for Long-Horizon Task Generalization. Long-horizon tasks require more than executing a
long sequence of planned steps. Current agent studies have made substantial progress on task decomposition, planning,
and reasoning-action interleaving, including least-to-most decomposition (Zhou et al., 2023), plan-and-solve prompting
(Wang et al., 2023a), ReAct-style reasoning and acting (Yao et al., 2023b), and adaptive decomposition (Prasad et al.,
2024). Recent long-horizon agents further extend this paradigm through automatic curricula and multi-stage agendas,
as in open-ended embodied agents (Wang et al., 2024a), autonomous scientific-discovery agents (Lu et al., 2024),
and long-term task-oriented agents that maintain standing intentions across sessions or trigger conditions (Shi et al.,
2026b). However, many long-horizon systems still assume that the task goal is explicitly given, the environment remains
sufficiently stable, and success mainly depends on aligning planning and action over many steps. This makes them
vulnerable when user intent changes, the original goal becomes infeasible, hidden constraints emerge, intermediate plans
fail, or the agent must decide on its own what should be done next. Proactiveness is therefore a necessary ingredient



                                                                                                                       106
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


for generalizing long-horizon agency beyond fixed task scripts, especially in open-ended domains such as autonomous
research and scientific discovery. The key missing capability is proactive agents’ self-initiative: the ability to notice
that the current plan may fail, identify that a new direction is needed, and generate the next useful objective without
waiting for a human to specify it. Difficult long-horizon tasks often involve potential failures, hidden constraints,
unexpected discoveries, and unexplored spaces where even human experts may not know in advance what the next
correct step should be. In such settings, a successful proactive agent does not merely align itself to a predefined sequence
of actions; it continuously maintains task validity by tracking the evolving situation, modeling possible world states,
anticipating failure points, and revising or reprioritizing goals. Existing work on long-horizon tasks already points in
this direction by emphasizing persistent commitments and suspend-resume boundaries (Shi et al., 2026b; Zhang, 2026a),
while plan repair and pre-emptive maintenance show how agents can preserve useful parts of a plan instead of restarting
from scratch when conditions change (Fox et al., 2006; White et al., 2015). Future work should therefore move from
alignment-centric long-horizon execution over fixed planning or action sequences toward initiative-driven generalization:
agents should self-initiate checks, anticipate failures, update agendas, request clarification, and adjust action modes so
that each step remains valid under changing user, task, and environmental conditions. Such self-initiative may be crucial
for enabling agents to handle obstacles that are difficult to specify in advance, discover new paths that were not provided
