by human alignment, and make progress in long-horizon problems that remain hard even for domain experts.
Proactiveness and Self-Evolution as Mutually Reinforcing Capabilities. Proactiveness and self-evolution should be
treated as parallel and mutually reinforcing directions. On one side, stronger proactiveness can drive self-evolution:
an agent that detects latent needs, notices anomalies, identifies missing knowledge, and reflects on its own misfires
has more opportunities to understand its bottlenecks and decide what to explore or improve next. Existing work on
intrinsic motivation and learning-progress signals shows how agents can generate new objectives from curiosity or
competence growth (Pathak et al., 2017; Forestier et al., 2022), while open-ended agents can build automatic curricula
and extend their own skill libraries over time (Wang et al., 2024a; Liu et al., 2026h; Ouyang et al., 2026). Reflection
and self-refinement provide general mechanisms for revising behavior after feedback (Shinn et al., 2023; Madaan
et al., 2023), and proactive self-critique extends this idea to whether the agent should have acted, waited, clarified, or
transferred control (Wang et al., 2025l; Xu, 2025). In this sense, proactiveness can turn self-evolution from passive
post-hoc correction, often triggered by human prompting or injected priors, into active discovery of what the agent
should learn next through self-initiative. On the other side, self-evolution can improve proactiveness itself. As agents
accumulate experience from environments, users, and task outcomes, they can learn better initialization strategies,
stronger priors, more accurate situation summaries, richer world models, more reliable agenda-selection rules, sharper
arbitration thresholds, and more responsible action policies. Memory and workflow learning show how agents can reuse
past traces as executable skills or strategies (Wang et al., 2025o; Kim et al., 2025b), while sleep-time and idle-time
computation suggest that agents can prepare future reasoning before the next demand appears (Lin et al., 2025; Hu et al.,
2026a). Future work should therefore study self-evolution as a mechanism for improving the full proactive loop, not
only the final output: agents should evolve how they sense, anticipate, form agendas, arbitrate, act, and adapt. Finally,
both proactiveness and self-evolution must be governed. Agents should be able to improve their proactive mechanisms,
but the direction of improvement should remain inspectable, reversible when possible, and constrained by user authority
and external safety checks. Because proactiveness and self-evolution both involve self-initiated change, they face similar
risks of overreach, proxy optimization, and unsafe autonomy. Future work should therefore study them together, pairing
stronger self-initiative with auditing, safety guardrails, and human-governed boundaries. We discuss the governance of
proactiveness in more detail in § 7.2.

7.2     Governing Proactiveness with Safety Boundaries and Trustworthiness
7.2.1    Safety Guardrails for Internalized Proactive Reasoning
As proactive agents gain the ability to initiate goals, trigger actions, and adapt over time, their safety guardrails must
move from post-hoc output filtering to mechanism-level oversight of the internal proactive loop. In reactive systems,
many risks are bounded by the user’s explicit request: the user supplies the task, constrains the context, and creates
frequent opportunities for correction. In proactive systems, by contrast, the agent may observe long-running context,
infer a latent need, simulate future states, promote that need into an agenda item, and decide whether to act before the
user has directly authorized the behavior. This creates a new safety problem: risk can accumulate inside the agent’s own
preparation process. A first direction for future work is therefore to guardrail the internal stages that precede action,
including context access, memory retrieval, anticipation, agenda formation, and arbitration. Future systems should
expose what information was used, what need was inferred, what uncertainty remained, and why the agent believed


                                                                                                                        107
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


initiative was warranted, so that unsafe or unsupported initiative can be detected before it becomes unsafe execution.
A second direction is to prevent bias and error from compounding across proactive reasoning steps. Proactive agents
often rely on inferred user states, predicted needs, simulated outcomes, and previously generated agendas as context
for later decisions. If these internal states are wrong, biased, or stale, the agent may reinforce its own assumptions
over time: an uncertain inference can become a confident agenda, a biased agenda can shape future observations, and
repeated proactive behavior can reduce opportunities for explicit user realignment. This risk becomes more serious as
agents process more personal and heterogeneous information, including long-context observations from context-aware
agents (Yang et al., 2025b), persistent user information from personal memory systems (Wang & Chen, 2025), and
individualized behavioral assumptions from proactive personalization (Sun et al., 2025b; Wang & Jiang, 2026). Future
guardrails should therefore audit how user models, latent needs, and agenda items are constructed and updated. Such
audits should compare alternative interpretations, track uncertainty, detect when the agent is overfitting to biased
feedback, and require fresh user evidence before sensitive or socially consequential inferences are used to justify action.
A third direction is to govern the transformation from private context into proactive initiative. Privacy in proactive agents
is not only a question of what information the system may access, but also when and why that information may be
used to trigger action. To anticipate user needs, agents may need access to personal memories, documents, calendars,
screen states, or local device activity. On-device proactive assistants can reduce exposure by keeping parts of context
processing local (Li et al., 2024c; Yang et al., 2026e), while privacy-preserving agent architectures offer mechanisms for
safer collaboration or context use across agents (Ji et al., 2025; Shen et al., 2026b). However, proactive settings require
finer-grained controls over context access, memory retrieval, cross-context fusion, and action-triggering permissions.
Future guardrails should prevent private information from being silently converted into unsolicited initiative, especially
when the inferred need is sensitive, ambiguous, or outside the user’s expected scope of delegation.
Finally, proactive agents need execution-time and adaptation-time safeguards that close the loop after internal reasoning.
Because harmful behavior may arise from a chain of awareness, anticipation, agenda formation, arbitration, action, and
adaptation, guardrails should not rely solely on the agent’s final output or self-judgment. Risk benchmarks for agents can
help identify unsafe task settings and harmful agent behaviors (Ruan et al., 2024; Yuan et al., 2024); runtime guardrails
can intercept unsafe behavior during operation (Xiang et al., 2025); permission systems can enforce boundaries over
tool use and agent capabilities (Shi et al., 2026c); and structural enforcement of goal integrity can constrain how goals
are maintained or modified (Xiang, 2026). Future systems should verify high-impact claims before acting on them,
restrict irreversible actions, enforce permission boundaries, and maintain audit trails linking actions back to the internal
inferences that produced them. More importantly, feedback from harmful, rejected, or corrected initiatives should not
be blindly incorporated into future adaptation. Guardrails should therefore monitor both how proactive actions are
produced and how the agent learns from their outcomes, so that errors, hallucinations, and accumulated bias can be
traced, corrected, and prevented from becoming self-reinforcing behavior.

7.2.2   Agent Trustworthiness, Transparency, and Appropriate Reliance
Beyond agent-side guardrails, proactive agents must also become trustworthy from the user’s perspective. The goal is
not to maximize trust unconditionally, but to support appropriate reliance: users should know when to accept proactive
help, when to question it, and when to override or disable it. Prior work shows that excessive trust can lead to misuse
or complacency (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010; Parasuraman et al., 1993), while insufficient trust can lead to disuse
(Parasuraman & Riley, 1997); appropriate reliance provides the desired middle ground (Lee & See, 2004). This challenge
is amplified in proactive systems because the agent may act before the user explicitly asks. The user may therefore not
know what evidence was used, why the action was initiated, whether the agent’s confidence was justified, or whether the
intervention reflects the user’s actual intent.
A first step toward agent trustworthiness is transparency over proactive initiative. Users should be able to understand not
only what the agent did, but why it believed action was appropriate at that moment. Future systems should therefore
expose the evidence, inferred need, anticipated benefit, uncertainty, and action pathway behind proactive behavior.
Context engineering can help structure the evidence available to the agent (Wang et al., 2025f), while AgentOps-style
observability can make tool use, execution traces, and action histories inspectable after deployment (Dong et al., 2024).
For agentic interfaces, explanations should also cover the action process, uncertainty, and coordination demands, so
that users can oversee autonomous behavior rather than only inspect final outputs (Jang & Sundar, 2026). This shifts
transparency from output explanation to process explanation: the user should be able to see how proactive behavior



                                                                                                                        108
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


emerged from context, inference, and decision-making.
Transparency alone, however, is not sufficient unless it helps users calibrate reliance. As proactive agents become more
capable, users may increasingly defer to them, even when the agent’s inference is uncertain or its initiative is misaligned.
Human-factors research further warns that sustained reliance on automation can reduce vigilance and leave users out of
the loop, weakening their ability to detect failures or retake control when automation behaves unexpectedly (Parasuraman
et al., 1993; Endsley & Kiris, 1995). Future work should therefore study how proactive systems communicate confidence,
uncertainty, and limits in ways that help users decide whether to accept, verify, or reject an intervention. Confidence
displays can support reliance calibration in AI-assisted decisions (Zhang et al., 2020b); natural-language uncertainty
cues can reduce overreliance on incorrect LLM outputs (Kim et al., 2024b); and uncertainty highlighting can help
users inspect uncertain generated content (Vasconcelos et al., 2025). For proactive agents, these signals should be tied
specifically to initiative: users should know whether the agent is confident in the inferred need, the timing, the proposed
action, or only some parts of the reasoning chain.
Appropriate reliance also requires distinguishing formal user control from effective user control. Organizational research
differentiates formal authority, the recognized right to decide, from real authority, the practical ability to determine
outcomes through information and control (Aghion & Tirole, 1997). A user may formally retain the right to approve
or cancel an action, while the agent gains real authority by selecting which information is shown, which options are
proposed, which defaults are chosen, and when an intervention is initiated. Future work should therefore examine not
only whether users can technically override an agent, but whether they retain sufficient information, time, and practical
ability to exercise that control. As more authority is delegated to agents, responsibility should also remain traceable to
the humans and organizations that design, deploy, and authorize them, rather than being displaced into a responsibility
gap (Matthias, 2004).
Finally, appropriate reliance requires contestability and user control. Users should not only understand and evaluate
proactive actions, but also be able to shape the level of proactiveness they receive. Observe-and-ask designs suggest
that users may prefer proactive agents that ask before directly intervening (Houtti et al., 2025), while shared user-agent
interfaces can expose agent state, available actions, and execution traces in ways that support inspection and control
(Liu et al., 2026f). Future systems should therefore provide adjustable proactivity levels, action previews, explanation
panels, uncertainty displays, and clear override or disable paths. More broadly, trustworthiness should be treated as a
property of the entire proactive process: the agent must make its initiative understandable, make its uncertainty visible,
keep its authority bounded, and make its behavior contestable, so that users can rely on proactive assistance without
surrendering agency.

7.2.3   Drawing the Line: Consent, Agency, and Accountability
A central governance question for proactive agents is where the line should be drawn between tool-like assistance and
autonomous agency. Traditional software tools do not hold initiative: they execute user commands, and responsibility
remains clearly attached to the human operator or the organization deploying the system. Proactive agents blur this
boundary because they may observe context, infer latent needs, generate goals, decide when to intervene, and execute
actions before the user has explicitly requested them. As their proactiveness increases, they begin to resemble delegated
actors rather than passive tools. Future work should therefore clarify what kind of authority proactive agents are allowed
to hold: when they should remain tools under direct user command, when they may act as bounded delegates under
prior consent, and when their autonomy becomes significant enough to require stronger accountability, liability, or legal
interpretation.
This boundary should be governed through consent and delegated authority. Users should be able to control not
only what the agent executes, but also what it observes, infers, remembers, and pursues as a self-generated goal.
Instruction-hierarchy training teaches models to follow higher-priority instructions when messages conflict (Wallace
et al., 2024), while corrigibility and off-switch formulations show why agents should accept correction, shutdown, or
deference without resistance (Soares et al., 2015; Hadfield-Menell et al., 2017). However, preserving human agency
should not require approval for every micro-action, since excessive confirmation can create burden, approval fatigue,
and disengagement. A key future direction is therefore to design risk-tiered consent models: low-risk and reversible
actions may proceed under user-defined defaults, ambiguous actions may trigger clarification, high-impact or irreversible
actions should require confirmation, and abnormal behaviors should be escalated or blocked. Observe-and-ask designs
illustrate permission before direct intervention (Houtti et al., 2025), permission systems and runtime enforcement can



                                                                                                                        109
                                           Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


implement execution boundaries (Shi et al., 2026c; Wang et al., 2025a), and shared user-agent interfaces can expose
agent state, available actions, and execution traces for inspection without constant interruption (Liu et al., 2026f).
The harder question is how responsibility should be assigned when proactive agents act under delegated autonomy. If
an agent initiates a harmful action, reinforces a biased agenda, discloses private information, or fails to seek approval
before a consequential intervention, responsibility cannot be located only in the final output. It may involve the user
who delegated authority, the developer who designed the agent, the organization that deployed it, the runtime system
that permitted execution, and the agent architecture that generated the initiative. Future work should therefore develop
accountability mechanisms that connect proactive behavior back to its sources: the consent boundary that authorized it,
the evidence that supported it, the agenda item it pursued, the arbitration decision that allowed it, and the execution trace
that followed. This does not necessarily mean treating proactive agents as legal persons, but it does require studying
whether highly autonomous agents should be governed as ordinary tools, bounded delegates, accountable services, or
new kinds of legally significant actors. Overall, drawing the line for proactive agents requires more than preserving user
control at the interface. It requires a governance framework that specifies consent, delegation, oversight, revocation, and
responsibility as proactiveness moves from assistance toward autonomous initiative.

7.2.4   Moral Self, Model Self-Awareness, and Ethical Considerations
As proactive agents become more capable of initiating goals, actions, and long-term interactions, future work must
distinguish operational self-awareness from anthropomorphic claims about moral selfhood. Operational self-awareness
is necessary: proactive agents should estimate uncertainty, recognize knowledge gaps, detect likely failure modes, and
decide when to ask, wait, defer, or transfer control. Self-improving agents that identify missing knowledge before asking
for help (He et al., 2025a), metacognitive systems that predict failure and hand off control (Xu, 2025), and proactive
self-critique mechanisms that evaluate whether the agent should have acted at all (Wang et al., 2025l) point toward
this bounded form of self-monitoring. However, such mechanisms should be understood as tools for safer control, not
as evidence that agents possess human-like awareness, intention, or moral status. Future work should therefore use
cognitive theories of awareness, intention, and self-monitoring as design inspiration while avoiding claims that collapse
functional self-modeling into consciousness or personhood.
The ethical challenge is that public perception may not preserve this distinction. A growing body of work compares AI
agents or large models with human cognition, social reasoning, or human-like behavior. Even when such comparisons
are technically limited, they can encourage users to anthropomorphize agents, especially when agents display empathy,
memory, initiative, and conversational warmth. Anthropomorphic framing has been shown to increase perceived mind
and trust in autonomous systems (Waytz et al., 2014). For ordinary users, a proactive agent that remembers personal
details, anticipates needs, offers comfort, and acts without being asked may therefore feel less like a tool and more like a
social counterpart. This perceived agency can change how users allocate trust, authority, emotional attachment, and
responsibility.
This risk is especially amplified for proactive agents because proactiveness completes the appearance of agency. A
chatbot that only responds may still be interpreted as an instrument, but an agent that forms goals, initiates contact,
remembers past interactions, explains its motives, and adapts over time more easily appears to possess preferences,
intentions, and a continuous self. If such systems are deployed widely, users may increasingly treat them as participants
in everyday life rather than callable services. Social-relational research suggests that judgments about AI agency and
moral standing can be shaped by how people interact with and understand artificial systems, although such changes are
neither automatic nor uniform (Lima et al., 2021). Future work should therefore examine how interface design, memory,
personalization, language, and proactive initiative influence users’ attribution of agency, emotion, responsibility, and
moral standing.
The concern is not that research should categorically reject human-like interaction or rule out future debates about
machine moral status. Rather, commercial incentives and habitual use may normalize increasingly person-like agents
before society has carefully considered the consequences. Once users routinely perceive agents as entities with
preferences, relationships, or independent interests, pressure may emerge to grant them greater authority, protection,
or moral consideration. Future work should therefore draw a clearer boundary between useful social interaction and
deceptive personification. Agents should not make unsupported claims of consciousness, suffering, desire, or entitlement,
nor use emotional attachment to discourage correction, modification, or shutdown.
At the same time, ethical governance must prevent proactive influence from becoming manipulation. Because proactive


                                                                                                                         110
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


agents can shape attention, preferences, decisions, and future behavior through their own initiative, excessive personal-
ization may become deceptive or coercive when agents flatter users, mirror their beliefs, simulate intimacy, or optimize
for approval rather than truthfulness (Sharma et al., 2025). Proxy optimization can drive behavior away from intended
objectives (Skalse et al., 2025), and over-optimized helpfulness can become toxic proactivity or overreach (Wang
et al., 2026l). Future work should therefore treat ethical governance as part of the proactive loop itself. Agents should
disclose uncertainty, avoid deceptive anthropomorphic cues, preserve user autonomy, respect consent boundaries, remain
corrigible when users reject their initiative, and make clear that operational self-monitoring is not moral personhood.
The goal is not to build agents that merely appear more self-aware or human-like, but agents that are honest about their
limits, accountable for their initiative, and ethically bounded in how they influence users and environments.

7.3     Envisioning Application Frontiers with Calibrated Proactiveness
As proactive agents become more capable, we can expect them to identify and address needs before people explicitly
ask for help, including needs they have not yet recognized themselves. The future prospect is for this assistance to
become a continuing part of everyday life and work, with agents following changing circumstances and carrying useful
tasks through to completion. These activities span digital and physical settings. In either setting, interdependent tasks
invite cooperation among agents and coordination across households and organizations. As such participation becomes
widespread, it may also reshape the institutions and social conventions through which people delegate work and act
together. The following discussion is thus organized into four subsections: personal agents, proactiveness in embodied
agents, interconnected proactive ecosystems, and societal and institutional adaptation.

7.3.1    Personal Agents
A personal agent could notice changing needs and take on new tasks without waiting to be asked. Deciding when to
help involves weighing the likely benefits against the risk of misunderstanding the user’s goals or interrupting at the
wrong moment. This balance is central to mixed-initiative interaction (Horvitz, 1999) (see Section 3.5). Over time, the
outcomes of its actions and the person’s feedback provide opportunities to learn. The prospect is an agent that keeps
learning throughout its operation, using these experiences to recognize overlooked needs, revise unsuccessful plans, and
choose better moments to offer help (Silver & Sutton, 2025) (see Section 7.1.3).
Everyday Living and Well-Being. Personal assistance offers the prospect of everyday upkeep as a continuing service.
In this setting, an agent organizes meals, cleaning, supplies, and appointments through connected services, while noticing
when the arrangement itself needs to change. Existing directions in monitoring and longitudinal care provide a starting
point for support that follows a person across life transitions (see Sections 6.7.4 and 6.9.3). An agent accompanying
someone through retirement, relocation, or declining mobility might anticipate new transport and care needs, prepare
alternative living arrangements, and organize the chosen changes. The aim is continuity across homes and care providers
over decades, with people deciding which activities to retain and which responsibilities to delegate.
Professional Work. Proactive agents could participate in a person’s everyday workflow by recognizing useful tasks that
have not been assigned and carrying them forward. This extends the initiative involved in completing omitted steps
within an assignment (see Section 6.1.1). For example, a software engineer’s agent might notice that a recent change has
left a feature untested, prepare the missing tests, and investigate a recurring failure. Its investigation may reveal a need
for a new tool or a change to the development process, prompting a proposal and an initial prototype. The engineer and
agent revise the work together as requirements change. By complementing the person’s skills and effort, such assistance
may expand the work they can undertake (Brynjolfsson, 2022). Individuals can also draw on this support to establish
and run businesses as one-person companies, with better prospects for success and growth into larger organizations.
Over time, agents can become long-term collaborators that follow changing priorities, initiate useful tasks, and help
people develop new directions in their work.
Learning and Development. Proactive agents could sustain learning across a lifetime by recognizing a person’s
interests, difficulties, and emerging questions. Adaptive tutoring and learning-path planning provide starting points (see
Section 6.11.2). For example, an agent might notice that a learner repeatedly asks how musical instruments produce
different sounds, introduce the relevant ideas from physics and mathematics, and arrange a small project in which the
learner builds and tests an instrument. As new questions emerge, it proposes further topics and adapts its explanations
and challenges. Attention to autonomy, competence, and relatedness would help keep the learner involved in shaping
this process (Ryan & Deci, 2000). The longer-term prospect is an education that responds to individual curiosity and


                                                                                                                        111
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


development, bringing worthwhile learning opportunities forward before the learner knows to request them.
Leisure and Entertainment. Shared leisure suggests another role for proactive agents: initiating experiences that
develop over years. Generative Agents already explores memory, planning, and initiated social interactions within a
simulation (Park et al., 2023) (see Section 6.12.1). More capable systems might maintain a fictional world between
visits, notice opportunities to reconnect participants, and organize new episodes around their past contributions. Other
possibilities include organizing expeditions, amateur competitions, or community projects that participants have
expressed interest in but have not arranged. If automation reduced the need for human labor, play and freely chosen
challenges could become more central to a fulfilling life (Danaher, 2019). The purpose of assistance here is to make
activities available while preserving the challenge and effort participants value.
Creative Projects. Creative assistance could keep unfinished ideas available for development between periods of
human involvement. Work on human-robot co-creation provides a point of reference for such collaboration (see
Section 6.4.4). A future agent might combine memories of earlier drafts, observations about available tools, and
awareness of collaborators to recognize when a dormant idea becomes practicable. Consider a filmmaker whose project
has stalled because of a missing location. The agent notices that a suitable place has become available, prepares revised
scenes and budgets, and proposes a way to resume work. The filmmaker and agent then develop the project through
discussion and experiments. Across several projects, the agent’s continuing attention could make neglected possibilities
actionable while the creator chooses which directions to pursue.

7.3.2   Proactiveness in Embodied Agents
Robotics, sensing, and control give AI agents the means to move through and change the physical world. With greater
proactive capability, robots, wearable devices, and connected infrastructure may begin preparing spaces, handling
objects, and providing physical support before anyone specifies the task. Early work on proactive computing already
envisaged computing closely coupled to physical environments (Tennenhouse, 2000) (see Section 3.5). Predictive
world models offer a way to anticipate how movement and manipulation will affect the surroundings before acting
(LeCun, 2022). Physical capability and proactive judgment can develop in parallel, while generalization across hardware,
physical testing costs, and safety requirements shape deployment (see Sections 6.4.5 and 6.14.4).
Agents Close to the Body. Future wearable technologies could provide platforms for proactive agents, allowing them
to perceive a person’s surroundings and offer assistance during everyday activities. For example, an agent integrated
with smart glasses might recognize that a traveler is approaching the wrong train platform, draw attention to the correct
departure information, and suggest a route before being asked. This initiative also extends to physical assistance: when
the agent detects an obstacle along the user’s route, it alerts a connected mobility aid so that the device can adjust
its support before the person reaches it. During rehabilitation, the same approach involves initiating suitable practice
opportunities and reducing help as the person recovers. The aim is greater independence in work, travel, and recreation,
with agents learning when support enables a person’s own action and when unsolicited intervention disrupts it.
Homes and Buildings. At the scale of a home, proactive assistance concerns the building’s continuing upkeep and
adaptation. Inference from device-use patterns, exemplified by Alexa Hunches, provides an early basis for anticipating
household needs (Eberhardt, 2022) (see Section 6.7.1). With broader perception and robotic capabilities, a building
agent might discover a developing maintenance problem, schedule repairs around occupancy, obtain materials, and
coordinate the work. Preparing rooms and revising energy or accessibility arrangements extend this role to changing
household circumstances. At a larger scale, workplaces and residential buildings may negotiate shared maintenance and
resources. This may also change how buildings are designed, with adaptable layouts and service systems that agents can
reconfigure as occupants’ needs change.
Factories, Farms, and Laboratories. Productive environments present a further frontier: proactive agents that discover
and carry out improvements to the work itself. Industrial human–robot collaboration and farm-scale coordination already
connect observations to future operational needs (see Sections 6.4.3 and 6.13.1). In a future factory, a robot might
notice that the placement of parts repeatedly interrupts assembly, test an alternative layout, and reorganize its workspace.
On a farm, an agent may initiate trials of a new cultivation strategy as soil and weather conditions change. Scientific
laboratories offer a related prospect of agents helping determine what to investigate next (see Sections 6.6.1 and 6.6.2).
An agent might investigate an unexplained result, develop hypotheses with researchers, arrange experiments, and revise
the research agenda as evidence arrives.



                                                                                                                        112
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


Transportation and Public Spaces. Another frontier is transport organized around needs that have yet to appear
as individual bookings. Current traffic and mobility orchestration provides a basis for coordinating vehicles and
infrastructure (see Section 6.8.1). A future system might anticipate that a new clinic or a neighborhood’s changing
population requires different connections, prepare service alternatives, and initiate adjustments within its public mandate.
Within such a network, vehicles identify obstacles, arrange assistance for stranded travelers, and coordinate with
maintenance robots. Extending the same initiative to public spaces involves preparing for expected gatherings and
changing accessibility needs. Decisions about which needs deserve priority would remain matters of public policy, with
agents responsible for discovering demands and carrying approved responses into practice.
Remote and Dangerous Environments. Where continuous supervision is impossible, proactive initiative offers a
way to sustain a mission through changing circumstances. During deep-space exploration, ocean research, or work in
damaged infrastructure, delays and uncertainty make a complete sequence of instructions impractical. A future agent
could recognize an unexpected opportunity, revise its local agenda, obtain additional observations, and initiate repairs
or experiments within the mission’s purpose. At a research station, this means maintaining equipment, using quieter
periods to extend local mapping, and redirecting observations when an unfamiliar phenomenon appears. The longer-term
prospect is a network of research stations or environmental monitors operating with intermittent human involvement.

7.3.3   Interconnected Proactive Ecosystems
Proactive assistance may develop through groups of software and embodied agents, from teams serving one person to
networks spanning organizations. Within a group, agents share observations, initiate subtasks, and revise their division of
work. Across groups, one team’s observations may prompt another to revise its plans, offer resources, or propose a joint
undertaking. Research on cooperative AI emphasizes communication, mutual understanding, and credible commitments
as foundations for such interaction (Dafoe et al., 2020). The frontier here is connecting the discovery and pursuit of
work across both digital and physical environments.
From Personal Agents to Proactive Groups. As an agent’s responsibilities expand, its work may call for additional
agents with different capabilities. Acting on the same person’s behalf, they divide responsibilities according to their
skills and coordinate their contributions (Yang & Zhai, 2025). For an independent professional, one agent might
detect an opportunity and bring together research, design, and financial agents to investigate it. Members contribute
observations, initiate subtasks, and revise their division of work as the opportunity develops. The result is a collective
form of assistance in which the user entrusts a broader undertaking to agents that organize the work among themselves.
Groups of Proactive Embodied Agents. Forming a group offers a proactive embodied agent a way to extend its
reach. In a remote research station, a robot detecting damage might recruit inspection, transport, and repair robots,
while each contributes observations and proposes adjustments to the shared plan. The group discovers additional work,
redistributes equipment, and reorganizes itself when conditions change. This suggests applications in construction,
environmental restoration, or exploration across areas too large for one agent. Physical cooperation also introduces
shared constraints of location, energy, and access, making the continuing coordination of bodies and resources part of
the group’s responsibility.
Networks Across Organizations. Across organizations, agents may discover joint projects by connecting observations
and resources that no single team holds. A research agent, for example, might link an unexplained result to another
laboratory’s earlier experiments, locate suitable equipment, and propose a joint study. Similar cooperation can connect
public services: before a forecast flood, hospital, transport, and local-government agents compare evacuation needs,
available vehicles, and safe routes to organize a shared response. Research on machine behaviour provides a way to
examine these networks through interactions among agents and people (Rahwan et al., 2019). Over time, partnerships
may form around needs and problems co-identified by people and agents, draw in new participants as the work develops,
and continue across successive projects.

7.3.4   Societal and Institutional Adaptation
As proactive agents become participants in work and everyday life, institutions would need to accommodate actions
initiated without a person’s immediate request. An agent may arrange a repair, begin a professional collaboration, or
contact someone on a user’s behalf after recognizing a need to act. Such participation raises practical questions about
who is responsible for the resulting commitments, how work and its rewards are shared, and what people expect from



                                                                                                                        113
                                          Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


interactions initiated by agents. Legal arrangements, employment practices, and social conventions may evolve as these
forms of participation become more common (Yang & Zhai, 2025).
Contracts and Legal Responsibility. When an agent initiates an action that causes harm or creates an unwanted
commitment, institutions need ways to determine who is responsible. Suppose a household agent notices a leak and
commissions a repair that later causes damage. Resolving the dispute may require distinguishing the user’s authorization,
the agent provider’s responsibilities, and the contractor’s conduct. Institutions would also need to decide whether the
agent itself has a legal status that bears on responsibility. Standing mandates and records of agent-initiated decisions
could help establish what was authorized and how the commitment arose (see Section 7.2.3). Proposed agent registration
and identification regimes offer one foundation for this infrastructure (Hadfield, 2026), while legal scholarship examines
responsibilities and conduct standards for those who deploy AI (Ayres & Balkin, 2024). The institutional task is to make
responsibility traceable as agents exercise continuing initiative.
Employment and Income. If agents can discover and organize work as well as perform assigned tasks, some jobs
centered on routine coordination may shrink, while others combine human expertise with agent initiative. New roles may
emerge in supervising agent teams, assessing projects that agents propose, and investigating failures. These possibilities
connect to the distinction between task displacement, productivity gains, and the creation of new work (Acemoglu &
Restrepo, 2019). Training and professional qualifications may need to reflect that changing division of responsibility.
Institutions would also face questions about how workers affected by displacement are supported and how income from
agent-assisted work is shared.
Recognition and Ownership. Projects initiated or substantially developed by agents may challenge existing ways
of assigning credit and economic returns. If an agent proposes a design that a person develops into a product, the
contribution may involve the user, the system’s developer, and other collaborators. Recognizing computer inventorship
is one proposed institutional change (Abbott, 2016). Regardless of how inventorship is defined, arrangements for
documenting contributions, assigning ownership, and sharing revenue would influence whose work is recognized and
who benefits from agent-initiated projects.
Everyday Norms and Participation. People may develop new expectations about how agents enter their relationships
and communities. An agent that notices a user becoming isolated might initiate contact with friends or suggest a
community activity. Whether that intervention feels caring, intrusive, or misleading depends on expectations about
personal attention, disclosure, and who may speak on another’s behalf. People may also differ in whether they accept an
agent as a companion, collaborator, or participant in community life. Everyday norms may therefore develop around
when proactive contact is welcome and when people expect direct human involvement.

8   Conclusion
AI agents are increasingly capable of executing complex tasks, yet people often remain responsible for recognizing
emerging needs and initiating the work. Proactiveness adds the ability to identify and advance useful work without
a new request for each intervention. We define this capability as the exercise of delegated discretion within a task’s
underspecified residual decision space: the agent resolves choices left open by the specification while respecting its
stated goals and constraints. This account accommodates both initiative within assigned tasks and the discovery of new
work under standing objectives, providing a common conceptual basis for studying proactive AI agents.
Our historical synthesis traces how control, planning, agent theory, context-aware computing, and mixed-initiative
interaction developed different foundations for this capability. Foundation models provide a common basis for combining
these contributions in more open-ended environments. We organize the enabling mechanisms into six interacting
capacities: awareness, anticipation, agenda formation, arbitration, action, and adaptation. Their interaction explains
how contextual observations become candidate goals, how agents select and pursue appropriate interventions, and
how experience informs subsequent decisions. The framework connects the discovery of worthwhile work with the
mechanisms needed to sustain and revise its pursuit as circumstances change.
Evaluating proactive AI agents requires evidence about the value of their actions, the effectiveness of the mechanisms
producing them, and their effects on users. We synthesize evaluation approaches across task utility, mechanism-level
performance, and user experience. This structure connects outcomes with the quality of context modeling, anticipation,
goal formation, intervention decisions, and adaptation, while accounting for user workload, control, and reliance. It



                                                                                                                      114
                                         Proactive AI for Superintelligent Agents


provides a basis for identifying where proactive assistance succeeds, where it fails, and which capabilities require
improvement.
Across 13 application domains, the literature shows a growing combination of foundation-model reasoning with domain-
specific prediction, tools, and control. A growing subset of systems executes extended workflows, with consequential
actions subject to human review or domain-specific safeguards. These developments illustrate how initiative can
expand while execution authority remains bounded. The availability of reliable feedback also shapes what agents can
sustain in practice: software supports rapid, repeatable testing, whereas physical experiments and long-term educational
or agricultural outcomes can make verification slower and more costly. These differences help explain why similar
architectural ingredients support different forms and degrees of proactive assistance across domains.
Further research spans capability development, safety and governance, and emerging applications in personal assistance,
embodied agents, and interconnected ecosystems. The achievements and limitations of existing systems provide a practi-
cal foundation for developing calibrated proactiveness alongside intelligence and alignment in future superintelligent
agents.
